    A schematic of the training procedure is shown in Figure 1. Training a NEF only requires a reliable estimate of the outgoing radiance Lₒ for any query within the network’s input domain, making the procedure agnostic to the underlying emitter geometry.

    Sample generation. For each training batch, we draw queries uniformly from the emitter-space (Section 3.2). For the glossy head f_g^θ, we sample a position x̃ uniformly in the local bounding box, and a normal ñ such that the emitter is visible in its hemisphere avoiding queries with zero radiance, an outgoing direction ω̃ₒ uniformly on the upper hemisphere defined by ñ, and a roughness α uniformly in [0.1,1]. The diffuse head f_d^θ uses the same procedure restricted to (x̃,ñ). For deformable or animated emitters, we additionally sample a time parameter t∈[0,1] corresponding to the emitter’s state, encoded with an 8-band Fourier encoding [22] and provided as an extra conditioning input.

    Radiance targets. Target radiance is obtained via offline path tracing against the (possibly time-varying) emitter geometry. Bare emissive surfaces are handled with standard next-event estimation; emitters with non-emissive housing geometry that causes self-occlusion or internal interreflections (Figure 5) are handled with full path tracing inside the emitter assembly, so that higher-order transport is naturally absorbed into the training signal. We use 64 samples per radiance estimate as default across all emitters in this paper as we saw diminishing returns beyond this (see supplemental material for an ablation). Targets are generated on-the-fly rather than cached, so all reported training timings include the cost of path tracing.

    Optimization. We minimize a relative L₂ loss [25] between the network prediction and the path-traced target averaged over the batch, L(θ)=((D_θ-⟨Lₒ⟩)²)/(sg(D_θ)²+ε), where ε=0.01 and sg denotes a stop gradient operation. The relative loss prevents bright regions of the emitter-space from dominating the gradient and helps the multi-resolution hash encoding to allocate capacity uniformly across the field. We use Adam [18] with a learning rate of 10⁻³, a batch size of 2¹⁶, and use cosine annealing learning rate decay. The number of training iterations for each of our emitter types can be found in the supplemental material. Total wall-clock time on an RTX 4090 ranges from one minute for diffuse receiver with planar emitters to three hours for emitters with complex emissive effects, dominated by the cost of generating path-traced target values.

    3.5 Rendering

    Because NEF stores a pre-integrated estimate of the outgoing radiance reflected by the receiver, no integration is required at runtime. Unlike methods that integrate with respect to the emitter geometry or to a proxy representation of the emitter [14, 35, 43], our approach reduces the shading process to a single network evaluation per pixel. At render time, we first perform a G-buffer pass to obtain the (x,n,ωₒ,α) channels at each shading point. These are transformed into the emitter’s local frame via its current world transform M (Section 3.2), encoded, and fed to D_θ to obtain the outgoing radiance contribution pre-integrated with respect to the emitter.

    Visibility. As with existing analytical methods [15, 5], NEF does not inherently capture occlusions of the emissive field caused by the surrounding scene. For simple emitters, a single shadow ray toward the emitter center is often sufficient (Figure 4); for soft shadows, established techniques such as shadow mapping [41] or a small ray-tracing budget combined with a denoiser [16] apply directly, which we implemented in the supplemental material. Crucially, shadow rays are only required against non-emitter scene geometry: the NEF itself bakes in self-occlusion and internal interreflections within the emitter assembly (Figure 5).

    4 Results

    We show that NEF matches the quality of analytical solutions (Section 4.1) and extends beyond what they handle, supporting emissive meshes and deformable emitters (Section 4.2). We then compare against two sampling-based techniques, where NEF’s sampling-free formulation yields a runtime advantage (Section 4.3).

    4.1 Planar Emitters

    We compare against analytical integration for diffuse receivers [5] and Linearly Transformed Cosines (LTC) for glossy receivers [15]. As shown in Figure 4, our method matches the analytical reference for diffuse receivers under uniform emission, confirming its accuracy.

    For glossy receivers (Figure 10), the larger capacity of NEF allows it to achieve lower rendering error across various roughness values α compared to LTC, highlighting LTC’s remaining approximation error. The near-mirror regime (α→0) remains challenging for a finite neural representation; we show an example of the increase in error at lower roughness in the supplemental material.

    While analytical methods have lower per-frame shading costs for simple polygons, their runtime scales linearly O(V) with the number of emitter vertices V. This linear cost is especially noticeable for large emissive emitters, as highlighted in Table 1. We show the crossover point between the analytical methods and our GlossyNEF—267 emitter vertices—in the supplemental material. The generality and computational efficiency of our approach become especially relevant when extending beyond planar geometry.

    4.2 Complex Emitters

    A key advantage of our approach is that inference cost is determined by the complexity of the emissive field, not by the complexity of the underlying geometry. While NEF inference cost does scale with emissive field complexity—a highly spatially varying emitter benefits from a larger or more expressive network—this complexity is typically much lower than that of the geometry itself. Naively subdividing an emissive mesh increases its vertex count but leaves its emissive field largely unchanged, so the same NEF capacity suffices regardless of tessellation. All results in this paper share a single network configuration sized for the most demanding case (the Pierced Sphere, whose housing interreflections produce a high-frequency emissive field); for simpler emitters such as the planar quad, a smaller architecture would suffice with no perceptible loss in quality (see supplemental material).

    Higher-order Emissive Effects. Our NEF formulation can also capture higher-order emissive effects arising from multi-bounce light transport within the emitter, such as internal reflections toward a filament. By replacing direct light-source sampling with path tracing during training, multi-bounce contributions are integrated into the training signal. Figure 5 shows three assemblies in which internal interreflections meaningfully shape the emissive field: a Dragon mesh acting as a bare emitter, a Pierced Sphere whose shell partially occludes and reflects an internal filament, and a Lattice Box which houses a spherical emitter. Obtaining a noise-free reference for these assemblies is expensive—on the order of 1M samples per pixel—because the interior light paths are not captured by simple next-event estimation against the bare emissive geometry. The effect varies by assembly: interreflections produce only a mild overall brightening on the Dragon, whereas the Pierced Sphere and Lattice Box show light diffusing through the apertures, softening cast shadows and noticeably brightening regions that the bare-emitter leaves dark. NEF reproduces all three references faithfully.

    Non-uniform emission. Since our NEF representation is agnostic to the emissive profile of the light source, it naturally accommodates spatially varying emission without modification. Figure  (center) shows an emitter with a non-uniform radiance distribution. While some prior methods support textured emitters, they rely on approximations that introduce error [15].

    Dynamic and Deformable Emitters. To support dynamic or deformable emitters, we extend NEF with a time-varying parameter t. As with the higher-order emissive effects in the previous section, this only requires that training data collection account for the time-varying state of the emitter. Figure 6 shows a textured fireball whose time parameter indexes into frames of a source video. See Figure 11 for an emitter with deformable geometry. We encourage the reader to consult the supplemental video for a detailed demonstration of the results.

    4.3 Comparison to Sampling-based Methods

    Both online many-light sampling methods and proxy-based emitters [14, 35, 43] require an integration step at runtime. We compare against a representative of each category: ReSTIR [6] and an oracle proxy formulation.

    Many-light Sampling. Unlike ReSTIR, which operates entirely at runtime with no precomputation, NEF amortizes work into a one-time training phase in exchange for a constant-time per-pixel inference cost. To make this trade-off concrete, we construct a Cornell Box scene with 1,000 point lights treated as a single composite emitter: the lights support global rigid transformations, but are fixed relative to each other. A single NEF is trained on this composite.

    We evaluate equal-quality convergence against three baselines: path-traced direct illumination, ReSTIR DI (M=32, K=5), and ReSTIR DI paired with an OptiX denoiser. To reach NEF’s error level, ReSTIR requires ∼256 SPP without denoising, or ∼32 SPP with denoising (Figure 8). While both unbiased sampling baselines eventually surpass NEF at high sample counts, even the 32 SPP denoised case exceeds the typical per-frame budget of real-time pipelines. However, ReSTIR remains more general: it handles arbitrary per-light motion at runtime, whereas NEF requires the emitter configuration to be fixed at training time. Rigid transforms of the entire emitter group and pre-arranged relative motion of the emitters in the composition (via a time parameter, Section 4.2) are supported, but arbitrary independent light motion requires retraining.

    Proxy Emitters.

    Proxy representations—whether using 4D light-field slabs [14], a radiance volume with virtual point lights [35], or neural fields [43]—gather radiance by sampling and integrating a proxy representation. We compare NEF against an oracle proxy: an idealized proxy whose near-field queries return a noise-free reference and whose evaluation cost is treated as zero. Any sampling-based proxy method is bounded from below by this oracle, so the comparison reveals the minimum number of proxy evaluations required to match NEF’s pre-integrated estimate, regardless of how the proxy itself is represented.

    As shown in Figure 7, for the Pierced Sphere scene (Figure 5), the oracle proxy requires approximately 734 samples per pixel to match the accuracy of a single NEF query when combined with a learned importance sampling routine from [43]. Each of those samples still requires a BSDF evaluation at the shading point: at 1920×1080 resolution, the 734 GGX evaluations alone cost 2.9 ms per frame in an optimized CUDA kernel. This already exceeds NEF’s total inference cost of 2.5 ms, before any of the proxy queries or importance sampling are accounted for. Moreover, the cost of those proxy queries is not negligible in practice. As a data point, a half-precision torch.compile’d forward pass of the evaluation network from [43] takes 103 ms per emitter sample per full-HD frame, and 49 ms to output the importance sampling distributions on the same hardware as our NEF timings.

    5 Discussion

    Visibility and soft shadows. Similarly to analytical methods and proxy emitters, NEF only captures the unoccluded emission field. In practice, this is well-addressed by combining NEF shading with a small budget of path-traced visibility samples and a denoiser that are used as a ratio estimator [16]. This approach yields plausible soft shadows while preserving the noise-free direct illumination produced by the NEF. Even 1 shadow ray per pixel yields perceptually accurate soft shadows (see Figure 9), with further samples producing diminishing returns. This makes NEF compatible with standard real-time visibility pipelines at minimal additional cost.

    Storage and training. All results in this paper were generated using a single NEF architecture totaling 15 MB (or 30 MB for the glossy variant) per emitter. For simpler emitters, this is often excessive and can be reduced (see supplemental). Training is a one-time offline cost, ranging from approximately one minute for simple planar emitters to three hours for emitters with internal interreflections, depending primarily on the cost of generating path-traced training samples. Crucially, this cost is incurred once per emitter and can be amortized across multiple scenes.

    Multiple emitters in a scene. Currently, a scene with N emitters requires evaluating N independent NEFs and summing their contributions (unless emitters are close enough to be represented jointly by a single NEF), scaling linearly with N. We see two avenues to mitigate this. First, a shared decoding MLP could learn to disentangle latents from multiple emitters; however a naive sum-then-decode scheme retains a linear cost for the latent fetching. Second, future work could combine NEF with lighting hierarchies [37, 23] to achieve sub-linear scaling.

    Sampling training data. We generate training targets by path tracing the emitter assembly with next-event estimation. For emitters with housing geometry more intricate than those presented in this work—heavily enclosing the emissive surface or admitting light only through narrow apertures—this strategy can produce a sparse training signal: most paths fail to reach the emitter and contribute zero, leaving the network to learn from a small fraction of informative samples. As shown in recent work [11], light tracing [2] can reduce the number of zero-radiance contributions. Orthogonally, when the emissive field around the emitter exhibits high-frequency variation, adaptive sampling the training loss [10] could training data on the regions that need it most.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented Neural Emission Fields, a pre-integrated neural representation of direct illumination from non-trivial emitters. By moving the receiver-side integral into an offline training phase, NEF reduces shading to a single network evaluation per pixel, at a cost independent of the emitter’s geometric complexity. The same formulation handles a wide range of lighting scenarios—including spatially varying emission, internal interreflections, and deformable emitters—within a single, unified training procedure; trained models then act as portable lighting assets that can be placed in any scene under rigid transforms and uniform scaling. We hope NEF proves a useful step toward treating expensive direct illumination as a bakeable, reusable component of real-time rendering pipelines.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Linear Scaling of Analytical Methods

    As shown in Figure 12, the computational cost of analytical methods like LTC [15] scales linearly with the number of emitter vertices. In contrast, NEF inference time remains constant for a given emitter geometry, regardless of the density of its tessellation. For glossy receivers, our method reaches a performance crossover at 267 emitter vertices. Notably, NEF maintains a constant 2.5ms shading time even for highly complex emitters like the Stanford Dragon (436k vertices), where analytical methods would be computationally prohibitive.

    Appendix B Representation Parameters

    We use a single set of hash grid parameters for all encoded inputs. The GlossyNEF architecture shares the positional encoding between the diffuse and glossy head. The multiresolution hash table has eight levels, each level increases in size with a rate of √2 per level, the corresponding latent vector consists of four floats, and the hash table uses 2¹⁹ entries. The additional inputs to the neural network, and the overall memory budget in half-precision, are summarized in Table 2.

    Appendix C Architecture Ablation

    We ablate several architecture choices (see Table 3) of our NEF by training a GlossyNEF on the same Quad emitter with the same number of training iterations.

    Applying the multiresolution hash encoding on the outgoing direction as opposed to the reflected direction, which is a common encoding choice for neural representations, reduces quality across all roughness values α.

    Splitting the network into a diffuse and glossy head similarly performs better than unifying into a single head.

    The original NEF architecture shares the positional encoding between the diffuse and glossy head. Decoupling this multiresolution hash table (i.e. diffuse and glossy each use a different one) yields no quality improvement, although it adds more capacity and extra runtime.

    Appendix D Training Budget

    Table 4 reports the training cost for each NEF in the paper, measured on a single RTX 4090 GPU. All timings include the cost of generating path-traced radiance targets on-the-fly, which dominates iteration time for the more complex emitters. Iterations and per-emitter training time scale with the difficulty of the underlying radiance field: planar emitters with uniform emission converge in minutes, bare emissive meshes and spatially varying emitters in under fifteen minutes, while configurations involving internal interreflections or temporal variation require several hours, both because the radiance field itself is more complex and because each path-traced target costs more to generate.

    Appendix E Overspent Capacity

    The default NEF architecture is sized for the most demanding emitter in our set (the Pierced Sphere) and is excessive for simpler emissive fields. We ablate two capacity axes—the MLP and the multiresolution hash encoding—on a simple Quad emitter (Figure 13). The two axes have different effects: reducing the MLP size quickly degrades quality, as the network loses the capacity to decode the encoded latents. Shrinking the hash encoding, in contrast, yields the largest reduction in memory footprint at negligible cost in error, since most of the parameter budget lives in the hash tables and the Quad’s emissive field does not need the default spatial resolution. In practice, simple emitters can therefore be deployed with a substantially smaller hash table while keeping the MLP near its default size.

    Appendix F Low-roughness Materials

    While there are no theoretical constraints preventing NEF from being trained on low-roughness receivers, practical results indicate a bottleneck as α→0, as illustrated in Figure 14. This degradation occurs because the specular highlight sharpens into a high-frequency signal that exceeds the network’s representational capacity. Consequently, while training is technically feasible across the entire roughness spectrum, the model struggles to resolve the near-singular gradients of mirror-like reflections, leading to the observed increase in approximation error in the highlight regions.

    Appendix G Impact of Training Data Noise

    The training targets used throughout this paper are generated via path tracing with Monte Carlo integration, leaving residual variance in the supervision signal. The magnitude of this variance depends on the emitter: emitters that are hard to sample yield noisier targets. The Pierced Sphere is a particularly challenging case, as its internal interreflections must also be captured during training, making it one of the noisiest emitters in our set. In Figure 15 we ablate the number of Monte Carlo samples used per training estimate and observe diminishing returns beyond 64 samples. We therefore adopt S=64 for all emitters throughout the paper, noting that this budget could safely be reduced for simpler emitters.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：Neural Emission Fields 预积分异构发光体的直接光照，消除运行时积分与采样噪声。

要点：

  • 针对带遮挡外壳、高面数自发光网格、空间变化发射率、可变形装配体这类「非平凡光源」，现有方案要么砍成解析近似，要么退回运行时采样换噪声。
  • NEF 在光源周围体积内预计算照度，场由位置、法线、视方向与材质参数参数化，双头（漫反射/高光）结构让每个着色点一次网络求值就得到无噪声的无遮挡直接光。
  • 训练在光源本地坐标系完成，训好的 NEF 是可跨场景复用的便携光照资产；内部互反射、自遮挡、空间变化发射与形变都被吸收进表示，运行时零额外开销。

为什么值得看：实时光追里「复杂灯具 = 采样地狱」是常年痛点，把积分搬到烘焙期的思路可以直接替掉部分光源代理方案，尤其适合固定装配体的场景美术资产。

中文摘要：带遮挡外壳、高面数自发光网格、空间变化发射率和可变形装配体的直接光照一直是实时渲染的瓶颈：解析法只适用于简单光源几何，纯采样估计要很高采样预算才无噪声，代理表示仍需在运行时对出射辐射做积分。论文提出 Neural Emission Fields，在光源周围的体积内预计算照度，以位置、法线、视方向和材质参数为输入，用漫反射/高光双头结构让每个着色点一次网络求值即得无噪声的无遮挡直接光。由于在光源本地坐标系训练，训练好的场可作为跨场景复用的光照资产，内部互反射与形变都被吸收。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-05

本期推送：2026-10-23

Real-time Rendering of Pre-integrated Neural Emitters

Abstract

Direct illumination from non-trivial emitters with occluding housing, high-polygon emissive meshes, spatially varying emission, or deformable assemblies is a persistent bottleneck in real-time rendering. Current real-time solutions either rely on simplified analytical representations or fall back to runtime sampling. Analytical methods are restricted to simple emitter geometry, pure sampling-based estimators need high sampling budgets to be noise-free, and proxy representations still require runtime integration over outgoing radiance around the emitter. We present Neural Emission Fields (NEF), a representation that eliminates runtime integration by precomputing the illumination in the volume around the emitter. This neural field is parameterized by position, normal, view direction, and material parameters. Using a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture, it yields noise-free unoccluded direct illumination from a single network evaluation per shading point. Because training is performed in the emitter’s local frame, a trained NEF acts as a portable lighting asset reusable across scenes under rigid transforms. Internal interreflections, self-occlusion, spatially varying emission, and deformations are absorbed into the learned representation at zero additional runtime cost.

1 Introduction

Direct illumination is a major cost in real-time rendering pipelines, especially when emitters are non-trivial—luminaires with housing geometry that occludes the internal filament, emissive meshes with thousands of polygons, light sources with spatially varying or textured emission profiles, or deformable emitters that change shape over time. While path tracing [17] handles all of these correctly, converging to noise-free direct illumination from non-trivial emitters is incompatible with real-time rendering budgets. Existing alternatives that do meet those rendering budgets typically compromise on generality, accuracy, or noise-free output.

Analytical methods like Linearly Transformed Cosines (LTC) [15] are extremely fast but assume 2D polygonal emitters and scale linearly with the emitter’s vertex count. For more general emitters, Monte Carlo estimators of direct illumination, including reservoir methods [6], support arbitrary emitters but produce noise that must be removed by a denoiser, which often introduces unwanted temporal and spatial artifacts. Proxy-based representations [14, 35], including recent neural variants [43], sidestep both limitations by precomputing the outgoing radiance into a 4D near-field proxy, factoring out the cost of sampling paths within the emitter assembly. However, receiver points must still integrate over this proxy at runtime.

Our key insight is that this remaining runtime integration is avoidable. Rather than precomputing only the radiance leaving an emitter (which still needs to be integrated), we precompute the pre-integrated outgoing direct illumination with respect to a receiver point (any shaded surface point in the volume around the emitter). We represent this as a neural field parameterized by the receiver’s position, normal, view direction, and material parameters, learned by a neural network conditioned on a material model. By shifting the integration to a one-time precomputation phase, a single network evaluation replaces the entire integral over the (proxy) emitter.

Because the network is trained in the emitter’s local coordinate frame, the resulting model functions as a portable lighting asset. World-space queries are mapped into the emitter’s frame at shading time rather than baked into the network weights, so a trained NEF can be translated, rotated, and uniformly scaled at runtime without retraining. A single training run therefore amortizes across every scene and every instance in which the emitter is placed—much like a baked texture or precomputed BRDF.

This design facilitates several critical performance advantages over traditional methods. Inference cost is fundamentally decoupled from the geometric complexity of the emitter; the computational cost is determined by the network’s size rather than the polygon count of the emitter. Furthermore, because the receiver’s BRDF is incorporated into the learning objective, complex emissive effects are absorbed into the representation at no additional runtime cost. Finally, since the training phase relies solely on path-traced radiance estimates for training data, the same training procedure is used for simple planar polygons, complex emissive meshes, and deformable emitter assemblies.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    A reformulation of direct illumination as a pre-integrated, receiver-aware quantity, eliminating the runtime integration retained by prior analytical, sampling-based, and proxy-based methods.

  • •

    A neural emission field employing a two-headed diffuse/glossy architecture and reflected-direction encoding, yielding noise-free direct illumination and accurate specular highlights from a single network evaluation per shading point.

  • •

    Scene-independent training in the emitter’s local coordinate frame, so a single pre-trained NEF can be translated, rotated and scaled across different scenes without retraining.

  • •

    Extensions to complex emissive assemblies with internal interreflections, spatially varying emission, and deformable emitters which are non-trivial or unsupported in state-of-the-art real-time methods.

    • 2 Related Work

    We categorize previous work into three primary categories: analytical solutions, Monte Carlo estimators, and proxy-based representations. Finally, we discuss the broader context of using neural networks in the context of rendering.

    Analytical Solutions. Analytical closed-form solutions for simple emitter geometries (e.g., planar polygons) exist for various receiver types, including diffuse [5] or glossy receivers like the Phong distribution [3], and more general glossy reflections [15, 19, 20]. Analytical methods are extremely efficient for low-polygon emitters, but their cost scales linearly with the number of emitter vertices [3], making them prohibitively expensive for high-polygon emitters in real-time applications. Furthermore, even on supported geometry they diverge from a path-traced reference when receivers are glossy or emission is non-uniform [15]. Our neural approach achieves more accurate shading with respect to a ground truth solution, natively supports non-convex and non-planar emitters, and decouples cost from the emitter geometry, drastically reducing shading time for complex emissive meshes.

    Many-Light Sampling. Monte Carlo integration supports estimating direct illumination from any emitter but requires specialized sampling strategies to manage runtime noise. Early techniques addressed the many-lights problem by ranking lights according to their potential contribution [40] or by classifying them as important or unimportant to guide sampling [31]. In complex scenes, hierarchical representations [37, 23, 42] can be used to enable emitter sampling at sublinear cost. More recently, ReSTIR [6] introduced spatiotemporal reservoir resampling, achieving high-quality direct illumination under tight sampling budgets. Despite these advancements, the residual variance inherent to all Monte Carlo approaches typically necessitates a denoiser. In contrast, NEF avoids runtime sampling entirely, shifting the computational burden to a (one-time) per-emitter offline training phase.

    Classical Pre-integration. Precomputation in rendering [28] trades offline computations for runtime cost by tabulating light transport over a discretised parameter domain. Precomputed radiance transfer (PRT) [33] projects the transfer function at each surface point onto a low-order spherical harmonics basis, reducing shading under distant lighting to a dot product. All-frequency variants require non-linear wavelet approximations to keep storage tractable [26]. More fundamentally, PRT relies on the distant-lighting assumption, which breaks down for near-field emitters whose incident lighting varies with receiver position.

    A complementary line of work stores lighting in a volume rather than on surfaces. Irradiance volumes [12] and their dynamic, ray-traced successors [21] cache irradiance at probes on a grid and interpolate between them at runtime. For strongly spatially varying signals, such as the near field of a complex emitter, these caches require careful probe placement [32, 39] and fine discretisation to avoid interpolation and light-leaking artifacts.

    These approaches share a common limitation: the storage of a tabulated representation grows exponentially with the dimensionality of the signal. Pre-integrated direct illumination around a near-field emitter depends on receiver position (3D), normal (2D), and reflected direction (2D), which is already seven dimensions for a single glossy material. Conditioning on roughness to cover a continuous family of materials, as done in this paper, adds an eighth parameter. A regular grid with only 32 samples per dimension would already require 32⁸≈10¹² entries. Adding a time parameter for dynamic emitters worsens this further: a naive per-keyframe cache scales linearly with the number of keyframes, and complex temporal variation demands many of them. Like prior neural precomputation methods [27, 9], NEF sidesteps this curse of dimensionality by fitting a compact, global representation that efficiently captures correlations in the high-dimensional signal.

    Pre-integrated Emitters. Estimating the radiance emitted by complex light sources is non-trivial, particularly when light paths are obstructed by housing geometry or undergo multiple internal reflections. Early research tackled this by replacing the emitter with a 4D proxy geometry. Canned light sources represent the radiance leaving the emitter’s bounding surface as a 4D light field slab so that scene points can be illuminated by ray-tracing against the proxy rather than the intricate original geometry [14]. Later work decoupled a luminaire’s dual roles in rendering: a radiance volume captures its appearance when viewed directly, while virtual point lights approximate how it illuminates the surrounding scene [35]. Neural variants [43] reduced the storage requirements of these tabulated representations and combined it with a learned importance sampling distribution. Subsequent work learned radiance-field representations of the luminaire for faster evaluation [7], or relied on wavelet-compressed light fields for fast per-ray reconstruction and hierarchical importance sampling [4].

    Despite these advances, these methods still treat the proxy as an emitter that must be integrated at runtime. Each shading point integrates the product of the radiance sampled from the proxy’s 4D near-field and the material evaluation. In contrast, NEF pre-integrates this contribution offline, storing the full outgoing pre-integrated direct illumination to be queried at runtime.

    Rendering with Neural Networks. A common use of neural networks in rendering is capturing the radiance distribution during a training phase which amortizes over subsequent viewings of the scene. Early work anchored a learned radiance representation to scene geometry for interactive viewing from arbitrary directions [30]. Modern variants extend this idea to high-quality static scenes [13], rotatable environment lighting [27], scene animations [8], variable scene configurations [10, 34], and volumetric irradiance caching [9]. These methods all rely on offline, scene-specific training. Alternatively, a small neural representation can be trained online as a radiance cache [25] with the additional runtime cost of ray tracing and denoising. NEF differs in that it is an offline method whose representation is anchored in the emitter’s local 3D extent rather than on the 2D scene manifold, making it a portable, reusable asset across scenes.

    3 Neural Pre-integrated Emitters

    Prior proxy methods reduce the runtime cost of internal emitter transport but still leave the receiver-side integral to be evaluated per shading point. We close this remaining gap by learning the full pre-integrated direct illumination as a neural field around the emitter. Section 3.1 derives this formulation; Section 3.2 defines the emitter-local frame that makes the representation portable; Section 3.3 introduces the diffuse/glossy decomposition; Section 3.4 describes training; and Section 3.5 outlines rendering.

    3.1 Pre-integrated Emitter

    Computing the direct illumination Lₒ with respect to a complex emitter involves two layers of integration: the recursive internal light transport inside the emitter, and the receiver’s shading integral over the hemisphere. Proxy-emitter methods [14, 35, 43] already peel away the inner layer by precomputing internal transport into a function ℙ defined on a bounding surface. The receiver, however, must still integrate against ℙ at runtime. We take this idea one step further by absorbing the receiver’s direct illumination integral into the learned field D_θ itself:

    Lₒ(x,ωₒ)=∫_Ω[∫_Ω⋯ dωᵢ^′] (internal transport)fᵣ(x,ωᵢ,ωₒ) (ωᵢ·n) dωᵢ(reference)
    =∫_Ωℙ(t(x,ωᵢ),-ωᵢ) (baked offline)fᵣ(x,ωᵢ,ωₒ) (ωᵢ·n) dωᵢ(proxy)
    ≈D_θ(x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ,α) (baked offline)(ours)

    where (x,n,ωₒ) defines the world-space position, normal and outgoing direction at an intersection point, (x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ) are their counterparts expressed in the emitter’s local frame (Section 3.2), ωᵢ is the incident direction, t(x,ωᵢ) returns the point where the ray from x in direction ωᵢ intersects the proxy surface, α are the material parameters for the BRDF fᵣ, (ωᵢ·n) is the cosine foreshortening term, and Ω denotes the hemispherical integration domain.

    Crucially, a pre-integrated quantity is not a property of the emitter alone. Since the BRDF fᵣ appears inside the direct illumination integral, different receivers will observe different values of D_θ at the same (x,n). The receiver’s shading model is therefore part of what is being learned. We instantiate this using the GGX microfacet model [38] over a roughness range of α∈[0.1,1]. By exposing α as input to the network, a single trained NEF represents the full roughness range for that material. While we restrict our scope to GGX in this work, our approach is generic and can be extended to other materials, such as Disney or layered BRDFs, by extending the conditioning inputs and the training distribution.

    At runtime, evaluating D_θ requires only a single network inference at the shading point. This eliminates the need for any sampling of the proxy ℙ, importance sampling, and denoising.

    Because D_θ is agnostic to the source of the radiance field, all the complexity that would otherwise have to be handled at runtime is shifted to the offline solver and baked into the network weights. This includes complex effects such as self-occlusion, multi-bounce transport and non-uniform emission (Section 4.2)—effects that often violate the assumptions made by analytical methods such as LTC [15]. As a result, D_θ can stand in for a path-traced estimate of direct illumination from an emitter, provided the field can be trained to faithfully represent it.

    3.2 Emitter-space

    Our neural field is defined in the emitter’s local frame (see Figure 1). Given a rigid world transform M, we map a world-space shading configuration (x,n,ωₒ) to its local counterpart (x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ) by applying M⁻¹ to the position and the rotational part of M⁻¹ to the normal and outgoing directions.

    Pre-integrated direct illumination is only physically meaningful within a bounded region around the emitter. Emitted radiance falls off with distance, and beyond a certain range an emitter’s contribution becomes negligible. We therefore define the emitter-space as an axis-aligned bounding region in the local frame, sized to extend 20× the emitter’s largest extent on each axis—well beyond the 5× threshold at which the inverse-square law becomes an acceptable approximation for emitters [29]. Shading points inside this region are evaluated by a direct query of D_θ, which is sufficient for all emitters in this work.

    Analytical Fall-off. A simple heuristic to deal with points outside of the emitter-space, consists of clamping outside queries to the nearest boundary point and scaling the resulting shading value by (d_boundary/d_actual)², where d_boundary is the distance from the emitter center to the clamped boundary point and d_actual is the true distance from the emitter center to the shading point. As shown in Figure 2, this fall-off approach generates a result that is hard to visually distinguish from the ground truth reference. Alternatively, the emitter-space can be enlarged at training time to avoid the heuristic, potentially requiring a larger representation to get the desired level of accuracy everywhere in the emitter-space.

    Scene-independent placement. Anchoring the representation to the emitter’s local frame yields two practical benefits: scene-independence and free rigid placement at runtime. The trained NEF does not store scene-specific information, so the same parameters θ are reusable across scenes. At runtime, world-space shading configurations are mapped through M⁻¹ before being evaluated by D_θ. Since M is applied at shading time rather than baked into the network weights, translating or rotating the emitter is essentially free: it only changes the transformation applied to each query, not the representation itself. Uniform scaling is handled by folding the scale factor into M and scaling the emitter-space extent accordingly; non-uniform scaling and shears are not supported, as they would distort the learned angular distribution. A single NEF therefore defines a family of emitters related by similarity transformations, amortizing the training cost across all scenes and instances in which the emitter is placed (Figure 3).

    3.3 Diffuse–Glossy Separation

    Similarly to related work [27], we decompose our neural representation into separate diffuse f^θ_d(x̃,ñ) and glossy f_g^θ(x̃,ñ,r(ω̃ₒ,ñ),α) components. We compute the total pre-integrated direct illumination D_θ at a given shading point (x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ,α) as their sum:

    D_θ(x̃,ñ,ω̃ₒ,α)=ρ_d(x)·f^θ_d(x̃,ñ) (diffuse)+ρ_g(x)·f_g^θ(x̃,ñ,r(ω̃ₒ,ñ),α) (glossy).

    Here, tilde denotes properties in the local emitter-space defined in Section 3.2, ρ_d and ρ_g are factored-out diffuse and specular textures of the shading point x which retain high-frequency texture details [25], θ are the trainable parameters of the neural representation, r(ω̃ₒ,ñ) is the reflected outgoing direction vector ω̃ₒ around the normal ñ, and α is the GGX roughness parameter. For emitters that are only expected to see diffuse surfaces at runtime, the glossy head f_g^θ can be omitted during training (and during shading).

    All network inputs are normalized to [0,1]³, and a learned multi-resolution hash encoding  [24] is applied to both the position x̃ and the reflected direction r(ω̃ₒ,ñ). Encoding the reflected direction is critical for capturing the sharp highlights and complex reflections characteristic of low-roughness receiver geometry (see supplemental material), consistent with findings in the field of novel view synthesis [36]. Both the glossy and diffuse head use a 4-layer MLP of width 128 with ReLU activations. More details on the network architecture can be found in the supplemental material.

    3.4 Training

    A schematic of the training procedure is shown in Figure 1. Training a NEF only requires a reliable estimate of the outgoing radiance Lₒ for any query within the network’s input domain, making the procedure agnostic to the underlying emitter geometry.

    Sample generation. For each training batch, we draw queries uniformly from the emitter-space (Section 3.2). For the glossy head f_g^θ, we sample a position x̃ uniformly in the local bounding box, and a normal ñ such that the emitter is visible in its hemisphere avoiding queries with zero radiance, an outgoing direction ω̃ₒ uniformly on the upper hemisphere defined by ñ, and a roughness α uniformly in [0.1,1]. The diffuse head f_d^θ uses the same procedure restricted to (x̃,ñ). For deformable or animated emitters, we additionally sample a time parameter t∈[0,1] corresponding to the emitter’s state, encoded with an 8-band Fourier encoding [22] and provided as an extra conditioning input.

    Radiance targets. Target radiance is obtained via offline path tracing against the (possibly time-varying) emitter geometry. Bare emissive surfaces are handled with standard next-event estimation; emitters with non-emissive housing geometry that causes self-occlusion or internal interreflections (Figure 5) are handled with full path tracing inside the emitter assembly, so that higher-order transport is naturally absorbed into the training signal. We use 64 samples per radiance estimate as default across all emitters in this paper as we saw diminishing returns beyond this (see supplemental material for an ablation). Targets are generated on-the-fly rather than cached, so all reported training timings include the cost of path tracing.

    Optimization. We minimize a relative L₂ loss [25] between the network prediction and the path-traced target averaged over the batch, L(θ)=((D_θ-⟨Lₒ⟩)²)/(sg(D_θ)²+ε), where ε=0.01 and sg denotes a stop gradient operation. The relative loss prevents bright regions of the emitter-space from dominating the gradient and helps the multi-resolution hash encoding to allocate capacity uniformly across the field. We use Adam [18] with a learning rate of 10⁻³, a batch size of 2¹⁶, and use cosine annealing learning rate decay. The number of training iterations for each of our emitter types can be found in the supplemental material. Total wall-clock time on an RTX 4090 ranges from one minute for diffuse receiver with planar emitters to three hours for emitters with complex emissive effects, dominated by the cost of generating path-traced target values.

    3.5 Rendering

    Because NEF stores a pre-integrated estimate of the outgoing radiance reflected by the receiver, no integration is required at runtime. Unlike methods that integrate with respect to the emitter geometry or to a proxy representation of the emitter [14, 35, 43], our approach reduces the shading process to a single network evaluation per pixel. At render time, we first perform a G-buffer pass to obtain the (x,n,ωₒ,α) channels at each shading point. These are transformed into the emitter’s local frame via its current world transform M (Section 3.2), encoded, and fed to D_θ to obtain the outgoing radiance contribution pre-integrated with respect to the emitter.

    Visibility. As with existing analytical methods [15, 5], NEF does not inherently capture occlusions of the emissive field caused by the surrounding scene. For simple emitters, a single shadow ray toward the emitter center is often sufficient (Figure 4); for soft shadows, established techniques such as shadow mapping [41] or a small ray-tracing budget combined with a denoiser [16] apply directly, which we implemented in the supplemental material. Crucially, shadow rays are only required against non-emitter scene geometry: the NEF itself bakes in self-occlusion and internal interreflections within the emitter assembly (Figure 5).

    4 Results

    We show that NEF matches the quality of analytical solutions (Section 4.1) and extends beyond what they handle, supporting emissive meshes and deformable emitters (Section 4.2). We then compare against two sampling-based techniques, where NEF’s sampling-free formulation yields a runtime advantage (Section 4.3).

    4.1 Planar Emitters

    We compare against analytical integration for diffuse receivers [5] and Linearly Transformed Cosines (LTC) for glossy receivers [15]. As shown in Figure 4, our method matches the analytical reference for diffuse receivers under uniform emission, confirming its accuracy.

    For glossy receivers (Figure 10), the larger capacity of NEF allows it to achieve lower rendering error across various roughness values α compared to LTC, highlighting LTC’s remaining approximation error. The near-mirror regime (α→0) remains challenging for a finite neural representation; we show an example of the increase in error at lower roughness in the supplemental material.

    While analytical methods have lower per-frame shading costs for simple polygons, their runtime scales linearly O(V) with the number of emitter vertices V. This linear cost is especially noticeable for large emissive emitters, as highlighted in Table 1. We show the crossover point between the analytical methods and our GlossyNEF—267 emitter vertices—in the supplemental material. The generality and computational efficiency of our approach become especially relevant when extending beyond planar geometry.

    4.2 Complex Emitters

    A key advantage of our approach is that inference cost is determined by the complexity of the emissive field, not by the complexity of the underlying geometry. While NEF inference cost does scale with emissive field complexity—a highly spatially varying emitter benefits from a larger or more expressive network—this complexity is typically much lower than that of the geometry itself. Naively subdividing an emissive mesh increases its vertex count but leaves its emissive field largely unchanged, so the same NEF capacity suffices regardless of tessellation. All results in this paper share a single network configuration sized for the most demanding case (the Pierced Sphere, whose housing interreflections produce a high-frequency emissive field); for simpler emitters such as the planar quad, a smaller architecture would suffice with no perceptible loss in quality (see supplemental material).

    Higher-order Emissive Effects. Our NEF formulation can also capture higher-order emissive effects arising from multi-bounce light transport within the emitter, such as internal reflections toward a filament. By replacing direct light-source sampling with path tracing during training, multi-bounce contributions are integrated into the training signal. Figure 5 shows three assemblies in which internal interreflections meaningfully shape the emissive field: a Dragon mesh acting as a bare emitter, a Pierced Sphere whose shell partially occludes and reflects an internal filament, and a Lattice Box which houses a spherical emitter. Obtaining a noise-free reference for these assemblies is expensive—on the order of 1M samples per pixel—because the interior light paths are not captured by simple next-event estimation against the bare emissive geometry. The effect varies by assembly: interreflections produce only a mild overall brightening on the Dragon, whereas the Pierced Sphere and Lattice Box show light diffusing through the apertures, softening cast shadows and noticeably brightening regions that the bare-emitter leaves dark. NEF reproduces all three references faithfully.

    Non-uniform emission. Since our NEF representation is agnostic to the emissive profile of the light source, it naturally accommodates spatially varying emission without modification. Figure  (center) shows an emitter with a non-uniform radiance distribution. While some prior methods support textured emitters, they rely on approximations that introduce error [15].

    Dynamic and Deformable Emitters. To support dynamic or deformable emitters, we extend NEF with a time-varying parameter t. As with the higher-order emissive effects in the previous section, this only requires that training data collection account for the time-varying state of the emitter. Figure 6 shows a textured fireball whose time parameter indexes into frames of a source video. See Figure 11 for an emitter with deformable geometry. We encourage the reader to consult the supplemental video for a detailed demonstration of the results.

    4.3 Comparison to Sampling-based Methods

    Both online many-light sampling methods and proxy-based emitters [14, 35, 43] require an integration step at runtime. We compare against a representative of each category: ReSTIR [6] and an oracle proxy formulation.

    Many-light Sampling. Unlike ReSTIR, which operates entirely at runtime with no precomputation, NEF amortizes work into a one-time training phase in exchange for a constant-time per-pixel inference cost. To make this trade-off concrete, we construct a Cornell Box scene with 1,000 point lights treated as a single composite emitter: the lights support global rigid transformations, but are fixed relative to each other. A single NEF is trained on this composite.

    We evaluate equal-quality convergence against three baselines: path-traced direct illumination, ReSTIR DI (M=32, K=5), and ReSTIR DI paired with an OptiX denoiser. To reach NEF’s error level, ReSTIR requires ∼256 SPP without denoising, or ∼32 SPP with denoising (Figure 8). While both unbiased sampling baselines eventually surpass NEF at high sample counts, even the 32 SPP denoised case exceeds the typical per-frame budget of real-time pipelines. However, ReSTIR remains more general: it handles arbitrary per-light motion at runtime, whereas NEF requires the emitter configuration to be fixed at training time. Rigid transforms of the entire emitter group and pre-arranged relative motion of the emitters in the composition (via a time parameter, Section 4.2) are supported, but arbitrary independent light motion requires retraining.

    Proxy Emitters.

    Proxy representations—whether using 4D light-field slabs [14], a radiance volume with virtual point lights [35], or neural fields [43]—gather radiance by sampling and integrating a proxy representation. We compare NEF against an oracle proxy: an idealized proxy whose near-field queries return a noise-free reference and whose evaluation cost is treated as zero. Any sampling-based proxy method is bounded from below by this oracle, so the comparison reveals the minimum number of proxy evaluations required to match NEF’s pre-integrated estimate, regardless of how the proxy itself is represented.

    As shown in Figure 7, for the Pierced Sphere scene (Figure 5), the oracle proxy requires approximately 734 samples per pixel to match the accuracy of a single NEF query when combined with a learned importance sampling routine from [43]. Each of those samples still requires a BSDF evaluation at the shading point: at 1920×1080 resolution, the 734 GGX evaluations alone cost 2.9 ms per frame in an optimized CUDA kernel. This already exceeds NEF’s total inference cost of 2.5 ms, before any of the proxy queries or importance sampling are accounted for. Moreover, the cost of those proxy queries is not negligible in practice. As a data point, a half-precision torch.compile’d forward pass of the evaluation network from [43] takes 103 ms per emitter sample per full-HD frame, and 49 ms to output the importance sampling distributions on the same hardware as our NEF timings.

    5 Discussion

    Visibility and soft shadows. Similarly to analytical methods and proxy emitters, NEF only captures the unoccluded emission field. In practice, this is well-addressed by combining NEF shading with a small budget of path-traced visibility samples and a denoiser that are used as a ratio estimator [16]. This approach yields plausible soft shadows while preserving the noise-free direct illumination produced by the NEF. Even 1 shadow ray per pixel yields perceptually accurate soft shadows (see Figure 9), with further samples producing diminishing returns. This makes NEF compatible with standard real-time visibility pipelines at minimal additional cost.

    Storage and training. All results in this paper were generated using a single NEF architecture totaling 15 MB (or 30 MB for the glossy variant) per emitter. For simpler emitters, this is often excessive and can be reduced (see supplemental). Training is a one-time offline cost, ranging from approximately one minute for simple planar emitters to three hours for emitters with internal interreflections, depending primarily on the cost of generating path-traced training samples. Crucially, this cost is incurred once per emitter and can be amortized across multiple scenes.

    Multiple emitters in a scene. Currently, a scene with N emitters requires evaluating N independent NEFs and summing their contributions (unless emitters are close enough to be represented jointly by a single NEF), scaling linearly with N. We see two avenues to mitigate this. First, a shared decoding MLP could learn to disentangle latents from multiple emitters; however a naive sum-then-decode scheme retains a linear cost for the latent fetching. Second, future work could combine NEF with lighting hierarchies [37, 23] to achieve sub-linear scaling.

    Sampling training data. We generate training targets by path tracing the emitter assembly with next-event estimation. For emitters with housing geometry more intricate than those presented in this work—heavily enclosing the emissive surface or admitting light only through narrow apertures—this strategy can produce a sparse training signal: most paths fail to reach the emitter and contribute zero, leaving the network to learn from a small fraction of informative samples. As shown in recent work [11], light tracing [2] can reduce the number of zero-radiance contributions. Orthogonally, when the emissive field around the emitter exhibits high-frequency variation, adaptive sampling the training loss [10] could training data on the regions that need it most.

    6 Conclusion

    We presented Neural Emission Fields, a pre-integrated neural representation of direct illumination from non-trivial emitters. By moving the receiver-side integral into an offline training phase, NEF reduces shading to a single network evaluation per pixel, at a cost independent of the emitter’s geometric complexity. The same formulation handles a wide range of lighting scenarios—including spatially varying emission, internal interreflections, and deformable emitters—within a single, unified training procedure; trained models then act as portable lighting assets that can be placed in any scene under rigid transforms and uniform scaling. We hope NEF proves a useful step toward treating expensive direct illumination as a bakeable, reusable component of real-time rendering pipelines.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Linear Scaling of Analytical Methods

    As shown in Figure 12, the computational cost of analytical methods like LTC [15] scales linearly with the number of emitter vertices. In contrast, NEF inference time remains constant for a given emitter geometry, regardless of the density of its tessellation. For glossy receivers, our method reaches a performance crossover at 267 emitter vertices. Notably, NEF maintains a constant 2.5ms shading time even for highly complex emitters like the Stanford Dragon (436k vertices), where analytical methods would be computationally prohibitive.

    Appendix B Representation Parameters

    We use a single set of hash grid parameters for all encoded inputs. The GlossyNEF architecture shares the positional encoding between the diffuse and glossy head. The multiresolution hash table has eight levels, each level increases in size with a rate of √2 per level, the corresponding latent vector consists of four floats, and the hash table uses 2¹⁹ entries. The additional inputs to the neural network, and the overall memory budget in half-precision, are summarized in Table 2.

    Appendix C Architecture Ablation

    We ablate several architecture choices (see Table 3) of our NEF by training a GlossyNEF on the same Quad emitter with the same number of training iterations.

    Applying the multiresolution hash encoding on the outgoing direction as opposed to the reflected direction, which is a common encoding choice for neural representations, reduces quality across all roughness values α.

    Splitting the network into a diffuse and glossy head similarly performs better than unifying into a single head.

    The original NEF architecture shares the positional encoding between the diffuse and glossy head. Decoupling this multiresolution hash table (i.e. diffuse and glossy each use a different one) yields no quality improvement, although it adds more capacity and extra runtime.

    Appendix D Training Budget

    Table 4 reports the training cost for each NEF in the paper, measured on a single RTX 4090 GPU. All timings include the cost of generating path-traced radiance targets on-the-fly, which dominates iteration time for the more complex emitters. Iterations and per-emitter training time scale with the difficulty of the underlying radiance field: planar emitters with uniform emission converge in minutes, bare emissive meshes and spatially varying emitters in under fifteen minutes, while configurations involving internal interreflections or temporal variation require several hours, both because the radiance field itself is more complex and because each path-traced target costs more to generate.

    Appendix E Overspent Capacity

    The default NEF architecture is sized for the most demanding emitter in our set (the Pierced Sphere) and is excessive for simpler emissive fields. We ablate two capacity axes—the MLP and the multiresolution hash encoding—on a simple Quad emitter (Figure 13). The two axes have different effects: reducing the MLP size quickly degrades quality, as the network loses the capacity to decode the encoded latents. Shrinking the hash encoding, in contrast, yields the largest reduction in memory footprint at negligible cost in error, since most of the parameter budget lives in the hash tables and the Quad’s emissive field does not need the default spatial resolution. In practice, simple emitters can therefore be deployed with a substantially smaller hash table while keeping the MLP near its default size.

    Appendix F Low-roughness Materials

    While there are no theoretical constraints preventing NEF from being trained on low-roughness receivers, practical results indicate a bottleneck as α→0, as illustrated in Figure 14. This degradation occurs because the specular highlight sharpens into a high-frequency signal that exceeds the network’s representational capacity. Consequently, while training is technically feasible across the entire roughness spectrum, the model struggles to resolve the near-singular gradients of mirror-like reflections, leading to the observed increase in approximation error in the highlight regions.

    Appendix G Impact of Training Data Noise

    The training targets used throughout this paper are generated via path tracing with Monte Carlo integration, leaving residual variance in the supervision signal. The magnitude of this variance depends on the emitter: emitters that are hard to sample yield noisier targets. The Pierced Sphere is a particularly challenging case, as its internal interreflections must also be captured during training, making it one of the noisiest emitters in our set. In Figure 15 we ablate the number of Monte Carlo samples used per training estimate and observe diminishing returns beyond 64 samples. We therefore adopt S=64 for all emitters throughout the paper, noting that this budget could safely be reduced for simpler emitters.

item.title: 给神经辐射缓存补上高光：按反射方向参数化，缓存预滤波入射辐射 ｜ Neural Caching of Prefiltered Radiance for Specular Lighting
item.description:
一句话：用反射方向 + 粗糙度相关的辐射目标，让在线 NRC 在镜面/高光场景收敛更快。

要点：

  • 原版 Neural Radiance Caching 为实时路径追踪提供在线神经光照表示，但对视角与粗糙度高度敏感的高光不友好。
  • 改动两点：用反射方向而不是视线方向参数化缓存；学习与粗糙度相关的预滤波入射辐射，再用 split-sum 近似与预计算 BRDF 积分图组合出射辐射。
  • 在 Bunny 与 Specular Sponza 上，收敛到累积路径追踪参考更快、高光质量优于对照的 NRC 基线，且在线训练仍保持实时性能、缓存在渲染过程中自适应。

为什么值得看：NRC 是实时路径追踪降噪/加速的主流路线，这篇的改动量很小却直指高光质量，适合直接在自己引擎的 GI 缓存里做 A/B。

中文摘要：神经辐射缓存（NRC）为实时路径追踪提供在线学习的场景光照表示，但高光反射强烈依赖视方向与粗糙度，难以直接表示。论文提出面向高光的 NRC 变体：用反射方向参数化缓存，学习与粗糙度相关的预滤波入射辐射，再通过 split-sum 近似与预计算的 BRDF 积分图重建出射辐射。在 Bunny 与 Specular Sponza 上的对比显示，相比所评测的 NRC 基线，该方法更快收敛到累积路径追踪参考且高光质量更好，在线训练方式也维持了实时性能，缓存可在渲染过程中持续自适应。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-23

Neural Caching of Prefiltered Radiance for Specular Lighting

Abstract

Neural Radiance Caching (NRC) [17] provides an online neural representation of scene illumination for real-time path tracing. This paper presents an NRC variant tailored to specular lighting through a reflection-direction parameterization and a roughness-dependent radiance target. Our network predicts prefiltered incoming radiance at individual surface points, which is combined with a precomputed BRDF integration map using the split-sum approximation to estimate outgoing radiance. On Bunny and Specular Sponza, the reported comparisons indicate faster convergence to the accumulated path-tracing reference and improved specular-lighting quality relative to the evaluated NRC baselines. Our online-trained method maintains real-time performance while adapting its cache during rendering.

1 Introduction

Specular reflection depends strongly on viewing direction and surface roughness, making its representation challenging for radiance caching. Neural Radiance Caching (NRC) [17] learns scene illumination online to accelerate path tracing. We target specular lighting by parameterizing the cache with the reflected viewing direction and learning roughness-dependent prefiltered incoming radiance for split-sum reconstruction.

The main goal of path-tracing is to calculate the solution of Light Transport Equation (LTE) [10]:

Lₒ(ωₒ)=Lₑ(ωₒ)+∫_H⁺Lᵢ(ωᵢ)fₛ(ωᵢ,ωₒ)\cos(θᵢ) dωᵢ.

(1)

Here, Lₑ is the radiance emitted in direction ωₒ, Lᵢ is the radiance arriving from direction ωᵢ, and fₛ is the bidirectional scattering distribution function (BSDF). The angle θᵢ is measured between the surface normal n at position x and ωᵢ. We omit the position argument for brevity. For reflection, the BSDF is restricted to a bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF). In this work, we consider its specular component. Estimating the integral is computationally expensive, motivating approaches that cache previously computed lighting information.

Traditional radiance caching approaches like[12] (and analogues) are based on several heuristics that are difficult to implement and tend to produce artefacts that need special care to be suppressed [20]. Other progressive rendering and reconstruction approaches (for example [14]) also uses handcrafted mathematic models which makes their implementation and testing inside and existing rendering system a challenging task. At the same time NRC[17] reduces such complexity by way of abstraction of internal radiance cache representation via neural network. This method represents scene illumination with a multilayer perceptron that maps hit ray positions and directions to radiance values of the scattered light. The approach is lightweight and it is designed to continuously train in real-time to support dynamic scenes while ensuring predictable performance and resource usage. The research presents a multitude of methods to regulate and stabilize the output of the neural network like self-training and path termination that are omitted in our paper. The idea of encoding input data was also explored in these papers [15][22][16].

Our method parameterizes the cache to represent specular reflection, including mirror-like and rough glossy reflection. Following the reflection-direction parameterization used in [22], we use the viewing direction reflected about the surface normal as a network input. We also use the split-sum approximation [11] to separate prefiltered lighting from the final BRDF reconstruction. The cache predicts roughness-dependent filtered radiance, while the BRDF integration lookup supplies the final Fresnel-dependent reconstruction. Together, these terms approximate the reflected component of Equation (1).

2 Previous Work

2.1 Microfacet Specular BRDF

Microfacet theory is a popular approach to modelling surface reflection and transmission. In this theory, surfaces are modelled as a collection of small microfacets, with their aggregated statistical behaviour determining the observed scattering of light. The microfacet specular BRDF is an expression that describes the scattering of light from a surface composed of microfacets. To compute BRDF from such a model, local lighting effects at the microfacet level need to be considered, such as microfacet occlusion, shadowing, and interreflection. An expression representing BRDF consists of two statistical measures, a microfacet normalized distribution function(NDF) of facets represented as D and a shadowing-masking function between facets G, and a Fresnel reflectance factor F. All of that is combined in a general Cook-Torrance [8][7] microfacet specular shading model. Here h is the halfway-vector between ωᵢ,ωₒ.

fᵣ(ωᵢ,ωₒ)=(D(h)F(ωₒ,h)G(ωᵢ,ωₒ))/(4(n·ωᵢ)(n·ωₒ))

(2)

For the implementation of those terms, we used ones implemented in the Falcor rendering framework [4] and thoroughly described in Disney’s research paper [5]. In the presented paper NDF is represented as a modified Trowbridge-Reitz(GGX)[21] distribution. For the Fresnel term the Schlick approximation [19] is used. For the shadowing-masking function modified GGX model[23] is used with reparametrization presented in Disney’s research paper to dampen the shine on small roughness values.

2.2 Split sum approximation

The reflected component of Equation (1) can be estimated by importance sampling. Let p(ωᵢ) denote the probability density of the sampled incoming direction, measured with respect to solid angle. We use the NDF-based sampling implementation provided by Falcor. For N samples ω_i,k, the estimator is

Lₒ(ωₒ)=Lₑ(ωₒ)+∫_H⁺Lᵢ(ωᵢ)fᵣ(ωᵢ,ωₒ)\cos(θᵢ) dωᵢ ≈Lₑ(ωₒ)+1/N∑ₖ₌₁^N(Lᵢ(ω_i,k)fᵣ(ω_i,k,ωₒ)\cos(θ_i,k))/(p(ω_i,k)).

(3)

Even with importance sampling, many samples may be required for high-quality results. Karis [11] approximates the reflected-radiance estimate by separating it into two averages:

Lₒ(ωₒ)-Lₑ(ωₒ) ≈(1/N∑ₖ₌₁^NLᵢ(ω_i,k))(1/N∑ₖ₌₁^N(fᵣ(ω_i,k,ωₒ)\cos(θ_i,k))/(p(ω_i,k))).

(4)

The first factor represents prefiltered environment radiance. The practical prefilter in [11] samples the GGX normal distribution and uses normalized cosine weighting. During prefiltering, the viewing direction is assumed perpendicular to the filtering surface, so n=ωₒ. The filtering normal is aligned with the reflected viewing direction used for lookup. Incoming directions ωᵢ remain sampled over the hemisphere. This normal-view assumption introduces approximation error at grazing viewing angles.

The second factor is the BRDF integration map. With Schlick’s Fresnel approximation, it is represented by two coefficients stored in a lookup texture indexed by roughness and the cosine of the viewing angle. Our method uses this split-sum factorization and BRDF integration lookup to reconstruct outgoing radiance from the neural cache.

2.3 Neural radiance cache

We examined various methods employing neural networks (and multilayer perceptron specifically) for providing scene information. Neural methods are increasingly being used for rendering in various applications. The recent method of spatio-directional neural representations replaces traditional discrete representations with an MLP for reconstructing 3D geometry-aware solutions. The most widely adopted strategy currently is Neural Radiance Fields[13], the science publication of which inspired a multitude of works [3][22] in the novel view synthesis problem.

Gradually, the interest in neural approaches for global illumination increased. There has been a significant effort to improve sampling[16] and denoising of Monte Carlo global illumination algorithms [2][6][9]. The current work is based on NRC [17] where researchers use small neural networks that undergo online training to store and predict indirect global illumination for real-time path tracing. Further development shows the significant advantage of using hash grid parametric encoding for NRC[15].

3 Proposed method

Our method uses a single multilayer perceptron to predict prefiltered incoming radiance at a queried position, reflection direction, and roughness. The network is trained during rendering to adapt to scene changes. We divide rendering into three passes. The first generates training paths with multiple surface bounces. The second traces rendering paths and stores the surface information needed to query the cache, terminating paths earlier than the training pass. Both passes use Monte Carlo integration and importance sampling for continuation directions. The third queries the cache and reconstructs outgoing radiance using the BRDF integration lookup.

For each surface hit, we collect the radiance and path-throughput information along the continuation of the training path. These data are used to reconstruct an RGB incoming-radiance target Y, which is stored in the training buffer together with its cache query. Different sampled paths can produce different targets for the same query.

The cache query is q=(φ(x),ω_refl,ρ), where x is the surface position, φ is its hash-grid encoding, and ρ is the surface roughness. For an outgoing direction ωₒ pointing away from the surface, the reflected direction is ω_refl=2(n·ωₒ)n-ωₒ. We hash-grid encode positions [15] and pass reflection direction and roughness directly to the MLP. Each query produces an RGB estimate of the filtered incoming radiance. The roughness input conditions the cached lighting on the reflection lobe.

We train the network using mean squared error (MSE). Under squared-error loss, the population-optimal predictor is the conditional mean of the training target given the cache query,

L̂^*(q)=𝔼[Y|q].

(5)

The sampling distribution and target weighting therefore determine the radiance filter represented by the cache. The network and optimization configuration follow [17]. To reduce fluctuations during online adaptation, we use an exponential moving average of the optimized network weights. The final pass combines the predicted radiance with the stored BRDF integration map to estimate outgoing specular radiance in the camera direction. This reconstruction retains the split-sum approximation and its grazing-angle limitations.

4 Experiments and Results

We use the ray-tracing pipeline in Falcor [4] and the MLP implementation in tiny-cuda-nn [18]. All images were rendered at a resolution of 1920×1080 on an Intel Core i7-8700K processor with an NVIDIA RTX 3080 Ti graphics card. We evaluate image quality using FLIP [1], SSIM [24], and MSE on each rendering frame. MSE is displayed on a logarithmic scale because its values span a wide range. The reference image is obtained by accumulating the regular path tracer over 4000 frames.

Our findings indicate that the modifications have not resulted in any discernible performance degradation while improving convergence and output quality. The BRDF integration map is precomputed and queried during rendering. The changes to the neural network inputs do not negatively influence the other major NRC components.

We compare our method with the NRC baseline and an NRC variant trained only on initial hits. We include the initial-hit variant because removing training targets from multiple hits along a path reduced NRC output quality in our tests. The two variants are distinguished in the comparison plots.

Figure  presents a qualitative comparison after 1000 rendering frames. The displayed images were adjusted for improved visibility. The FLIP results indicate closer agreement with the accumulated reference for our method than for the evaluated NRC baselines. Figure 1 shows the evolution of the quality metrics during training and indicates faster convergence for our method. On Bunny, our method achieves better image quality than the NRC baseline after 1000 frames.

5 Conclusion

We presented an NRC variant for real-time specular-lighting approximation that predicts roughness-dependent prefiltered incoming radiance and reconstructs outgoing radiance using the split-sum approximation. On Bunny and Specular Sponza, the reported comparisons show faster convergence and improved output quality relative to the evaluated NRC baselines while maintaining the same level of performance. The evaluated method uses hash-grid position encoding, a reflection-direction input, and split-sum reconstruction. It retains the grazing-angle limitations of the split-sum approximation. Online training enables the cache to adapt during rendering, motivating further investigation of its behavior in dynamic scenes.

（参考文献见原文。）

item.title: H2-Ray：3DGS 走光追也能不炸，负载均衡 BVH + 路径复用 + 统一求交 ｜ A Hybrid and Hierarchical Ray Tracing Method for Efficient 3D Gaussian Rendering
item.description:
一句话：针对高斯分布不均、相邻光线路径重复、高斯/三角混合求交三个瓶颈各给一招。

要点：

  • 负载失衡：Load-Balanced Spatial BVH 把场景切成均匀网格，用密度感知表示把全局不均衡工作量转成均衡的局部遍历单元。
  • 路径冗余：Ray-Cluster Path Reuse 让一条代理光线与邻近光线共享遍历状态，摊薄重复遍历开销。
  • 异构求交：Unified Intersection Engine 用模式复用的数据通路同时处理高斯与三角形求交，共享约 40% 的浮点数据通路。

为什么值得看：3DGS 想吃到二次光照、畸变相机与景深就得走光追，而光追下的负载均衡与求交效率正是引擎侧最难啃的部分，这篇的三招都可移植。

A Hybrid and Hierarchical Ray Tracing Method for Efficient 3D Gaussian Rendering

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a powerful representation for real-time neural reconstruction and rendering. While existing 3DGS systems rely on rasterization for efficiency, recent work explores ray tracing to enable secondary lighting, highly distorted cameras, and depth-of-field effects. However, compared with rasterization, ray-traced 3DGS introduces three major challenges: (1) the highly non-uniform spatial distribution of massive numbers of Gaussian primitives creates severe load imbalance; (2) neighboring pixels often generate rays with highly similar traversal paths, leading to substantial redundant traversal overhead; and (3) supporting both Gaussian and triangle primitives yields heterogeneous intersection workloads that are not well matched to existing GPU architectures. We present H2-Ray, a hybrid and hierarchical ray tracing architecture for efficient 3D Gaussian rendering. H2-Ray introduces three techniques. Load-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH) partitions the scene into uniform grids and uses density-aware representations to convert an imbalanced global workload into balanced local traversal units.
