    where G_φ,ψ is the four-step generator, ℂ=(c,R(S,I)), and z̃ₜ is a re-noised student sample. Since full-step sampling of the backbone is blurry, the composed student is already sharper than its teacher, and plain distribution matching pulls it back toward this blur: the adapted student ends below its own starting point (sec:abl-guidance). We therefore amplify the structural signal of the teacher. With ẑ₀(ℂ) the clean prediction of the teacher and ẑ₀(ℂ_∅) its prediction after the tokens of the structural video are removed from the reference sequence, the teacher score is computed from

    ẑ₀ʷ=ẑ₀(ℂ)+(w-1)(ẑ₀(ℂ)-ẑ₀(ℂ_∅)).

    		(6)

    In ℂ_∅ the first frame and the prompt are kept unchanged. The difference isolates what the structural video contributes, such as contours, layout, and character positions, so with w>1 the student is pushed toward a target that is sharper and more decisive than the teacher itself. Setting w=1 recovers plain distribution matching. The extrapolation follows classifier-free guidance [Ho and Salimans, 2021], which distribution matching applies to the text condition of the teacher [Yin et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026]. Here it acts on the structural condition alone. The fake-score model is a separate rank-128 LoRA initialized at the teacher, updated five times per generator update with learning rates of 2×10⁻⁶ and 10⁻⁵ for the fake-score model and the generator. We set w=1.5 and run 800 iterations, each one fake-score update, at the cost of one additional teacher forward pass per generator update (app:implementation).

    3.4 Causal Streaming Extension

    To generate video incrementally, we extend the same two-stage design to block-causal attention. The clip is split into blocks of at most five latent frames. We adapt the bidirectional control LoRA with teacher forcing so that each block attends to the prompt, the first frame, the structure of itself and the five preceding blocks, and the clean frames of the five preceding blocks, never to a later block. We then freeze this causal control LoRA and post-train a separate acceleration LoRA, initialized from the bidirectional four-step LoRA, on the student’s own block-by-block rollouts, with the bidirectional control model as the structure-guided teacher (w=1.5). Each rollout is generated without gradients and replayed as one teacher-forced sequence, so that the gradient reaches both how each block is generated and how it serves as context for later blocks. At inference, we merge the acceleration LoRA into the backbone, keep the control LoRA attached, sample each block in four steps, and update the fixed-window key–value cache before outputting the block immediately. With a streaming VAE decoder [Chen et al., 2026a] that decodes each block without future latents, the causal model renders 768p video in real time at up to 28 FPS.

    4 Engine-Aligned Paired Data

    A renderer learns to follow structure only from pairs in which the target video actually follows the structure. Conditions estimated from real videos, such as predicted depth or segmentation, carry the errors of the estimator and differ from the engine proxies that the renderer receives at test time. We therefore collect pairs whose condition is exported by an engine or fitted to the target, and use a pair as structural supervision only when its condition matches the target in time and carries enough structure. We then describe the data sources (sec:sources), the checks that decide how each source is used (sec:alignment), and the construction of prompts (sec:captions).

    4.1 Data Sources

    The training set contains 136K samples, about 243 hours of video. Every clip is a 158-frame window at 24 fps and 768p resolution. The data cover diverse sources and control types (fig:data), listed below with the condition each one supplies.

  • •

    Magpie[Zhan et al., 2026] records human-played Unreal Engine gameplay across many scenes at 60 fps, together with a synchronized grey block-out of the scene. The block-out gives the layout, the large geometry, the bodies and motion of the characters, and the camera of every frame, while materials and lighting are left to the model.

  • •

    CARLA[Dosovitskiy et al., 2017] provides urban and rural driving. Among the buffers that the simulator exports, we use semantic segmentation, which paints every class in one flat colour and thus specifies the class layout of the scene without its appearance.

  • •

    Engine recordings consist of frames together with depth, object masks, camera poses, and skeletons on shared timestamps. We render the depth as grey shading, with distant regions and the sky set to black, so that it conveys the shape of the scene near the camera.

  • •

    Blender renders of animated scenes are paired with the white-box of their scene, which describes the scene layout and the motion of the main character.

  • •

    UnrealZoo[Zhong et al., 2025] provides Unreal Engine 5 environments in first- and third-person views. Its condition combines object masks and skeletons, with one colour per object and the skeleton of each character drawn on top.

  • •

    YouTube videos [Ju et al., 2024] provide clips for body-motion conditioning. We keep videos with a clear protagonist, fit the SMPL body [Loper et al., 2015] of the protagonist with GVHMR [Shen et al., 2024] using camera and depth from VGGT [Wang et al., 2025a] and Depth Anything 3 [Lin et al., 2026b], and render it from the target camera as a grey body on a white background. This SMPL body video gives the position, pose, and motion of the protagonist, while the environment and clothing come from the first frame and text.

  • •

    WildWorld[Li et al., 2026c], a public dataset of Monster Hunter Wilds gameplay, and OmniWorld[Zhou et al., 2026], which collects footage of AAA games such as Cyberpunk 2077, contribute rich game appearance. Their structural annotations follow the frames less closely, so we use them as appearance data and supply only a first frame.

item.title: Budgeted-GS：整座城市的 3DGS 塞不进显存？先算「场景到底需要多少高斯」 ｜ Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD
item.description:
一句话：把训练好的 3DGS 变成多分辨率分解树，一个质量参数按显存选 LOD。

要点：

  • 后处理式方案：一次几秒钟的构建把任意已训练 3DGS 转成 factor 树，即矩匹配聚合的多分辨率层级，运行时单个质量参数按目标设备显存选每视角的 LOD。
  • 理论依据是可测量的容量下界与「预算—误差」规律，由相空间最优传输推出；选择规则用近期覆盖定理证明哪些基元可安全丢弃。
  • 同一理论也用于训练：预算中心训练先测场景需要多少基元再按该规模训练，避免先练满再压缩的浪费；在 13 个公开场景上按预注册协议验证了下界。

为什么值得看：城市级 3DGS 落地的门槛就是显存与 LOD，这里给的是「先算容量再训练/选 LOD」的定量方法，比经验性抽稀更适合工程化。

中文摘要：3DGS 画质与实时性都很好，但整城规模下单模型就有数百万基元、数 GB 显存，消费级 GPU 无法高质量实时渲染。Budgeted-GS 是一种后处理方法：用几秒钟的构建把任意已训练模型转成 factor 树——矩匹配聚合构成的多分辨率层级，之后一个质量参数就能按目标设备显存为每个视角选合适 LOD，同城级模型可服务显存差异很大的 GPU。理论基于相空间最优传输推出的「预算—误差」规律与可测量容量下界，并用覆盖定理证明哪些基元冗余；同一理论也支撑预算中心训练，在 13 个公开场景上完成验证。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-02

本期推送：2026-10-23

Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting achieves excellent visual quality with real-time rendering, but at the scale of entire cities it does not fit: a trained model carries millions of primitives and gigabytes of memory, and real-time rendering at high quality on a consumer GPU remains out of reach. We introduce Budgeted-GS, a post-hoc method that turns any trained 3DGS model into a factoring tree, a multi-resolution hierarchy of moment-matched aggregates. After a construction pass of a few seconds, a single quality parameter then selects, for each view, the level of detail that fits the memory of the target device, so the same city-scale model serves GPUs with widely different memory capacities. When a new scene is to be trained, the same theory applies: instead of growing a full-sized model and compressing it afterwards, budget-centered training first measures how many primitives the scene needs and then trains the model directly at that size, avoiding the wasted effort of optimizing primitives that are later discarded. Both methods are grounded in a measurable capacity floor, a budget–error law derived from optimal transport in phase space; selection rules certified by recent covering theorems decide which primitives are redundant. The floor answers how many primitives a scene actually needs and how many can safely be given up. We validate the floor on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol, and exercise both methods from object scenes to an official city capture, rendering it at native 1920×1080, full SH, in real time on one consumer GPU.

1 Introduction

Real-time radiance-field rendering of captured scenes is now routine at object and room scale. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [14] represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussians rendered by projective splatting with depth-sorted α-compositing. At city scale it does not fit: a trained model carries millions of primitives and gigabytes of memory, and real-time rendering at high quality on a consumer GPU remains out of reach. The obstacles are structural. At training time the standard recipe is to densify a large model and then compress it; the primitives are optimized for a different capacity, and the time spent on the removed half is wasted. At deploy time the only degradation mode offered by streaming renderers such as Gaussian Point Splatting (GPS [29]) is random subsampling. And beneath both sits an unanswered question: nobody can say what the right budget is. The question “how many primitives do I need here?” is answered by habit, because no principled budget–error floor has been available either at training or deployment time.

This paper answers it with a rate–distortion theory of rendering primitives: a trained model is a point on a rate–distortion curve; its primitive count is its budget, its error a function of that budget. The theory has two mathematical halves. The capacity floor, derived from optimal transport in phase space (position × direction, where rendering primitives and renderers are both natural objects), says that if the scene’s phase-space measure has dₚₛ-dimensional support, the minimal achievable error with N primitives falls as N^-2/dₚₛ (Zador’s law). The collapse license comes from the 2025 resolution of the three-dimensional Kakeya set conjecture [36]: the Wang–Zahl union-volume estimate, in weighted (continuous-opacity) form, certifies that wherever Gaussians locally over-cover space, they merge into few representatives with bounded volumetric loss. The floor tells a budget what it can achieve; the license tells it where redundancy lives and what may be merged or dropped.

The floor and the license are operationalized as two methods. On the deployment side, the floor’s allocation law (Nⱼ^*∝Kⱼsⱼ/dⱼ per tile) is realized as a factoring tree (Factoring LOD, Section 5), an octree of scale bands with moment-matched equivalent planks, driven by a one-parameter pixel-footprint scheduler. A single trained model sweeps a continuous memory–quality curve instead of a single fixed operating point. On the training side, Budget-Centered Training (BCT, Section 5.1) trains the densifier directly at the floor’s knee, so the model is born at the right size instead of growing huge and being pruned afterwards. Beyond rendering, the floor answers how many primitives a scene needs, how much of it is redundancy, and how a fixed budget should split across a city. Measuring it on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol shows published compressors lying on an essentially flat frontier. Their reported gains come from redundancy, not from proximity to capacity (Section 6.1). At city scale the same discipline turns real-time. A retrain of the official city model serves the official test trajectory at native 1920×1080, full SH, on one consumer GPU—to our knowledge the first post-hoc, full-SH result on a consumer GPU in this regime (Section 6.6).

Contributions.

  • •

    We introduce Factoring LOD, a post-hoc layer that converts one trained model into a factoring tree with a one-parameter scheduler; it renders a city-scale scene at high quality in real time within whatever memory the consumer GPU has.

  • •

    We propose Budget-Centered Training, which trains the densifier directly at the floor-located budget; the model is born at the right size instead of growing huge and being pruned afterwards; it leads the train-then-prune route at every matched budget, in a single training run.

  • •

    We establish the theory beneath the problem: a measurable capacity floor that answers, for any city-scale 3DGS scene, how many primitives it actually needs, and therefore how many can safely be given up.

    • 2 Related Work

    Rendering large-scale scenes. Every classic representation solved scale with its own multiresolution answer. Points: surfel splatting [27], QSplat’s sphere hierarchy [30], and Potree’s out-of-core octree generation [31] stream large point clouds at interactive rates. Meshes: progressive meshes [10] introduced view-dependent refinement, and Nanite [13] virtualizes micropolygon geometry in production engines. Voxels: sparse voxel octrees [19] ray-march gigavoxel volumes. What these systems share, a coarse-to-fine hierarchy carrying a per-frame budget, is exactly what a raw 3DGS model [14] lacks: it is a flat set of primitives with no hierarchy at all.

    Data structures for large-scale 3DGS scenes. Inside the 3DGS world, the standard answer is a spatial structure coupled to training. Octree-GS builds an octree of level-of-detail clusters [28]; Scaffold-GS anchors Gaussians on a sparse grid [23]; multiresolution hash grids organize NeRF-side training [25]; CityGaussian partitions the scene into blocks with distance-based LOD [21], following the block decomposition of Block-NeRF [33]; hierarchical 3DGS trains a chunk pyramid [15]; concurrent efforts pursue out-of-core streaming hierarchies [38] and LOD-aware training [18]; GPS streams an octree with distance shells [29] (our cross-renderer comparisons use it, Section 5). These structures carry the indexing, but the budget lives in the training pipeline: levels and blocks are fixed when training ends. Our factoring tree is built post-hoc from any model, selects per (leaf, scale-band) instead of per block or level, and grounds the selection in measurable redundancy and pixel-footprint criteria (Section 5); Section 6.4 compares directly against Octree-GS and CityGaussianV2’s runtime LOD [22].

    Quality and memory control for large-scale 3DGS scenes. Once a model exists, a large family controls its size: MCMC-based densification [16] and regularization-based pruning [24] budget during training; LightGaussian [4], Compact3DGS [20], RDO-Gaussian [35], EAGLES [6], RadSplat [26], PUP 3D-GS [9], and RAP [39] prune, quantize, distill, or reselect primitives after training; 2DGS changes the primitive itself to a surfel for surface quality [11]. All of these act once, at training or export time, and expose no runtime memory–quality trade-off or error bound. Our budget parameter acts on any trained model continuously and renderer-agnostically; LightGaussian’s own score, applied post-hoc through our export path, yields a Vanilla-flat budget axis to 25% of the primitives on city-scale scenes (Section 6.6); and rasterizer accelerators [8, 3] are composable with it: they render the selected set faster, while the parameter decides what is selected.

    3 Overview

    Budgeted-GS applies one budget discipline at every stage of a scene’s life cycle (Fig. 1). The capacity floor (Section 4) gives, for any scene, the minimal achievable rendering error at a primitive count N; it is stated as theorems and measured per scene with a preregistered protocol (Section 6.1). Two methods spend the budget where the floor says. Budget-Centered Training (Section 5.1) reads the floor’s knee N^* off the measured curve and trains the densifier directly at that budget. Factoring LOD (Section 5) converts any trained model into a factoring tree whose one-parameter pixel-footprint scheduler selects, per view, exactly the working set that fits the memory at hand. Section 6 reports the experiments. The supplementary material carries the proofs.

    4 An optimal-transport theory for 3D Gaussian primitives

    Why should the budget be a design variable, and how should it be spent? On real data, reconstruction error falls steeply as the budget grows, then flattens into a shallow floor. This section develops a theory that predicts where that floor lies: from primitives and rendering at the bottom, through construction and capacity, up to the selection rules on top. Concretely, for a quality target Q, the theory yields (i) the minimal primitive count a scene requires, (ii) the redundant subset of its primitives, and (iii) the allocation of a fixed budget across a city.

    4.1 Rendering as optimal transport in phase space

    Prior work has employed optimal transport in 3DGS only in narrow, task-specific roles, including Wasserstein losses between Gaussian mixtures [32], radial-optimal-transport fitting of structured Gaussians [41], and capacity control in multi-view stylization [37]. To our knowledge, we are the first to formulate rendering as optimal transport in phase space.

    Definition 1(Phase space and primitives).

    ℙ:=X×Ω, the product of scene space X⊂ℝ³ (the unit ball) and the direction sphere Ω=S², is phase space; a cell Q=V×C (spatial plank × directional cone) obeys Δx·Δξ≥c (the uncertainty bound). A rendering primitive is a triple (Q,w,ρ): cell, opacity weight w, value model ρ. Three families exist. Point primitives take the limit Δx→0. Wave primitives are Gaussian wave packets with ΔxΔξ\asympc, the family of 3DGS surfels and 2DGS plates. Field primitives are continuous densities, such as NeRF/SDF. A representation is a parameterized measure family {μ_θ}_θ∈Θ on ℙ.

    Definition 2(Rendering coupling and marginalization).

    For view v and parameters θ, the renderer defines a joint measure π_v,θ on ℙ×Pixelᵥ, the pixel grid of view v, with source marginal μ_θ and pixel marginal ν_v,θ (pixel masses S(p):=ν_v,θ({p})); the pixel colour is the conditional expectation

    I_v,θ(p)=∫_ℙρ(x) dπ_v,θ(x|p).

    		(1)

    4.2 An optimal-transport view of 3DGS

    The framework rests on four axioms: every representation induces a phase-space distribution μ_θ; the renderer is a legal transport and the image is its coupling marginal; every construction algorithm’s objective is expressible as one transport cost; a single source is transported to all view targets. For 3DGS-style compositing, this coupling is the familiar compositing rule: π_v,θ(p,{i})∝wᵢ(p)=αᵢ(p)Tᵢ(p) with Tᵢ=∏_jrendering transport: the renderer transports μ_θ to per-view pixel marginals; the second is representation formation: given complexity comp_F(θ)≤N, minimize the transport cost

    ℝᵣₑₛ(N)=\min_θ∑ᵥ∫_ℙ×Pixelᵥc dπ_v,θ, c(x,p):=\lVertρ(x)-cᵍᵗᵥ(p)\rVert².

    		(2)

    Gradient training, sampling, meshing, and voxelization are solvers of the second problem; their outputs are measured by the transport residual (their convergence is proved or cited to classical sources in the supplementary material). The bottom layer is one theorem: the renderer really is a legal transport, rendering is conditional expectation, and the error splits into a tight three-term chain.

    Theorem 3(The renderer, the rendering map, and the error chain).

    Under measurable ray–pixel assignment, bounded transmittance-weighted mass, and Lipschitz regularity, every (v,θ) admits a canonical coupling π_v,θ with marginals (μ_θ,ν_v,θ), determined by the rendering rule and weakly continuous in θ. With projection Jacobian J_Π and footprint kernel G, the pixel probability kernel is κᵥ(p, dx)∝w(x)G(p-Π(x))\lvert\detJ_Π(x)\rvert1_V(x), In the audited low-opacity domain, the pieces combine into a tight three-term chain: the operator norm is sharp (\lVertPᵥf\rVert_L²(Pixelᵥ)≤√μᵥ\lVertf\rVert_L²(ℙ)), the blending gap is second-order in the max opacity ε (with multiplicity M(x): \lvertC(x)-L(x)\rvert≤(K^′)/(2)M(x)²ε²+O(K^′M(x)ε³)), and

    \lVertν_v,θ-νᵍᵗᵥ\rVert_L²≤√ℓᵥ \lVertμ_θ-μ_S\rVert_L²+(K^′)/(2)ε²\lVertM²\rVert_L²+ε_target(v),

    		(3)

    a tight three-term chain: source gap, blending gap, target map; here μᵥ=∑ₚS(p) is the transported mass of view v, ℓᵥ the Lipschitz constant of the target map, K^′ the compositing Lipschitz constant, and measure norms are taken over densities with respect to the phase-space reference measure, the source one over the normalized source marginal of the coupling.

    Forming a representation under a budget is itself an optimal-transport problem [12, 34], and its duality is what makes the floor certifiable.

    Theorem 4(Representation formation as restricted optimal transport).

    For compositing with normalized coupling π̃ₚ, the loss decomposes as L(θ)=ℂ(θ)-V(θ): the transport cost ℂ minus the conditional variance V. For atomic families with quadratic cost, \inf_\lvertsuppμ_θ\rvert≤N∫\minᵢ\lVertx-yᵢ\rVert² dμ_S=W₂²-optimal quantization, and Lloyd’s algorithm is monotone. The certificate follows: the residual satisfies ℝ_free(N)≤ℝᵣₑₛ(N) with gap decomposition Δ(θ)=Δ_coupl(θ)+Δ_src(θ)≥0; for every dual-feasible (φ,ψ) the certificate

    L(θ)≥∫_ℙφ dμ_θ+∑ₚS(p)ψ(p)-V(θ)

    		(4)

    lower-bounds achieved error; and with target colour measure ν_c of intrinsic dimension d_c≤3, ℝ_free(N)\asympC_d_c\lVertν_c\rVert_d_c/(d_c+2)N^-2/d_c.

    4.3 The capacity floor

    How fast must this residual fall as the budget N grows? Classical high-resolution quantization theory [40, 7] answers exactly this, and the rendering instance, whose source is the phase-space measure of Definition 1, obeys the same law:

    Theorem 5(The capacity floor of the rendering instance).

    Imported from classical high-resolution quantization [40, 7] through the transport formulation above, with the lower bound additionally assuming view completeness (the view set separates the source): if the phase-space measure μ_S has dₚₛ-dimensional support with density λ, the minimal achievable rendering error with N primitives obeys

    ℝ(N) \asymp C_dₚₛ \lVertλ\rVert_dₚₛ/dₚₛ+2 N^-2/dₚₛ.

    		(5)

    On surface scenes the phase-space support is four-dimensional (surface position × incident-direction hemisphere), so ℝ(N)∝N^-1/2. For the cartoon class with appearance smoothness p and resolution L, ℝ_F(N,L)^1/2\asympC₁KN^-1/2(\logN)ᶜ+C₂K^′L⁻ᵖ with optimal allocation N^*\asympM^p/(p+1), L^*\asympM^1/(2(p+1)); width brackets sandwich ℝ_F^free≤ℝ_F≤C width.

    The free relaxation of Theorem 4 is target-limited (rate N^-2/d_c), while this rendering instance is source-limited at N^-2/dₚₛ with dₚₛ≥d_c: the requirement that primitives must render, not merely match colours, is what slows the rate. The floor is certifiable rather than assumed: the duality chain L+V=ℂ≥ℂ_free≥D evaluates, per budget and per test view, a lower bound on the achievable error (Eq. (4)). It is also measurable, and Section 6.1 reports the curve for 13 public scenes.

    Three supporting results, proved, cited, or labelled as sketches in the supplementary material, round out the framework: gradient training is a legitimate solver of the restricted-transport problem and attains the classical rates of sampling, Lloyd, and meshing; cross-view colour agreement is structural, and the new-view error is bounded by the training error plus an angular-regularity term; and across primitive families on surfaces, triangles achieve N⁻¹, point-like primitives N^-1/2, and isotropic voxels N^-1/4. One part reads as a prediction: the optimal cell is an anisotropic, covariance-ellipsoidal atom, exactly what 3DGS fits, and exactly what the moment-matched aggregates of the factoring tree (Section 5.2) construct.

    4.4 The selection rules

    The floor is one half of the mathematics; the other half is a set of selection rules, theorems that decide which primitives may be merged or dropped at a given budget. Here a rendering primitive is viewed geometrically, as a plank(μ,R,h,α): an oriented box centered at μ, rotated by R, of half-extents h=3σ, carrying the opacity α as its weight. We state the rules here; the proofs are in the supplementary material.

    Definition 6(Essentially distinct tubes and the convex Wolff axioms).

    Sets U,V⊂ℝ³ are essentially distinct if \lvertU∩V\rvert≤\tfrac12\max(\lvertU\rvert,\lvertV\rvert); throughout, T is a set of essentially distinct δ×δ×1 tubes in the unit ball, so \lvertT\rvert\asympδ². Following [36] (Def. 1.3), Tobeys the Katz–Tao convex Wolff axioms with error C if

    #{T∈T: T⊂W} ≤ C \lvertW\rvert \lvertT\rvert⁻¹ for every convexW⊂ℝ³,

    		(6)

    i.e. no convex set concentrates more tubes than its volume admits; a Kakeya-type arrangement (one tube per δ-separated direction) satisfies (6) with C\lesssim1.

    Theorem 7(Weighted covering—the collapse license).

    (i) (Unweighted; [36], Thm. 1.2.) For every ε>0 there is K>1 such that, for all δ>0 small: if T satisfies (6) with C\lesssim1 and every a×b×2 prism contains at most 100abδ⁻² tubes of T, and Y(T)⊂T has \lvertY(T)\rvert≥λ₀\lvertT\rvert, then

    \lvert\bigcup_T∈TY(T)\rvert ≥ δ^ελ₀^K∑_T∈T\lvertT\rvert.

    (ii) (Weighted, rendering form.) If each tube carries a weight function w_T\colonT→[0,1] of per-tube mass \lvertT\rvert⁻¹ ∫_Tw_T≥λ(w)\gtrsim1, then the saturated weighted union volume |U|_w:=∫\min(1,∑_Tw_T(x)) dx obeys |U|_w \gtrsim λ(w)^K+1δ^ε∑_T∫_Tw_T: thresholding costs only constants depending on ε, so the weighted form loses nothing beyond the ε-loss of (i).

    Lemma 8(Scale truncation).

    For cartoon-class fields, atoms whose projected footprint is below the pixel scale can be dropped or collapsed with bounded loss.

    Theorem 9(Adaptive covering rate).

    For f∈ℂ_K (piecewise C²/H² cartoon fields) there is an N-atom combination of plates and tubes with \lVertf-f_N\rVert_L²≤CK N^-1/2(\logN)ᶜ; conversely, some f^*∈ℂ_K forces every N-atom combination to obey \lVertf^*-f_N\rVert_L²≥c₀K(N\log₂N)^-1/2.

    Corollary 10(Budget allocation).

    Minimizing the geometric + appearance error C₁KN^-1/2+C₂K^′L⁻ᵖ under the parameter budget M\asympN(L+1)² yields N^*\asympM^p/(p+1) and L^*\asympM^1/(2(p+1)); across scale bands sⱼ=2ʲs₀ the band budgets decay exponentially, mⱼ∝2^-jγ.

    Theorem 7 is the union-volume estimate of Wang–Zahl [36], the theorem behind the 2025 resolution of the three-dimensional Kakeya set conjecture, reinterpreted with continuous opacity weights—to our knowledge the first rendering use of this theory. It certifies when a family of rendering primitives can be collapsed into fewer representatives without forfeiting more than an ε-fraction of volumetric mass, and its one-line corollary caps the packing density of any convex region at CΔ_\max(T) (the Katz–Tao constant of Definition 6), which is what keeps the scale-band decomposition of Section 5 bounded. Together with Zador’s law (5), the four statements answer, in order: how much error is unavoidable (the floor), which groups are redundant (collapse), what may be dropped outright (truncation), and how a fixed budget should be split (allocation). Stated as questions (how many primitives does this scene need, how much of it is redundancy, how should a fixed budget be split across a city), the theory answers all three; the rest of the paper measures the answers and builds methods on them.

    5 Budgeted-GS: training and deployment

    The floor and the selection rules are operationalized two ways: at training time, budget-centered training grows the model the floor prescribes (Section 5.1); at deployment time, the factoring tree and its pixel-footprint scheduler serve, per view, exactly the working set that fits the memory at hand (Sections 5.2 and 5.3).

    Both halves of our system follow from one observation: a trained model is a redundant, multi-scale arrangement of oriented boxes (each primitive occupies a box of half-extents h=3σ weighted by its opacity), and budget control means removing that redundancy without visible loss. Three principles govern every selection rule in this paper; they are the operational form of the theorems stated in Section 4.

    The first principle is the collapse license: a group of primitives that locally over-covers space, many overlapping boxes of comparable scale in one region, can be merged into a few representatives with bounded volumetric loss (Theorem 7; the moment-matching counterpart of the optimal-atom prediction, Section 4). This licenses the moment-matched aggregates of the factoring tree and opacity-ranked pruning inside redundancy-flagged regions.

    The second is scale truncation: a primitive whose projected footprint is below the pixel scale can be dropped or collapsed with bounded image error (Lemma 8; the U2 projection-error regime). This licenses the pixel-footprint threshold t=c·d/f of the scheduler and the stopping rule that freezes density control once pruning stops paying for itself.

    The third is budget allocation: under a fixed primitive budget, coarser scale bands deserve exponentially more budget than finer ones (Corollary 10; the Kⱼsⱼ/dⱼ law); the same footprint rule instantiates this allocation per view. The three principles are grounded in recent union-volume estimates for unions of convex sets [36] and classical adaptive-approximation rates [2]; measured error rates on synthetic scenes match the prediction within measurement noise.

    5.1 Budget-centered training

    The floor answers “how many primitives do I need at quality Q?”, and the answer is also a training prescription. Traditional pipelines train a large model and compress it: the primitives are optimized for a different capacity, and the training time spent on the removed half is wasted. BCT instead locates the knee N^* from the measured curve (Fig. 2; the budget with the largest steepest-window slope, Section 6.1), then trains the MCMC densifier directly at cap=N^*: the initial primitive count is set to a fixed initial fraction of N^* and the refine-stop fraction to a second, both scaled by the measured redundancy θ_waste=Nₒₚₜ/N_full.

    Standard 3DGS densification/pruning is driven by positional gradients and opacity. We keep densification but replace the pruning signal by the θ redundancy map (the collapse license; supplementary material): θ is computed per region from the local factoring of the model: regions with high local multiplicity (low θ) are over-covered and are exactly where primitives can be removed with the smallest approximation loss; pruning inside θ-flagged regions removes primitives by opacity. A rate-based stopping criterion freezes density control once validation improvement falls below ε=0.5 dB.

    5.2 The factoring tree

    A trained model is frozen, but the hardware it must run on is not: the same city has to serve a render farm, a desktop, a laptop, and a VR headset, and at the far end it has to render in real time on a consumer GPU. The floor’s allocation law (budget should follow Kⱼsⱼ/dⱼ per tile and per view) turns this into a selection problem. Concretely, applied per tile j (regularity Kⱼ, extent sⱼ, distance dⱼ), Corollary 10 yields the level-selection law

    Nⱼ^*(v)∝Kⱼ√Aⱼ(v)\asymp(Kⱼ sⱼ)/(dⱼ),\hskip18.49988pteⱼ²\asymp(c² Kⱼsⱼ)/(dⱼ)·(∑ₖKₖsₖ/dₖ)/(N)·occⱼ.\normalsize

    		(7)

    with Aⱼ(v) the projected screen area of tile j in view v. For uniform regularity it reduces to the classical screen-space-error heuristic and adds what it lacks: rougher tiles draw more budget, occluded tiles pay the visibility factor, and the per-tile error is certificate-verifiable.

    Given a trained model with N primitives (means μᵢ, rotations Rᵢ, scales σᵢ, opacities αᵢ, SH colors), we first convert each primitive to a plank(μ,R,h=3σ,α). The scene bounding box is partitioned by a GPU octree (leaf capacity 4096); the structure lives in what its nodes store (below), and within each leaf the planks are split into scale bandsℓ=⌊\log₂(s/s_base)⌋ where s=\maxh and s_base is the 5% quantile of s. Each (leaf, band) group is then factored into at most 256 equivalent planks by batch moment matching: within a group, planks are ordered by Morton code (spatial locality), split into consecutive buckets, and each bucket is replaced by a single plank conserving

    W=∑ᵢαᵢ|Vᵢ|, c^*=(∑ᵢαᵢ|Vᵢ|μᵢ)/(W),(8)
    T^*=∑ᵢαᵢ|Vᵢ|((μᵢ-c^*)(μᵢ-c^*)^⊤+\tfrac13Rᵢ diag(hᵢ)² Rᵢ^⊤),

    i.e. weighted volume, centroid, and inertia tensor; the equivalent plank is (c^*,R^*,h^*,w^*) from the eigendecomposition of T^* with w^*=W/|V^*|∈[0,1] (Fig. 3c). Colors enter as opacity-weighted first moments of the SH coefficients (DC and higher bands separately).

    The internal nodes of the octree receive the same treatment bottom-up, so every (node, band) has one aggregate plank. The raw primitives are retained in Morton order for the finest tier. Construction on multi-million-primitive scenes takes seconds on one GPU, and the aggregate representation is 119× smaller than the input (supplementary material).

    5.3 The pixel-footprint scheduler

    At render time, for camera position p and focal length f (pixels), each (leaf, band) with mean scale s̄ and centroid distance d is assigned to one of three tiers by the threshold t=c·d/f:

  • •

    raw: members individually resolvable (s̄≥t) ⇒ render the original Gaussians;

  • •

    fine: the cluster resolvable but members not (s̄

  • •

    coarse: sub-pixel (h̄

    • c is a single scalar budget parameter: c=1 means exactly resolvable (the reference tier), larger c progressively collapses sub-c-pixel content (scale truncation; supplementary material), and c<1 keeps members below the pixel scale (super-resolving regime); on distant aerial cameras most bands are already sub-pixel at c=1, and our real-time renderer operates at c≈0.3 there (Section 6.6).

    6 Experiments

    We validate the theory and both methods end to end: the floor itself across 13 public scenes, then Budget-Centered Training, then Factoring LOD from object scenes to city scale, closing with ablations and efficiency.

    6.1 The floor, measured across 13 scenes

    The floor is measured with a preregistered protocol (criteria frozen before data collection; all verdicts frozen before reading results; 3 fixed seeds; JSON certificates at every stage, supplementary material): on each scene, MCMC training at cap 2×10⁶ followed by opacity-prune to N and fine-tune yields the empirical floor curve R(N) at 9 budgets; the preregistered floor-intactness test asks that no scan point crosses the fitted floor by more than \log₁₀(0.8); published operating points are re-anchored to their own baseline at matched capacity ratio with a 5% (0.22 dB) tolerance; and a duality certificate lower-bounds the achieved error at every (budget, view).

    On a synthetic cartoon control with the same protocol, the chord lands directly on Zador’s law (-0.549/-0.548/-0.551, R²=0.997). On the 13 public scenes (seed 0; 3 seeds on garden/room/bonsai) chord slopes are seed-stable (±0.004–0.011) but all fall outside the preregistered band [-0.55,-0.45], a registered negative. The reading-window audit explains it: the SfM point clouds have TWO-NN intrinsic dimension 1.9–2.05, and the steepest three-band windows reach -0.41 to -0.53 across scenes and seeds (bonsai -0.46/-0.49/-0.53; room -0.469→-0.496 when the fine-tune budget is quadrupled), straddling the predicted -1/2. Floor intactness holds 13/13; the duality certificate holds at every (band, view) on room with tightness 0.28→0.03 (Table S10, full data in supplementary material).

    The published frontier is flat: every compression method with a same-paper (N,PSNR) pair defines a resolution-invariant two-point trajectory (Fig. S3). Across Compact3DGS and EAGLES on all 13 scenes plus Mini-Splatting [5] and RadSplat [26] at dataset level, these slopes occupy [-0.28,+0.09] with mean -0.04: removing 60–70% of a converged model’s primitives costs under 1 dB across the surveyed compressors, while the floor law (asymptote -1/2, reached end-to-end on the synthetic control and bracketed by our steepest windows) is an order of magnitude steeper. Published compression operates deep in the over-budgeted regime: its reported gains ride the redundancy θ_waste=Nₒₚₜ/N_full that the floor makes measurable, not proximity to capacity. The universal (model-free) colour-quantization floor, a lower bound on every representation at budget N computed from test images alone, confirms it: all 26 published operating points lie above the band (Fig. S4).

    Three questions therefore have checkable answers: certified compression headroom (measure the floor once, place any candidate point on it; with our measured estimator looseness folded in, headroom is certified on eight published points, up to +1.9 dB); when lossless is impossible (the gap decomposition separates structural coupling loss from source capacity); and the right budget: the floor knee N^* is the budget where the steepest-window slope is largest, which is exactly where BCT trains (Section 5.1).

    6.2 Training-side results

    The redundancy signal and the stopping rule behave as the floor predicts across the synthetic and Mip-NeRF 360 scenes, under the same preregistered discipline as the floor study (3 fixed seeds on garden/room/bonsai, seed 0 elsewhere; matched near-N runs).

    On the 13-scene study, BCT is faster and better in the same-ruler sense at the budgets where it is asked to exceed a train-then-prune point: at the matched compact3DGS room budget, 529k, BCT reaches 31.94±0.04 dB (three seeds, re-measured protocol) against the published Compact3DGS (30.23 dB; the original high draw was 31.20). An earlier protocol generation of the same comparison makes the capacity point directly: two audit runs agree on 31.21 dB at cap 670k, where that generation’s prune pipeline needs 1M primitives for the same 31.21 dB—BCT spends 33% fewer primitives for the same rendering quality. (All Table 1 room rows are re-measured under the current protocol; the audit generation is kept protocol-separated.) The same-ruler comparison over six scenes (Table 1) is the honest version of this claim: at counter BCT beats both published points (+0.24/+0.58 dB) and our prune scan (+1.90 dB vs. the 500k scan point), at bonsai 640k it beats EAGLES (+0.86), and at kitchen 1131k it beats Compact3DGS by +1.70 dB; only at flowers does it stay below the published compressors (-0.29/-0.71 dB), while still leading our own prune pipeline there (+0.44/+0.65 dB); and at garden both budgets beat the published points (+0.24/+0.44 dB). The honest summary: BCT leads our train-then-prune pipeline at every matched budget, and it now beats the published compressor points on five of six scenes (all but flowers). The single loss is diagnostic rather than accidental: flowers is the only scene whose measured knee sits at the full scanned budget (θ_waste=1.0, Section 6.1)—source-limited, not redundancy-limited—so there is nothing for budget selection to spend there. Its decisive advantage is budget selection at the floor knee (33% fewer primitives at matched quality) plus a single 78-minute run instead of the 175-minute train–prune–fine-tune route (measured on room: 125 min training at 1M + 50 min prune+fine-tune). An extension to the outdoor scenes of the study (bicycle, stump, treehill), where the published points sit highest above the floor, appears in Table S4.

    Table 1 records the tuned variants: in all 7 runs (across three scenes and two budgets each, the initial-fraction/stop schedule variants) the original recipe (SfM init of 100k primitives, refine to convergence) is best or tied, a negative ablation confirming that BCT needs no hyper-parameter search, and that the gains above are not tuning artifacts. Timing (measured on room, shared A100 under neighbor load; ratios are same-card): BCT 78±7 min over three seeds; the traditional route for the same budget (train at 1M, prune, fine-tune) ≈175 min, 2.2× slower for lower quality (Table 1).

    6.2.1 Outdoor extension

    The same-ruler BCT comparison extended to the three outdoor scenes of the study (bicycle, stump, treehill) at the published compressor budgets, plus the frontier reading of the outcome. Protocol identical to Table 1 (seed 0, same eval, original recipe: SfM init 100k primitives, refine to convergence). “ours-prune” = the matched-budget point of the same-ruler train-then-prune scan of Section 6.1 (nearest scan band; interpolated in \logN to the tabular budget).

    The outdoor extension (Table S4) makes the floor’s practical value testable in both directions. BCT, which spends the floor’s answer directly at a budget, lands on the same curve as our train→prune →fine-tune scan (differences ≤0.15 dB); the two procedures agree because both consume the budget the floor says the scene can carry. The published compressor points at the same budgets are 0.8–2.9 dB above that curve. Their gains therefore do not come from capacity: on stump, where the published points are 2.7–2.9 dB above our measured floor at matched budgets, the measured training-time redundancy θ_waste fully accounts for the reported gap (frontier analysis, Section 6.1).

    6.2.2 Budget-aware density control at the ceiling

    Table S5, Fig. S2, and Fig. S14a: on lego our budget-aware training with the BCT stop rule (Section 5.1) reaches 36.85 dB with 151k primitives: the same quality as Vanilla with 339k (44% of the budget, -0.34 dB), and +0.23 dB over MCMC at a 12% smaller budget. The full Pareto curve (Fig. S2) dominates MCMC at every tested budget. Perceived, not just measured: Fig. S5 shows the two models side by side on a held-out view with the residual amplified 10×; on this view the 151k model is better than Vanilla (24.88 vs. 21.46 dB; the aggregate mean is -0.34 dB over the full test set), and the largest residuals are structural edges rather than texture (mean |Δ|=0.013).

    6.2.3 Generalization

    Table S6 generalizes the stop rule to four further scenes (chair, ship, bonsai, room).

    Post-hoc, the redundancy signal keeps its value on the indoor scenes (seed-0 runs): pruning the trained model by the BCT stop rule dominates random pruning at every matched budget on bonsai and room; e.g. at 70% kept, a 32-view 3DGS re-render of the same checkpoints measures 31.10/35.64 dB for θ-pruning vs. 28.10/29.56 dB random (+3.0/+6.1 dB). Fig. S6 shows the corresponding renders: at matched 70% budget the θ-guided models stay close to their full renders, while random pruning visibly degrades foliage and edges.

    The contribution-scored export of the score export of Section 5 is a pure ranking of an already-trained model, so it applies to any primitive set. Table S7 applies it to the trained lego/bonsai/room models and the two Mip-NeRF 360 indoor scenes, evaluated by the same CityGaussian test protocol that produced the training-side numbers. On every scene and every budget, the score ranking beats opacity-ordered pruning, the baseline the same protocol ships, by +2.7 to +7.9 dB (PSNR), with large margins also in SSIM and LPIPS. At 50% the margin costs almost nothing: -0.13 and -0.54 dB on room and bonsai versus the full model. At 25% the loss is substantial (3.1–13.9 dB), which is the expected behavior on already-compressed models: these trained models are down to 36–66% of Vanilla, so they carry less removable redundancy than Block_A (where 24% of primitives are invisible from every training view and the curve is flat to 25%). The clean division of labor: the score export recovers what a post-hoc pass can, and the training-side BCT is the tool where a fixed quality target must be met.

    The two stages also compose. On room, we build factoring trees over two roots, the full model (1.66M primitives) and the budget-centered model trained at the floor’s knee (529k), and deploy both through the same scheduler at a matched budget of ≈520k rendered primitives (34 held-out views, LOD render protocol). The BCT-born tree renders 34.19 dB, within 0.16 dB of its own root; the full-born tree, collapsed to the same budget, renders 22.83 dB. Budget-centered training is thus the correct front end for factoring-tree deployment: a model born at the floor’s budget passes through the tree essentially unchanged, because it contains almost no redundancy for the tree to lose (per-tier data in the supplementary material).

    6.3 The LOD quality window

    On garden (Table 2), the residual-proxy adaptive selector recovers 0.49 dB over the fixed threshold at a comparable primitive count (1.05×).

    On the city-scale model the near-lossless window is even wider (Table 3): c=4 renders 68% of the primitives at -0.05 dB (visual comparisons: Fig. S12 for the garden tiers, Fig. S10 for the same ladder on room). This asymmetry (garden vs. city aerial), quantified by the orbit sweep of Fig. S7, matches the theory: the aerial model is already tessellated at its training viewing distance, so sub-pixel redundancy is exhausted at small c; the surplus is in super-pixel collapse. Across the full ladder the single model sweeps a continuous memory–quality curve (Fig. S15); re-rendering the same tiers through the GPS renderer reproduces it within 0.5 dB (c=4 is lossless under both renderers), and the ∼20.8 dB operating point costs 110.6 MB against GPS’s full 1926 MB (17×; same-budget numbers and byte-level accounting in the supplementary material).

    6.4 Comparison with training-coupled LOD

    The most closely related systems are LOD hierarchies coupled to training: Octree-GS [28] trains a multi-level anchor structure and selects levels per view; CityGaussian [21] and its V2 [22] partition large scenes and load blocks by level at runtime. Our layer is complementary by construction: it is built post-hoc from any trained model, exposes a continuous budget parameter, and is renderer-agnostic. Recent concurrent work reaches consumer-GPU city scale by training the LOD itself, out-of-core streaming hierarchies [38] and LoD-aware training [18], so the axes are complementary rather than competing: their budgets are fixed at training time, ours are chosen per deployment on the same trained model. Table S8 frames the head-to-head on MatrixCity and makes the structural difference concrete. Re-rendering the official Octree-GS Block_all checkpoint (8.01M stored anchors, each decoding to 10 neural Gaussians at render time) under a held-out split reproduces its level curve (27.23 dB at 145k visible anchors, degrading gracefully to 19.5 dB at 29k), a trained representation whose level set is fixed at training time. On the other side, CityGaussianV2’s runtime LOD cannot be evaluated post-hoc on the official Aerial release: its renderer requires a per-partition partitioning file and one trained checkpoint per partition block, artifacts of its partitioned training that the published single checkpoint does not include. Our post-hoc layer, in contrast, consumes that same 8.56M checkpoint as-is and sweeps the continuous c curve of Table 3 on it. Runtime memory tells the same story: while rendering the same Block_all views at 1600×900 through each side’s official path on the same 4080 SUPER, the VRAM peak is 30.4 GiB for Octree-GS (steady-state 15.9 GiB) and 4.4 GiB for ours (6.9× lower at peak; Table S8); the decoded-per-frame neural representation is intrinsically memory-heavy, independent of the fps gap.

    6.5 Pruning baselines

    The θ+opacity rule’s city-scale behavior is measured on Block_A (Table S9): the redundancy signal localizes sacrifice at city scale just as it does on lego (Section 6.2.2).

    At matched budgets, Table S9 compares two post-hoc exports of the same trained model against LightGaussian [4], RAP [39], and a faithful single-pass reimplementation of PUP 3D-GS’s Fisher sensitivity score [9] (diagonal Fisher over means and scales, applied through the same export path): the θ+opacity rule (coverage redundancy) and the contribution-scored export of Section 5 (render-aware ranking; the score itself is LightGaussian’s, faithfully reimplemented and applied through our post-hoc export path). The score export matches Vanilla exactly at 50% and 25% of the primitives and dominates all three baselines on all three metrics at 10% (+0.45 dB PSNR over LightGaussian, +0.80 dB over RAP, +0.37 dB over the PUP score); one 234 s scoring pass, no retraining. The axis extends where no baseline reports numbers: 13.49 dB at 5%, 12.97 dB at 2.5%, 12.53 dB at 1.3% of the primitives. Absolute Block_A values are low by protocol design (DC-only evaluation against real photographs); the table’s purpose is the ordering of methods under one identical pipeline, not absolute quality. θ+opacity keeps a complementary role: it is the best LPIPS export at every extreme budget (0.547 vs. 0.557 for the score export at 10%; 0.601 for RAP), consistent with its design of removing perceptually redundant mass. The score export, in turn, keeps street markings and facades legible at 10% where LightGaussian blurs and RAP collapses (Fig. S9).

    The scheduler itself emits a standard primitive stream (means, quaternions, scales, opacities, SH), consumable by any splatting rasterizer; the export pipeline and render-aware scoring are described in the supplementary material.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把训练好的 3DGS 变成多分辨率分解树，一个质量参数按显存选 LOD。

要点：

  • 后处理式方案：一次几秒钟的构建把任意已训练 3DGS 转成 factor 树，即矩匹配聚合的多分辨率层级，运行时单个质量参数按目标设备显存选每视角的 LOD。
  • 理论依据是可测量的容量下界与「预算—误差」规律，由相空间最优传输推出；选择规则用近期覆盖定理证明哪些基元可安全丢弃。
  • 同一理论也用于训练：预算中心训练先测场景需要多少基元再按该规模训练，避免先练满再压缩的浪费；在 13 个公开场景上按预注册协议验证了下界。

为什么值得看：城市级 3DGS 落地的门槛就是显存与 LOD，这里给的是「先算容量再训练/选 LOD」的定量方法，比经验性抽稀更适合工程化。

中文摘要：3DGS 画质与实时性都很好，但整城规模下单模型就有数百万基元、数 GB 显存，消费级 GPU 无法高质量实时渲染。Budgeted-GS 是一种后处理方法：用几秒钟的构建把任意已训练模型转成 factor 树——矩匹配聚合构成的多分辨率层级，之后一个质量参数就能按目标设备显存为每个视角选合适 LOD，同城级模型可服务显存差异很大的 GPU。理论基于相空间最优传输推出的「预算—误差」规律与可测量容量下界，并用覆盖定理证明哪些基元冗余；同一理论也支撑预算中心训练，在 13 个公开场景上完成验证。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-02

本期推送：2026-10-23

Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD

Abstract

3D Gaussian Splatting achieves excellent visual quality with real-time rendering, but at the scale of entire cities it does not fit: a trained model carries millions of primitives and gigabytes of memory, and real-time rendering at high quality on a consumer GPU remains out of reach. We introduce Budgeted-GS, a post-hoc method that turns any trained 3DGS model into a factoring tree, a multi-resolution hierarchy of moment-matched aggregates. After a construction pass of a few seconds, a single quality parameter then selects, for each view, the level of detail that fits the memory of the target device, so the same city-scale model serves GPUs with widely different memory capacities. When a new scene is to be trained, the same theory applies: instead of growing a full-sized model and compressing it afterwards, budget-centered training first measures how many primitives the scene needs and then trains the model directly at that size, avoiding the wasted effort of optimizing primitives that are later discarded. Both methods are grounded in a measurable capacity floor, a budget–error law derived from optimal transport in phase space; selection rules certified by recent covering theorems decide which primitives are redundant. The floor answers how many primitives a scene actually needs and how many can safely be given up. We validate the floor on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol, and exercise both methods from object scenes to an official city capture, rendering it at native 1920×1080, full SH, in real time on one consumer GPU.

1 Introduction

Real-time radiance-field rendering of captured scenes is now routine at object and room scale. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [14] represents a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussians rendered by projective splatting with depth-sorted α-compositing. At city scale it does not fit: a trained model carries millions of primitives and gigabytes of memory, and real-time rendering at high quality on a consumer GPU remains out of reach. The obstacles are structural. At training time the standard recipe is to densify a large model and then compress it; the primitives are optimized for a different capacity, and the time spent on the removed half is wasted. At deploy time the only degradation mode offered by streaming renderers such as Gaussian Point Splatting (GPS [29]) is random subsampling. And beneath both sits an unanswered question: nobody can say what the right budget is. The question “how many primitives do I need here?” is answered by habit, because no principled budget–error floor has been available either at training or deployment time.

This paper answers it with a rate–distortion theory of rendering primitives: a trained model is a point on a rate–distortion curve; its primitive count is its budget, its error a function of that budget. The theory has two mathematical halves. The capacity floor, derived from optimal transport in phase space (position × direction, where rendering primitives and renderers are both natural objects), says that if the scene’s phase-space measure has dₚₛ-dimensional support, the minimal achievable error with N primitives falls as N^-2/dₚₛ (Zador’s law). The collapse license comes from the 2025 resolution of the three-dimensional Kakeya set conjecture [36]: the Wang–Zahl union-volume estimate, in weighted (continuous-opacity) form, certifies that wherever Gaussians locally over-cover space, they merge into few representatives with bounded volumetric loss. The floor tells a budget what it can achieve; the license tells it where redundancy lives and what may be merged or dropped.

The floor and the license are operationalized as two methods. On the deployment side, the floor’s allocation law (Nⱼ^*∝Kⱼsⱼ/dⱼ per tile) is realized as a factoring tree (Factoring LOD, Section 5), an octree of scale bands with moment-matched equivalent planks, driven by a one-parameter pixel-footprint scheduler. A single trained model sweeps a continuous memory–quality curve instead of a single fixed operating point. On the training side, Budget-Centered Training (BCT, Section 5.1) trains the densifier directly at the floor’s knee, so the model is born at the right size instead of growing huge and being pruned afterwards. Beyond rendering, the floor answers how many primitives a scene needs, how much of it is redundancy, and how a fixed budget should split across a city. Measuring it on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol shows published compressors lying on an essentially flat frontier. Their reported gains come from redundancy, not from proximity to capacity (Section 6.1). At city scale the same discipline turns real-time. A retrain of the official city model serves the official test trajectory at native 1920×1080, full SH, on one consumer GPU—to our knowledge the first post-hoc, full-SH result on a consumer GPU in this regime (Section 6.6).

Contributions.

  • •

    We introduce Factoring LOD, a post-hoc layer that converts one trained model into a factoring tree with a one-parameter scheduler; it renders a city-scale scene at high quality in real time within whatever memory the consumer GPU has.

  • •

    We propose Budget-Centered Training, which trains the densifier directly at the floor-located budget; the model is born at the right size instead of growing huge and being pruned afterwards; it leads the train-then-prune route at every matched budget, in a single training run.

  • •

    We establish the theory beneath the problem: a measurable capacity floor that answers, for any city-scale 3DGS scene, how many primitives it actually needs, and therefore how many can safely be given up.

    • 2 Related Work

    Rendering large-scale scenes. Every classic representation solved scale with its own multiresolution answer. Points: surfel splatting [27], QSplat’s sphere hierarchy [30], and Potree’s out-of-core octree generation [31] stream large point clouds at interactive rates. Meshes: progressive meshes [10] introduced view-dependent refinement, and Nanite [13] virtualizes micropolygon geometry in production engines. Voxels: sparse voxel octrees [19] ray-march gigavoxel volumes. What these systems share, a coarse-to-fine hierarchy carrying a per-frame budget, is exactly what a raw 3DGS model [14] lacks: it is a flat set of primitives with no hierarchy at all.

    Data structures for large-scale 3DGS scenes. Inside the 3DGS world, the standard answer is a spatial structure coupled to training. Octree-GS builds an octree of level-of-detail clusters [28]; Scaffold-GS anchors Gaussians on a sparse grid [23]; multiresolution hash grids organize NeRF-side training [25]; CityGaussian partitions the scene into blocks with distance-based LOD [21], following the block decomposition of Block-NeRF [33]; hierarchical 3DGS trains a chunk pyramid [15]; concurrent efforts pursue out-of-core streaming hierarchies [38] and LOD-aware training [18]; GPS streams an octree with distance shells [29] (our cross-renderer comparisons use it, Section 5). These structures carry the indexing, but the budget lives in the training pipeline: levels and blocks are fixed when training ends. Our factoring tree is built post-hoc from any model, selects per (leaf, scale-band) instead of per block or level, and grounds the selection in measurable redundancy and pixel-footprint criteria (Section 5); Section 6.4 compares directly against Octree-GS and CityGaussianV2’s runtime LOD [22].

    Quality and memory control for large-scale 3DGS scenes. Once a model exists, a large family controls its size: MCMC-based densification [16] and regularization-based pruning [24] budget during training; LightGaussian [4], Compact3DGS [20], RDO-Gaussian [35], EAGLES [6], RadSplat [26], PUP 3D-GS [9], and RAP [39] prune, quantize, distill, or reselect primitives after training; 2DGS changes the primitive itself to a surfel for surface quality [11]. All of these act once, at training or export time, and expose no runtime memory–quality trade-off or error bound. Our budget parameter acts on any trained model continuously and renderer-agnostically; LightGaussian’s own score, applied post-hoc through our export path, yields a Vanilla-flat budget axis to 25% of the primitives on city-scale scenes (Section 6.6); and rasterizer accelerators [8, 3] are composable with it: they render the selected set faster, while the parameter decides what is selected.

    3 Overview

    Budgeted-GS applies one budget discipline at every stage of a scene’s life cycle (Fig. 1). The capacity floor (Section 4) gives, for any scene, the minimal achievable rendering error at a primitive count N; it is stated as theorems and measured per scene with a preregistered protocol (Section 6.1). Two methods spend the budget where the floor says. Budget-Centered Training (Section 5.1) reads the floor’s knee N^* off the measured curve and trains the densifier directly at that budget. Factoring LOD (Section 5) converts any trained model into a factoring tree whose one-parameter pixel-footprint scheduler selects, per view, exactly the working set that fits the memory at hand. Section 6 reports the experiments. The supplementary material carries the proofs.

    4 An optimal-transport theory for 3D Gaussian primitives

    Why should the budget be a design variable, and how should it be spent? On real data, reconstruction error falls steeply as the budget grows, then flattens into a shallow floor. This section develops a theory that predicts where that floor lies: from primitives and rendering at the bottom, through construction and capacity, up to the selection rules on top. Concretely, for a quality target Q, the theory yields (i) the minimal primitive count a scene requires, (ii) the redundant subset of its primitives, and (iii) the allocation of a fixed budget across a city.

    4.1 Rendering as optimal transport in phase space

    Prior work has employed optimal transport in 3DGS only in narrow, task-specific roles, including Wasserstein losses between Gaussian mixtures [32], radial-optimal-transport fitting of structured Gaussians [41], and capacity control in multi-view stylization [37]. To our knowledge, we are the first to formulate rendering as optimal transport in phase space.

    Definition 1(Phase space and primitives).

    ℙ:=X×Ω, the product of scene space X⊂ℝ³ (the unit ball) and the direction sphere Ω=S², is phase space; a cell Q=V×C (spatial plank × directional cone) obeys Δx·Δξ≥c (the uncertainty bound). A rendering primitive is a triple (Q,w,ρ): cell, opacity weight w, value model ρ. Three families exist. Point primitives take the limit Δx→0. Wave primitives are Gaussian wave packets with ΔxΔξ\asympc, the family of 3DGS surfels and 2DGS plates. Field primitives are continuous densities, such as NeRF/SDF. A representation is a parameterized measure family {μ_θ}_θ∈Θ on ℙ.

    Definition 2(Rendering coupling and marginalization).

    For view v and parameters θ, the renderer defines a joint measure π_v,θ on ℙ×Pixelᵥ, the pixel grid of view v, with source marginal μ_θ and pixel marginal ν_v,θ (pixel masses S(p):=ν_v,θ({p})); the pixel colour is the conditional expectation

    I_v,θ(p)=∫_ℙρ(x) dπ_v,θ(x|p).

    4.2 An optimal-transport view of 3DGS

    The framework rests on four axioms: every representation induces a phase-space distribution μ_θ; the renderer is a legal transport and the image is its coupling marginal; every construction algorithm’s objective is expressible as one transport cost; a single source is transported to all view targets. For 3DGS-style compositing, this coupling is the familiar compositing rule: π_v,θ(p,{i})∝wᵢ(p)=αᵢ(p)Tᵢ(p) with Tᵢ=∏_jrendering transport: the renderer transports μ_θ to per-view pixel marginals; the second is representation formation: given complexity comp_F(θ)≤N, minimize the transport cost

    ℝᵣₑₛ(N)=\min_θ∑ᵥ∫_ℙ×Pixelᵥc dπ_v,θ, c(x,p):=\lVertρ(x)-cᵍᵗᵥ(p)\rVert².

    		(2)

    Gradient training, sampling, meshing, and voxelization are solvers of the second problem; their outputs are measured by the transport residual (their convergence is proved or cited to classical sources in the supplementary material). The bottom layer is one theorem: the renderer really is a legal transport, rendering is conditional expectation, and the error splits into a tight three-term chain.

    Theorem 3(The renderer, the rendering map, and the error chain).

    Under measurable ray–pixel assignment, bounded transmittance-weighted mass, and Lipschitz regularity, every (v,θ) admits a canonical coupling π_v,θ with marginals (μ_θ,ν_v,θ), determined by the rendering rule and weakly continuous in θ. With projection Jacobian J_Π and footprint kernel G, the pixel probability kernel is κᵥ(p, dx)∝w(x)G(p-Π(x))\lvert\detJ_Π(x)\rvert1_V(x), In the audited low-opacity domain, the pieces combine into a tight three-term chain: the operator norm is sharp (\lVertPᵥf\rVert_L²(Pixelᵥ)≤√μᵥ\lVertf\rVert_L²(ℙ)), the blending gap is second-order in the max opacity ε (with multiplicity M(x): \lvertC(x)-L(x)\rvert≤(K^′)/(2)M(x)²ε²+O(K^′M(x)ε³)), and

    \lVertν_v,θ-νᵍᵗᵥ\rVert_L²≤√ℓᵥ \lVertμ_θ-μ_S\rVert_L²+(K^′)/(2)ε²\lVertM²\rVert_L²+ε_target(v),

    		(3)

    a tight three-term chain: source gap, blending gap, target map; here μᵥ=∑ₚS(p) is the transported mass of view v, ℓᵥ the Lipschitz constant of the target map, K^′ the compositing Lipschitz constant, and measure norms are taken over densities with respect to the phase-space reference measure, the source one over the normalized source marginal of the coupling.

    Forming a representation under a budget is itself an optimal-transport problem [12, 34], and its duality is what makes the floor certifiable.

    Theorem 4(Representation formation as restricted optimal transport).

    For compositing with normalized coupling π̃ₚ, the loss decomposes as L(θ)=ℂ(θ)-V(θ): the transport cost ℂ minus the conditional variance V. For atomic families with quadratic cost, \inf_\lvertsuppμ_θ\rvert≤N∫\minᵢ\lVertx-yᵢ\rVert² dμ_S=W₂²-optimal quantization, and Lloyd’s algorithm is monotone. The certificate follows: the residual satisfies ℝ_free(N)≤ℝᵣₑₛ(N) with gap decomposition Δ(θ)=Δ_coupl(θ)+Δ_src(θ)≥0; for every dual-feasible (φ,ψ) the certificate

    L(θ)≥∫_ℙφ dμ_θ+∑ₚS(p)ψ(p)-V(θ)

    		(4)

    lower-bounds achieved error; and with target colour measure ν_c of intrinsic dimension d_c≤3, ℝ_free(N)\asympC_d_c\lVertν_c\rVert_d_c/(d_c+2)N^-2/d_c.

    4.3 The capacity floor

    How fast must this residual fall as the budget N grows? Classical high-resolution quantization theory [40, 7] answers exactly this, and the rendering instance, whose source is the phase-space measure of Definition 1, obeys the same law:

    Theorem 5(The capacity floor of the rendering instance).

    Imported from classical high-resolution quantization [40, 7] through the transport formulation above, with the lower bound additionally assuming view completeness (the view set separates the source): if the phase-space measure μ_S has dₚₛ-dimensional support with density λ, the minimal achievable rendering error with N primitives obeys

    ℝ(N) \asymp C_dₚₛ \lVertλ\rVert_dₚₛ/dₚₛ+2 N^-2/dₚₛ.

    		(5)

    On surface scenes the phase-space support is four-dimensional (surface position × incident-direction hemisphere), so ℝ(N)∝N^-1/2. For the cartoon class with appearance smoothness p and resolution L, ℝ_F(N,L)^1/2\asympC₁KN^-1/2(\logN)ᶜ+C₂K^′L⁻ᵖ with optimal allocation N^*\asympM^p/(p+1), L^*\asympM^1/(2(p+1)); width brackets sandwich ℝ_F^free≤ℝ_F≤C width.

    The free relaxation of Theorem 4 is target-limited (rate N^-2/d_c), while this rendering instance is source-limited at N^-2/dₚₛ with dₚₛ≥d_c: the requirement that primitives must render, not merely match colours, is what slows the rate. The floor is certifiable rather than assumed: the duality chain L+V=ℂ≥ℂ_free≥D evaluates, per budget and per test view, a lower bound on the achievable error (Eq. (4)). It is also measurable, and Section 6.1 reports the curve for 13 public scenes.

    Three supporting results, proved, cited, or labelled as sketches in the supplementary material, round out the framework: gradient training is a legitimate solver of the restricted-transport problem and attains the classical rates of sampling, Lloyd, and meshing; cross-view colour agreement is structural, and the new-view error is bounded by the training error plus an angular-regularity term; and across primitive families on surfaces, triangles achieve N⁻¹, point-like primitives N^-1/2, and isotropic voxels N^-1/4. One part reads as a prediction: the optimal cell is an anisotropic, covariance-ellipsoidal atom, exactly what 3DGS fits, and exactly what the moment-matched aggregates of the factoring tree (Section 5.2) construct.

    4.4 The selection rules

    The floor is one half of the mathematics; the other half is a set of selection rules, theorems that decide which primitives may be merged or dropped at a given budget. Here a rendering primitive is viewed geometrically, as a plank(μ,R,h,α): an oriented box centered at μ, rotated by R, of half-extents h=3σ, carrying the opacity α as its weight. We state the rules here; the proofs are in the supplementary material.

    Definition 6(Essentially distinct tubes and the convex Wolff axioms).

    Sets U,V⊂ℝ³ are essentially distinct if \lvertU∩V\rvert≤\tfrac12\max(\lvertU\rvert,\lvertV\rvert); throughout, T is a set of essentially distinct δ×δ×1 tubes in the unit ball, so \lvertT\rvert\asympδ². Following [36] (Def. 1.3), Tobeys the Katz–Tao convex Wolff axioms with error C if

    #{T∈T: T⊂W} ≤ C \lvertW\rvert \lvertT\rvert⁻¹ for every convexW⊂ℝ³,

    		(6)

    i.e. no convex set concentrates more tubes than its volume admits; a Kakeya-type arrangement (one tube per δ-separated direction) satisfies (6) with C\lesssim1.

    Theorem 7(Weighted covering—the collapse license).

    (i) (Unweighted; [36], Thm. 1.2.) For every ε>0 there is K>1 such that, for all δ>0 small: if T satisfies (6) with C\lesssim1 and every a×b×2 prism contains at most 100abδ⁻² tubes of T, and Y(T)⊂T has \lvertY(T)\rvert≥λ₀\lvertT\rvert, then

    \lvert\bigcup_T∈TY(T)\rvert ≥ δ^ελ₀^K∑_T∈T\lvertT\rvert.

    (ii) (Weighted, rendering form.) If each tube carries a weight function w_T\colonT→[0,1] of per-tube mass \lvertT\rvert⁻¹ ∫_Tw_T≥λ(w)\gtrsim1, then the saturated weighted union volume |U|_w:=∫\min(1,∑_Tw_T(x)) dx obeys |U|_w \gtrsim λ(w)^K+1δ^ε∑_T∫_Tw_T: thresholding costs only constants depending on ε, so the weighted form loses nothing beyond the ε-loss of (i).

    Lemma 8(Scale truncation).

    For cartoon-class fields, atoms whose projected footprint is below the pixel scale can be dropped or collapsed with bounded loss.

    Theorem 9(Adaptive covering rate).

    For f∈ℂ_K (piecewise C²/H² cartoon fields) there is an N-atom combination of plates and tubes with \lVertf-f_N\rVert_L²≤CK N^-1/2(\logN)ᶜ; conversely, some f^*∈ℂ_K forces every N-atom combination to obey \lVertf^*-f_N\rVert_L²≥c₀K(N\log₂N)^-1/2.

    Corollary 10(Budget allocation).

    Minimizing the geometric + appearance error C₁KN^-1/2+C₂K^′L⁻ᵖ under the parameter budget M\asympN(L+1)² yields N^*\asympM^p/(p+1) and L^*\asympM^1/(2(p+1)); across scale bands sⱼ=2ʲs₀ the band budgets decay exponentially, mⱼ∝2^-jγ.

    Theorem 7 is the union-volume estimate of Wang–Zahl [36], the theorem behind the 2025 resolution of the three-dimensional Kakeya set conjecture, reinterpreted with continuous opacity weights—to our knowledge the first rendering use of this theory. It certifies when a family of rendering primitives can be collapsed into fewer representatives without forfeiting more than an ε-fraction of volumetric mass, and its one-line corollary caps the packing density of any convex region at CΔ_\max(T) (the Katz–Tao constant of Definition 6), which is what keeps the scale-band decomposition of Section 5 bounded. Together with Zador’s law (5), the four statements answer, in order: how much error is unavoidable (the floor), which groups are redundant (collapse), what may be dropped outright (truncation), and how a fixed budget should be split (allocation). Stated as questions (how many primitives does this scene need, how much of it is redundancy, how should a fixed budget be split across a city), the theory answers all three; the rest of the paper measures the answers and builds methods on them.

    5 Budgeted-GS: training and deployment

    The floor and the selection rules are operationalized two ways: at training time, budget-centered training grows the model the floor prescribes (Section 5.1); at deployment time, the factoring tree and its pixel-footprint scheduler serve, per view, exactly the working set that fits the memory at hand (Sections 5.2 and 5.3).

    Both halves of our system follow from one observation: a trained model is a redundant, multi-scale arrangement of oriented boxes (each primitive occupies a box of half-extents h=3σ weighted by its opacity), and budget control means removing that redundancy without visible loss. Three principles govern every selection rule in this paper; they are the operational form of the theorems stated in Section 4.

    The first principle is the collapse license: a group of primitives that locally over-covers space, many overlapping boxes of comparable scale in one region, can be merged into a few representatives with bounded volumetric loss (Theorem 7; the moment-matching counterpart of the optimal-atom prediction, Section 4). This licenses the moment-matched aggregates of the factoring tree and opacity-ranked pruning inside redundancy-flagged regions.

    The second is scale truncation: a primitive whose projected footprint is below the pixel scale can be dropped or collapsed with bounded image error (Lemma 8; the U2 projection-error regime). This licenses the pixel-footprint threshold t=c·d/f of the scheduler and the stopping rule that freezes density control once pruning stops paying for itself.

    The third is budget allocation: under a fixed primitive budget, coarser scale bands deserve exponentially more budget than finer ones (Corollary 10; the Kⱼsⱼ/dⱼ law); the same footprint rule instantiates this allocation per view. The three principles are grounded in recent union-volume estimates for unions of convex sets [36] and classical adaptive-approximation rates [2]; measured error rates on synthetic scenes match the prediction within measurement noise.

    5.1 Budget-centered training

    The floor answers “how many primitives do I need at quality Q?”, and the answer is also a training prescription. Traditional pipelines train a large model and compress it: the primitives are optimized for a different capacity, and the training time spent on the removed half is wasted. BCT instead locates the knee N^* from the measured curve (Fig. 2; the budget with the largest steepest-window slope, Section 6.1), then trains the MCMC densifier directly at cap=N^*: the initial primitive count is set to a fixed initial fraction of N^* and the refine-stop fraction to a second, both scaled by the measured redundancy θ_waste=Nₒₚₜ/N_full.

    Standard 3DGS densification/pruning is driven by positional gradients and opacity. We keep densification but replace the pruning signal by the θ redundancy map (the collapse license; supplementary material): θ is computed per region from the local factoring of the model: regions with high local multiplicity (low θ) are over-covered and are exactly where primitives can be removed with the smallest approximation loss; pruning inside θ-flagged regions removes primitives by opacity. A rate-based stopping criterion freezes density control once validation improvement falls below ε=0.5 dB.

    5.2 The factoring tree

    A trained model is frozen, but the hardware it must run on is not: the same city has to serve a render farm, a desktop, a laptop, and a VR headset, and at the far end it has to render in real time on a consumer GPU. The floor’s allocation law (budget should follow Kⱼsⱼ/dⱼ per tile and per view) turns this into a selection problem. Concretely, applied per tile j (regularity Kⱼ, extent sⱼ, distance dⱼ), Corollary 10 yields the level-selection law

    Nⱼ^*(v)∝Kⱼ√Aⱼ(v)\asymp(Kⱼ sⱼ)/(dⱼ),\hskip18.49988pteⱼ²\asymp(c² Kⱼsⱼ)/(dⱼ)·(∑ₖKₖsₖ/dₖ)/(N)·occⱼ.\normalsize

    		(7)

    with Aⱼ(v) the projected screen area of tile j in view v. For uniform regularity it reduces to the classical screen-space-error heuristic and adds what it lacks: rougher tiles draw more budget, occluded tiles pay the visibility factor, and the per-tile error is certificate-verifiable.

    Given a trained model with N primitives (means μᵢ, rotations Rᵢ, scales σᵢ, opacities αᵢ, SH colors), we first convert each primitive to a plank(μ,R,h=3σ,α). The scene bounding box is partitioned by a GPU octree (leaf capacity 4096); the structure lives in what its nodes store (below), and within each leaf the planks are split into scale bandsℓ=⌊\log₂(s/s_base)⌋ where s=\maxh and s_base is the 5% quantile of s. Each (leaf, band) group is then factored into at most 256 equivalent planks by batch moment matching: within a group, planks are ordered by Morton code (spatial locality), split into consecutive buckets, and each bucket is replaced by a single plank conserving

    W=∑ᵢαᵢ|Vᵢ|, c^*=(∑ᵢαᵢ|Vᵢ|μᵢ)/(W),(8)
    T^*=∑ᵢαᵢ|Vᵢ|((μᵢ-c^*)(μᵢ-c^*)^⊤+\tfrac13Rᵢ diag(hᵢ)² Rᵢ^⊤),

    i.e. weighted volume, centroid, and inertia tensor; the equivalent plank is (c^*,R^*,h^*,w^*) from the eigendecomposition of T^* with w^*=W/|V^*|∈[0,1] (Fig. 3c). Colors enter as opacity-weighted first moments of the SH coefficients (DC and higher bands separately).

    The internal nodes of the octree receive the same treatment bottom-up, so every (node, band) has one aggregate plank. The raw primitives are retained in Morton order for the finest tier. Construction on multi-million-primitive scenes takes seconds on one GPU, and the aggregate representation is 119× smaller than the input (supplementary material).

    At render time, for camera position p and focal length f (pixels), each (leaf, band) with mean scale s̄ and centroid distance d is assigned to one of three tiers by the threshold t=c·d/f:

    raw: members individually resolvable (s̄≥t) ⇒ render the original Gaussians;

  • •

    fine: the cluster resolvable but members not (s̄

    coarse: sub-pixel (h̄

    • c is a single scalar budget parameter: c=1 means exactly resolvable (the reference tier), larger c progressively collapses sub-c-pixel content (scale truncation; supplementary material), and c<1 keeps members below the pixel scale (super-resolving regime); on distant aerial cameras most bands are already sub-pixel at c=1, and our real-time renderer operates at c≈0.3 there (Section 6.6).

    6 Experiments

    We validate the theory and both methods end to end: the floor itself across 13 public scenes, then Budget-Centered Training, then Factoring LOD from object scenes to city scale, closing with ablations and efficiency.

    6.1 The floor, measured across 13 scenes

    The floor is measured with a preregistered protocol (criteria frozen before data collection; all verdicts frozen before reading results; 3 fixed seeds; JSON certificates at every stage, supplementary material): on each scene, MCMC training at cap 2×10⁶ followed by opacity-prune to N and fine-tune yields the empirical floor curve R(N) at 9 budgets; the preregistered floor-intactness test asks that no scan point crosses the fitted floor by more than \log₁₀(0.8); published operating points are re-anchored to their own baseline at matched capacity ratio with a 5% (0.22 dB) tolerance; and a duality certificate lower-bounds the achieved error at every (budget, view).

    On a synthetic cartoon control with the same protocol, the chord lands directly on Zador’s law (-0.549/-0.548/-0.551, R²=0.997). On the 13 public scenes (seed 0; 3 seeds on garden/room/bonsai) chord slopes are seed-stable (±0.004–0.011) but all fall outside the preregistered band [-0.55,-0.45], a registered negative. The reading-window audit explains it: the SfM point clouds have TWO-NN intrinsic dimension 1.9–2.05, and the steepest three-band windows reach -0.41 to -0.53 across scenes and seeds (bonsai -0.46/-0.49/-0.53; room -0.469→-0.496 when the fine-tune budget is quadrupled), straddling the predicted -1/2. Floor intactness holds 13/13; the duality certificate holds at every (band, view) on room with tightness 0.28→0.03 (Table S10, full data in supplementary material).

    The published frontier is flat: every compression method with a same-paper (N,PSNR) pair defines a resolution-invariant two-point trajectory (Fig. S3). Across Compact3DGS and EAGLES on all 13 scenes plus Mini-Splatting [5] and RadSplat [26] at dataset level, these slopes occupy [-0.28,+0.09] with mean -0.04: removing 60–70% of a converged model’s primitives costs under 1 dB across the surveyed compressors, while the floor law (asymptote -1/2, reached end-to-end on the synthetic control and bracketed by our steepest windows) is an order of magnitude steeper. Published compression operates deep in the over-budgeted regime: its reported gains ride the redundancy θ_waste=Nₒₚₜ/N_full that the floor makes measurable, not proximity to capacity. The universal (model-free) colour-quantization floor, a lower bound on every representation at budget N computed from test images alone, confirms it: all 26 published operating points lie above the band (Fig. S4).
