    This work was supported in part by National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 62272011.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix 0.A Text2PhyX Dataset Details

    0.A.1 Overview

    As introduced in the main text, Text2PhyX is a large-scale, text-conditioned 3D physical property dataset designed to resolve the inherent ambiguity of predicting object mechanics from pure visual inputs. The dataset is built upon a diverse collection of 1,700 unique 3D assets, which are sourced from two distinct domains to ensure both quality and real-world complexity: approximately 1,000 high-quality 3D meshes from the Objaverse dataset, and 700 3D gs (gs) models reconstructed from in-the-wild 2D images using SAM 3D Objects.

    To support flexible, text-driven physical predictions, we generate 8 distinct textual descriptions paired with corresponding physical parameters for each base object. Consequently, Text2PhyX comprises a total of 13,600 data triplets. Each triplet consists of:

  • 1.

    A 3D object representation (dense OpenCLIP semantic voxels extracted from multi-view renderings).

  • 2.

    A text description specifying the material or physical state of the object’s constituent parts.

  • 3.

    The ground-truth dense physical parameters, specifically Young’s Modulus (E), Poisson’s Ratio (ν), and Density (ρ), assigned at the voxel level.

    • The entire dataset is partitioned at the object level into a training set of 12,600 samples from 1,575 objects and a testing set of 1,000 samples from 125 held-out objects, providing a robust benchmark for text-conditioned 3D physical parameter regression.

    0.A.2 Gallery with Physics Property

    To intuitively demonstrate the diversity and granularity of Text2PhyX, Figure A5 provides a visual gallery showcasing various objects alongside their part-level segmentations and corresponding physical property heatmaps.

    Multi-View Renderings and Semantic Segmentation.

    To mitigate the ambiguity of single-view observations and extract robust 3D OpenCLIP voxels, we uniformly render multiple views from the upper hemisphere of each object. Based on these visual features and vlm-generated keywords, objects are accurately segmented into constituent parts. As shown in the second column of Figure A5, a snowman is segmented into its body, arms, and nose; a potted grass is separated into the planter and the green grass; and a bag is distinctly divided into the fabric body and plastic handles. This fine-grained part-level segmentation is crucial for applying localized, text-driven physical controls.

    Voxel-Wise Physical Property Heatmaps.

    Building upon the part segmentation, Text2PhyX provides dense, voxel-wise annotations for three key physical properties. As visualized in the rightmost three columns of Figure A5, different semantic parts within the same object exhibit distinctly different physical values, reflecting their assigned materials. For example, the wooden trunk of the tree shows a significantly higher Young’s Modulus (E) compared to its leaves, while the plastic handles of the bag exhibit different densities (ρ) and elasticity compared to the fabric body. These detailed heatmaps confirm that our automated, text-guided pipeline successfully assigns physically plausible and spatially accurate parameters across a wide variety of complex 3D objects.

    0.A.3 OpenCLIP-Driven 3D Semantic Segmentation

    Overview

    To endow our volumetric representation with open-vocabulary semantic understanding suitable for physics-based simulation, we distill dense, high-dimensional semantic features from a pre-trained 2D vision-language foundation model (specifically OpenCLIP) into a continuous 3D feature field. Furthermore, to ensure physical accuracy during stress propagation, we extend these surface features into the unobservable internal volume using a robust ray-casting strategy.

    2D Feature Extraction

    Given a set of multi-view RGB images {Iₖ} of the scene, we first extract 2D semantic feature maps using a pre-trained OpenCLIP image encoder. Since vision transformers typically output features at a lower resolution than the input image, we obtain a dense feature map Fₖ∈ℝ^512×512×768 for each image Iₖ, where 768 is the dimensionality of the OpenCLIP latent space.

    3D Feature Distillation via Volumetric Rendering

    Unlike heuristic multi-view projection methods that suffer from occlusion ambiguities, we lift the 2D semantic features into 3D using a physics-inspired volumetric rendering framework. We freeze the density field σ obtained from a pre-trained RGB NeRF and introduce a continuous 3D feature field Φ:ℝ³→ℝ^D, parameterized by a neural network or a feature grid.

    During optimization, we render the expected 3D feature F̂(r) along a camera ray r using the accumulated transmittance T(t). This naturally handles occlusions by dropping the transmittance to zero behind visible surfaces. We optimize the feature field Φ by minimizing the discrepancy between the rendered ray features F̂(r) and the corresponding ground-truth OpenCLIP features Fₖ(r) sampled from the 2D feature maps. We employ the negative cosine similarity loss as our distillation objective:

    L_distill=-1/N∑ₖ∑ᵣ(F̂(r)·Fₖ(r))/(∥F̂(r)∥₂∥Fₖ(r)∥₂)

    where N is the total number of sampled rays. By minimizing this loss, the 3D feature field learns to encode view-consistent semantic priors strictly on the visible surfaces.

    Internal Volume Filling via Even-Odd Rule

    While the volumetric rendering successfully distills features onto the object’s surface, physics-based simulations require semantic and physical properties (e.g., Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio ν) to be defined throughout the object’s interior. Since internal voids are unobservable from external cameras, their features remain undefined.

    To bridge this gap, we employ a hierarchical ray-casting strategy based on the classic even-odd rule. For a given unassigned voxel v in the 3D space, we cast multiple rays uniformly distributed over a sphere towards infinity. Along each ray, we count the number of intersections with the object’s surface (defined by a density threshold on σ). If the intersection count is consistently odd across the majority of the casted rays, the voxel v is robustly classified as being inside the object, effectively handling complex concavities.

    Finally, for each identified internal voxel, we assign its semantic feature by performing nearest-neighbor interpolation from the optimized surface feature field Φ. This ensures that the internal volume inherits semantically and physically consistent properties from its closest bounding surface, yielding a complete volumetric representation ready for downstream simulation.

    Open-Vocabulary Querying

    Once the 3D feature distillation is complete, the scene can be queried using natural language. Given a user-provided text prompt (e.g., "a red apple" or "the handle of the mug"), we encode the text into a 768-dimensional embedding t using the OpenCLIP text encoder.

    To perform 3D semantic segmentation, we compute the cosine similarity between the text embedding t and the distilled 3D feature fₚ of each primitive: S(p,t)=(fₚ·t)/(∥fₚ∥₂∥t∥₂) Primitives with a similarity score S(p,t) exceeding a predefined threshold are segmented as belonging to the target object. This continuous similarity field not only enables robust part-level segmentation but also facilitates downstream tasks such as language-guided robotic grasping and interaction.

    0.A.4 vlm labeling

    To further illustrate the automated data generation pipeline described in Section 3.3, Figure A4 provides a concrete example of our text-guided property assignment process. As discussed in the main text, relying solely on visual inputs for physical parameter prediction is inherently ill-posed. To resolve this, we utilize a vlm to generate diverse, physically plausible textual descriptions and assign corresponding physical parameters.

    In this example, the input consists of multi-view RGB renderings of a soda can and its extracted 3D representation. During the augmentation phase, the vlm generates a novel semantic condition: “The soda can is now made of a very hard plastic.” Rather than blindly guessing the physical values, the vlm grounds its assignment by querying external knowledge bases. As shown in the generated JSON metadata, the model explicitly provides its reasoning trace (“from wiki”) to prevent hallucination.

    Based on this grounded knowledge, the vlm determines an appropriate scaling factor (multiplier: 0.113) for the material transition from standard aluminum to hard plastic. This multiplier is then applied to the default Young’s Modulus (E) of the object (“original_E_mean”: 249999920.0) to compute the updated physical parameter (“new_E_mean”: 28249996.8) for the specified part (“soda can”). This transparent, physics-aware reasoning process ensures that the generated text-parameter pairs in Text2PhyX remain strictly consistent and physically accurate across all 13,600 data triplets.

    Appendix 0.B Additional Evaluation and Analysis

    0.B.1 Human-Annotated Text Generalization

    To further evaluate text generalization beyond Text2PhyX, we construct a human-annotated test set of 30 objects. For each material category, we query The Engineering Toolbox to obtain plausible physical-property ranges, retrieve corresponding object images, and reconstruct 3D assets using SAM 3D Objects. We sample two material-property configurations from the queried ranges and run physics simulation for each sample. Human annotators then watch these videos and provide the corresponding natural language descriptions, making this evaluation independent of the text-generation pipeline used to build Text2PhyX.

    0.B.2 Unconditional Cross-Dataset Validation

    To evaluate whether our framework is tied only to Text2PhyX, we also compare Pixie, VoMP, and our model under an unconditional protocol using an empty text input. We train and test the methods on the Pixie dataset, the VoMP dataset, and Text2PhyX, respectively. This setting is not designed to test text controllability; rather, it checks whether the voxel-based feed-forward architecture remains competitive when reduced to the same unconditional setting as prior feed-forward methods.

item.title: JointLight：把人像重光照的辐照度图当「蓝图」，但噪声得先去掉 ｜ JointLight: Human-Centric Video Relighting with Asynchronous RGB-Irradiance Joint Modeling
item.description:
一句话：异步联合建模 RGB 与辐照度、分阶段去噪时间表，两阶段训练补齐控制精度。

要点：

  • 端到端重光照把光传输隐进网络里，可控性差；直接用路径追踪辐照度图当显式蓝图又带瑕疵、拖累生成质量。
  • 关键观察：噪声破坏能去掉高频瑕疵而保留低频光传输，因此采用异步联合建模——在同一模型里用不同时间表分别去噪 RGB 与真值辐照度帧。
  • 两阶段训练，第二阶段引入域匹配策略弥合「辐照度提示」与「真值辐照度」的域差，从而获得细粒度光照控制。

为什么值得看：虚拟制片与游戏内人像重光照都受限于光照可控性，把辐照度当显式中间量并解决其域差，是比纯端到端更可调的路线。

中文摘要：人像场景中的光传输建模长期困难：扩散模型推动了重光照研究，但精确光照控制仍落后，主因是缺少多样、高质量且标注精确的视频重光照数据。端到端方法把光传输隐式学进网络，可控性变差；另一些工作用路径追踪辐照度线索作为显式蓝图，但这类线索带瑕疵，直接当控制信号会拖累生成质量。JointLight 观察到噪声破坏会去掉高频瑕疵而保留低频光传输，于是采用异步联合建模：训练时用不同时间表同时去噪 RGB 与真值辐照度帧，第二阶段再用域匹配弥合辐照度线索与真值之间的域差。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-23

JointLight: Human-Centric Video Relighting with Asynchronous RGB-Irradiance Joint Modeling

© cc

Abstract.

Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real-world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/JointLight/

Keywords:

Human-Centric Video Relighting, Diffusion Models, Irradiance Map, Illumination Control ††cc-license: by-nc-nd

1. Introduction

Lighting fundamentally affects how we perceive a scene. Modifying lighting while preserving scene identity enables a wide range of applications, such as artistic creation, film production, augmented reality, and computer vision research. Fundamentally, relighting requires an understanding of how light interacts with the scene. Traditional graphics pipelines simulate physical light transport with explicit geometry and materials. For objects and portraits, meticulously calibrated studio equipment [(Debevec, 2012)] is used to reconstruct geometry and capture reflectance fields. However, real-world scenes comprise complex combinations of objects and persons, of which the geometry and material properties are impractical to capture. Relighting of human-centric scenes in diverse indoor and outdoor environments thus remains a challenging task.

With the advent of powerful generative models, relighting with a single image or video input has drawn increasing attention. It is an innately ill-posed problem, since geometry, material, and lighting are all coupled in the single input. Some works [(Zhang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025c)] construct degradation pairs for real-world images or videos and train end-to-end diffusion models for relighting. These methods, lacking explicit physical light transport modeling, are typically constrained to text prompts or environment maps as conditioning inputs, failing to offer precise control over lighting parameters such as light source angles. Some other works [(Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)] utilize graphics engines to construct synthetic data, enabling relighting with environment maps as a condition. Such synthetic data are limited to simple object-centric scenes, hindering generalization to complex human-centric real-world scenarios. More importantly, implicit light transport modeling within neural networks cannot guarantee physical accuracy.

Recent advances in monocular geometry estimation [(Wang et al., 2025e; Wang et al., 2025f; Lin et al., 2025; Mescheder et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)] have opened new avenues for scene relighting. While monocular point clouds serve as a coarse geometric proxy, they are unsuitable for direct integration into traditional graphics pipelines due to single-layer geometry and artifacts from depth discontinuities at object boundaries. With a diffuse white BRDF and physics-based rendering, this proxy produces an irradiance cue that characterizes the scene’s diffuse light transport, as illustrated in Figure 3. Although this irradiance cue remains plagued by artifacts and exhibits a significant domain gap relative to the ground-truth irradiance map, we propose that this discrepancy can be effectively bridged through noise corruption. The key observation is that after blending with a certain amount of Gaussian noise, the rough irradiance cue and ground-truth irradiance map become indistinguishable. In this way, noise corruption mitigates the domain gap by removing high-frequency artifacts and preserving low-frequency content. We then model this rough irradiance distribution via the diffusion process. During training, the model jointly denoises RGB video and irradiance maps with separate timestep scheduling, learning to transform a noised irradiance cue into a pixel-aligned fine-grained irradiance map. At inference time, we render the irradiance cue using a geometry estimate and the target lighting with a path tracer. The irradiance cue is then noised and jointly denoised with the RGB video.

For training data, we develop a large-scale human-centric multi-illumination video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. It contains 68K synthetic videos from 6.8K dynamic scenes across 30 artist-made 3D environments. A character performing random actions is placed in the center of the camera, where random camera shake and camera movement are applied. Each scene is rendered with 10 different lighting conditions sampled from 821 HDR environment maps, of which 20% are set to rotating.

Experimental results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art realistic video relighting approaches in both relighting fidelity and video quality. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of our key designs. To summarize, we present three main contributions:

  • •

    An asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint-modeling approach with separate timestep scheduling, plus a domain matching strategy that bridges the gap between noisy irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps.

  • •

    A high-quality human-centric multi-illumination video dataset with paired irradiance maps across diverse indoor and outdoor lighting conditions. This dataset will be publicly released to advance research in human-centric video relighting and intrinsic decomposition.

  • •

    Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on video relighting in both visual quality and lighting fidelity.

    • 2. Related Work

    Human-centric scene relighting.

    While object-centric [(Jin et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2024; Bharadwaj et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2025)] and portrait-centric [(Lv et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2023; Saito et al., 2024; Chaturvedi et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Zhang et al., 2024)] static relighting have been extensively explored, human-centric video relighting in dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes remains underexplored. Many works [(Zhang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2024)] rely on degradation pairs with text prompts or environment maps, but provide only coarse control and often produce stylized results. [(Liang et al., 2026)] use path tracing rendering as an anchor point to online optimize static relighting results, which cannot extend to dynamic scenes. DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] curates synthetic multi-illumination data with simple objects and paired G-buffers, training separate inverse and forward rendering models. UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] further extends this to end-to-end video relighting. However, both methods input environment maps directly without explicit light transport guidance, limiting generalization in complex scenes with occlusions. In contrast, our method targets general dynamic scenes beyond portraits and employs physically-based irradiance cues to achieve more accurate lighting control.

    Several related systems target narrower capture settings or different control interfaces. SwitchLight [(Kim et al., 2024)] decomposes a single portrait using a physics-guided architecture and relights it from an environment map, whereas DifFRelight [(He et al., 2024)] learns subject-specific facial-performance relighting from light-stage data. Relightable Full-Body Gaussian Codec Avatars [(Wang et al., 2025d)] models local and non-local light transport for captured, personalized avatars. ReLumix [(Wang et al., 2025b)] propagates the illumination of one artist-relit reference frame through a video rather than taking a target environment map directly. The commercial Runway Relight Scene system [(Runway, 2026)] instead uses text descriptions to edit the atmosphere of short videos. These methods demonstrate complementary progress, but do not address pixel-aligned, environment-map-controlled relighting of general monocular human-centric videos in the wild.

    RGB↔X [(Zeng et al., 2024a)] shows pixel-aligned irradiance maps can serve as lighting control signals, but require an existing clean irradiance map as input. DiLightNet [(Zeng et al., 2024b)], PractiLight [(Erel et al., 2025)], and Lightit [(Kocsis et al., 2024)] compute irradiance cues from target lighting and coarse depth, but misalignment with the input image due to noisy geometry undermines relighting quality. Portrait-specific relighting methods such as Total Relighting [(Pandey et al., 2021)] focus on human faces and use image-based lighting without path-traced shadows, which is suitable for portrait photography but less applicable to general scenes.

    Joint cross-modal modeling.

    Diffusion models have been applied to jointly model pixel-aligned attributes such as depth [(Li et al., 2025; Byung-Ki et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025a)], motion [(Chefer et al., 2025)], and PBR attributes [(Xi et al., 2025b; He et al., 2025)]. Joint modeling approaches include dual-stream cross-attention [(Li et al., 2025; Byung-Ki et al., 2025)] and various single-model injection paradigms [(Chefer et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2025a; Xi et al., 2025b; He et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a)]. Most such methods assume clean auxiliary modalities; in contrast, we must handle imperfect irradiance cues with substantial geometry artifacts—a domain-gap issue largely unexplored in prior work. The use of per-modality asynchronous timestep schedules has been explored in UniDiffuser [(Bao et al., 2023)], AVDiT [(Wang et al., 2024a)], and Uni-Renderer [(Chen et al., 2025b)], but none addresses imperfect auxiliary modalities at inference time. Our key contribution is applying this idea to the RGB-irradiance pairing, combined with domain matching and hijacked inference to handle noisy real-world irradiance cues.

    Multi-illumination dataset.

    Training a video relighting network requires paired multi-illumination data with lighting annotation. Existing datasets [(Murmann et al., 2019; Teufel et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023)] mainly cover static images in restricted scenarios, and prior works [(Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)] use only simple rendered scenes. Unreal Engine 5 [(Epic Games, 2019)] enables high-quality human-centric multi-illumination video synthesis with accurate lighting annotation.

    3. Preliminary

    Our study builds on a transformer-based latent diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. The architecture comprises a 3D Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and a diffusion transformer (DiT) of spatio-temporal transformer blocks. Each block integrates 3D spatio-temporal self-attention, cross-attention, feed-forward network, and gate modulation. The generative process can be defined as a mapping between samples x₁ from a noise distribution to samples from a data distribution x₀ in terms of an ordinary differential equation (ODE),

    (1)dzₜ=v_Θ(zₜ,t)dt,

    where the velocity v is parameterized by the weights Θ of the diffusion transformer and t denotes the timestep. The noise scheduling follows the Rectified Flow framework [(Liu et al., 2022; Esser et al., 2024)]. Let z₀ denote a clean latent, ε∼ℕ(0,I) a Gaussian-noise latent, and t∈[0,1] a continuous noise level, where t=0 is clean data and t=1 is noise. Rectified Flow defines a straight interpolation

    (2)zₜ=ψₜ(z₀|ε)=(1-t)z₀+tε.

    The target velocity along this path is uₜ=ε-z₀. The Conditional Flow Matching objective regresses this vector field with an MSE loss:

    (3)L_CFM=𝔼_t,z₀,ε[\lVertv_Θ(zₜ,t)-(ε-z₀)\rVert²₂],

    where v_Θ is the predicted velocity. At inference, integrating the learned ODE from noise toward data produces a clean sample.

    4. Training Dataset

    We build an automated UE5 pipeline for multi-illumination videos. Our assets include 30 3D environments, 60 characters, 600 body animations, 20 facial expressions, and 821 HDR environment maps. Figure 4 overviews the dataset. For each scene, a character is randomly placed and animated, while the camera is assigned random distance, rotation, and oscillation. Ray intersection tests prevent interpenetration. We use UE5’s real-time global illumination system Lumen [(Tan, 2024)] for efficient low-frequency approximation, and add a directional light to match the brightest region of the environment map. LightingOnly mode renders the irradiance map synchronously. Each scene is rendered under 10 illuminations, with 20% using rotary lighting. In total, we render 68K videos at 832×480 resolution, 94 frames each, with paired irradiance maps. Lighting parameters are recorded, and prompts are generated using a video understanding model [(Zhang et al., 2025a)]. Among the 30 scene environments, 12 are indoor scenes and 18 are outdoor scenes. The 821 HDR environment maps are collected from public resources such as Poly Haven, covering diverse illumination conditions including outdoor daytime, indoor, and outdoor nighttime settings. We pair the MetaHuman characters with Mixamo animations and mainly keep in-place motions such as talking, dancing, and fighting, while filtering out large-displacement motions such as walking and running to better match our camera setup.

    The set contains 31 male-presenting and 29 female-presenting characters; 22 dark-, 12 medium-, and 26 light-skinned characters; and 4 child, 43 adult, and 13 older characters. Our dataset focuses on human-centric indoor and outdoor scenarios, enabling precise lighting control over human subjects. Despite being trained purely on synthetic data, our model generalizes well to real-world videos. We attribute this to the high photorealism of UE5-rendered content, which substantially reduces the sim-to-real gap compared to prior Blender-based synthetic datasets. This aligns with observations from prior works trained exclusively on UE-rendered videos, such as ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)] and Context-as-Memory [(Yu et al., 2025)].

    5. Method

    We first describe how to construct the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ for an input video V^I, then present our asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling and hijacked inference strategy for generating the relit video V and refined irradiance map Êᶜᵘᵉ.

    5.1. Irradiance cue

    An irradiance cue describes diffuse light transport obtained by rendering scene geometry with target lighting. Previous works [(Zeng et al., 2024b; Erel et al., 2025)] use monocular depth [(Bhat et al., 2023)] and unproject it to a mesh. We instead use monocular point-cloud estimation [(Wang et al., 2025e; Wang et al., 2025f)] to obtain metric-level geometry and smoother meshes. We convert each estimated point cloud into a per-frame mesh and remove triangles spanning depth discontinuities with a fixed threshold-based mask. We assign a spatially uniform white diffuse BRDF , illuminate the mesh with the target environment map, and render it using Mitsuba 3 [(Jakob et al., 2022)]. Repeating this process independently for every frame yields the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ∈ℝ^F×H×W×3 for an input video V. Per-frame estimation avoids accumulating global reconstruction drift, but geometry errors, removed boundary triangles, and temporal inconsistency still create a substantial gap from the ground-truth irradiance E (Figure 3).

    5.2. Joint modeling with separate timestep scheduling

    Noise Corruption.

    Directly using the imperfect irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ causes model confusion due to pixel misalignment. To retain its low-frequency lighting prior while suppressing artifacts, we corrupt it with Gaussian noise ε:

    (4)Eᶜᵘᵉₜ=(1-t)Eᶜᵘᵉ+tε.

    In this way, the high-frequency artifacts are removed and the global light transport prior is preserved. Simple hole filling or spatial blurring cannot reliably reconstruct light transport around undefined geometry and may erase useful low-frequency lighting structure; joint denoising instead learns how much of the corrupted cue to retain. To exploit this prior, we jointly model irradiance maps and RGB videos within the diffusion framework.

    Model design.

    Given an input video V^I and a text prompt p, we train a model v_Θ that jointly denoises the relit RGB video V and irradiance map E using separate timesteps t_V and t_E. This allows the model to learn denoising under mismatched noise levels and enables inference with noisy irradiance conditions (Section 5.3). As illustrated in Figure 2, we concatenate the latents of noisy RGB video z_t_V^V, noisy irradiance map z_t_E^E and input video z₀^I along the frame dimension and feed into the transformer. This simple strategy allows the 3D spatial-temporal self-attention to cover input, irradiance and relit frames, enabling cross-modal understanding. While asynchronous timestep scheduling has been explored in prior multi-modal diffusion work [(Bao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2025b)], our contribution lies in applying it to the RGB-irradiance pairing, where the auxiliary modality is imperfect at inference time. This motivates our domain matching strategy and hijacked inference pipeline, which are essential for bridging the gap to noisy real-world irradiance cues.

    Modality disambiguation.

    Since the three input modalities share pixel alignment, we apply the same RoPE [(Su et al., 2024)] to assign shared spatial-temporal positions. To distinguish modalities, we introduce a learnable modality embedding on top of the timestep embedding, whose gate modulation already conditions features on timestep. Unlike prior designs that inject modality embeddings into latent features, this better avoids modality mixture in our setting.

    Domain matching

    Since the model only observes the ground-truth irradiance map E during standard training, conditioning on imperfect irradiance cues at inference introduces a domain gap. We address this with a domain matching paradigm: at random training iterations, we replace the noisy irradiance map zₜ^E with the noisy cue zₜ^Eᶜᵘᵉ. This encourages denoising towards a probability path closer to the high-quality manifold and improves both RGB and irradiance generation. This design is fundamentally different from previous joint cross-modal modeling methods, which usually assume clean and reliable modalities during both training and inference. In contrast, our framework is explicitly designed for imperfect irradiance cues with domain discrepancies, which are common in practical relighting settings. It also differs from prior irradiance-conditioned methods that directly feed the estimated cue into the generator, making them more vulnerable to accumulated geometry and rendering errors.

    5.3. Hijacked asynchronous inference strategy

    In Section 5.1 we show how to construct the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ, given an input video and a target lighting condition. In order to utilize it during inference, we design a hijacked conditional inference strategy that guides the sampling process towards the probability path indicated by the irradiance cue. We illustrate this process in Figure 3. Specifically, we obtain the noisy irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ_tₕ with Eq. 4, where tₕ is the hijack timestep. Before tₕ, at each timestep only the noisy RGB latents are updated while the irradiance latents remain fixed at Eᶜᵘᵉ_tₕ. After tₕ, the two modalities are denoised together. This strategy effectively utilizes low-frequency lighting prior provided by the noisy irradiance map, while removing high-frequency artifacts by joint denoising. The hyperparameter tₕ controls the amount of noise that is added to the irradiance cue, offering a flexible tradeoff between generation quality and lighting fidelity. In practice, we find that tₕ=0.6T works well for most cases. When the irradiance cue is reliable, a smaller tₕ helps preserve more high-frequency appearance details. When the cue is noisy or less aligned, a larger tₕ is preferable because it suppresses artifacts more aggressively.

    6. Experiments

    Implementation details.

    We fine-tune Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [(Wan et al., 2025)] for 12K steps at 832×480 resolution using a learning rate of 10⁻⁵ and batch size 16. Domain matching is applied only during the last 4K steps. We apply this second-stage training after the first-stage joint modeling has largely converged, and empirically find that 4K steps are sufficient for the model to adapt to the imperfect irradiance-cue distribution. To further mitigate the visual characteristics of synthetic training data, we adopt a noise augmentation strategy inspired by ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)]: a moderate level of noise (equivalent to 200–500 diffusion timesteps) is added to the conditional video latent during training, which discourages the model from relying on domain-specific synthetic cues and improves robustness at real-world inference time. We set the hijack timestep to tₕ=0.6T for every experiment and do not retune it case by case.

    Baselines

    We compare our method with the publicly available video relighting method DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] and Light-X [(Liu et al., 2025a)]. Image relighting methods DiLightNet [(Zeng et al., 2024b)] and Neural-Gaffer [(Jin et al., 2024)] are also included. We adopt the Cosmos [(Agarwal et al., 2025)] implementation version of DiffusionRenderer for a fair comparison. These methods allow environment maps as control signals. We additionally include prompt-based relighting methods, including IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025b)], Light-A-Video [(Zhou et al., 2025)], TC-Light [(Liu et al., 2025b)]. For environment-map-conditioned methods we use the identical target HDR map; prompt-based methods instead receive best-effort captions derived from the target lighting, so exact direction and intensity cannot be guaranteed.

    Datasets

    We use the test subset of our synthetic dataset for quantitative evaluation. It contains 100 test cases: 50 static-lighting cases (SynthStatic) and 50 rotary-lighting cases (SynthDynamic), each with an input video, relit target, and target environment map. For qualitative comparison, test cases are sampled from the HumanVid [(Wang et al., 2024b)] dataset. Since there is no publicly available video relighting dataset for quantitative evaluation, we follow previous video relighting methods such as DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] by using our proposed synthetic dataset for the video benchmark. To test cross-dataset generalization independently of our synthetic renderer, we additionally evaluate static images from HumanOLAT [(Teufel et al., 2025)].

    Metrics.

    We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. We also conduct a user study on visual quality and illumination accuracy. Following prior works [(Jin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)], we avoid per-channel rescaling and instead compare results directly with ground truth, enabling faithful evaluation of relighting fidelity.

    6.1. Evaluation

    Qualitative comparison

    Figures 5 and  6 compare vertical and horizontal cases, respectively; the latter includes SynthStatic examples. Prompt-based methods including IC-Light, TC-Light, and Light-A-Video produce appealing lighting styles, but cannot precisely control lighting direction or ambient color because text prompts are ambiguous. These methods often produce warm tones and can retain hard input shadows, as in the second case of Figure 5. Light-X and Neural Gaffer inherits much of the input lighting distribution and mainly modifies color tone, while DiLightNet produces low-quality results caused by inaccurate material estimates. DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight performs reasonably well in terms of light direction and color. However, inaccurate material estimation yields unrealistic skin and clothing textures (Figs. 6 and 5). It also causes identity drift, demonstrated on the third case of Figure 6. More importantly, implicit light transport modeling sometimes fails to produce physically correct results. In Fig. 5 (third case), DiffusionRenderer mistakes yellow ambient light for the main source, ignoring the actual moon light. In contrast, our method models light transport with guidance from the path-traced irradiance cue, facilitating physically accurate illumination control. Although trained on human-centric data, our method also generalizes to the cat example in Figure  6.

    Quantitative comparison

    Table 1 confirms the qualitative observation that DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight respond more faithfully to environment maps than the other baselines. We evaluate on 100 test cases in total, with 50 cases from SynthStatic and 50 from SynthDynamic. For prompt-based methods, we ask GPT 5.4 to describe the lighting in the ground truth video and use the caption as text prompt input. For image-based methods, we perform relighting frame by frame. Our method obtains the best PSNR and LPIPS on SynthStatic, while UniRelight obtains the best SSIM. On SynthDynamic, our method is best on all three metrics. The larger advantage under rotating illumination indicates that explicit irradiance guidance improves controllability when the target lighting changes over time.

    HumanOLAT evaluation

    We synthesize ground-truth relit images from HumanOLAT OLAT captures under 100 HDR environment maps. We apply the provided foreground masks before computing metrics and do not perform per-channel rescaling. Table 2 shows that our model, trained without HumanOLAT data, achieves the best performance among all evaluated methods. Qualitative comparison is presented in Figure 11

    User study

    A user study evaluated perceptual quality on in-the-wild videos. Participants viewed the relighting results, the input video, and the environment map, and rated methods from 1 to 5 on visual quality (VQ) and lighting fidelity (LF). The study involved 13 in-lab users, and average scores are reported in Table 1. We evaluate 15 indoor and outdoor test cases in total. Before the study, we explain that visual quality measures the overall perceptual realism, including artifacts and temporal stability, while lighting fidelity evaluates how well the generated result matches the target illumination in terms of light direction, shadow, and highlight consistency. Compared to baselines, our results are consistently preferred on both dimensions.

    Dynamic scenes with dynamic illumination

    Thanks to explicit light transport guidance from asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling, our method naturally extends to dynamic scenes with dynamic illumination. Figure 7 shows results sampled every 10 frames. Our method faithfully follows the sun direction and produces physically plausible lighting effects.

    Runtime

    For an 81-frame, 832×480 video sampled with 50 diffusion steps on one NVIDIA A800 GPU, the full pipeline takes 223 s: 22.8 s for depth estimation, 38.2 s for mesh conversion, 18.8 s for Mitsuba rendering, and 141.9 s for neural generation (minor overhead accounts for the remaining time). Under the same evaluation setting, UniRelight, DiffusionRenderer, and Light-A-Video take 1077 s, 1629 s, and 1822 s, respectively. Thus, external reconstruction and rendering are not the main runtime bottleneck.

    7. Ablation study

    Qualitative ablation

    We conduct ablation study on our asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling and domain matching strategy with qualitative results in Figure 10. Without the asynchronous joint modeling training paradigm, simply using the irradiance cue as control signal, the model fails to follow the light transport. Joint modeling alone does not sufficiently bridge the domain gap; domain matching is essential for producing pixel-aligned irradiance maps and physically plausible RGB results. Without it, the denoised irradiance maps exhibit black edges and blurred details, leading to suboptimal outputs. In contrast, the full recipe generates pixel-aligned RGB and irradiance images, producing physically accurate and visually plausible results.

    Quantitative ablation

    We report quantitative ablation results in Tables 3 and 4. We additionally train a no-irradiance variant that receives only the target HDR environment map under the same data and optimization protocol, analogous to HDR-conditioned implicit relighting. All ablation models are trained for 6K steps, with domain matching applied during the final 2K steps. HDR map conditioning does not provide pixel-aligned guidance for light distribution, which produces less accurate relighting results compared to irradiance conditioning. Joint modeling irradiance and RGB alone brings limited gains because the imperfect irradiance cue still causes a noticeable train-test mismatch. Introducing hijacked conditional generation and asynchronous timestep scheduling progressively improves both lighting fidelity and visual quality, while the domain matching strategy delivers the final performance boost by explicitly aligning the cue distribution with inference-time inputs. We also compare different modality embedding strategies and find that injecting the modality cue through the time embedding performs best, likely because it modulates the denoising process globally and reduces the ambiguity between RGB appearance and irradiance guidance.

    8. Discussion

    We present JointLight, a human-centric video relighting framework that jointly models RGB and irradiance asynchronously. We also introduce a high-quality human-centric multi-illumination synthetic dataset covering indoor and outdoor scenarios, paired with ground-truth irradiance maps. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model achieves state-of-the-art relighting quality and fidelity.

    Robustness to geometry errors

    Our method depends on monocular geometry only through the rendered irradiance cue. Because geometry is estimated independently per frame, errors do not accumulate as global reconstruction drift. Noise injection suppresses high-frequency defects such as jagged boundaries, holes, and aliased shadows, but cannot recover light transport that is absent from severely incorrect geometry. Aggressive subject or camera motion can also produce blur and occlusion errors. Incorrect depths or holes near discontinuities may distort the path-traced cue and can cause light leakage (the bottom-right case in Figure 9).

    Limitations and Future Work

    First, irradiance provides diffuse transport only and therefore cannot explicitly or physically control full specular transport. Video priors can synthesize plausible moderate highlights on skin and hair, but these effects are not guaranteed to follow the target illumination; polished metal, mirrors, and glass remain difficult. A failure case is shown in the bottom-right case of Figure 9. Second, suppressing high-frequency cue errors can also attenuate texture-rich appearance, occasionally over-smoothing fine facial details around the eyes and mouth. Future work could jointly reason about geometry, material, diffuse and specular transport, and use detail-preserving or preference-based post-training. Extending the control representation beyond environment maps to local spotlights or flashlights is another promising direction.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62322210, 62561160115), the Beijing Major Science and Technology Project (No. Z251100008125009), the Royal Society (IEC \233596), and the Innovation Funding of ICT, CAS (No. E561100).

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：异步联合建模 RGB 与辐照度、分阶段去噪时间表，两阶段训练补齐控制精度。

要点：

  • 端到端重光照把光传输隐进网络里，可控性差；直接用路径追踪辐照度图当显式蓝图又带瑕疵、拖累生成质量。
  • 关键观察：噪声破坏能去掉高频瑕疵而保留低频光传输，因此采用异步联合建模——在同一模型里用不同时间表分别去噪 RGB 与真值辐照度帧。
  • 两阶段训练，第二阶段引入域匹配策略弥合「辐照度提示」与「真值辐照度」的域差，从而获得细粒度光照控制。

为什么值得看：虚拟制片与游戏内人像重光照都受限于光照可控性，把辐照度当显式中间量并解决其域差，是比纯端到端更可调的路线。

中文摘要：人像场景中的光传输建模长期困难：扩散模型推动了重光照研究，但精确光照控制仍落后，主因是缺少多样、高质量且标注精确的视频重光照数据。端到端方法把光传输隐式学进网络，可控性变差；另一些工作用路径追踪辐照度线索作为显式蓝图，但这类线索带瑕疵，直接当控制信号会拖累生成质量。JointLight 观察到噪声破坏会去掉高频瑕疵而保留低频光传输，于是采用异步联合建模：训练时用不同时间表同时去噪 RGB 与真值辐照度帧，第二阶段再用域匹配弥合辐照度线索与真值之间的域差。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-23

JointLight: Human-Centric Video Relighting with Asynchronous RGB-Irradiance Joint Modeling

© cc

Abstract.

Understanding and modeling light transport in human-centric scenes is a longstanding challenge. While recent progress in diffusion models has boosted research in relighting, precise illumination control still lags, primarily due to the scarcity of diverse, high-quality, precisely labeled video relighting datasets. Existing end-to-end relighting approaches model light transport implicitly through neural networks, which substantially complicates controllability. In contrast, some works resort to path-traced irradiance cues as an explicit blueprint for light transport. However, such constructed irradiance cues are prone to artifacts and hinder generative quality when directly used as control signals. With the key observation that noise corruption removes high-frequency artifacts and preserves low-frequency light transport, we introduce an asynchronous joint-modeling paradigm that facilitates fine-grained illumination control. During two-stage training, we force the model to jointly denoise RGB and ground-truth irradiance frames with separate timesteps scheduling. A domain matching strategy is applied to the second stage to bridge the domain gap between irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps. At inference time, we introduce an asynchronous hijacked generation pipeline that facilitates flexible illumination control. For training data, we develop a multi-illumination high-quality synthetic video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model exhibits robust generalization to real-world scenarios and outperforms prior approaches in both lighting fidelity and generative quality. Project page: http://www.geometrylearning.com/JointLight/

Keywords:

Human-Centric Video Relighting, Diffusion Models, Irradiance Map, Illumination Control ††cc-license: by-nc-nd

1. Introduction

Lighting fundamentally affects how we perceive a scene. Modifying lighting while preserving scene identity enables a wide range of applications, such as artistic creation, film production, augmented reality, and computer vision research. Fundamentally, relighting requires an understanding of how light interacts with the scene. Traditional graphics pipelines simulate physical light transport with explicit geometry and materials. For objects and portraits, meticulously calibrated studio equipment [(Debevec, 2012)] is used to reconstruct geometry and capture reflectance fields. However, real-world scenes comprise complex combinations of objects and persons, of which the geometry and material properties are impractical to capture. Relighting of human-centric scenes in diverse indoor and outdoor environments thus remains a challenging task.

With the advent of powerful generative models, relighting with a single image or video input has drawn increasing attention. It is an innately ill-posed problem, since geometry, material, and lighting are all coupled in the single input. Some works [(Zhang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025c)] construct degradation pairs for real-world images or videos and train end-to-end diffusion models for relighting. These methods, lacking explicit physical light transport modeling, are typically constrained to text prompts or environment maps as conditioning inputs, failing to offer precise control over lighting parameters such as light source angles. Some other works [(Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)] utilize graphics engines to construct synthetic data, enabling relighting with environment maps as a condition. Such synthetic data are limited to simple object-centric scenes, hindering generalization to complex human-centric real-world scenarios. More importantly, implicit light transport modeling within neural networks cannot guarantee physical accuracy.

Recent advances in monocular geometry estimation [(Wang et al., 2025e; Wang et al., 2025f; Lin et al., 2025; Mescheder et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a)] have opened new avenues for scene relighting. While monocular point clouds serve as a coarse geometric proxy, they are unsuitable for direct integration into traditional graphics pipelines due to single-layer geometry and artifacts from depth discontinuities at object boundaries. With a diffuse white BRDF and physics-based rendering, this proxy produces an irradiance cue that characterizes the scene’s diffuse light transport, as illustrated in Figure 3. Although this irradiance cue remains plagued by artifacts and exhibits a significant domain gap relative to the ground-truth irradiance map, we propose that this discrepancy can be effectively bridged through noise corruption. The key observation is that after blending with a certain amount of Gaussian noise, the rough irradiance cue and ground-truth irradiance map become indistinguishable. In this way, noise corruption mitigates the domain gap by removing high-frequency artifacts and preserving low-frequency content. We then model this rough irradiance distribution via the diffusion process. During training, the model jointly denoises RGB video and irradiance maps with separate timestep scheduling, learning to transform a noised irradiance cue into a pixel-aligned fine-grained irradiance map. At inference time, we render the irradiance cue using a geometry estimate and the target lighting with a path tracer. The irradiance cue is then noised and jointly denoised with the RGB video.

For training data, we develop a large-scale human-centric multi-illumination video dataset with paired irradiance maps using a powerful game engine. It contains 68K synthetic videos from 6.8K dynamic scenes across 30 artist-made 3D environments. A character performing random actions is placed in the center of the camera, where random camera shake and camera movement are applied. Each scene is rendered with 10 different lighting conditions sampled from 821 HDR environment maps, of which 20% are set to rotating.

Experimental results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art realistic video relighting approaches in both relighting fidelity and video quality. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of our key designs. To summarize, we present three main contributions:

  • •

    An asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint-modeling approach with separate timestep scheduling, plus a domain matching strategy that bridges the gap between noisy irradiance cues and ground-truth irradiance maps.

  • •

    A high-quality human-centric multi-illumination video dataset with paired irradiance maps across diverse indoor and outdoor lighting conditions. This dataset will be publicly released to advance research in human-centric video relighting and intrinsic decomposition.

  • •

    Extensive experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art results on video relighting in both visual quality and lighting fidelity.

    • 2. Related Work

    Human-centric scene relighting.

    While object-centric [(Jin et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024b; Wu et al., 2024; Bharadwaj et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2025)] and portrait-centric [(Lv et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2023; Saito et al., 2024; Chaturvedi et al., 2025; Mei et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Zhang et al., 2024)] static relighting have been extensively explored, human-centric video relighting in dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes remains underexplored. Many works [(Zhang et al., 2025b; Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2024)] rely on degradation pairs with text prompts or environment maps, but provide only coarse control and often produce stylized results. [(Liang et al., 2026)] use path tracing rendering as an anchor point to online optimize static relighting results, which cannot extend to dynamic scenes. DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] curates synthetic multi-illumination data with simple objects and paired G-buffers, training separate inverse and forward rendering models. UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] further extends this to end-to-end video relighting. However, both methods input environment maps directly without explicit light transport guidance, limiting generalization in complex scenes with occlusions. In contrast, our method targets general dynamic scenes beyond portraits and employs physically-based irradiance cues to achieve more accurate lighting control.

    Several related systems target narrower capture settings or different control interfaces. SwitchLight [(Kim et al., 2024)] decomposes a single portrait using a physics-guided architecture and relights it from an environment map, whereas DifFRelight [(He et al., 2024)] learns subject-specific facial-performance relighting from light-stage data. Relightable Full-Body Gaussian Codec Avatars [(Wang et al., 2025d)] models local and non-local light transport for captured, personalized avatars. ReLumix [(Wang et al., 2025b)] propagates the illumination of one artist-relit reference frame through a video rather than taking a target environment map directly. The commercial Runway Relight Scene system [(Runway, 2026)] instead uses text descriptions to edit the atmosphere of short videos. These methods demonstrate complementary progress, but do not address pixel-aligned, environment-map-controlled relighting of general monocular human-centric videos in the wild.

    RGB↔X [(Zeng et al., 2024a)] shows pixel-aligned irradiance maps can serve as lighting control signals, but require an existing clean irradiance map as input. DiLightNet [(Zeng et al., 2024b)], PractiLight [(Erel et al., 2025)], and Lightit [(Kocsis et al., 2024)] compute irradiance cues from target lighting and coarse depth, but misalignment with the input image due to noisy geometry undermines relighting quality. Portrait-specific relighting methods such as Total Relighting [(Pandey et al., 2021)] focus on human faces and use image-based lighting without path-traced shadows, which is suitable for portrait photography but less applicable to general scenes.

    Joint cross-modal modeling.

    Diffusion models have been applied to jointly model pixel-aligned attributes such as depth [(Li et al., 2025; Byung-Ki et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025a)], motion [(Chefer et al., 2025)], and PBR attributes [(Xi et al., 2025b; He et al., 2025)]. Joint modeling approaches include dual-stream cross-attention [(Li et al., 2025; Byung-Ki et al., 2025)] and various single-model injection paradigms [(Chefer et al., 2025; Xi et al., 2025a; Xi et al., 2025b; He et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025a)]. Most such methods assume clean auxiliary modalities; in contrast, we must handle imperfect irradiance cues with substantial geometry artifacts—a domain-gap issue largely unexplored in prior work. The use of per-modality asynchronous timestep schedules has been explored in UniDiffuser [(Bao et al., 2023)], AVDiT [(Wang et al., 2024a)], and Uni-Renderer [(Chen et al., 2025b)], but none addresses imperfect auxiliary modalities at inference time. Our key contribution is applying this idea to the RGB-irradiance pairing, combined with domain matching and hijacked inference to handle noisy real-world irradiance cues.

    Multi-illumination dataset.

    Training a video relighting network requires paired multi-illumination data with lighting annotation. Existing datasets [(Murmann et al., 2019; Teufel et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023)] mainly cover static images in restricted scenarios, and prior works [(Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)] use only simple rendered scenes. Unreal Engine 5 [(Epic Games, 2019)] enables high-quality human-centric multi-illumination video synthesis with accurate lighting annotation.

    3. Preliminary

    Our study builds on a transformer-based latent diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)]. The architecture comprises a 3D Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and a diffusion transformer (DiT) of spatio-temporal transformer blocks. Each block integrates 3D spatio-temporal self-attention, cross-attention, feed-forward network, and gate modulation. The generative process can be defined as a mapping between samples x₁ from a noise distribution to samples from a data distribution x₀ in terms of an ordinary differential equation (ODE),

    (1)dzₜ=v_Θ(zₜ,t)dt,

    where the velocity v is parameterized by the weights Θ of the diffusion transformer and t denotes the timestep. The noise scheduling follows the Rectified Flow framework [(Liu et al., 2022; Esser et al., 2024)]. Let z₀ denote a clean latent, ε∼ℕ(0,I) a Gaussian-noise latent, and t∈[0,1] a continuous noise level, where t=0 is clean data and t=1 is noise. Rectified Flow defines a straight interpolation

    (2)zₜ=ψₜ(z₀|ε)=(1-t)z₀+tε.

    The target velocity along this path is uₜ=ε-z₀. The Conditional Flow Matching objective regresses this vector field with an MSE loss:

    (3)L_CFM=𝔼_t,z₀,ε[\lVertv_Θ(zₜ,t)-(ε-z₀)\rVert²₂],

    where v_Θ is the predicted velocity. At inference, integrating the learned ODE from noise toward data produces a clean sample.

    4. Training Dataset

    We build an automated UE5 pipeline for multi-illumination videos. Our assets include 30 3D environments, 60 characters, 600 body animations, 20 facial expressions, and 821 HDR environment maps. Figure 4 overviews the dataset. For each scene, a character is randomly placed and animated, while the camera is assigned random distance, rotation, and oscillation. Ray intersection tests prevent interpenetration. We use UE5’s real-time global illumination system Lumen [(Tan, 2024)] for efficient low-frequency approximation, and add a directional light to match the brightest region of the environment map. LightingOnly mode renders the irradiance map synchronously. Each scene is rendered under 10 illuminations, with 20% using rotary lighting. In total, we render 68K videos at 832×480 resolution, 94 frames each, with paired irradiance maps. Lighting parameters are recorded, and prompts are generated using a video understanding model [(Zhang et al., 2025a)]. Among the 30 scene environments, 12 are indoor scenes and 18 are outdoor scenes. The 821 HDR environment maps are collected from public resources such as Poly Haven, covering diverse illumination conditions including outdoor daytime, indoor, and outdoor nighttime settings. We pair the MetaHuman characters with Mixamo animations and mainly keep in-place motions such as talking, dancing, and fighting, while filtering out large-displacement motions such as walking and running to better match our camera setup.

    The set contains 31 male-presenting and 29 female-presenting characters; 22 dark-, 12 medium-, and 26 light-skinned characters; and 4 child, 43 adult, and 13 older characters. Our dataset focuses on human-centric indoor and outdoor scenarios, enabling precise lighting control over human subjects. Despite being trained purely on synthetic data, our model generalizes well to real-world videos. We attribute this to the high photorealism of UE5-rendered content, which substantially reduces the sim-to-real gap compared to prior Blender-based synthetic datasets. This aligns with observations from prior works trained exclusively on UE-rendered videos, such as ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)] and Context-as-Memory [(Yu et al., 2025)].

    5. Method

    We first describe how to construct the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ for an input video V^I, then present our asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling and hijacked inference strategy for generating the relit video V and refined irradiance map Êᶜᵘᵉ.

    5.1. Irradiance cue

    An irradiance cue describes diffuse light transport obtained by rendering scene geometry with target lighting. Previous works [(Zeng et al., 2024b; Erel et al., 2025)] use monocular depth [(Bhat et al., 2023)] and unproject it to a mesh. We instead use monocular point-cloud estimation [(Wang et al., 2025e; Wang et al., 2025f)] to obtain metric-level geometry and smoother meshes. We convert each estimated point cloud into a per-frame mesh and remove triangles spanning depth discontinuities with a fixed threshold-based mask. We assign a spatially uniform white diffuse BRDF , illuminate the mesh with the target environment map, and render it using Mitsuba 3 [(Jakob et al., 2022)]. Repeating this process independently for every frame yields the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ∈ℝ^F×H×W×3 for an input video V. Per-frame estimation avoids accumulating global reconstruction drift, but geometry errors, removed boundary triangles, and temporal inconsistency still create a substantial gap from the ground-truth irradiance E (Figure 3).

    5.2. Joint modeling with separate timestep scheduling

    Noise Corruption.

    Directly using the imperfect irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ causes model confusion due to pixel misalignment. To retain its low-frequency lighting prior while suppressing artifacts, we corrupt it with Gaussian noise ε:

    (4)Eᶜᵘᵉₜ=(1-t)Eᶜᵘᵉ+tε.

    In this way, the high-frequency artifacts are removed and the global light transport prior is preserved. Simple hole filling or spatial blurring cannot reliably reconstruct light transport around undefined geometry and may erase useful low-frequency lighting structure; joint denoising instead learns how much of the corrupted cue to retain. To exploit this prior, we jointly model irradiance maps and RGB videos within the diffusion framework.

    Model design.

    Given an input video V^I and a text prompt p, we train a model v_Θ that jointly denoises the relit RGB video V and irradiance map E using separate timesteps t_V and t_E. This allows the model to learn denoising under mismatched noise levels and enables inference with noisy irradiance conditions (Section 5.3). As illustrated in Figure 2, we concatenate the latents of noisy RGB video z_t_V^V, noisy irradiance map z_t_E^E and input video z₀^I along the frame dimension and feed into the transformer. This simple strategy allows the 3D spatial-temporal self-attention to cover input, irradiance and relit frames, enabling cross-modal understanding. While asynchronous timestep scheduling has been explored in prior multi-modal diffusion work [(Bao et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Chen et al., 2025b)], our contribution lies in applying it to the RGB-irradiance pairing, where the auxiliary modality is imperfect at inference time. This motivates our domain matching strategy and hijacked inference pipeline, which are essential for bridging the gap to noisy real-world irradiance cues.

    Modality disambiguation.

    Since the three input modalities share pixel alignment, we apply the same RoPE [(Su et al., 2024)] to assign shared spatial-temporal positions. To distinguish modalities, we introduce a learnable modality embedding on top of the timestep embedding, whose gate modulation already conditions features on timestep. Unlike prior designs that inject modality embeddings into latent features, this better avoids modality mixture in our setting.

    Domain matching

    Since the model only observes the ground-truth irradiance map E during standard training, conditioning on imperfect irradiance cues at inference introduces a domain gap. We address this with a domain matching paradigm: at random training iterations, we replace the noisy irradiance map zₜ^E with the noisy cue zₜ^Eᶜᵘᵉ. This encourages denoising towards a probability path closer to the high-quality manifold and improves both RGB and irradiance generation. This design is fundamentally different from previous joint cross-modal modeling methods, which usually assume clean and reliable modalities during both training and inference. In contrast, our framework is explicitly designed for imperfect irradiance cues with domain discrepancies, which are common in practical relighting settings. It also differs from prior irradiance-conditioned methods that directly feed the estimated cue into the generator, making them more vulnerable to accumulated geometry and rendering errors.

    5.3. Hijacked asynchronous inference strategy

    In Section 5.1 we show how to construct the irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ, given an input video and a target lighting condition. In order to utilize it during inference, we design a hijacked conditional inference strategy that guides the sampling process towards the probability path indicated by the irradiance cue. We illustrate this process in Figure 3. Specifically, we obtain the noisy irradiance cue Eᶜᵘᵉ_tₕ with Eq. 4, where tₕ is the hijack timestep. Before tₕ, at each timestep only the noisy RGB latents are updated while the irradiance latents remain fixed at Eᶜᵘᵉ_tₕ. After tₕ, the two modalities are denoised together. This strategy effectively utilizes low-frequency lighting prior provided by the noisy irradiance map, while removing high-frequency artifacts by joint denoising. The hyperparameter tₕ controls the amount of noise that is added to the irradiance cue, offering a flexible tradeoff between generation quality and lighting fidelity. In practice, we find that tₕ=0.6T works well for most cases. When the irradiance cue is reliable, a smaller tₕ helps preserve more high-frequency appearance details. When the cue is noisy or less aligned, a larger tₕ is preferable because it suppresses artifacts more aggressively.

    6. Experiments

    Implementation details.

    We fine-tune Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [(Wan et al., 2025)] for 12K steps at 832×480 resolution using a learning rate of 10⁻⁵ and batch size 16. Domain matching is applied only during the last 4K steps. We apply this second-stage training after the first-stage joint modeling has largely converged, and empirically find that 4K steps are sufficient for the model to adapt to the imperfect irradiance-cue distribution. To further mitigate the visual characteristics of synthetic training data, we adopt a noise augmentation strategy inspired by ReCamMaster [(Bai et al., 2025)]: a moderate level of noise (equivalent to 200–500 diffusion timesteps) is added to the conditional video latent during training, which discourages the model from relying on domain-specific synthetic cues and improves robustness at real-world inference time. We set the hijack timestep to tₕ=0.6T for every experiment and do not retune it case by case.

    Baselines

    We compare our method with the publicly available video relighting method DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)], UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] and Light-X [(Liu et al., 2025a)]. Image relighting methods DiLightNet [(Zeng et al., 2024b)] and Neural-Gaffer [(Jin et al., 2024)] are also included. We adopt the Cosmos [(Agarwal et al., 2025)] implementation version of DiffusionRenderer for a fair comparison. These methods allow environment maps as control signals. We additionally include prompt-based relighting methods, including IC-Light [(Zhang et al., 2025b)], Light-A-Video [(Zhou et al., 2025)], TC-Light [(Liu et al., 2025b)]. For environment-map-conditioned methods we use the identical target HDR map; prompt-based methods instead receive best-effort captions derived from the target lighting, so exact direction and intensity cannot be guaranteed.

    Datasets

    We use the test subset of our synthetic dataset for quantitative evaluation. It contains 100 test cases: 50 static-lighting cases (SynthStatic) and 50 rotary-lighting cases (SynthDynamic), each with an input video, relit target, and target environment map. For qualitative comparison, test cases are sampled from the HumanVid [(Wang et al., 2024b)] dataset. Since there is no publicly available video relighting dataset for quantitative evaluation, we follow previous video relighting methods such as DiffusionRenderer [(Liang et al., 2025)] and UniRelight [(He et al., 2025)] by using our proposed synthetic dataset for the video benchmark. To test cross-dataset generalization independently of our synthetic renderer, we additionally evaluate static images from HumanOLAT [(Teufel et al., 2025)].

    Metrics.

    We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)]. We also conduct a user study on visual quality and illumination accuracy. Following prior works [(Jin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025; He et al., 2025)], we avoid per-channel rescaling and instead compare results directly with ground truth, enabling faithful evaluation of relighting fidelity.

    6.1. Evaluation

    Qualitative comparison

    Figures 5 and  6 compare vertical and horizontal cases, respectively; the latter includes SynthStatic examples. Prompt-based methods including IC-Light, TC-Light, and Light-A-Video produce appealing lighting styles, but cannot precisely control lighting direction or ambient color because text prompts are ambiguous. These methods often produce warm tones and can retain hard input shadows, as in the second case of Figure 5. Light-X and Neural Gaffer inherits much of the input lighting distribution and mainly modifies color tone, while DiLightNet produces low-quality results caused by inaccurate material estimates. DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight performs reasonably well in terms of light direction and color. However, inaccurate material estimation yields unrealistic skin and clothing textures (Figs. 6 and 5). It also causes identity drift, demonstrated on the third case of Figure 6. More importantly, implicit light transport modeling sometimes fails to produce physically correct results. In Fig. 5 (third case), DiffusionRenderer mistakes yellow ambient light for the main source, ignoring the actual moon light. In contrast, our method models light transport with guidance from the path-traced irradiance cue, facilitating physically accurate illumination control. Although trained on human-centric data, our method also generalizes to the cat example in Figure  6.

    Quantitative comparison

    Table 1 confirms the qualitative observation that DiffusionRenderer and UniRelight respond more faithfully to environment maps than the other baselines. We evaluate on 100 test cases in total, with 50 cases from SynthStatic and 50 from SynthDynamic. For prompt-based methods, we ask GPT 5.4 to describe the lighting in the ground truth video and use the caption as text prompt input. For image-based methods, we perform relighting frame by frame. Our method obtains the best PSNR and LPIPS on SynthStatic, while UniRelight obtains the best SSIM. On SynthDynamic, our method is best on all three metrics. The larger advantage under rotating illumination indicates that explicit irradiance guidance improves controllability when the target lighting changes over time.

    HumanOLAT evaluation

    We synthesize ground-truth relit images from HumanOLAT OLAT captures under 100 HDR environment maps. We apply the provided foreground masks before computing metrics and do not perform per-channel rescaling. Table 2 shows that our model, trained without HumanOLAT data, achieves the best performance among all evaluated methods. Qualitative comparison is presented in Figure 11

    User study

    A user study evaluated perceptual quality on in-the-wild videos. Participants viewed the relighting results, the input video, and the environment map, and rated methods from 1 to 5 on visual quality (VQ) and lighting fidelity (LF). The study involved 13 in-lab users, and average scores are reported in Table 1. We evaluate 15 indoor and outdoor test cases in total. Before the study, we explain that visual quality measures the overall perceptual realism, including artifacts and temporal stability, while lighting fidelity evaluates how well the generated result matches the target illumination in terms of light direction, shadow, and highlight consistency. Compared to baselines, our results are consistently preferred on both dimensions.

    Dynamic scenes with dynamic illumination

    Thanks to explicit light transport guidance from asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling, our method naturally extends to dynamic scenes with dynamic illumination. Figure 7 shows results sampled every 10 frames. Our method faithfully follows the sun direction and produces physically plausible lighting effects.

    Runtime

    For an 81-frame, 832×480 video sampled with 50 diffusion steps on one NVIDIA A800 GPU, the full pipeline takes 223 s: 22.8 s for depth estimation, 38.2 s for mesh conversion, 18.8 s for Mitsuba rendering, and 141.9 s for neural generation (minor overhead accounts for the remaining time). Under the same evaluation setting, UniRelight, DiffusionRenderer, and Light-A-Video take 1077 s, 1629 s, and 1822 s, respectively. Thus, external reconstruction and rendering are not the main runtime bottleneck.

    7. Ablation study

    Qualitative ablation

    We conduct ablation study on our asynchronous RGB-irradiance joint modeling and domain matching strategy with qualitative results in Figure 10. Without the asynchronous joint modeling training paradigm, simply using the irradiance cue as control signal, the model fails to follow the light transport. Joint modeling alone does not sufficiently bridge the domain gap; domain matching is essential for producing pixel-aligned irradiance maps and physically plausible RGB results. Without it, the denoised irradiance maps exhibit black edges and blurred details, leading to suboptimal outputs. In contrast, the full recipe generates pixel-aligned RGB and irradiance images, producing physically accurate and visually plausible results.

    Quantitative ablation

    We report quantitative ablation results in Tables 3 and 4. We additionally train a no-irradiance variant that receives only the target HDR environment map under the same data and optimization protocol, analogous to HDR-conditioned implicit relighting. All ablation models are trained for 6K steps, with domain matching applied during the final 2K steps. HDR map conditioning does not provide pixel-aligned guidance for light distribution, which produces less accurate relighting results compared to irradiance conditioning. Joint modeling irradiance and RGB alone brings limited gains because the imperfect irradiance cue still causes a noticeable train-test mismatch. Introducing hijacked conditional generation and asynchronous timestep scheduling progressively improves both lighting fidelity and visual quality, while the domain matching strategy delivers the final performance boost by explicitly aligning the cue distribution with inference-time inputs. We also compare different modality embedding strategies and find that injecting the modality cue through the time embedding performs best, likely because it modulates the denoising process globally and reduces the ambiguity between RGB appearance and irradiance guidance.

    8. Discussion

    We present JointLight, a human-centric video relighting framework that jointly models RGB and irradiance asynchronously. We also introduce a high-quality human-centric multi-illumination synthetic dataset covering indoor and outdoor scenarios, paired with ground-truth irradiance maps. Trained exclusively on this dataset, our model achieves state-of-the-art relighting quality and fidelity.

    Robustness to geometry errors

    Our method depends on monocular geometry only through the rendered irradiance cue. Because geometry is estimated independently per frame, errors do not accumulate as global reconstruction drift. Noise injection suppresses high-frequency defects such as jagged boundaries, holes, and aliased shadows, but cannot recover light transport that is absent from severely incorrect geometry. Aggressive subject or camera motion can also produce blur and occlusion errors. Incorrect depths or holes near discontinuities may distort the path-traced cue and can cause light leakage (the bottom-right case in Figure 9).

    Limitations and Future Work

    First, irradiance provides diffuse transport only and therefore cannot explicitly or physically control full specular transport. Video priors can synthesize plausible moderate highlights on skin and hair, but these effects are not guaranteed to follow the target illumination; polished metal, mirrors, and glass remain difficult. A failure case is shown in the bottom-right case of Figure 9. Second, suppressing high-frequency cue errors can also attenuate texture-rich appearance, occasionally over-smoothing fine facial details around the eyes and mouth. Future work could jointly reason about geometry, material, diffuse and specular transport, and use detail-preserving or preference-based post-training. Extending the control representation beyond environment maps to local spotlights or flashlights is another promising direction.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (No. 62322210, 62561160115), the Beijing Major Science and Technology Project (No. Z251100008125009), the Royal Society (IEC \233596), and the Innovation Funding of ICT, CAS (No. E561100).

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: Golden Anchor：首帧图越「好看」，生成的视频反而越差 ｜ Golden Anchor for Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：锚图审美分与下游视频质量弱相关，结构与纹理分甚至负相关；改为按视频反馈选锚图。

要点：

  • 现代图生视频管线里锚图由文生图模型合成，但锚图的美学/质量分与下游视频质量只有弱相关，结构—纹理分在视觉与运动两个维度上都呈负相关。
  • 按图像奖励微调 T2I 会得到结构细节更密的锚图，图像指标更高，却在所测每个 I2V 模型上降低视频奖励并让下游运动变得不可预测。
  • Golden Anchor Learning 用冻结 I2V 模型生成候选视频、把视频奖励转成图像级偏好，用 DPO 微调 T2I 生成器；四个 I2V 模型上都有效。

为什么值得看：做生成式过场/贴图管线时，「先出高质量参考图再生成视频」这条默认链路可能是错的，锚图应当按下游任务指标而不是图像指标来挑。
