We demonstrate this binding capability with 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly binding the anisotropic Gaussian primitives to the learned skinning fields.

    3D Gaussian Representation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [28] represents a scene using anisotropic Gaussian primitives G={G_g}_g=1^N_G, each parameterized as:

    G_g={μ_g, R_g, s_g, α_g, c_g},

    		(25)

    where μ_g∈ℝ³ is the center, R_g∈SO(3) is the rotation matrix, s_g∈ℝ₊³ contains the principal-axis scales, α_g∈[0,1] is the opacity, and c_g denotes the spherical harmonic (SH) appearance coefficients. The corresponding 3D covariance matrix is:

    Σ_g=R_gS_gS_g^⊤R_g^⊤, S_g=diag(s_g).

    		(26)

    For rendering, each 3D Gaussian is projected to a screen-space Gaussian, whose color contribution is accumulated through depth-ordered alpha blending. Animating the Gaussian representation therefore requires updating the center and covariance of each Gaussian according to the underlying physical deformation.

    Continuous Gaussian Binding. Let μ_g⁰ denote the rest center of the g-th Gaussian. Since the neural skinning fields are spatially continuous, we directly evaluate Wᵢ(μ_g⁰) at its rest center. Following the deformation map in Eq. (1), we construct the local affine transformation for each Gaussian as:

    T_g(z)≡[A_g(z) t_g(z)]=[I₃ 0]+∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐWᵢ(μ_g⁰)Zᵢ,

    		(27)

    where A_g∈ℝ^3×3 is the linear part of the affine transformation, which may include rotation, scaling, and shear, and t_g∈ℝ³ is its translation. We evaluate the skinning weights once at each Gaussian’s rest center and use these fixed weights throughout its kernel. The resulting local affine transformation is updated from the current reduced coordinates.

    Gaussian Kernel Deformation. Let Σ_g⁰ denote the rest covariance. Applying the local affine transformation T_g(z) to the Gaussian kernel gives:

    μ_g(z)=A_g(z)μ_g⁰+t_g(z),(28)
    Σ_g(z)=A_g(z)Σ_g⁰A_g(z)^⊤.

    The center therefore follows the skinned point motion, while the covariance captures the induced rotation and anisotropic deformation of the Gaussian kernel. The opacity and SH coefficients retain their rest values.

    Runtime Coupling. At runtime, we advance the reduced coordinates z using Eq. (10). At each frame, these coordinates determine the local affine maps in Eq. (27), which update the Gaussian centers and covariances through Eq. (28), driving physics-based animation of the Gaussian representation.

    IV Experiments

    IV-AImplementation Details

    For the 3D shape encoder, we adopt the pre-trained Michelangelo [67] model which consists of one cross-attention block and eight self-attention blocks; the output latent set Fₛ∈ℝ^M×d has M=256 and d=768. For each 3D object, we re-center and normalize it into a bounding volume of [-1,1]³. For the 3D shape encoder, we sample 4096 points on the object surface as input. For cubature points sampling, we first sample 100k points on the surface, and then voxelize the space into a 128³ grid to obtain interior points to form the complete candidate cubature point set. For each training batch, we randomly sample 1000 cubature points from the candidate point set for potential energy computation, following the same strategy as previous work [9, 44]. In each batch, we randomly sample 1024 subspace coordinate vectors z for training. Our framework is trained on 4 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs. The learning rate is linearly increased to 5×10⁻⁴ within the first 1% of training iterations (warm-up), and then gradually decreased using the cosine decay schedule until reaching the minimum value of 5×10⁻⁵.

    IV-BEvaluation of Learned Skinning Fields

    Baselines. We compare our method with the following baselines: Simplicits [44], RigNet [62], M-I-A [20], Anymate [14], and Puppeteer [52] on the ShapeNet [7] and RigNet [62] datasets. Simplicits trains a separate neural network for each object to output skinning fields through self-supervised learning. The other baselines are supervised neural rigging and skinning methods that output object joints, bones, and skinning weights in a feed-forward manner. These methods are pretrained on expert-annotated datasets, then fine-tuned for comparison.

    Evaluation Metrics. Since our framework is entirely self-supervised and does not rely on annotated skinning data as ground truth, we draw from matrix analysis [22, 4] and spectral theory [54, 13] to propose three quantitative metrics that measure structural independence, numerical stability, and spectral balance of the skinning weights matrix W∈ℝ^N×K, where N is the number of vertices and K is the number of handles or bones. To ensure a fair comparison, we perform ℓ₂-normalization on each column of W before evaluation for all methods, resulting in the matrix Ŵ.

    (1) Orthogonality Metric. We first measure the pairwise orthogonality among handle or bone influence vectors as:

    Ωₒᵣₜₕ=1/K(K-1)∥ Ŵ^⊤Ŵ-I ∥₂²,

    		(29)

    where I is the K×K identity matrix. A smaller Ωₒᵣₜₕ indicates that different handle or bone weights are more decorrelated and capture distinct deformation subspaces. Since each column of Ŵ is ℓ₂-normalized, Ωₒᵣₜₕ is bounded within [0,1], and a smaller value indicates that each handle or bone encodes an independent deformation mode.

    (2) Log-Condition Number Metric. To evaluate the numerical stability of the skinning basis, we compute the log-scaled condition number [21] of the Gram matrix:

    κ_\log=\log₂(1+(λ_\max(Ŵ^⊤Ŵ))/(λ_\min(Ŵ^⊤Ŵ))),

    		(30)

    where λ_\max and λ_\min are the largest and smallest eigenvalues of Ŵ^⊤Ŵ. κ_\log lies within [1,+∞); a smaller value indicates a well-conditioned deformation basis, where small transformations result in stable geometric responses.

    (3) Spectrum Entropy Metric. To assess the balance of spectral energy distribution across skinning weights, we define the spectrum entropy metric [13, 54] as:

    H_spec=-(1)/(\logK)∑ᵢ₌₁^Kpᵢ\logpᵢ, pᵢ=(λᵢ)/(∑ⱼλⱼ),

    		(31)

    where {λᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K are the eigenvalues of Ŵ^⊤Ŵ. H_spec is bounded within [0,1], where higher values indicate more uniform spectral energy and balanced, expressive deformation modes.

    Results. We first evaluate neural skinning on unseen objects from the test set of the RigNet [62] dataset to assess generalization. The RigNet dataset provides annotated skinning data; we fine-tune the pretrained feed-forward neural skinning baselines using these annotations, whereas our model is trained only on the 3D meshes. Table  reports the quantitative comparison on unseen objects. Our method significantly outperforms the baselines across all three evaluation metrics, demonstrating its generalization ability. We further evaluate our method on the ShapeNet dataset [7], which provides clearly defined object categories. Our model is trained jointly across all categories, and all baselines are evaluated on the corresponding test sets. Because Simplicits can only be trained on a single object at a time, we train an individual Simplicits model for each object. The quantitative results in Table  show that our method consistently outperforms all baselines. In Fig. 8 and Fig. 11, we compare the qualitative skinning results with the baselines. Our method produces more physically consistent, geometrically orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results. Fig. 9 and Fig. 11 further show that our method generalizes to unseen objects and produces high-quality skinning results. For additional results, please refer to the supplementary material.

    Deformable Shape Family. In Fig. 12, our method uses a single model to infer skinning fields for a deformable shape family, while Simplicits [44] must be trained separately for each geometry. This comparison demonstrates the efficiency and cross-shape generalization of our framework.

    Rig-Complementary Neural Skinning Fields. We evaluate the neural skinning fields learned with our self-supervised rig-complementarity objective on characters from the RigNet dataset [62], which provides the skeletal rigs and associated LBS skinning weights. Fig. 13 shows the learned fields across diverse character geometries and rig structures, with spatially varying patterns over the body and appendages. We further examine the resulting complementary elastic responses under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences in Sec. IV-D.

    IV-CAblation Studies

    To validate our design choices, we conduct ablation studies covering both the key components of the proposed Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy and the rig-space complementarity term in the rig-complementary setting, using the RigNet [62] dataset. As shown in Table , we remove or modify the PISSL components to assess their individual effects on model performance. Specifically, we evaluate the smoothness loss Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ, the orthogonality constraint Lₒᵣₜₕ, the skinning normalization process, the ONI [26] layer, and conflict-aware gradient correction using ConFIG [37]. The quantitative results demonstrate that these components maintain the numerical stability and orthogonality of the learned neural skinning fields, which are essential for well-conditioned and physically consistent deformation behavior. In Fig. 14, we visualize the skinning results obtained without the potential energy loss Lₚₒₜ, where the model fails to produce physically interpretable skinning fields. Fig. 13 further compares neural skinning fields learned with and without L_comp. Without this term, the visualized fields form broad regions across the head, torso, and limbs. Incorporating L_comp changes these distributions, with visible differences in the ears, wings, and limb regions across multiple characters. These comparisons illustrate the effect of rig-space complementarity learning on the spatial organization of the skinning fields.

    IV-DDiverse Real-Time Physics-Based Animation

    We next examine the broader animation scope enabled by PhysSkin++. Its discretization-agnostic neural skinning fields support efficient reduced dynamics for controllable and collision-aware animation, rig-complementary animation, and direct binding to 3D Gaussian representations.

    Time Efficiency. We first evaluate the time efficiency of our skinning-based subspace animation. We compare it with a classical FEM method using implicit time integration and an MPM method using explicit time integration. For these two full-space physical simulators, we use open-source high-performance GPU implementations [9, 68]. All methods are evaluated on the same CPU and GPU hardware. As shown in Table , our method demonstrates excellent time efficiency.

    Controllable and Collision-Aware Animation. Beyond unconstrained deformation, we qualitatively examine how the learned neural skinning subspaces respond to prescribed controls and environmental contact. As shown in Fig. 4(a), the Dirichlet boundary conditions enforce zero displacement over the prescribed upper regions, while the unconstrained geometry deforms under gravity. In the interactive sequences of Fig. 4(b), the lower region of each object is fixed by Dirichlet boundary conditions, while Gaussian-kernel-weighted dragging provides localized control over the remaining deformable domain. Fig. 4(c) further demonstrates contact with planar environments across diverse shapes and boundary orientations, with the contact response modeled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (14). We further evaluate collision-aware animation involving multiple objects. In the rigid–deformable sequences of Fig. 5(a), a rigid body is released from an elevated position and falls under gravity onto a deformable object. Contact between the two objects is modeled by the point-pair IPC-style barrier in Eq. (15), while contact with the supporting floor is handled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (14). In the deformable–deformable sequences of Fig. 5(b), multiple deformable objects are released from elevated positions and fall under gravity. Contacts among the falling objects are resolved using the point-pair IPC-style barrier in Eq. (15), while their contact with the supporting floor is modeled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (14). These results demonstrate controllable deformation and multi-object interaction within the PhysSkin++ skinning-based reduced representation.

    Rig-Complementary Animation. We evaluate the resulting rig-complementary animation under both interactive control and user-authored animation sequences, as shown in Fig. 7. For interactive rig control, we implement a Polyscope-based graphical interface [48] that allows users to manipulate bone poses at runtime. The resulting rig motion defines the primary animation, while PhysSkin++ computes the corresponding complementary elastic response. For user-authored rig animation, we obtain source skeletal animation sequences from Mixamo [1] and retarget them to the target character rigs using Auto-Rig Pro [3]. In both settings, PhysSkin++ augments the primary rig animation with temporally evolving, physics-based complementary deformation.

    Discretization-Agnostic 3D Gaussian Animation. Owing to the discretization-agnostic nature of our neural skinning formulation, the learned deformation fields can be evaluated directly on 3D Gaussian primitives without introducing an underlying mesh discretization. Following the 3D Gaussian binding formulation in Sec. III-F, we evaluate PhysSkin++ on the ShapeSplat dataset [42], which contains 3D Gaussian reconstructions of objects from ShapeNet [7]. As shown in Fig. 15, the learned fields are queried at the Gaussian rest centers, and the induced local affine deformation updates both the centers and anisotropic covariances to produce coherent physics-based animation. We encourage readers to visit our project page for additional animation videos.

    V Conclusion

    In this paper, we present PhysSkin++, a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. A neural skinning fields autoencoder learns continuous skinning fields directly from static geometries to define a skinning-based subspace mapping. Our Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy promotes physically plausible deformations through a self-supervised objective and stabilizes joint optimization through on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction. At runtime, a reduced dynamics formulation advances the reduced coordinates and supports Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable contact. Beyond purely physics-driven animation, we extend the deformation representation with prescribed rig displacement and the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term, enabling complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animations without enforcing the complementarity constraint at runtime. The continuous deformation map also enables discretization-agnostic binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussian representations. Experiments demonstrate that PhysSkin++ achieves outstanding performance on generalizable neural skinning while enabling real-time physics-based animation. As a limitation, our current formulation does not incorporate semantic priors for modeling complex geometries. Future work will explore such priors to improve the expressiveness of the learned skinning-based subspace mapping.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：自监督学神经蒙皮场构造紧凑形变子空间，支持刚体控制、接触与 rig 动画绑定。

要点：

  • 跨形状、跨空间离散化地泛化实时物理动画一直很难；PhysSkin++ 从静态几何学出连续的神经蒙皮场，用它构造紧凑的形变子空间，从而把降维动力学做成可复用的表示。
  • 神经蒙皮场自编码器直接预测与形状相关的形变子空间，无需逐物体训练；训练不依赖仿真轨迹，用物理自监督 + 蒙皮场归一化与冲突感知梯度校正，稳定物理与正交约束下的联合优化。
  • 学到的表示支持带用户控制与接触交互的高效降维动力学，并能把动画直接绑定到网格、点云与 3D Gaussians；对给定 rig 动画还引入自监督互补性目标，运行时不必再解互补约束就能得到弹性响应。

为什么值得看：蒙皮 + 物理形变是引擎动画系统里最贵也最手工的一环；把「形变子空间」变成网络输出、且能直接绑到点云/3DGS，意味着资产格式和动画管线可以一起简化。

中文摘要：跨不同 3D 形状与空间离散化地泛化实时物理动画仍然困难。PhysSkin++ 从静态几何学习连续的神经蒙皮场，用其构造紧凑的形变子空间：神经蒙皮场自编码器直接预测与形状相关的子空间，无需逐物体训练；为摆脱对仿真轨迹的依赖，作者提出物理自监督学习策略，结合蒙皮场归一化与冲突感知梯度校正，在物理约束与正交约束下稳定联合优化。所得表示支持带用户控制与接触的高效降维动力学，并可把动画直接绑定到网格、点云与 3D Gaussians；对给定 rig 动画引入自监督互补性目标，在不于运行时强制互补约束的前提下学出弹性响应。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·引擎架构（English）

原文发布：2026-10-19

本期推送：2026-10-23

PhysSkin++: Real-Time and Generalizable Physics-Based Animation via Self-Supervised Neural Skinning

Abstract

Generalizing real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and spatial discretizations remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce PhysSkin++, a physics-informed framework that learns continuous neural skinning fields from static geometries to construct compact deformation subspaces. Specifically, we propose a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder that predicts shape-dependent deformation subspaces without per-object network training. To learn these subspaces without simulation trajectories, we develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning strategy that combines skinning-field normalization with conflict-aware gradient correction, stabilizing joint optimization under physical and orthogonality constraints. The learned representation supports efficient reduced dynamics with user control and contact interactions, together with direct animation binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussians. For prescribed rig animation, we further introduce a self-supervised complementarity objective to learn complementary elastic responses without enforcing complementarity constraints at runtime. Experiments demonstrate cross-shape generalization of the learned skinning fields, real-time reduced simulation, and applications to controllable, collision-aware, and rig-complementary animation. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/PhysSkin_plus/.

Index Terms:

Physics-based animation, geometric deep learning, reduced-order modeling, self-supervised learning.

I Introduction

Real-time physics-based animation is a long-standing goal in computer vision and graphics, underpinning applications in VR/AR authoring, character animation, and interactive digital content creation. To support such applications, an animation system must provide a compact yet expressive motion representation that captures physically plausible deformations, accommodates user control and interactions, and remains computationally efficient for real-time animation.

Subspace physics-based animation [2, 10] addresses this by learning a low-dimensional motion subspace for efficient computation, and then lifting the result back to the full space using a subspace mapping. However, classical methods [2, 51] optimize a single linear subspace mapping matrix tied to a particular mesh topology and resolution, which prevents generalization across different spatial discretizations. Recently, neural methods [10, 49] have emerged as promising alternatives by using neural networks to learn subspace mappings that naturally handle arbitrary spatial discretizations. These approaches, however, must still train a separate network per object and fail to generalize to different 3D shapes. In parallel, recent transformer-based approaches learn physical dynamics directly from simulation trajectories across diverse objects and physical systems [15, 58]. Although this data-driven route enables generalizable neural simulation, it requires extensive trajectory supervision and does not explicitly construct a low-dimensional deformation subspace for reduced-order animation. These limitations motivate a central question: How can we learn a physics-consistent deformation subspace mapping that generalizes across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations directly from static geometries, without relying on supervised training data?

In this work, we introduce PhysSkin++ (Fig. 1), a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. In the spirit of Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) [43], we use continuous skinning fields to define a deformation subspace mapping, with handle transformations serving as the reduced coordinates for full-space 3D object deformation. To construct this representation directly from static geometries, we introduce a Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder. Specifically, PhysSkin++ employs a transformer-based point cloud encoder to extract latent shape features from surface samples, while a cross-attention decoder predicts continuous neural skinning fields at arbitrary spatial locations. PhysSkin++ requires no simulation trajectories, skinning annotations, or category-specific priors. This mesh-free, discretization-agnostic representation generalizes across object categories, topologies, and resolutions.

Learning such a deformation subspace mapping purely from geometry is highly non-trivial. A physically meaningful subspace must exhibit low potential energy, reflecting deformation modes compatible with physically plausible behavior; spatial smoothness, ensuring coherent deformations; and orthogonality, promoting independence among the deformation modes. We therefore formulate a self-supervised objective consisting of potential-energy, smoothness, and orthogonality terms. However, jointly optimizing these terms often leads to conflicts in gradient magnitude and direction, making naive joint optimization unstable. To overcome this optimization challenge, we introduce a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy. First, we apply on-the-fly skinning-field normalization, which regulates the scale of the learned skinning weights and prevents numerical drift during training. Second, we incorporate a conflict-aware gradient correction mechanism [37] to resolve destructive interference among gradients of the loss terms, enabling balanced optimization and stable convergence. Together, these mechanisms enable PhysSkin++ to learn a physically consistent deformation subspace mapping directly from static geometries, with spatially smooth and approximately orthogonal skinning fields.

At runtime, we advance the reduced coordinates through implicit reduced dynamics and map them to full-space deformations through the learned skinning-based subspace mapping. To support controllable and collision-aware animation, we incorporate Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and multi-object contact into this formulation. Prescribed boundary displacements are enforced through a boundary-compatible deformation map, while external forces and contact interactions are incorporated through their corresponding energy terms. This formulation supports both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable interactions within the learned deformation subspaces. Moreover, the continuous deformation map can be directly bound to different spatial discretizations, including 3D Gaussian representations [28], enabling physics-based animation of diverse object representations within the same reduced dynamics framework.

Beyond purely physics-driven animation, PhysSkin++ also supports rig-complementary animation when an artist-authored LBS rig is available. Artist-authored rigs provide intuitive low-dimensional control, but their kinematic deformations alone cannot reproduce physical elastic responses, while increasing the complexity of a rig places a greater burden on animation authoring. Complementary dynamics [65, 6] addresses this tension by augmenting a prescribed rig animation with complementary physical deformations. Following this principle, PhysSkin++ treats the user-authored rig-based animation as the primary animation and learns neural skinning fields for complementary elastic response. We augment the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term defined by the rig Jacobian, encouraging the learned deformation subspace to be complementary to the prescribed rig animation space. At runtime, the resulting reduced dynamics enriches the prescribed animation with physics-based complementary displacement without enforcing the rig-space complementarity constraint at every step. Both animation settings share the continuous skinning representation and reduced dynamics framework.

Experiments on various datasets evaluate the learned skinning fields and demonstrate real-time physics-based animation across diverse shapes, controls, interactions, and spatial discretizations. Our contributions are:

  • •

    We present PhysSkin++, a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations by learning neural skinning fields directly from static geometries. Its Neural Skinning Fields Autoencoder employs a transformer-based shape encoder and a cross-attention decoder to predict continuous skinning fields.

  • •

    We develop a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy that incorporates on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction, enabling stable joint optimization of multiple self-supervised loss terms.

  • •

    We develop a controllable and collision-aware reduced dynamics formulation that supports Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and multi-object contact, together with discretization-agnostic binding of the continuous deformation map to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussian representations.

  • •

    We support rig-complementary animation by extending the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term defined by the rig Jacobian. This enables physics-based complementary elastic responses under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences without enforcing the rig-space complementarity constraint at runtime.

    • A preliminary version of this work has been published as PhysSkin [30]. The present article extends the conference version in four aspects. First, we develop a reduced dynamics formulation for controllable and collision-aware animation, supporting prescribed boundary displacements, interactive control, environmental interaction, and multi-object contact. Second, we provide a discretization-agnostic binding formulation for 3D Gaussian representations, updating both Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances through local affine transformations determined by the learned skinning fields and current reduced coordinates. Third, we extend the deformation representation with prescribed rig displacement and the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term. These extensions support complementary elastic deformation for prescribed rig animations without enforcing the complementarity constraint at runtime. Finally, we expand the experimental evaluation to cover controllable and collision-aware animation, 3D Gaussian animation, and self-supervised rig-complementarity learning, including rig-complementary animation under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences.

    II Related Work

    Neural Physics-Based Animation. Subspace physics-based animation [2, 57, 10] is an effective method for accelerating animation computations. Its core idea is to learn a low-dimensional motion subspace for efficient computation, and then lift the result back to the full space using a subspace mapping. Recently, fully neural approaches have been proposed to directly learn subspace mapping by neural networks. Data-driven methods [17, 50, 10, 68, 9] represented by CROM [10] learn the mapping for a single object by fitting neural networks to motion sequences from physical simulators, but they have limited generalization ability to unseen motion patterns. In parallel, recent transformer-based approaches learn physical dynamics directly from simulation trajectories across rigid, deformable, and particle-based systems [15, 58, 12, 19]. Data-free methods [49, 41, 44, 59, 8] learn a low-energy subspace mapping by physics-informed learning without requiring motion sequences, but pure neural network approaches often struggle to converge to high-quality subspace representations. Recently, Simplicits [44] learns neural skinning weight functions as a physics-informed subspace mapping by minimizing a quadratic energy subject to orthogonality constraints, which stabilizes training compared to purely neural models but limits generalization due to its per-object network design. Our method overcomes these limitations with a neural skinning fields autoencoder that outputs skinning weights generalizing across diverse 3D shapes, enabling real-time subspace physics-based animation. Our physics-informed neural subspace formulation retains explicit reduced-order dynamics and complements approaches that learn dynamics directly from simulation trajectories.

    Neural Rigging and Skinning Representations. Another classical reduced deformation representation is skeletal rigging-based animation [5, 16, 39]. Recently, based on 3D shape VAEs [64, 67], many works [14, 53, 20, 36, 62, 66, 52] have performed supervised learning from expert-annotated 3D object rigging and skinning datasets to infer objects’ joints, bones, and skinning weights through a feed-forward network. However, some methods are limited to specific categories of 3D shapes such as characters [62, 20] or animals [55, 60], as they incorporate category-specific priors [39, 69] such as predefined skeletal structures or semantic constraints, making it difficult to generalize to other object categories. Works represented by Anymate [14] learn from annotated 3D object rigging and skinning datasets and design category-agnostic network architectures, thereby enabling the ability to generalize across diverse object categories and demonstrating stronger generalization capabilities. However, these methods heavily rely on expert-annotated data [14, 35, 34, 60, 40], which are costly and difficult to scale. In contrast, our work employs self-supervised learning to train neural skinning fields directly from static 3D geometries without any annotated data.

    III Method

    III-AFramework Overview and Problem Formulation

    PhysSkin++ is a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. As illustrated in Fig. 2, our neural skinning fields autoencoder predicts continuous skinning fields from static geometry to define a deformation subspace mapping. The autoencoder is trained through Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) under physical and numerical constraints. At runtime, we advance reduced coordinates to animate objects with boundary conditions, interactive control, and contact. Beyond purely physics-driven animation, PhysSkin++ also supports rig-complementary animation by learning complementary deformation subspaces for prescribed rigs. Moreover, the continuous deformation map supports binding to mesh vertices, sampled points, and 3D Gaussians.

    Classical full-space physics-based animation methods [51, 38, 27, 61, 31, 63] typically use explicit or implicit time integrators to update the object’s motion state. Explicit time integrators are often constrained by stability conditions [33], while implicit time integrators require solving a large nonlinear optimization problem in the high-dimensional full space. PhysSkin++ instead represents the deformation using continuous neural skinning fields and advances only the corresponding reduced-order subspace coordinates through implicit time integration. This lower-dimensional optimization reduces computational cost [6], enabling real-time physics-based animation.

    Continuous Skinning-Based Deformation Representation. To model full-space 3D object deformations within a reduced-order subspace, in the spirit of Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) [43], we represent the deformation map x=φ(X,z(t)) using a weighted sum of m affine displacement transformations:

    φ(X,z)=X+∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐWᵢ(X)Zᵢ\beginbmatrixX 1\endbmatrix.

    		(1)

    Here, X∈ℝ³ is a point in undeformed space and x∈ℝ³ is its deformed position, m is the number of skinning handles, Wᵢ:ℝ³→ℝ is the continuous skinning weight function associated with handle i, and Zᵢ∈ℝ^3×4 parameterizes its affine displacement. The vector z=flat(Z)∈ℝ¹²ᵐ stacks all handle parameters and serves as the reduced-order subspace coordinates, compactly representing the full-space deformation of n spatial sample points, where m≪n. We first describe the representation and learning procedure for purely physics-driven animation, and then introduce the prescribed rig displacement and rig-space complementarity objective in Sec. III-E.

    III-BNeural Skinning Fields Autoencoder

    We train a neural skinning fields autoencoder to predict spatially continuous skinning weights across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. The resulting mesh-free representation supports the skinning-based real-time animation described in Sec. III-D. Unlike existing neural subspace methods [44, 10] that train a separate neural network for each object, our single feed-forward network generalizes across diverse objects, improving scalability and practicality.

    Neural 3D Shape Encoding. We use the transformer-based point cloud encoder Michelangelo [67] to extract a highly compressed latent set Fₛ∈ℝ^M×d for a given 3D shape via a cross-attention block and several self-attention blocks:

    Fₛ=SelfAttn^(1:L)(CrossAttn(Qₛ,γ(P))),

    		(2)

    where Qₛ∈ℝ^M×d is a set of learnable shape latent tokens, P∈ℝ^N×6 is the sampled surface point cloud with N points, each point consisting of 3D coordinates and normals, γ(·) is point-wise positional encoding, SelfAttn^(1:L)(·) indicates a stack of L self-attention layers that iteratively improve the shape latent representation, M is the number of latents, and d is the dimension of each latent. In practice, the shape encoder is pretrained on the ShapeNet dataset [7] via a signed distance field (SDF) reconstruction task [47] to learn generalizable geometric priors. We then freeze the encoder parameters during training to enhance efficiency.

    Neural Skinning Fields Decoding. To obtain spatially continuous skinning fields, we decode the shape latent set Fₛ obtained from Eq. (2) into spatially varying skinning weights. We first assign m learnable skinning handle tokens Qₕ∈ℝ^m×d, and then use a cross-attention block to extract a skinning handle latent set Fₕ∈ℝ^m×d from the shape latent set Fₛ:

    Fₕ=CrossAttn(Qₕ,SelfAttn(Fₛ)).\vskip3.00003pt

    		(3)

    Next, for any spatial query point X, we use another cross-attention block to extract a point-wise skinning feature Fₚ∈ℝᵈ from the skinning handle latent set Fₕ:

    Fₚ=CrossAttn(γ(X),Fₕ).\vskip3.00003pt

    		(4)

    Finally, we concatenate the point-wise skinning feature Fₚ with the positional encoding of the query point, and use a ResNet-style MLP to compute the skinning fields:

    W(X)=MLP(Fₚ⊕γ(X)),\vskip1.99997pt

    		(5)

    where W(X)∈ℝᵐ is the skinning weight vector at point X, and ⊕ denotes the concatenation operator. To promote orthogonality among different skinning modes, we apply an Orthogonalization by Newton’s Iteration (ONI) module [26] at the final layer of the MLP, and we adopt ELU as the activation function in the MLP, which allows learning flexible and expressive skinning-based deformation subspaces without enforcing non-negativity on the learned skinning modes. We denote the full autoencoder by Φ_θ and its skinning weight output at X by Φ_θ(X). The continuous fields can be queried throughout the object, while cubature points specify locations for physics-informed training and numerical integration.

    Cubature Points Sampling. In the classical Finite Element Method (FEM) [51], the object’s volume is typically discretized into a tetrahedral mesh [23] to facilitate numerical solutions of physical equations. Unlike triangle surface meshes commonly used for rendering, which only contain surface points, tetrahedral meshes include interior volumetric elements that better capture the object’s spatial structure. To train the neural skinning fields autoencoder, we sample cubature points both on the object’s surface and inside its volume, with each cubature point serving as a spatial query point X for computing the potential energy Eₚₒₜ during subspace learning and skinning-based real-time animation. This sampling captures volumetric deformation behavior that surface-only sampling cannot, in contrast to popular 3D Shape VAEs [64] that only sample surface points. To sample interior cubature points, we first convert the object’s surface mesh into a watertight mesh [24, 25], then uniformly sample points in the voxelized spatial grid using ray tracing [45], and classify points as being outside the object if the ray intersects the surface mesh and the dot product with the normal is negative. For surface cubature points, we employ Sharp Edge Sampling (SES) [11] to better capture geometric details.

    III-CPhysics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning

    To learn a deformation subspace mapping directly from static geometry without annotated skinning data or precomputed simulation trajectories, we train the neural skinning fields autoencoder with a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy. The learned skinning fields should be spatially smooth and mutually independent, while inducing low-energy deformations. We therefore formulate a self-supervised objective consisting of potential-energy, smoothness, and orthogonality terms:

    L_subspace(θ)=Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ(θ)+λₚₒₜLₚₒₜ(θ)+λₒᵣₜₕLₒᵣₜₕ(θ),

    		(6)

    where λₚₒₜ and λₒᵣₜₕ weight the potential-energy and orthogonality losses, respectively. The additional objective for rig-complementary learning is introduced in Sec. III-E.

    Physical Constraints. To encourage physically plausible deformations, we construct a low-energy subspace [49] by minimizing the expected potential energy of deformations induced by randomly sampled subspace coordinates z∈ℝ¹²ᵐ:

    Lₚₒₜ(θ)=𝔼_z∼ℕ[Eₚₒₜ^θ(φ(X,z))],\vskip3.99994pt

    		(7)

    where z is defined in Sec. III-A, and ℕ=ℕ(0,μ²I₁₂ₘ) denotes a Gaussian distribution over ℝ¹²ᵐ with μ=0.2. The expectation is estimated by averaging the potential energy over sampled subspace coordinates within a training batch. Here, Eₚₒₜ^θ(φ(X,z)) denotes the object’s potential energy evaluated using the deformation map induced by z under the current network parameters θ, with spatial integration approximated using cubature points. During training, we linearly interpolate the potential energy computation from the linear elasticity [56] model to the Neo-Hookean [29] model to enhance training stability [44]. Besides the low-energy constraint imposed by Lₚₒₜ, we also expect Φ_θ(X) to be spatially smooth, so we introduce a spatial smoothness loss:

    Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ(θ)=𝔼_X∼S∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐ∥∇Φ_θⁱ(X)∥²,

    		(8)

    where S denotes the set of sampled cubature points introduced in Sec. III-B, and ∇Φ_θⁱ is the spatial gradient of the i-th skinning weight function at point X under the current network parameters θ.

    Orthogonality Constraint. To enhance subspace expressiveness, we introduce a loss that promotes orthogonality among the learned skinning weight functions:

    Lₒᵣₜₕ(θ)=𝔼_D∼S[∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐ∑_\beginsubarraycj=1 j≠i\endsubarrayᵐ(Φ_θⁱ(X_D)^⊤Φ_θʲ(X_D))²],

    		(9)

    where D denotes a training batch of cubature points sampled from the overall set S, and X_D represents the corresponding point matrix within the batch.

    Stable Joint Optimization. Simplicits [44] jointly penalizes deviations from orthogonality and unit magnitude. We instead ℓ₂-normalize each column of the skinning weight matrix evaluated at the batch points on the fly. This normalization regulates the scale of the learned modes and prevents numerical drift during training, thereby facilitating optimization of the orthogonality objective and promoting more independent neural skinning fields. However, gradients of the self-supervised loss terms can differ substantially in magnitude and conflict in direction, making naive joint optimization unstable. To overcome this challenge, we complement our on-the-fly skinning-field normalization with ConFIG [37] to correct conflicting gradients and stabilize joint optimization. In Fig. 3, we visualize the evolution of different skinning modes during optimization, demonstrating that our physics-informed self-supervised framework progressively organizes the initially unstructured skinning representations into low-energy, approximately orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results, which are then used for real-time physics-based animation as detailed in Sec. III-D.

    III-DSkinning-Based Real-Time Animation

    The learned neural skinning fields define a continuous subspace mapping through which reduced coordinates determine full-space deformations for physics-based animation. We first describe the basic reduced dynamics, and then incorporate boundary conditions, external control, and contact energies. Rig-complementary dynamics is introduced separately in Sec. III-E.

    Subspace Dynamics. With the skinning-based subspace representation, we can create motions with physically plausible deformations directly in the reduced-order subspace. We discretize the governing Newtonian physical equations using standard implicit time integration and update the subspace coordinates z over time as:

    zₜ₊₁=\undersetz\arg\min 1/2h²∥z-2zₜ+zₜ₋₁∥_M²+Eₚₒₜ(φ(X,z)),

    		(10)

    where h is the time step size, ∥·∥_M is the norm induced by the reduced mass matrix M, and Eₚₒₜ is the potential energy that induces the internal force, with Eₚₒₜ supporting general hyperelastic material models. This formulation can be solved using standard Newton-based methods [46]. The much lower subspace dimensionality allows efficient optimization of Eq. (10) [6], enabling real-time physics-based animation.

    Reduced Dynamics with Control and Contact. We extend Eq. (10) by augmenting its elastic potential with the energies associated with each animation setting. Let φ_D denote the deformation map satisfying the prescribed Dirichlet boundary conditions. For a fixed boundary displacement field and fixed constrained region, we update the reduced coordinates via:

    zₜ₊₁=\undersetz\arg\min1/2h²∥z-2zₜ+zₜ₋₁∥_M²+Eₚₒₜ (φ_D(X,z))(11)
    +E_force(z,t)+E_bnd(z)+E_coll(z).

    Here, E_force accounts for the effects of gravity or user-defined actuation forces, E_bnd models penalty-based environment interaction, and E_coll accounts for inter-object contact. In the absence of boundary constraints, φ_D reduces to φ. Activating the relevant terms in Eq. (11) supports controllable and collision-aware animation.

    Boundary and External Control. We enforce prescribed boundary displacements through Dirichlet boundary conditions and project global or localized external forces into the reduced space to drive and interactively control object deformation.

    Dirichlet Boundary Conditions. Let Ω⊂ℝ³ denote the object’s rest domain and Γ_D⊆∂Ω its Dirichlet boundary. We define an indicator d:Ω→{0,1} for the unconstrained region, with d=0 on Γ_D and d=1 elsewhere, and let g:Ω→ℝ³ be a displacement field that matches the prescribed displacement on Γ_D. Following a boundary-compatible construction, we modify the deformation map in Eq. (1) as:

    φ_D(X,z)=X+g(X)+d(X)∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐWᵢ(X)Zᵢ\beginbmatrixX 1\endbmatrix.

    		(12)

    This construction is equivalent to modulating the runtime skinning fields by d(X). Consequently, the displacement induced by the reduced coordinates vanishes on Γ_D, where g directly specifies the prescribed boundary displacement for arbitrary reduced coordinates. Different boundary configurations are specified by selecting different subsets of ∂Ω. As shown in Fig. 4(a), varying the constrained region produces distinct boundary-conditioned deformation behavior under the same reduced formulation.

    External Force and Interactive Control. External controls are represented as full-space force fields and then mapped to the reduced coordinates through the deformation map. Let J_φ denote the Jacobian of the active deformation map with respect to the reduced coordinates. A full-space force fₓ(t) gives:

    f_z(t)=J_φ^⊤fₓ(t), E_force(z,t)=-f_z(t)^⊤z.

    		(13)

    This linear potential applies to forces held fixed during each reduced solve. It covers global force fields, such as gravity, and localized user-defined actuation forces. Different controls share the same force-to-coordinate mapping while differing in how fₓ(t) is constructed. For interactive dragging, we construct a Gaussian-kernel-weighted local force around the selected point and update the drag target position from the current user input at each frame before applying Eq. (13). As shown in Fig. 4(b), localized dragging enables direct manipulation of different character geometries.

    Contact-Aware Multi-Object Dynamics. We handle contact through boundary-penalty environment interaction and point-based IPC-style collision energies, with the latter supporting both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable interaction.

    Boundary-Penalty Environment Interaction. We model simple environmental interactions, such as plane collision, as penalty constraints to prescribed geometric boundaries. Let Γ_E denote an environment boundary, and let A be the active set of animation points within its influence region. For each active point j, we compute a boundary target x̄ⱼ∈Γ_E from the current environment geometry. The boundary penalty is:

    E_bnd(z)=∑_j∈A∥φ_D(Xⱼ,z)-x̄ⱼ∥₂².

    		(14)

    The active set and targets are held fixed when differentiating this energy. The resulting full-space derivatives are mapped to the reduced coordinates using the same deformation-map Jacobian J_φ as in Eq. (13). For plane-collision scenarios, such as an inclined ramp, Γ_E is instantiated as a finite rectangular boundary with a prescribed normal. The target x̄ⱼ is obtained by projecting the current point onto the boundary plane and restricting it to the finite boundary extent. Moving or rotating the boundary updates its geometry, active points, and boundary targets. As shown in Fig. 4(c), the same boundary-penalty formulation supports contact with planar environments across diverse object geometries and boundary orientations.

    IPC-Style Collision Energy. For multi-object interaction, we use sampled integration points as collision primitives and construct a contact set ℂ by querying neighboring points from different objects. For each contact c, we store a contact direction n_c and define the contact gap d_c as the signed separation along this direction. We normalize this gap by the contact radius r_c>0, i.e., d̂_c=d_c/r_c, and use the following point-based log barrier inspired by Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) [32]:

    E_b,c=\begincases-(d̂_c-1)²\log(d̂_c-rₚ),&rₚ

    		(15)

    We assemble the collision term as E_coll=k_c∑_c∈ℂE_b,c, defining an IPC-style barrier over sampled point pairs. Here, 0≤rₚ<1 specifies the minimum normalized contact gap, and k_c controls the contact stiffness. The barrier is finite only for d̂_c>rₚ.

    Rigid–Deformable Interaction. We model rigid-body motion with a global rigid transformation, while the deformable geometry evolves according to the neural skinning deformation map. At the beginning of each time step, the transformed rigid surface samples and current deformable points are used to construct the active contact pairs. For each pair, the point-pair barrier in Eq. (15) is evaluated from the contact gap between the rigid and deformable sides. The rigid transformation is treated as prescribed input to this reduced deformable solve. As shown in Fig. 5(a), this formulation handles rigid–deformable contact across different object pairs and motions.

    Deformable–Deformable Interaction. For K deformable objects, each object i maintains its own reduced coordinates zᵢ, material parameters, and subspace dimension. We concatenate the reduced coordinates into the global reduced variable z=[z₁^⊤,…,z_K^⊤]^⊤ and sum the per-object inertial, elastic, and control energies. Cross-object contacts couple these states through the same point-pair barrier in Eq. (15). For a contact c between objects a and b, let J_φ,a and J_φ,b denote their deformation-map Jacobians with respect to zₐ and z_b, respectively, evaluated at the corresponding contact points. With the contact direction and radius held fixed during differentiation, the contact gap is affine in z. Applying the chain rule to the barrier energy gives the following reduced derivatives, showing only the nonzero blocks for objects a and b:

    J_c=(∂d_c)/(∂z)=n_c^⊤[ J_φ,a -J_φ,b ],(16)
    ∇_zE_b,c=J_c^⊤(∂E_b,c)/(∂d_c), ∇_z²E_b,c=J_c^⊤(∂²E_b,c)/(∂d_c²)J_c.

    At each reduced solve step, we assemble these per-contact derivatives into the global gradient and Hessian of E_coll(z), directly coupling the reduced states of contacting objects. As shown in Fig. 5(b), the resulting coupled system jointly resolves contacts among multiple deformable objects.

    III-ERig-Complementary Animation

    Beyond purely physics-driven animation, PhysSkin++ also supports rig-complementary animation when an artist-authored LBS rig is available. The prescribed rig deformation serves as the primary animation, while complementary elastic deformation is parameterized by reduced coordinates through the learned neural skinning fields. We first describe the rig-based deformation and then introduce the rig-space complementarity objective used during self-supervised learning.

    Rig-Based Deformation Representation. Consider a skeletal rig with n_b bones, pose parameters p, and rest pose p⁰. Let G_b(p)∈SE(3) be the global transformation of bone b, obtained by composing its local transformations along the kinematic hierarchy. We denote by A_b(p)∈ℝ^3×4 the affine transform induced by the relative bone motion G_b(p)G_b(p⁰)⁻¹. With rig skinning weights W_bʳⁱᵍ(X), LBS [43] maps a rest-space point as:

    φ_rig(X,p)=∑_b=1^n_bW_bʳⁱᵍ(X)A_b(p)\beginbmatrixX 1\endbmatrix.

    		(17)

    Here, A_b(p) moves the point from the rest configuration according to bone b, and the weighted sum blends the bone-transformed positions. Subtracting the rest position gives the rig displacement u_rig(X,p)=φ_rig(X,p)-X. This formulation is efficient and directly controllable, but its kinematic deformations alone cannot produce physical elastic responses.

    For rig-complementary animation, we augment the representation in Eq. (1) with the prescribed rig displacement:

    φ(X,p,z)=X+u_rig(X,p)(18)
    +∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐW_θ,iᶜᵒᵐᵖ(X)Zᵢ\beginbmatrixX 1\endbmatrix.

    The neural skinning term defines the complementary elastic displacement u_comp(X,z). Both animation settings share the continuous skinning parameterization, with rig-complementary animation incorporating the prescribed rig displacement.

    Rig-Space Complementarity Constraint. Fig. 6 summarizes our self-supervised rig-complementarity training pipeline.

    For a batch D of N_D cubature points, we stack the rig and complementary displacements as u_rig(p),u_comp(z)∈ℝ^3N_D. We denote the rig Jacobian by J_rig=∂u_rig(p)/∂p. To prevent the physical component from duplicating motion expressible by the rig, we seek complementary displacements satisfying:

    J_rig^⊤u_comp=0.

    		(19)

    This condition makes the complementary displacement orthogonal to the rig motion subspace spanned by the columns of J_rig under the Euclidean inner product.

    To impose this condition for arbitrary subspace coordinates z, we arrange the batch point matrix as X_D∈ℝ^3×N_D and collect the predicted complementary weights in W_θᶜᵒᵐᵖ(X_D)∈ℝ^N_D×m. Consistent with Eq. (18), the corresponding discrete skinning matrix is constructed as:

    B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖ=I₃⊗[(1ₘ^⊤⊗\beginbmatrixX_D 1_N_D^⊤\endbmatrix^⊤)(20)
    ⊙(W_θᶜᵒᵐᵖ(X_D)⊗1₄^⊤)].

    Here, ⊗ and ⊙ denote the Kronecker and Hadamard products, respectively, and B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖ∈ℝ^3N_D×12m. The displacement stacking and the flattening of handle parameters use the ordering consistent with this matrix, so that u_comp=B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖz.

    We use a linear control parameterization of the prescribed rig, yielding a constant rig Jacobian J_rig[6]. Since u_comp=B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖz, the complementarity condition in Eq. (19) holds for arbitrary z when:

    J_rig^⊤B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖ=0.

    		(21)

    We optimize the predicted complementary skinning weights using the following rig-space complementarity loss:

    L_comp(θ)=𝔼_(D,ℝ)[∥J_rig^⊤B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖ∥_F²],

    		(22)

    where ℝ denotes the prescribed rig and its Jacobian is evaluated on the same batch points as B_lbsᶜᵒᵐᵖ. The rig-complementary training objective augments Eq. (6):

    L_rig(θ)=L_subspace(θ)+λ_compL_comp(θ),

    		(23)

    where L_subspace is the self-supervised subspace learning objective defined in Eq. (6), L_comp is the rig-space complementarity loss defined in Eq. (22), and λ_comp is a weighting hyperparameter. We optimize the resulting objective using the on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction described in Sec. III-C.

    Rig-Driven Complementary Dynamics. At runtime, the deformation representation in Eq. (18) expresses object deformation through the prescribed rig displacement and a complementary elastic displacement parameterized by the reduced coordinates. The rig trajectory {pₜ} is supplied as an external kinematic input, such as an animator-authored pose sequence. Given the prescribed pose pₜ₊₁, we update the complementary coordinates through implicit reduced dynamics:

    zₜ₊₁=\undersetz\arg\min 1/2h²∥z-2zₜ+zₜ₋₁∥_M²(24)
    +Eₚₒₜ (X+u_comp(X,z)+u_rig(X,pₜ₊₁)).

    The complementarity loss in Eq. (22) encourages the condition in Eq. (19) during training, allowing the runtime solve to optimize only the complementary coordinates without additional complementarity constraints. As shown in Fig. 7, this formulation supports both interactive rig control and user-authored rig animation sequences, enriching their kinematic deformation with physics-based complementary elastic response.

    III-FDiscretization-Agnostic Animation Binding

    A key advantage of representing skinning weights as continuous neural fields is the resulting discretization-agnostic deformation map. The learned fields can be evaluated directly at mesh vertices, sampled points, and neural scene primitives, allowing the same reduced physical state to deform different spatial discretizations. We demonstrate this binding capability with 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly binding the anisotropic Gaussian primitives to the learned skinning fields.

    3D Gaussian Representation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [28] represents a scene using anisotropic Gaussian primitives G={G_g}_g=1^N_G, each parameterized as:

    G_g={μ_g, R_g, s_g, α_g, c_g},

    		(25)

    where μ_g∈ℝ³ is the center, R_g∈SO(3) is the rotation matrix, s_g∈ℝ₊³ contains the principal-axis scales, α_g∈[0,1] is the opacity, and c_g denotes the spherical harmonic (SH) appearance coefficients. The corresponding 3D covariance matrix is:

    Σ_g=R_gS_gS_g^⊤R_g^⊤, S_g=diag(s_g).

    		(26)

    For rendering, each 3D Gaussian is projected to a screen-space Gaussian, whose color contribution is accumulated through depth-ordered alpha blending. Animating the Gaussian representation therefore requires updating the center and covariance of each Gaussian according to the underlying physical deformation.

    Continuous Gaussian Binding. Let μ_g⁰ denote the rest center of the g-th Gaussian. Since the neural skinning fields are spatially continuous, we directly evaluate Wᵢ(μ_g⁰) at its rest center. Following the deformation map in Eq. (1), we construct the local affine transformation for each Gaussian as:

    T_g(z)≡[A_g(z) t_g(z)]=[I₃ 0]+∑ᵢ₌₁ᵐWᵢ(μ_g⁰)Zᵢ,

    		(27)

    where A_g∈ℝ^3×3 is the linear part of the affine transformation, which may include rotation, scaling, and shear, and t_g∈ℝ³ is its translation. We evaluate the skinning weights once at each Gaussian’s rest center and use these fixed weights throughout its kernel. The resulting local affine transformation is updated from the current reduced coordinates.

    Gaussian Kernel Deformation. Let Σ_g⁰ denote the rest covariance. Applying the local affine transformation T_g(z) to the Gaussian kernel gives:

    μ_g(z)=A_g(z)μ_g⁰+t_g(z),(28)
    Σ_g(z)=A_g(z)Σ_g⁰A_g(z)^⊤.

    The center therefore follows the skinned point motion, while the covariance captures the induced rotation and anisotropic deformation of the Gaussian kernel. The opacity and SH coefficients retain their rest values.

    Runtime Coupling. At runtime, we advance the reduced coordinates z using Eq. (10). At each frame, these coordinates determine the local affine maps in Eq. (27), which update the Gaussian centers and covariances through Eq. (28), driving physics-based animation of the Gaussian representation.

    IV Experiments

    IV-AImplementation Details

    For the 3D shape encoder, we adopt the pre-trained Michelangelo [67] model which consists of one cross-attention block and eight self-attention blocks; the output latent set Fₛ∈ℝ^M×d has M=256 and d=768. For each 3D object, we re-center and normalize it into a bounding volume of [-1,1]³. For the 3D shape encoder, we sample 4096 points on the object surface as input. For cubature points sampling, we first sample 100k points on the surface, and then voxelize the space into a 128³ grid to obtain interior points to form the complete candidate cubature point set. For each training batch, we randomly sample 1000 cubature points from the candidate point set for potential energy computation, following the same strategy as previous work [9, 44]. In each batch, we randomly sample 1024 subspace coordinate vectors z for training. Our framework is trained on 4 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs. The learning rate is linearly increased to 5×10⁻⁴ within the first 1% of training iterations (warm-up), and then gradually decreased using the cosine decay schedule until reaching the minimum value of 5×10⁻⁵.

    IV-BEvaluation of Learned Skinning Fields

    Baselines. We compare our method with the following baselines: Simplicits [44], RigNet [62], M-I-A [20], Anymate [14], and Puppeteer [52] on the ShapeNet [7] and RigNet [62] datasets. Simplicits trains a separate neural network for each object to output skinning fields through self-supervised learning. The other baselines are supervised neural rigging and skinning methods that output object joints, bones, and skinning weights in a feed-forward manner. These methods are pretrained on expert-annotated datasets, then fine-tuned for comparison.

    Evaluation Metrics. Since our framework is entirely self-supervised and does not rely on annotated skinning data as ground truth, we draw from matrix analysis [22, 4] and spectral theory [54, 13] to propose three quantitative metrics that measure structural independence, numerical stability, and spectral balance of the skinning weights matrix W∈ℝ^N×K, where N is the number of vertices and K is the number of handles or bones. To ensure a fair comparison, we perform ℓ₂-normalization on each column of W before evaluation for all methods, resulting in the matrix Ŵ.

    (1) Orthogonality Metric. We first measure the pairwise orthogonality among handle or bone influence vectors as:

    Ωₒᵣₜₕ=1/K(K-1)∥ Ŵ^⊤Ŵ-I ∥₂²,

    		(29)

    where I is the K×K identity matrix. A smaller Ωₒᵣₜₕ indicates that different handle or bone weights are more decorrelated and capture distinct deformation subspaces. Since each column of Ŵ is ℓ₂-normalized, Ωₒᵣₜₕ is bounded within [0,1], and a smaller value indicates that each handle or bone encodes an independent deformation mode.

    (2) Log-Condition Number Metric. To evaluate the numerical stability of the skinning basis, we compute the log-scaled condition number [21] of the Gram matrix:

    κ_\log=\log₂(1+(λ_\max(Ŵ^⊤Ŵ))/(λ_\min(Ŵ^⊤Ŵ))),

    		(30)

    where λ_\max and λ_\min are the largest and smallest eigenvalues of Ŵ^⊤Ŵ. κ_\log lies within [1,+∞); a smaller value indicates a well-conditioned deformation basis, where small transformations result in stable geometric responses.

    (3) Spectrum Entropy Metric. To assess the balance of spectral energy distribution across skinning weights, we define the spectrum entropy metric [13, 54] as:

    H_spec=-(1)/(\logK)∑ᵢ₌₁^Kpᵢ\logpᵢ, pᵢ=(λᵢ)/(∑ⱼλⱼ),

    		(31)

    where {λᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^K are the eigenvalues of Ŵ^⊤Ŵ. H_spec is bounded within [0,1], where higher values indicate more uniform spectral energy and balanced, expressive deformation modes.

    Results. We first evaluate neural skinning on unseen objects from the test set of the RigNet [62] dataset to assess generalization. The RigNet dataset provides annotated skinning data; we fine-tune the pretrained feed-forward neural skinning baselines using these annotations, whereas our model is trained only on the 3D meshes. Table  reports the quantitative comparison on unseen objects. Our method significantly outperforms the baselines across all three evaluation metrics, demonstrating its generalization ability. We further evaluate our method on the ShapeNet dataset [7], which provides clearly defined object categories. Our model is trained jointly across all categories, and all baselines are evaluated on the corresponding test sets. Because Simplicits can only be trained on a single object at a time, we train an individual Simplicits model for each object. The quantitative results in Table  show that our method consistently outperforms all baselines. In Fig. 8 and Fig. 11, we compare the qualitative skinning results with the baselines. Our method produces more physically consistent, geometrically orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results. Fig. 9 and Fig. 11 further show that our method generalizes to unseen objects and produces high-quality skinning results. For additional results, please refer to the supplementary material.

    Deformable Shape Family. In Fig. 12, our method uses a single model to infer skinning fields for a deformable shape family, while Simplicits [44] must be trained separately for each geometry. This comparison demonstrates the efficiency and cross-shape generalization of our framework.

    Rig-Complementary Neural Skinning Fields. We evaluate the neural skinning fields learned with our self-supervised rig-complementarity objective on characters from the RigNet dataset [62], which provides the skeletal rigs and associated LBS skinning weights. Fig. 13 shows the learned fields across diverse character geometries and rig structures, with spatially varying patterns over the body and appendages. We further examine the resulting complementary elastic responses under interactive rig control and user-authored animation sequences in Sec. IV-D.

    IV-CAblation Studies

    To validate our design choices, we conduct ablation studies covering both the key components of the proposed Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy and the rig-space complementarity term in the rig-complementary setting, using the RigNet [62] dataset. As shown in Table , we remove or modify the PISSL components to assess their individual effects on model performance. Specifically, we evaluate the smoothness loss Lₛₘₒₒₜₕ, the orthogonality constraint Lₒᵣₜₕ, the skinning normalization process, the ONI [26] layer, and conflict-aware gradient correction using ConFIG [37]. The quantitative results demonstrate that these components maintain the numerical stability and orthogonality of the learned neural skinning fields, which are essential for well-conditioned and physically consistent deformation behavior. In Fig. 14, we visualize the skinning results obtained without the potential energy loss Lₚₒₜ, where the model fails to produce physically interpretable skinning fields. Fig. 13 further compares neural skinning fields learned with and without L_comp. Without this term, the visualized fields form broad regions across the head, torso, and limbs. Incorporating L_comp changes these distributions, with visible differences in the ears, wings, and limb regions across multiple characters. These comparisons illustrate the effect of rig-space complementarity learning on the spatial organization of the skinning fields.

    IV-DDiverse Real-Time Physics-Based Animation

    We next examine the broader animation scope enabled by PhysSkin++. Its discretization-agnostic neural skinning fields support efficient reduced dynamics for controllable and collision-aware animation, rig-complementary animation, and direct binding to 3D Gaussian representations.

    Time Efficiency. We first evaluate the time efficiency of our skinning-based subspace animation. We compare it with a classical FEM method using implicit time integration and an MPM method using explicit time integration. For these two full-space physical simulators, we use open-source high-performance GPU implementations [9, 68]. All methods are evaluated on the same CPU and GPU hardware. As shown in Table , our method demonstrates excellent time efficiency.

    Controllable and Collision-Aware Animation. Beyond unconstrained deformation, we qualitatively examine how the learned neural skinning subspaces respond to prescribed controls and environmental contact. As shown in Fig. 4(a), the Dirichlet boundary conditions enforce zero displacement over the prescribed upper regions, while the unconstrained geometry deforms under gravity. In the interactive sequences of Fig. 4(b), the lower region of each object is fixed by Dirichlet boundary conditions, while Gaussian-kernel-weighted dragging provides localized control over the remaining deformable domain. Fig. 4(c) further demonstrates contact with planar environments across diverse shapes and boundary orientations, with the contact response modeled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (14). We further evaluate collision-aware animation involving multiple objects. In the rigid–deformable sequences of Fig. 5(a), a rigid body is released from an elevated position and falls under gravity onto a deformable object. Contact between the two objects is modeled by the point-pair IPC-style barrier in Eq. (15), while contact with the supporting floor is handled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (14). In the deformable–deformable sequences of Fig. 5(b), multiple deformable objects are released from elevated positions and fall under gravity. Contacts among the falling objects are resolved using the point-pair IPC-style barrier in Eq. (15), while their contact with the supporting floor is modeled by the boundary-penalty energy in Eq. (14). These results demonstrate controllable deformation and multi-object interaction within the PhysSkin++ skinning-based reduced representation.

    Rig-Complementary Animation. We evaluate the resulting rig-complementary animation under both interactive control and user-authored animation sequences, as shown in Fig. 7. For interactive rig control, we implement a Polyscope-based graphical interface [48] that allows users to manipulate bone poses at runtime. The resulting rig motion defines the primary animation, while PhysSkin++ computes the corresponding complementary elastic response. For user-authored rig animation, we obtain source skeletal animation sequences from Mixamo [1] and retarget them to the target character rigs using Auto-Rig Pro [3]. In both settings, PhysSkin++ augments the primary rig animation with temporally evolving, physics-based complementary deformation.

    Discretization-Agnostic 3D Gaussian Animation. Owing to the discretization-agnostic nature of our neural skinning formulation, the learned deformation fields can be evaluated directly on 3D Gaussian primitives without introducing an underlying mesh discretization. Following the 3D Gaussian binding formulation in Sec. III-F, we evaluate PhysSkin++ on the ShapeSplat dataset [42], which contains 3D Gaussian reconstructions of objects from ShapeNet [7]. As shown in Fig. 15, the learned fields are queried at the Gaussian rest centers, and the induced local affine deformation updates both the centers and anisotropic covariances to produce coherent physics-based animation. We encourage readers to visit our project page for additional animation videos.

    V Conclusion

    In this paper, we present PhysSkin++, a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. A neural skinning fields autoencoder learns continuous skinning fields directly from static geometries to define a skinning-based subspace mapping. Our Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy promotes physically plausible deformations through a self-supervised objective and stabilizes joint optimization through on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction. At runtime, a reduced dynamics formulation advances the reduced coordinates and supports Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable contact. Beyond purely physics-driven animation, we extend the deformation representation with prescribed rig displacement and the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term, enabling complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animations without enforcing the complementarity constraint at runtime. The continuous deformation map also enables discretization-agnostic binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussian representations. Experiments demonstrate that PhysSkin++ achieves outstanding performance on generalizable neural skinning while enabling real-time physics-based animation. As a limitation, our current formulation does not incorporate semantic priors for modeling complex geometries. Future work will explore such priors to improve the expressiveness of the learned skinning-based subspace mapping.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: ML-IST：碰撞内切球树别再贪心一遍遍建，网络一次预测完，已接进 Jolt 与 Bullet ｜ Fast Construction of Inner Sphere Trees Using Machine Learning
item.description:
一句话：把内切球生成改成集合预测问题，单卡比单核 CPU 快 2.0–2.6 倍，集成后 55.89 FPS。

要点：

  • 复杂非凸物体的碰撞检测是物理仿真、VR 与机器人的瓶颈；内切球树（IST）查询快，但构建是串行贪心、开销极大，既拖慢预处理也限制运行时使用。
  • ML-IST 把叶球生成重构成单次集合预测：网络从多通道体素几何直接预测一固定数量的内切球候选，用可微覆盖反馈修正粗预测并在更细尺度补残余空洞，最后用轻量几何投影保证合法性。
  • 单卡实现相比单核 CPU 构建，在 64–512 球的目标容量下平均把叶球生成时间降到 1/2.0–1/2.6；已集成进 Jolt Physics 与 Bullet，alpha-puzzle 基准上达 55.89 FPS，高于传统 IST、GImpact 与凸分解。

为什么值得看：这是「AI 直接替换引擎内核构件」最干净的样本：输出是可验证的几何加速结构，不是黑盒预测，还给出两个主流物理引擎里的实测帧率——能照着评估自己项目的碰撞管线。

中文摘要：复杂非凸物体的碰撞检测是物理仿真、虚拟现实与机器人的瓶颈。内切球树（IST）能高效回答邻近与穿透查询，但叶球构建是串行贪心过程，计算昂贵，限制大规模预处理与运行时使用。论文提出 ML-IST，把叶球生成重构为单次集合预测问题：网络从多通道体素几何预测固定数量的内切球候选，用可微覆盖反馈修正粗预测并在更细尺度填补残余空隙，再用轻量几何投影保证合法性。在测试集上，单卡实现相对单核 CPU 构建把平均叶球生成时间降低 2.0–2.6 倍（目标容量 64–512 球）；作者将其集成进 Jolt Physics 与 Bullet，alpha-puzzle 基准达到 55.89 FPS。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·引擎架构（English）

原文发布：2026-10-08

本期推送：2026-10-23

Fast Construction of Inner Sphere Trees Using Machine Learning

Abstract

Collision detection for complex non-convex objects is a bottleneck in physics simulation, virtual reality, and robotics. Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer proximity and penetration queries efficiently, but their greedy leaf-sphere construction is sequential and computationally expensive, which limits both large-scale preprocessing and runtime use. In this work, we present ML-IST, a machine-learning-based method that reformulates leaf-sphere generation as a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback corrects the coarse prediction and fills residual gaps at finer scales, and a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Averaged over the test set, a single-GPU implementation of ML-IST reduces mean leaf-generation time by a factor of 2.0–2.6 over single-core CPU construction across target capacities of 64–512 spheres, and qualitative results on complex models show multiscale sphere distributions that follow principal volumes and slender features. We further integrate ML-IST into the Jolt Physics and Bullet engines; in an alpha-puzzle benchmark it reaches 55.89 FPS, the highest among the compared representations (conventional IST, GImpact, and convex decomposition). These results support learned leaf generation as a practical component for fast, runtime construction of detailed collision representations.

Keywords: inner sphere tree; collision detection; machine learning.

1 Introduction

Collision detection is essential to realism and responsiveness in virtual reality, physics simulation, robotic path planning, and medical interaction. For objects with complex non-convex features, such as holes, recesses, and thin structures, an effective collision representation must support efficient queries while accurately describing the occupied interior. Many acceleration structures have been developed for this purpose, including convex-body distance tests [1], convex-hull constructions [2], and exterior bounding-volume hierarchies [3, 4]. Sphere hierarchies approximate a model with nested spheres and have long been used for time-critical collision detection and medial-axis approximation [5, 6]. Among them, the inner sphere tree (IST) [7] places non-overlapping inscribed spheres inside the object and organizes them hierarchically, approximating the occupied volume compactly and supporting proximity and penetration queries.

Although ISTs are efficient at query time, their construction remains expensive. Conventional leaf generation uses a greedy iterative strategy over a signed distance field (SDF) [8], which encodes boundary clearance and inside–outside information and is widely used in collision-related computation [9]: the largest admissible inner sphere is repeatedly located in voxel space, and the residual feasible region is updated after every placement. The procedure is therefore inherently sequential and cannot fully exploit the parallelism of modern GPUs; construction time grows with voxel resolution, geometric complexity, and the target number of leaf spheres. Prior IST research has emphasized hierarchical organization, query performance, and penetration-depth estimation, whereas the cost of generating the leaf spheres has received less attention. Reducing this cost would benefit both large-scale preprocessing and rapid, runtime construction of collision representations.

Recent progress in deep learning has produced data-driven representations of three-dimensional geometry [10, 11] and neural implicit models such as DeepSDF and Occupancy Networks, which learn continuous geometric fields from spatial coordinates [12, 13]. For collision-related computation, Zesch et al. predict signed distances for deformable objects from a deformation code and a query point [14], and neural builders have been used to accelerate the construction of spatial subdivisions such as k-d trees and BVHs [15]. These methods demonstrate that search- or optimization-intensive geometric procedures can be transferred to offline training and approximated by a forward pass at runtime. They primarily predict query-level quantities, such as an SDF value, an occupancy probability, or a collision state, or they target exterior spatial subdivision for traversal optimization. ML-IST instead predicts an explicit, reusable set of interior spheres from multichannel voxel geometry, providing the leaves for a conventional IST hierarchy.

To this end, we propose ML-IST (machine-learning-based inner sphere tree generation), which reformulates leaf-sphere construction as the prediction of a fixed-capacity candidate set. Given a normalized 3D model, a multistage network predicts candidate centers, radii, and objectness scores from a multichannel voxel representation: it first establishes coarse coverage with large base spheres and then corrects them and fills residual gaps at finer scales through differentiable coverage feedback, after which a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Inference requires a single network forward pass. The contribution of this work is threefold. First, it formulates IST leaf generation as fixed-capacity sphere-set prediction. Second, it combines coarse prediction with differentiable coverage feedback and bounded multiscale refinement. Third, it evaluates generation time against the conventional greedy builder and demonstrates the predicted proxy in rigid-body and physics-engine benchmarks, including runtime construction inside Jolt Physics and Bullet.

The scope of this work is the leaf-sphere generation stage, which is the dominant construction cost in a conventional IST, rather than the replacement of the complete IST framework. The predicted spheres can still be organized into a conventional hierarchy and used by existing collision-query procedures, so ML-IST is a hybrid approach that moves much of the geometric search from online construction to offline training. This design supports both offline batch preprocessing and the runtime construction of detailed collision representations for objects that appear only after a physics engine has started; Section 5 evaluates the latter setting.

2 Learning-Based Inner Sphere Tree Generation

Conventional IST leaf generation repeatedly searches for admissible inner spheres and updates the remaining volume. This sequential process becomes expensive as voxel resolution and target sphere count increase. ML-IST replaces the search with a learned mapping from voxel geometry to a fixed-capacity sphere set. The pipeline comprises multichannel input construction, base-sphere prediction, coverage-feedback generation, and multiscale refinement, followed by lightweight geometric projection.

As illustrated in Fig. 1, the network first predicts large base spheres to represent the principal interior regions. A differentiable renderer converts these spheres into voxel-level coverage feedback. A second encoder uses this feedback to guide limited corrections to the base spheres and predict medium and fine residual spheres for the remaining gaps. All branches are evaluated within a single network forward pass; the resulting leaves can subsequently be organized into a conventional IST hierarchy.

2.1 Multichannel Voxel Geometry Representation

Let Ωᵢₙ denote the interior of a 3D model. The objective is to generate a sphere set that covers the principal interior volume with limited exterior coverage and severe overlap under a finite candidate budget. ML-IST predicts K candidates from the voxel input V in a single pass. Each candidate is represented by its center ĉᵢ, radius r̂ᵢ, and activation confidence, or objectness, ôᵢ∈[0,1]. Centers and radii are expressed in input-grid units, and the candidate set is denoted by Ŝ.

Model geometry is resampled onto a grid of resolution R³ to construct the seven-channel input:

V=[Mᵢₙ,Dₙₒᵣₘ,Φₙₒᵣₘ,B,X,Y,Z].

(1)

The binary mask Mᵢₙ equals 1 for interior voxels and 0 for exterior voxels. The interior distance field D estimates, in grid units, the distance from an interior point to the model boundary ∂Ω:

D(p)≈\min_q∈∂Ω∥p-q∥₂, p∈Ωᵢₙ.

(2)

This distance approximates an upper bound on the admissible radius of a sphere centered at p and provides the geometric basis for subsequent constraints and radius projection. The implementation reads a preprocessed distance field when available; otherwise, it computes the Euclidean distance transform from the interior mask.

Dₙₒᵣₘ is scaled by the 99th percentile of interior distances, with a minimum scaling factor of 1, and clipped to [0,1]. The signed-distance channel Φₙₒᵣₘ is robustly normalized by the 99th percentile of absolute SDF values and clipped to [-1,1].
