    The proposed method accelerates phase-based collision detection by optimizing the order of exact mesh checks in the narrow phase, without modifying the underlying collision detector. This is achieved by using the collision probabilities predicted by the hypernetwork-based model to approximate the optimal check order. In this subsection, we evaluate whether the proposed method can reduce the time cost of phase-based collision detection.

    First, we construct 9 simulated environments with different clutter levels, where the number of obstacles ranges from 10 to 90. In each environment, the obstacle positions are randomly generated during initialization and then kept fixed, and we randomly sample 100000 poses of the Panda robot for collision detection. For each pose, we perform two collision detection operations: one using BVH alone and the other using BVH combined with our method. The average detection time and its decomposition in each environment are shown in Fig. 8. We have the following observations: (i) over all detections, BVH combined with our method reduces the average detection time compared with BVH alone. The acceleration effect is generally more evident in cluttered environments, achieving a 37% speedup in the scenario with 60 obstacles. Moreover, as environmental clutteredness increases, a higher proportion of detection time is spent on collision cases. (ii) in collision cases, BVH combined with our method incurs additional costs for probability prediction and check-order construction, but it reduces the time spent on mesh checks by examining more likely colliding pairs earlier and enabling earlier termination. (iii) in non-collision cases, all object pairs in the narrow phase must be checked. Therefore, check-order optimization does not reduce mesh-check time and may slightly increase the total detection time. Overall, although our method introduces additional operations, it reduces the narrow-phase mesh-check time in collision cases by adjusting the check order, thereby accelerating phase-based collision detection. The improvement is substantial in cluttered environments. Since the proposed method accelerates collision detection by reordering mesh checks in the narrow phase, it can also be applied to other phase-based methods. As shown in Table IV, our method substantially reduces the detection time of Octree-based collision detection in the environments with 50 and 70 obstacles shown in Fig. 8.

    The generalization capability of the proposed model across robot arms has been evaluated in Sec. IV-A. We further validate whether the proposed method can accelerate phase-based collision detection for the unseen UR5 without any additional training. The experiments are conducted in two more complex environments containing 100 and 120 obstacles. As shown in Table V, our method effectively reduces the detection time for UR5, indicating that the proposed check-ordering strategy can generalize to other robot arms.

    Finally, we compare our method with the surface area heuristic (SAH) and the distance-based heuristic (DBH), which use geometric metrics as coarse proxies for collision likelihood to adjust the check order. In the environment with 50 obstacles shown in Fig. 8, we randomly resample 1000 robot poses and perform collision detection with the two heuristics and our method. The results are shown in Table VI. Both SAH and DBH can accelerate BVH-based collision detection. However, because these heuristics are simple but coarse, their resulting check orders show noticeable discrepancies from those produced by our model, leading to inferior acceleration performance.

    IV-CAcceleration for Sampling-based Motion Planning

    As mentioned earlier, sampling-based motion planning involves numerous collision detection operations, which are typically accelerated by phase-based collision detection methods. In this subsection, we evaluate whether the proposed collision-detection acceleration method can improve the performance of sampling-based motion planners. Three planners, RRT [27], RRT-Connect [28], and BIT* [29], are implemented using OMPL. For each planner, we compare two collision detection settings: BVH alone and BVH combined with our method. The simulation environment with 50 obstacles is the same as that shown in Fig. 8. For each planner, we generate 100 random start-goal configuration pairs in the environment and set a time budget of 5 seconds for finding a feasible solution. Each planner is run 50 times for each configuration pair and stops when either a feasible solution is found or the time budget is exhausted.

    The execution results are shown in Table VII. For all three planners, combining BVH with our method reduces the average time cost required to find a feasible solution, with RRT-Connect achieving about 22% acceleration. Since the proposed method improves the efficiency of phase-based collision detection, the planners can perform more sampling and collision-checking operations within the same time budget. This enables more thorough exploration of the configuration space, resulting in improved planning success rates for all three planners in the cluttered environment.

    Furthermore, it is worth emphasizing that the planner-level acceleration reported above is achieved under CPU-only inference during planning. GPU support is only required when MFN is invoked to process previously unseen object meshes. After the corresponding CPN parameters are generated, they can be reused for subsequent predictions. This design avoids retraining the entire collision predictor when new object meshes appear.

    V Conclusion

    In this paper, we propose a learning-based method to accelerate phase-based collision detection in sampling-based motion planning by optimizing the check order in the narrow phase. First, we formulate the expected time cost of the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion that minimizes this expectation. Second, we design a hypernetwork-based model to learn and predict the priors required to construct an approximate optimal check order, while maintaining low computational complexity and good generalization capability. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces the time cost of phase-based collision detection in cluttered environments, and further improves the efficiency and success rate of sampling-based motion planners.

    In practical applications, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing phase-based collision detection frameworks, since it only adjusts the check order in the narrow phase without modifying the underlying collision detector. This non-intrusive design enables straightforward deployment in a wide range of sampling-based motion planning systems with minimal implementation effort. Furthermore, since collision detection often dominates the computational cost of motion planning in cluttered environments, the proposed acceleration strategy has the potential to provide substantial performance gains in real-world robotic applications that require frequent collision checking, such as manipulation, navigation, and motion planning in confined spaces.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把窄相期望代价写成可学习的目标，用模型排出检查顺序，杂乱场景里加速明显。

要点：

  • 分相碰撞检测里，宽相用层级结构快速剔除明显不相交的物体对，窄相才对剩下的对做详细检查；但现有实现按宽相返回的默认顺序检查，几乎没优化过顺序。
  • 作者先形式化窄相阶段的期望时间代价，并推导出最优检查顺序，再用学习方法预测该顺序，使「早发现碰撞、早退出」成为常态。
  • 收益集中在杂乱环境：宽相剪枝后仍留下大量物体对、窄相占总检测时间大头时，重排顺序能显著降低总体开销。

为什么值得看：碰撞检测是引擎里最热的代码路径之一，这篇给的不是新结构而是「检查顺序」这个几乎零成本杠杆——不需要换加速结构就能吃到加速比。

中文摘要：碰撞检测对基于采样的运动规划是必要但昂贵的开销。常见的分相方法里，宽相用层级结构快速排除明显不相交的物体对，窄相对剩余物体对做详细检查；然而窄相通常按宽相返回的默认顺序执行，几乎没有对检查顺序做显式优化，在混杂环境中仍有大量物体对残留时，窄相会占据总检测时间的显著部分。论文提出用学习优化窄相检查顺序：先形式化窄相的期望时间代价并推导最优顺序，再用学习模型预测顺序，从而更早命中碰撞并提前退出，在杂乱场景中显著加速整体检测。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·引擎架构（English）

原文发布：2026-09-24

本期推送：2026-10-23

Learning-Accelerated Narrow-Phase Collision Detection via Check Ordering for
Sampling-Based Motion Planning

Abstract

Collision detection is critical for ensuring the safety of planned paths in sampling-based motion planning. However, it imposes a non-negligible computational burden on motion planners, motivating extensive studies on collision-detection acceleration. In commonly used phase-based collision-detection methods, the broad phase employs hierarchical structures to rapidly discard object pairs that are clearly collision-free, while the subsequent narrow phase performs detailed collision checks on the remaining object pairs whose collision status cannot be determined by the broad phase. Although these methods effectively reduce the number of detailed checks through broad-phase pruning, the narrow phase is usually executed in the default order returned by the broad phase, with little explicit optimization of the check order. This leaves room for further acceleration, especially in cluttered environments where many object pairs may remain after the broad phase and the narrow phase can account for a significant portion of the total detection time. In this work, we propose a learning-based method to accelerate phase-based collision detection by optimizing the check order in the narrow phase. We first formulate the expected time cost of the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion that minimizes this expectation. Since the priors required by this criterion are difficult to obtain in advance, we design a hypernetwork-based model to predict collision probabilities, which are then used to approximate the optimal check order. The resulting order guides the execution of exact mesh checks in the narrow phase, thereby reducing detection time without replacing the underlying geometric collision checker. Simulation results show that our method effectively accelerates phase-based collision detection and improves the efficiency and success rate of sampling-based motion planning, especially in cluttered environments.

Index Terms:

Sampling-based motion planning, phase-based collision detection, narrow-phase detection, optimal check order, hypernetwork-based model.

I Introduction

Sampling-based motion planning constructs feasible paths by sampling the robot’s configuration space and connecting collision-free configurations [1]. Among its key processes, collision detection determines whether the robot collides with surrounding obstacles at each sampled configuration, serving as a basis for ensuring the safety of the generated paths. In typical geometric collision detection, the surface geometry of each object is represented as a mesh composed of numerous triangles. This applies to both robot components and environmental obstacles, where each triangle defines a small region of the object’s surface. Therefore, a direct collision check between two objects, referred to as a mesh check, involves a large number of triangle-triangle intersection computations [2], making it computationally expensive. Since each sampled configuration may require checking many object pairs, collision detection often accounts for a substantial portion of the total computational cost in sampling-based motion planning [3]. Consequently, numerous studies have been conducted to accelerate collision detection [4], and several studies have shown that such acceleration can improve the performance of sampling-based motion planners [5][6].

Among these studies, phase-based collision detection is one of the most widely used acceleration paradigms, including methods based on Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVH) [7], Octrees [8], and Spatial Hashing [9]. These methods divide the detection into two phases: the broad phase and the narrow phase. In the broad phase, coarse geometric representations, such as bounding volumes or spatial partitions, are used to perform efficient overlap tests and quickly discard object pairs that are clearly collision-free. Then, in the subsequent narrow phase, mesh checks are performed only on the remaining object pairs whose collision status cannot be determined by the broad phase. Therefore, phase-based methods achieve acceleration primarily through broad-phase pruning, and their differences mainly lie in the coarse representations and exclusion strategies used in the broad phase.

Compared with the broad phase, the narrow phase has received relatively limited attention in existing phase-based methods. In most implementations, mesh checks are performed on the remaining object pairs from the broad phase one by one, following the default order returned by the broad-phase traversal, without explicit check-order optimization. In cluttered environments, the robot is often in close proximity to obstacles, which limits the ability of the coarse broad phase to exclude object pairs. As a result, many object pairs still need to be processed during the narrow phase. Due to the high computational complexity of the mesh check, the narrow phase can account for a significant portion of the overall detection time, as shown in Fig. 1. This indicates that optimizing the narrow phase can provide further acceleration for phase-based collision detection.

Therefore, in this work, we aim to accelerate the narrow phase by adjusting the order of mesh checks, so that object pairs more likely to collide are examined earlier. This enables earlier termination once a collision is detected, thereby reducing the expected detection time. However, constructing an effective check order requires prior information about the object pairs, such as their collision probabilities, which is difficult to obtain in advance. To address this, we propose a hypernetwork-based learning model to predict the required priors and use them to guide narrow-phase check ordering. Importantly, the proposed method does not replace exact mesh checks with learning-based predictions; instead, it only reorders exact checks, preserving the reliability of the underlying geometric collision detector. In summary, our main contributions are:

  • •

    We propose to accelerate the phase-based collision detection by optimizing the check order in the narrow phase. By modeling the expected time cost of the narrow phase, we derive an optimal check-ordering criterion that minimizes this expectation.

  • •

    We design a hypernetwork-based model to predict the priors required for constructing an approximate optimal check order, with an emphasis on generalization and low computational complexity.

  • •

    Simulation results show that the proposed method accelerates phase-based collision detection in cluttered environments, thereby improving both the efficiency and success rate of sampling-based motion planners.

    • II Background

    Collision detection determines whether the meshes of robot components intersect with those of environmental obstacles. A straightforward implementation is to perform mesh checks on all object pairs. However, since mesh checks are computationally expensive, collision detection can become time-consuming, motivating extensive research on acceleration methods. Existing approaches can be broadly categorized into phase-based methods, which reduce the number of mesh checks, and learning-based methods, which reduce the computational cost of individual checks.

    Phase-based methods divide collision detection into two phases: the broad phase and the narrow phase. Acceleration is primarily achieved in the broad phase, where coarse geometric representations are used to enclose objects and enable simple overlap tests. Object pairs that clearly do not collide can then be quickly discarded without performing detailed mesh checks. For example, BVH [7] organizes objects or geometric primitives into a hierarchy of bounding volumes. Since these volumes are usually simple shapes, such as boxes or spheres, their overlap can be tested much more efficiently than mesh intersections. If two bounding volumes do not overlap, the object pairs contained in them can be directly excluded from further mesh checks. Similarly, Octrees [8] recursively divide the environment into octants and construct a hierarchical spatial index, thereby reducing the number of object pairs requiring mesh checks by excluding non-intersecting nodes. Spatial Hashing [9] partitions the workspace into grid cells and checks only object pairs mapped to the same or neighboring cells, efficiently filtering out pairs that are guaranteed to be collision-free. In addition, some studies have explored parallel or hardware-friendly implementations of phase-based collision detection [10]. Although these methods differ in their broad-phase representations and exclusion strategies, their subsequent narrow phase is usually similar: mesh checks are performed on the remaining object pairs in the order returned by the broad phase, without explicit optimization of the check order.

    In contrast, learning-based methods aim to approximate mesh-check results using data-driven models, achieving faster predictions at the cost of possible prediction errors. Early studies used multilayer perceptrons [11] and Support Vector Machines (SVMs) [12] to learn collision boundaries, but these methods were mainly limited to relatively simple objects and offered limited advantages in prediction efficiency. To improve efficiency, Pan et al. [13] proposed a method that stores prior collision results and uses them to predict collisions for new robot poses, based on the observation that nearby poses may share similar collision states. Das et al. [14] learned a collision proxy using a perceptron classifier with a computationally efficient kernel, and further showed that a forward-kinematics kernel is more suitable for measuring the similarity between two robot poses [15]. Verghese et al. [16] and Han et al. [17] further decomposed the configuration space into multiple subspaces, each associated with a separate predictor, thereby improving prediction accuracy and reducing prediction time. These methods mainly focus on the trade-off between prediction accuracy and computational complexity. However, they are typically designed for fixed environments and may suffer from limited generalization. Moreover, when learning-based predictions are used to replace exact mesh checks, false predictions may waste computational resources or even compromise path safety. Therefore, deterministic phase-based methods remain widely used in motion planning systems. Although learning-based predictors could be applied to the narrow phase, directly replacing mesh checks still introduces the risks of incorrect predictions and limited generalization.

    To further accelerate phase-based collision detection while preserving deterministic collision-checking results, this paper focuses on optimizing the check order in the narrow phase. Some heuristic strategies, such as the surface-area-based [18] and distance-based [19] rules, use geometric features as indirect proxies for collision likelihood and can be used to adjust the check order. However, these heuristics do not explicitly model the expected time cost of the narrow phase or provide an optimality criterion for check ordering. Therefore, we formulate the expected narrow-phase time cost and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion. Instead of replacing exact mesh checks, the proposed hypernetwork-based model predicts the priors required to approximate this criterion and uses them only to reorder mesh checks in the narrow phase.

    III Narrow-Phase Optimization in
    Phase-based Collision Detection

    In this section, we first introduce the principle of phase-based collision detection using BVH as an example, and discuss the potential for optimization in the narrow phase. Then, we formulate a time cost model for the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion that minimizes the expected time cost. Next, we propose a hypernetwork-based model to learn and predict the priors required to approximate the optimal check order. Finally, we summarize the proposed learning-accelerated phase-based collision detection method for sampling-based motion planning.

    III-APhase-based Collision Detection

    Phase-based methods divide the collision detection process into the broad phase and the narrow phase. The basic idea is to use bounding volumes and hierarchical structures in the broad phase to quickly exclude object pairs that are clearly collision-free, thereby reducing the number of remaining object pairs that require detailed mesh checks in the narrow phase. In this way, phase-based methods avoid performing mesh checks on all object pairs and thus accelerate collision detection. We use the widely adopted BVH as an example, as shown in Fig. 2. Suppose BVH is applied to detect collisions between the robot component link1 and four obstacles.

  • •

    Broad phase: As illustrated in Fig. 2b, bounding volumes are constructed for link1 and each obstacle, and a hierarchy, i.e., a BVH tree, is built for the bounding volumes of all obstacles. Since bounding volumes are usually simple shapes, such as the Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) used in Fig. 2b, testing whether two boxes overlap, referred to as a box check, is much simpler than performing a mesh check. Moreover, if two boxes do not overlap, the objects enclosed by them cannot collide. Therefore, based on the BVH tree in Fig. 2c, if a parent box does not overlap with the box of link1, its child boxes can be directly excluded. Otherwise, box checks are further performed for its child boxes until the leaf nodes of the tree are reached.

  • •

    Narrow phase: Since the bounding-volume hierarchy used in the broad phase is coarse, an overlap between a leaf node in the BVH tree and the box of link1 does not necessarily indicate an actual collision. As a result, in the narrow phase shown in Fig. 2c, mesh checks are still required for the object pairs remaining from the broad phase, because their collision status cannot be determined by the box check alone. The default check order in the narrow phase is determined by the order in which the remaining object pairs are generated during broad-phase traversal, and this order is not explicitly optimized for narrow-phase collision checking.

    • Existing phase-based methods mainly differ in the hierarchical structures, bounding volumes, and exclusion strategies used in the broad phase. However, the remaining object pairs after the broad phase are typically checked one by one using mesh checks in the narrow phase. This leaves room for further acceleration, especially in cluttered environments. In such environments, the robot may be close to obstacles, limiting the ability of the broad phase to exclude object pairs and leaving many pairs to be processed in the narrow phase. Since mesh checks are much more expensive than box checks, the narrow phase can account for a large portion of the overall detection time. Therefore, phase-based collision detection can be further improved by optimizing the narrow phase.

    III-BNarrow Phase Modeling and Optimal Check Order

    In the narrow phase of phase-based collision detection, mesh checks are performed on object pairs whose collision status cannot be determined by the broad phase. Since collision detection only needs to determine whether at least one collision occurs, the narrow phase terminates either after all object pairs are verified as collision-free or immediately once a collision is detected. Therefore, to reduce the expected time cost of the narrow phase, object pairs with higher collision probabilities and lower check costs should be examined earlier. This enables earlier termination of the narrow phase. Building on this idea, we formulate the time cost of the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion.

    Suppose there are n≥2 object pairs {m₁,m₂,…,mₙ} that require mesh checks in the narrow phase. For each object pair mᵢ, let pᵢ denote its collision probability and tᵢ denote the time cost of its mesh check. A check order is denoted by a permutation σ=[s₁,s₂,…,sₙ], where sᵢ is the index of the object pair checked at the i-th position. Assuming that collision events of different object pairs are independent, the expected time cost 𝔼(T_σ) of the narrow phase under the order σ is

    \beginsplit𝔼(T_σ)=&t_s₁+(1-p_s₁)t_s₂+(1-p_s₁)(1-p_s₂)t_s₃ &+⋯+(1-p_s₁)⋯(1-p_sₙ₋₁)t_sₙ =&∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ(∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ))t_sᵢ.\endsplit(1)

    In the following, we show that the expected time cost is minimized by sorting object pairs in nonincreasing order of pᵢ/tᵢ.

    Theorem 1

    Assume that collision events of different object pairs are independent. An optimal check order that minimizes the expected time cost 𝔼(T_σ) in (1) is given by σᵒ=[sᵒ₁,sᵒ₂,…,sᵒₙ], where for any i

    Proof: Consider an arbitrary check order σᵃ=[s₁,…,sₗ,sₗ₊₁…,sₙ] and another order σᵇ=[s₁,…,sₗ₊₁,sₗ…,sₙ] obtained by swapping the adjacent elements sₗ and sₗ₊₁ of σᵃ, where l∈{1,2,…,n-1}.

    According to (1), the expected time costs of the narrow phase under σᵃ and σᵇ are

    𝔼(T_σᵃ)=∑ᵢ₌₁ˡ⁻¹(∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ))t_sᵢ(2)
    +∏ⱼ₌₁ˡ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ)(t_sₗ+(1-p_sₗ)t_sₗ₊₁)
    +∑ᵢ₌ₗ₊₂ⁿ(∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ))t_sᵢ,

    and

    𝔼(T_σᵇ)=∑ᵢ₌₁ˡ⁻¹(∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ))t_sᵢ(3)
    +∏ⱼ₌₁ˡ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ)(t_sₗ₊₁+(1-p_sₗ₊₁)t_sₗ)
    +∑ᵢ₌ₗ₊₂ⁿ(∏ⱼ₌₁ⁱ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ))t_sᵢ.

    Subtracting (3) from (2), we obtain the time difference as

    𝔼(T_σᵃ)-𝔼(T_σᵇ)
    =∏ⱼ₌₁ˡ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ)(t_sₗ+(1-p_sₗ)t_sₗ₊₁-t_sₗ₊₁-(1-p_sₗ₊₁)t_sₗ)
    =∏ⱼ₌₁ˡ⁻¹(1-p_sⱼ)(p_sₗ₊₁t_sₗ-p_sₗt_sₗ₊₁).

    Thus, it follows that 𝔼(T_σᵃ)>𝔼(T_σᵇ) if and only if (p_sₗ)/(t_sₗ)<(p_sₗ₊₁)/(t_sₗ₊₁). In other words, if (p_sₗ)/(t_sₗ)<(p_sₗ₊₁)/(t_sₗ₊₁), then swapping sₗ and sₗ₊₁ results in a check order with a lower expected time cost in the narrow phase. Moreover, for any check order whose elements are not in nonincreasing order of pᵢ/tᵢ, we can swap neighboring elements to construct a better check order that reduces the expected time cost of the narrow phase, until the optimal check order σᵒ is achieved. ∎

    III-CHypernetwork-based model

    Although the optimal check-ordering criterion is derived in Theorem 1, the priors (pᵢ,tᵢ) required to construct the optimal order are difficult to obtain in advance. We address this issue using a learning-based method, with the following considerations. First, since prediction and check-order construction introduce additional operations into phase-based collision detection, the learning model should maintain a balance between prediction accuracy and computational complexity. Second, the model should generalize well to environments and object meshes beyond those used during training. Third, since the check time tᵢ is difficult to predict accurately and may vary across hardware platforms, we use the predicted collision probability p̂ᵢ as a practical proxy for the optimal score pᵢ/tᵢ. This approximation is motivated by the empirical observation in Fig. 3, where the check order obtained by sorting object pairs in descending order of p̂ᵢ is highly similar to the optimal order σᵒ computed using p̂ᵢ/tᵢ, where p̂ is predicted by our model. To further validate this approximation, we collect statistics from extensive computations on different hardware platforms, involving 10000 narrow phase cases, 100000 object pairs, and more than 2000 meshes of varying shapes. The results are summarized in Table I. On the one hand, using p̂ as a proxy for p̂/t produces a check order with high correlation and order similarity to that obtained from p̂/t. On the other hand, although the distribution of tᵢ varies across hardware platforms, its variation is relatively small and does not substantially change the ordering induced by p̂/t. Since our study focuses on the ordering rather than the exact values of p̂/t, using p̂ as a practical proxy is reasonable.

    Then, we propose a hypernetwork-based model to predict the collision probability of each object pair in the narrow phase, as shown in Fig. 4. The model consists of a MeshFeatureNet (MFN) and a CollisionPredictionNet (CPN), where the network parameters of CPN are generated by MFN. The rationale behind this design is that object pairs differ in two aspects: the meshes of the two objects and their relative pose. In sampling-based motion planning, the meshes of the robot and obstacles usually remain fixed, while their relative poses change frequently. As a result, during collision-probability prediction, the component related to relative poses is invoked much more frequently than the component related to meshes. Moreover, since meshes are much more complex than relative poses, using a single shared network to process both mesh geometry and relative pose makes it difficult to balance computational complexity and generalization. Most existing collision-prediction methods rely on such shared structure, which often prioritizes low complexity at the cost of generalization [13][15]. Inspired by hypernetworks [23], which generate the parameters of a target network using another network, we use MFN to generate the parameters of CPN. In this way, mesh-related information and pose-related information are handled separately, enabling a better balance between efficiency and generalization. Specifically, the two components are designed as follows:

  • •

    MeshFeatureNet: MFN uses two MeshNets [22] and one Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) to extract features from two input meshes. It outputs the parameters of CPN and a set of key points that compactly encode the geometry of the object pair. In this way, MFN focuses on the mesh-related information and transfers this information to CPN through its outputs. After training, the outputs of MFN are stored in memory, and a library is maintained for object pairs with known meshes. It is worth noting that, although MFN has a more complex architecture than CPN, its forward pass is only required when an object pair with previously unknown meshes appears during prediction.

  • •

    CollisionPredictionNet: CPN loads the parameters generated by MFN and predicts the collision probability. Although its external input is only the relative pose, the loaded parameters and the key points transformed by the relative pose implicitly encode mesh-related information. Therefore, CPN only needs to model the collision probability under different relative poses for two specific meshes, making it possible to use a compact network structure for efficient prediction.

    • When the environment remains unchanged, the proposed model can directly use the CPN with loaded parameters to make predictions. When unknown obstacles appear, object pairs with new meshes only need to pass through MFN once to obtain the corresponding CPN parameters and key points. Afterward, predictions for new poses are still made by the loaded CPN. Therefore, although MFN is more computationally expensive than CPN, its impact on the overall detection time is negligible due to its infrequent use. As a result, the proposed MFN-CPN structure maintains low computational complexity while improving generalization.

    The hypernetwork-based model is trained in a supervised manner using labeled collision-check samples of the form {(m_robᵢ,m_obsⱼ,T_i,j,k,c_i,j,k)}_k=1,…,N_i,j for each object pair (i,j), where N_i,j is the number of relative poses, m_robᵢ denotes the mesh of the i-th robot component, m_obsⱼ denotes the mesh of the j-th obstacle, T_i,j,k is the k-th relative pose between the two meshes, and c_i,j,k∈{0,1} is the corresponding mesh-check label. During training, (m_robᵢ,m_obsⱼ,T_i,j,k) are used as inputs, and c_i,j,k is used as the supervised signal. Since the parameters of CPN are generated by MFN, the trainable parameters are those of MFN. The forward propagation of the model is

    {\beginaligned &(φ_i,j,P_i,j)←MFN(m_robᵢ,m_obsⱼ;θ), &P^′_i,j,k=R_i,j,k·P_i,j+v_i,j,k, &p̂_i,j,k←CPN(P^′_i,j,k;φ_i,j),\endaligned.

    		(4)

    where θ denotes the parameters of MFN, φ_i,j denotes the generated parameters of CPN, and P_i,j denotes the key points generated by the MFN, P^′_i,j,k denotes the key points transformed according to the relative pose T_i,j,k, and R_i,j,k and v_i,j,k are the rotation matrix and translation vector induced by T_i,j,k. The model is trained using the cross-entropy loss

    l(θ)=-∑_i,j∑ₖ₌₁^N_i,j(c_i,j,k\lnp̂_i,j,k+(1-c_i,j,k)\ln(1-p̂_i,j,k)).

    		(5)

    In summary, the proposed acceleration method for phase-based collision detection in sampling-based motion planning is illustrated in Fig. 5. The method focuses on the narrow phase and accelerates collision detection by adjusting the check order of mesh checks. First, the hypernetwork-based model predicts the collision probability of each object pair remaining after the broad phase. Then, these object pairs are sorted in descending order of their predicted collision probabilities to approximate the optimal check order. Finally, exact mesh checks are performed according to the constructed check order.

    IV Simulations

    The simulations are built using MoveIt! in Robot Operating System (ROS). The robot model is the Franka Emika Panda, and the obstacle models are selected from ModelNet40 [24]. BVH-based collision detection, including both the broad and narrow phases, is implemented using the Flexible Collision Library (FCL) [25] with default parameters in the source code. The sampling-based motion planners are implemented using the Open Motion Planning Library (OMPL) [26]. All simulations are conducted on the same computer platform with Ubuntu 20.04, an Intel Core i7-11800H CPU, 32GB RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU.

    For training the hypernetwork-based model, we construct the dataset using 9 components of the Panda robot model and 252 obstacle models randomly selected from ModelNet40, forming 9×252 mesh pairs. For each mesh pair, 100000 relative poses are randomly generated to create collision-check samples. The ground-truth labels, i.e., collision or non-collision, are obtained by mesh checks using FCL. During training, we use the Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) optimizer with 1000 epochs and a learning rate of 10⁻⁶. At test time, the mesh information and relative pose, represented by a rotation matrix and a translation vector, are directly available from the simulation environment and used as inputs for network prediction.

    IV-APerformance of Hypernetwork-based Model

    In this subsection, we evaluate the prediction performance of the hypernetwork-based model, using Fastron [14] as the baseline. Fastron is implemented using the provided code [14] with default parameters and evaluated on the same testing data as our model. The testing dataset is divided into two parts. The seen part contains 2160 mesh pairs, consisting of 9 robot components and 240 obstacles used during training, with 2000 randomly generated relative poses for each mesh pair. The unseen part contains 432 mesh pairs, consisting of 9 robot components and 48 obstacles not used during training, with 2000 randomly generated relative poses for each mesh pair. Each relative pose, together with the corresponding mesh pair, forms a collision-check sample. We compare the proposed model with Fastron in terms of accuracy, True Positive Rate (TPR), True Negative Rate (TNR), and average prediction time. Since the collision label of each sample is binary, the predicted collision probability is binarized using a threshold of 0.5, where values greater than 0.5 are classified as collision and values no greater than 0.5 as non-collision.

    The comparison results are shown in Table II: compared with Fastron, the proposed hypernetwork-based model achieves higher prediction accuracy on both seen and unseen object pairs, while requiring less prediction time. This result is consistent with our design motivation of improving generalization while maintaining high accuracy and low computational complexity. Moreover, the hypernetwork-based model achieves a higher TPR than Fastron, with only a slightly lower TNR. This indicates that our model tends to be more conservative, prioritizing the detection of potential collisions over the exclusion of non-collision cases. In contrast, Fastron adopts a support-vector-based model, which tends to form larger prediction margins around non-collision samples. Overall, the proposed model demonstrates advantages in prediction accuracy, prediction speed, and generalization ability. In addition, the results also show that learning-based predictions are not always perfectly accurate. However, in our method, the predicted collision probabilities are used only to optimize the check order in the narrow phase, rather than to replace exact mesh checks. Therefore, prediction errors do not directly change the final collision-detection result, but only affect the efficiency of the checking process. This allows our method to benefit from learning-based prediction while preserving the reliability of the underlying geometric collision detector. It is also worth noting that, although the hypernetwork-based model is designed for object pairs in the narrow phase, its underlying design idea may inspire future research on collision prediction with more complex inputs, such as predicting collisions involving multiple objects simultaneously.

    To evaluate whether the proposed model can generalize to other robot arms without additional training, we test it on an unseen robotic arm, the Universal Robots UR5. Specifically, we use the same obstacle set as that in Table II, but replace the Panda links with the seven links of the UR5 to construct new robot-obstacle mesh pairs. For each mesh pair, we randomly sample 2000 relative poses to generate collision-check samples for prediction. As shown in Table III, the model effectively predicts collisions for UR5 with both seen and unseen obstacles, demonstrating its generalization capability across environments and robot arms.

    IV-BAcceleration on Phase-based Collision Detection

    The proposed method accelerates phase-based collision detection by optimizing the order of exact mesh checks in the narrow phase, without modifying the underlying collision detector. This is achieved by using the collision probabilities predicted by the hypernetwork-based model to approximate the optimal check order. In this subsection, we evaluate whether the proposed method can reduce the time cost of phase-based collision detection.

    First, we construct 9 simulated environments with different clutter levels, where the number of obstacles ranges from 10 to 90. In each environment, the obstacle positions are randomly generated during initialization and then kept fixed, and we randomly sample 100000 poses of the Panda robot for collision detection. For each pose, we perform two collision detection operations: one using BVH alone and the other using BVH combined with our method. The average detection time and its decomposition in each environment are shown in Fig. 8. We have the following observations: (i) over all detections, BVH combined with our method reduces the average detection time compared with BVH alone. The acceleration effect is generally more evident in cluttered environments, achieving a 37% speedup in the scenario with 60 obstacles. Moreover, as environmental clutteredness increases, a higher proportion of detection time is spent on collision cases. (ii) in collision cases, BVH combined with our method incurs additional costs for probability prediction and check-order construction, but it reduces the time spent on mesh checks by examining more likely colliding pairs earlier and enabling earlier termination. (iii) in non-collision cases, all object pairs in the narrow phase must be checked. Therefore, check-order optimization does not reduce mesh-check time and may slightly increase the total detection time. Overall, although our method introduces additional operations, it reduces the narrow-phase mesh-check time in collision cases by adjusting the check order, thereby accelerating phase-based collision detection. The improvement is substantial in cluttered environments. Since the proposed method accelerates collision detection by reordering mesh checks in the narrow phase, it can also be applied to other phase-based methods. As shown in Table IV, our method substantially reduces the detection time of Octree-based collision detection in the environments with 50 and 70 obstacles shown in Fig. 8.

    The generalization capability of the proposed model across robot arms has been evaluated in Sec. IV-A. We further validate whether the proposed method can accelerate phase-based collision detection for the unseen UR5 without any additional training. The experiments are conducted in two more complex environments containing 100 and 120 obstacles. As shown in Table V, our method effectively reduces the detection time for UR5, indicating that the proposed check-ordering strategy can generalize to other robot arms.

    Finally, we compare our method with the surface area heuristic (SAH) and the distance-based heuristic (DBH), which use geometric metrics as coarse proxies for collision likelihood to adjust the check order. In the environment with 50 obstacles shown in Fig. 8, we randomly resample 1000 robot poses and perform collision detection with the two heuristics and our method. The results are shown in Table VI. Both SAH and DBH can accelerate BVH-based collision detection. However, because these heuristics are simple but coarse, their resulting check orders show noticeable discrepancies from those produced by our model, leading to inferior acceleration performance.

    IV-CAcceleration for Sampling-based Motion Planning

    As mentioned earlier, sampling-based motion planning involves numerous collision detection operations, which are typically accelerated by phase-based collision detection methods. In this subsection, we evaluate whether the proposed collision-detection acceleration method can improve the performance of sampling-based motion planners. Three planners, RRT [27], RRT-Connect [28], and BIT* [29], are implemented using OMPL. For each planner, we compare two collision detection settings: BVH alone and BVH combined with our method. The simulation environment with 50 obstacles is the same as that shown in Fig. 8. For each planner, we generate 100 random start-goal configuration pairs in the environment and set a time budget of 5 seconds for finding a feasible solution. Each planner is run 50 times for each configuration pair and stops when either a feasible solution is found or the time budget is exhausted.

    The execution results are shown in Table VII. For all three planners, combining BVH with our method reduces the average time cost required to find a feasible solution, with RRT-Connect achieving about 22% acceleration. Since the proposed method improves the efficiency of phase-based collision detection, the planners can perform more sampling and collision-checking operations within the same time budget. This enables more thorough exploration of the configuration space, resulting in improved planning success rates for all three planners in the cluttered environment.

    Furthermore, it is worth emphasizing that the planner-level acceleration reported above is achieved under CPU-only inference during planning. GPU support is only required when MFN is invoked to process previously unseen object meshes. After the corresponding CPN parameters are generated, they can be reused for subsequent predictions. This design avoids retraining the entire collision predictor when new object meshes appear.

    V Conclusion

    In this paper, we propose a learning-based method to accelerate phase-based collision detection in sampling-based motion planning by optimizing the check order in the narrow phase. First, we formulate the expected time cost of the narrow phase and derive an optimal check-ordering criterion that minimizes this expectation. Second, we design a hypernetwork-based model to learn and predict the priors required to construct an approximate optimal check order, while maintaining low computational complexity and good generalization capability. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces the time cost of phase-based collision detection in cluttered environments, and further improves the efficiency and success rate of sampling-based motion planners.

    In practical applications, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing phase-based collision detection frameworks, since it only adjusts the check order in the narrow phase without modifying the underlying collision detector. This non-intrusive design enables straightforward deployment in a wide range of sampling-based motion planning systems with minimal implementation effort. Furthermore, since collision detection often dominates the computational cost of motion planning in cluttered environments, the proposed acceleration strategy has the potential to provide substantial performance gains in real-world robotic applications that require frequent collision checking, such as manipulation, navigation, and motion planning in confined spaces.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: Walk Like This：给一段风格参考片段，物理角色就能用那种走法听摇杆 ｜ Walk Like This: Stylized Locomotion for Physics-Based Characters through Example-Driven Diffusion
item.description:
一句话：风格编码器 + 自回归扩散出运动学参考，RL 控制器跟踪，速度与风格解耦可实时调。

要点：

  • 现有数据驱动控制器需要显式风格标签，只能模仿训练分布内的动作；这里用定制采样策略把风格与功能性移动解耦，风格编码器从未标注的大规模动作数据里学出风格嵌入。
  • 风格嵌入条件化一个自回归扩散模型生成运动学参考，再由强化学习控制器跟踪；推理时用户只给一段风格参考片段和摇杆速度指令。
  • 加入 attention 偏置与速度指令校正提升可控性与风格强度；在物理仿真人形与真机上都能实时运行、连续调节风格。

为什么值得看：这是「引擎里 AI 当核心系统」的典型样本：动画不再靠美术逐段调曲线，而是用参考片段直接改风格，同时保持物理合理与实时——对云端/真机角色控制都直接可用。

中文摘要：物理人形控制的核心难题是超越功能性行走、做出有表现力的步态风格，但现有风格化控制器多为固定目标或只能模仿窄分布动作，训练后很难泛化到新风格；CAMDM 这类实时方案又依赖显式风格标签。Walk Like This 提出实时框架，让速度与风格独立可调：用定制采样策略把风格与功能性移动解耦，训练一个基于 transformer 的风格编码器，其输出条件化自回归扩散模型生成运动学参考，再由 RL 控制器跟踪。推理时用户给一段任意时长的风格参考片段加摇杆速度指令，配合 attention 偏置与速度指令校正提升可控性，在仿真人形与真机上均实现鲁棒的实时控制。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-23

Walk Like This: Stylized Locomotion for Physics- Based Characters through Example-Driven Diffusion

Abstract

We present a real-time framework for expressive legged locomotion that enables independent control over velocity and style. Unlike existing data-driven controllers, which typically require explicit style labels for training, our method efficiently leverages large-scale unstructured motion data and generalizes to unseen styles. We disentangle style from functional locomotion through a tailored sampling strategy used to train a style encoder whose output conditions an autoregressive diffusion model. During inference, the user provides a style reference clip and a joystick velocity command. The diffusion model then generates a kinematic reference tracked by a reinforcement learning controller. To improve user controllability and stylization strength, we propose an attention biasing mechanism and a velocity command correction strategy. We demonstrate our method on a physics-based humanoid character in simulation and on a physical robot, showcasing robust real-time control and continuous style modulation. The results can be best seen in our supplemental video111https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=roFnS6N7nJ4.

Keywords: Motion Generation, Physics-Based Control, Stylized Locomotion

1 Introduction

A central challenge in physics-based humanoid control is to move beyond functional locomotion and to perform tasks in an expressive gait style. Although some stylized locomotion controllers exist, they are typically designed around fixed objectives or limited to imitating a narrow distribution of motions [24, 30, 29, 7, 31], offering little flexibility for stylistic variation and generalization after training. Similarly, while CAMDM [3] achieves real-time stylized character control, its conditioning on explicit style labels prevents generalization to new styles. Style transfer offers an alternative by mapping style onto target motions [1, 14, 54], but these methods are not designed for real-time robotic tracking or interactive control. On the other hand, motion generators [35, 43, 50, 49] can be grounded in physics but lack expressive control over style. Hence, a real-time framework that adapts to unseen styles on humanoid robots is currently missing.

To fill this gap, we propose a framework for the interactive control of humanoid robots that enables real-time user control via joystick commands and an example motion clip that contains the desired style characteristics. This gives users intuitive control over both what the robot does and how it performs these movements. To enable this, we build a stylized generative motion model based on autoregressive diffusion [3]. Crucially, we condition the model on a style embedding that is extracted from a style example through a transformer-based encoder. We jointly train the diffusion model and style encoder on unlabeled data, and use a tailored sampling strategy to disentangle style from functional locomotion. Our method both generalizes to new styles and gives users the flexibility to provide style examples of any duration. We highlight both aspects in our experiments by extracting a style directly from a recorded human video demonstration.

To enhance style adherence and enable rapid style transitions, we introduce an inference-time technique that re-weights the attention scores within the diffusion model, outperforming standard classifier-free guidance (CFG) [11] both in efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, we add a velocity correction scheme that mitigates drift when following joystick commands. Finally, we bridge the gap between generated motion and hardware dynamics by pairing the diffusion model with a reinforcement learning (RL) tracking controller. This combines the expressive power of a motion generator with the robustness of an RL low-level controller, as we validate with closed-loop simulation and hardware deployment.

Our core contributions: (i) A generative motion-control framework enabling user control over locomotion and style, trained from large-scale unstructured datasets and demonstrated on hardware. (ii) An autoregressive diffusion model and style encoder that disentangle style from functional locomotion through an effective sampling strategy during training. (iii) An inference-time attention biasing technique to modulate stylization strength alongside a velocity correction scheme to mitigate drift. We validate each design choice through ablations.

2 Related Work

Our work builds upon advancements in kinematic motion synthesis and physics-based control. Tab. 1 contrasts our work with prior approaches.

Stylized Motion Generation

Stylized motion generation traditionally relies on style transfer from reference to content motion [48], with modern approaches utilizing network activation matching [1, 39, 16, 2] or diffusion models [54, 32, 55]. While they produce high-quality results, these methods are usually too slow for real-time use and depend heavily on the source content motion. Even when coupled with generative models to mitigate this dependency [54, 55], they still lack the performance and controllability required for interactive applications. In contrast, purely generative approaches are better suited for real-time interaction [3, 9, 40, 23, 51, 41, 38]. Closest to our work is CAMDM [3], a state-of-the-art interactive generator that uses an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on discrete labels. While CAMDM achieves real-time, high-quality synthesis, it is restricted to seen training styles, provides purely kinematic motion, and lacks explicit control over style intensity or transitions. We overcome these limitations by introducing a more general style conditioning mechanism, explicit control over stylization strength, and an RL tracker to enforce physicality.

Physics-Based Character Control

Physics-based RL is well-established for robust humanoid locomotion [33, 8, 57, 18, 21]. Compared to command-based strategies [33, 8, 19], tracking-based approaches offer superior style control [21, 36, 27], scaling from single references [27] to large datasets via mixture-of-experts [47, 20] or implicit rewards [24, 30, 29]. However, frameworks like CALM [42] fail to explicitly disentangle style from skills, and character-specific gait-design tools [7, 31, 25, 12] lack generalization. To enforce physical feasibility, recent trends combine kinematic diffusion with RL through iterative training [49], joint state-action prediction [13], or closed-loop fine-tuning [43], though these are often limited to simulation. RobotMDM [35] tackles the sim-to-real gap by fine-tuning the diffusion model. We instead train a tracking policy from scratch on a large dataset of diffusion-generated motions.

3 Background

We build on the framework of Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) [44, 52]. Given a noisy motion Mᵈ, whose noise level depends on the diffusion step d, an MDM M predicts the clean motion M⁰. Particularly relevant to our work is CAMDM [3], an autoregressive MDM that predicts the next F frames of motion M⁰_fut, conditioned on the past P frames of motion Mₚₛₜ, as well as future root trajectory C_fut and a discrete style label ℓ_syl:

M⁰_fut=M(Mᵈ_fut,d;Mₚₛₜ,C_fut,ℓ_syl).

(1)

The future root trajectory contains x-y coordinates and the root orientation of the character in all F future frames, computed by integrating world-frame velocity commands. M itself is a transformer-encoder [45] where all the inputs are tokenized individually. During inference, a pure noise sample is gradually denoised over multiple steps to reach the final clean prediction. We refer to [3, 44] for details.

4 Method

We develop a real-time interactive controller for stylized locomotion of physics-based characters, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Our framework contains two models: a kinematic, autoregressive diffusion model (Sec. 4.1) and an RL-based tracking controller (Sec. 4.3).

The diffusion model generates kinematic motions based on user velocity commands and a stylized motion clip. A style encoder learns to extract the style from the motion in a compressed latent space. Both the generator and the style encoder are trained jointly from an unstructured motion dataset. During inference, we propose two simple yet effective techniques to improve stylization and adherence to user commands (Sec. 4.2). First, we modify bias terms in the generator transformer’s attention layers. Second, we enable intuitive user control through a velocity correction module that mitigates global drift. To transfer the generated kinematic motions onto a physics-based character, we use an RL-based tracking controller. We train this controller on a large dataset generated through autoregressive rollouts of our diffusion model.

4.1 Kinematic Diffusion Model

We use an autoregressive diffusion model for predicting the character’s next F states M_fut, inspired by CAMDM [3] (see Sec. 3). We condition the model on the past P states Mₚₛₜ and motion differences Dₚₛₜ, future root states C_fut and a style condition c_syl:

M⁰_fut=M(Mᵈ_fut,d;Mₚₛₜ,Dₚₛₜ,C_fut,c_syl),

(2)

where M is a transformer-encoder. Inputs are tokenized individually per timestep through linear maps before being fed to the transformer, except the diffusion step d, for which we use a learned lookup table. We use a motion representation similar to [3], where the state at each timestep consists of the root position, orientation, joint orientations as well as link positions and orientations (details can be found in Appendix A.1). Unlike CAMDM, the future root states C_fut contain desired root yaw angles and not full rotations so that the character’s roll and pitch are fully controlled through the imposed style. Furthermore, we add past motion differences Dₚₛₜ as an additional condition, computed as position and rotation differences of consecutive frames in Mₚₛₜ. While the information in Dₚₛₜ is redundant, we found it to improve coherence during autoregressive rollouts, e.g., consistent swing directions of arms.

Encoding Style

We compute style embeddings c_syl by compressing a stylized motion clip M_syl to a latent representation using our style transformer 𝔼, i.e., c_syl=𝔼(M_syl). Contrary to discrete style labels [3], such inputs contain explicit information about the style and allow generalization outside the set of training styles [1]. The style transformer 𝔼 is also a transformer-encoder, where all frames of the style motion are tokenized through a linear projection. The transformer architecture is well suited to represent the various timespans S of different styles. In addition, we enforce ∥c_syl∥=1 through normalization which facilitates generalization [29, 15] and allows mixing styles through spherical linear interpolation. Inspired by the use of register tokens in vision transformers [4], we use an input-independent register token r in the inputs of the style transformer. It serves as a working space to capture relevant style information and we use its value after the final transformer layer as the output c_syl. See Fig. 2 for a visualization of the style encoder in the full model architecture.

Training

Both M and 𝔼 are trained jointly. We first sample a motion sequence from the training data and then sample P+F consecutive frames to get Mₚₛₜ and M_fut. The future root states C_fut are directly read from the motion. The model is then trained to reconstruct M_fut from a noisy version of it. For the style encoder, a different window of length S∈[S_\min,S_\max] is sampled from the same motion sequence to yield M_syl. Crucially, this dual sampling allows the style transformer to disentangle the style of the sequence from its content. We define content as the ground-projected root trajectory, while style encompasses all residual motion dynamics. The loss function combines a reconstruction loss with velocity, joint consistency, and foot sliding losses, adopted from [3].

4.2 Diffusion Model Inference

We deploy the diffusion model autoregressively, conditioning the prediction of the next F frames on its own past predictions, the style c_syl, and the future root states C_fut. The autoregressive nature of the model, however, comes with a number of limitations, which we address through inference-time adjustments.

Attention Bias

Conditioning on past motion gives the model a strong signal for how future motion should be generated, often leading it to ignore style conditioning and get stuck in a single style. To address this, we propose biasing the attention mechanism during inference. Specifically, attention in the transformer layers is computed as

attention(Q,K,V;B)=softmax((QK^⊤)/(√D)+B)V,

(3)

where Q,K,V∈ℝ^N×D are the query, key and value matrices, and B∈ℝ^N×N is the bias matrix with N being the number of tokens and D the model dimension. Typically, the bias matrix is set to 0, leaving the model full control over how different tokens attend to each other. We propose adding a bias w_syl≥0 to the attention scores of all queries toward the style token and a bias wₚₛₜ≤0 to those toward the past-motion tokens. This forces the model to respect the style token, facilitating style transitions and improving stylization strength.

Velocity Correction

The user controls the character through joystick commands (v_x,y,v_ψ) comprising heading, lateral, and yaw velocities, which are integrated over timesteps t∈{1,…,F} to form the trajectory conditioning signal C_fut for the diffusion model. During inference, the character can drift from the intended trajectory due to accumulation of prediction errors. Furthermore, the character is controlled through velocity commands expressed in the root heading frame. As the root naturally oscillates during movement, the generated trajectory depends heavily on where exactly in that cycle the diffusion model is triggered.

To alleviate these problems, we keep track of the character’s current position and yaw direction, pᶜᵘʳ_x,y and ψᶜᵘʳ, as well as the desired position and direction, pᵈᵉˢ_x,y and ψᵈᵉˢ. The current state is updated according to the diffusion model predictions whereas the desired state is computed by integrating the given joystick velocity commands (v_x,y,v_ψ). Whenever a new diffusion call is triggered, we apply a feedback correction to the velocity command to compute corrected joystick commands:

ṽ_x,y=v_x,y+kₚR_ψ(ψᶜᵘʳ)^⊤(pᵈᵉˢ_x,y-pᶜᵘʳ_x,y)(4)
ṽ_ψ=v_ψ+k_ψ(ψᵈᵉˢ-ψᶜᵘʳ).(5)

Here kₚ and k_ψ are feedback gains and R_ψ is the 2D rotation matrix about the yaw axis. These corrected commands ṽ are then used to generate the future root trajectory which is used as conditioning input for the diffusion model. By treating the deviation from the intended trajectory as an error signal, this formulation introduces a closed-loop correction that continuously steers the character back toward the user’s original commands. We prevent excessive corrections by projecting the desired state into a neighborhood of the current state during each timestep. Specifically, the desired position is clipped to be at most 0.5m away from the current position and the desired yaw is clipped into a 0.5rad range around the current orientation. We refer to Appendix A.1 for further details.

4.3 RL-Based Tracking Controller

We use RL to train a policy that tracks the generated kinematic motions, largely following related work [36, 27]. The policy predicts actions given observations and goal states. We refer to Appendix A.2 for details on the design of the action space, rewards, observations, and goal states.

Training Data

We avoid the computational overhead of querying the diffusion model during RL by generating a large motion dataset offline via autoregressive rollouts. To do so, we run the diffusion model conditioned on style clips randomly sampled from the diffusion model’s training data paired with randomly sampled joystick commands. This ensures that we cover the whole space of motions that can be generated by the diffusion model.

Deployment

We deploy the policy and diffusion model in an open loop: the diffusion model is conditioned on its own past predictions, rather than the real state of the character, which we found to improve stylization quality. Furthermore, an open-loop scheme allows training on a precomputed dataset instead of running the diffusion model online. This is feasible because we do not deal with precise object or environment interactions that require the diffusion model to adjust to the real-world data, as in other works [43, 53]. To avoid computational overhead from the style encoder, we precompute a set of style encodings and cache them during deployment.

5 Experiments and Results

We first compare our method to CAMDM [3] and analyze our style encoder. We then evaluate the attention biasing and velocity correction. Finally, we ablate our RL tracking policy and transfer our method onto a real robot. We refer to the Appendix for implementation details.

5.1 Diffusion Model

Quantitative Evaluation

We compare our diffusion model against CAMDM [3], the current state of the art in generative modeling of stylized motion and the only model directly applicable to our setting when evaluating seen styles (Tab. 1). Both models are trained on the 100STYLE dataset [23]. We report FID score [10], style accuracy, foot sliding, and positional and yaw errors with respect to the condition trajectory (see Appendix A.3). We summarize results in Tab. 2 and provide a qualitative comparison in Appendix A.3.1. Compared to CAMDM, our model generates motion that is closer to the real motion capture data, as indicated by the lower FID and higher style accuracy, while achieving similar results in terms of physicality and alignment to the trajectory conditions. Furthermore, we find that adding attention biasing at inference improves overall motion quality for both CAMDM and our model, which we discuss in more detail in Sec. 5.2.

Style Encoder

We highlight the interpolation and generalization capabilities of our style encoder. First, we encode styles from the 100STYLE dataset and spherically interpolate between the corresponding style latents. Next, we evaluate the generalization of our method by capturing videos of a person performing a given style. We then extract 120 frames of motion features from that video using an open-source pose estimation model [37] and pass them as input to the style encoder. Notably, no further processing after pose estimation is needed before feeding the clips to the style encoder. As seen in Fig. 3 and our supplemental video, our model interpolates smoothly between styles and even generalizes to a highly dynamic style such as jumping. For this experiment, we train the model on both the 100STYLE [23] and AMASS [22] datasets to improve generalization capabilities. Furthermore, Tab. 2 shows quantitative evaluations on a set of 10 styles of 100STYLE not included during training. Importantly, CAMDM is not applicable here, as it is inherently limited to seen styles. On unseen styles, our model reproduces their distinctive features and reaches style accuracy comparable to that on seen styles, but it struggles with finer details, leading to a higher FID. Visualizations of the motions generated for the test split can be found in Appendix A.3.1. Finally, we apply three additional probes to the style latents for further evidence of disentanglement between style and content (the ground-projected root trajectory). First, linear discriminant analysis [6] recovers style identity from the style latents with 95% accuracy across all styles of 100STYLE. Second, within-style variation of the style latents, computed across different clips of the same style, accounts for only 19% of the total style latent variance. Third, regressing content from the style latents alone yields R²=0.07, barely better than predicting the mean content.

Style Clip Sampling Strategy

We verify the importance of our style encoder sampling strategy by training a model where we always sample the same motion window for both style reference and past and future motion. Using the same motion window results in a sample diversity of 0.8\deg for joint angles across different generated motion windows, while using different motion windows (our approach) results in 5.5\deg. We refer to Appendix A.3.1 for qualitative results, which show that without our sampling scheme, the model collapses, causing all generated motion windows to repeat the reference motion. In contrast, with our sampling scheme, we can disentangle the style from the locomotion and generate diverse motion.

5.2 Inference Techniques

Attention Bias

We compare our proposed attention bias method to CFG [11] on past motion where the predicted motion is a weighted average of a fully conditioned and a masked prediction (see Appendix A.3). Tab. 2 shows how attention biasing significantly improves quality and stylization of generated motions. As it is a pure inference adjustment, we can apply it to both models, Ours + Bias and CAMDM + Bias, though the relative improvement is smaller for CAMDM because its discrete style labels are less informative than our style encodings. Improved stylization comes at the cost of more foot sliding, as negative weighting of past motion makes it more challenging to create coherent foot swings. Compared to CFG, attention biasing performs better in all metrics. We conjecture that this performance gap arises because the bias modifies the pre-softmax weights, so attention stays a normalized distribution over the same tokens and thus closer to the training regime. In contrast, CFG interpolates two separate in-distribution predictions at every denoising step, and the result of this guidance step may no longer lie in the training distribution. Qualitative results and a sensitivity analysis with respect to the bias weights can be found in the Appendix (Fig. A.5 and Fig. A.6 respectively).

We also investigate style transition behavior between the different methods more closely. As shown in the inset table, both our attention biasing and CFG achieve similar improvements over regular diffusion rollouts in transition success rates [3]. However, our method incurs much less computational overhead than CFG, which requires two model evaluations in each diffusion step.

Velocity Correction

We evaluate how closely the generated motion adheres to the intended trajectories, with and without velocity correction. To that end, we deploy the diffusion model with velocity commands corresponding to a number of predefined trajectories, such as squares, circles, figure eights, and randomized velocity commands. The quantitative results, reported in the inset table, highlight that our correction scheme significantly improves adherence to the given commands, indicated by the reduced drift and mean velocity error. We refer to Appendix A.3.1 and Fig. A.8 for qualitative results and details on the test trajectories.

5.3 Physics-Based Tracking

RL Tracking Policy

We evaluate how the choice of training data affects the RL policy’s tracking of diffusion-generated motions. Tab. 3 shows that training a policy on the original, non-diffusion-generated data has a significantly higher failure rate (falls per minute) when tracking diffusion output than when training on generated data. This happens because the policy trained on the diffusion output learns to correct artifacts, such as foot sliding, yielding improved stability at the cost of higher tracking errors and worse motion quality. We further compare our open-loop approach, where the diffusion model is conditioned on its own past predictions, with a closed-loop approach, where the diffusion model is conditioned on states estimated from the robot. The open-loop approach leads to better stylization since, in closed loop, the past simulated states differ in distribution from the past motions the diffusion model was trained on. Closed-loop execution leads to lower tracking errors, because the tracking errors enter the diffusion conditioning, pulling the generated motion toward what the policy executes rather than toward the intended style. Finally, we apply perturbation forces of 600N to the character root, resulting in lower motion quality, higher tracking errors, and significantly more failures for both open and closed loop. Open loop nevertheless remains more stable than closed loop. Recovery states can enter the diffusion conditioning in closed-loop mode, pushing the diffusion model out of distribution. In contrast, with an open-loop deployment the diffusion model’s generation stream stays uncorrupted and provides clean recovery targets for the policy. We found no degradation of motion quality over the whole time horizon of 20 minutes per rollout. The tracking evaluations discussed so far were performed for styles contained in the training set of both the diffusion model and RL policy. For styles that are generated by interpolating between style latents of training styles, as seen in Fig. 3, tracking performance stays consistent at an MPJAE of 7.9\deg and 0 falls. FID and style accuracy cannot be computed for such interpolated styles, as no ground-truth data exists.

Transfer to Physical Robot

We apply our method to a Unitree G1 humanoid robot (1.32m, 35kg, 29 DoF). After retargeting the human data to the G1 with ReActor [26], we train our model and deploy it zero-shot on the robot. Qualitative results, provided in Fig. 4 and our supplemental video, show that a single controller can robustly track diverse motion styles using different joystick inputs. The robustness of the open-loop mode carries over to hardware, including under disturbances. Throughout ∼4h of deployments, the robot successfully executed various trajectories and velocity commands across different styles without any failures. The diffusion model runs in real time on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Thor at ∼11ms per inference step and ∼17ms command-to-motion output latency, compared to 8ms/12ms for simulation on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.

6 Limitations

While our work presents a framework for general, stylized locomotion control, several limitations remain. The RL policy can correct artifacts of the diffusion model (foot sliding, hovering, ground penetration). However, there can be a mismatch between the kinematic motions and the commanded velocity, which manifests as the tracking policy taking extra in-between steps to maintain stability. Introducing implicit rewards to achieve natural gaits could present a solution to these issues [24, 30]. Our method works with styles that are agnostic to the direction of movement, such as flailing the arms or walking in a wide stance. For styles that are tightly coupled to the direction of movement, such as a moonwalk or cartwheels, our method requires matching velocity commands. Furthermore, styles that are largely described through a distinct root trajectory, such as rotating clockwise while walking, specify the same quantity as the joystick, creating an inherent conflict in the interface, which we resolve in favor of the user command. Finally, our current framework lets the model learn the style implicitly. A more explicit parameterization could allow users to partially stylize, for example, focusing only on the lower or upper body behavior of a style reference.

7 Conclusion

We presented a real-time system for expressive legged locomotion that enables simultaneous user control over velocity and style via an example-driven, autoregressive diffusion model. Through a style encoder that is trained with an effective sampling strategy on short, unstructured motion clips rather than fixed style labels, we enable physics-based characters to generalize to completely unseen styles, including those extracted from real-world videos. This flexible interface opens the door to various other style input modalities, such as artist-created animations.

Acknowledgments

We would like to thank Ioannis Dadiotis for his support with robot deployments.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Kinematic Diffusion Model

Motion Representation

We represent the motion state, similarly to CAMDM [3], as

m=(x,r,J,X,R),

(6)

with the position x∈ℝ³ and orientation r∈ℝ⁶ of the character’s root, the orientations of all its N_J joints J∈ℝ^N_J×6, and the positions X∈ℝ^N_B×3 and orientations R∈ℝ^N_B×6 of all its N_B links. We represent all rotations in 6D [56]. For joint orientations, we represent a child’s orientation in the kinematic chain by its orientation in the parent’s coordinate frame.

To train a model that is agnostic to the character’s global state, we transform all quantities, except the joint orientations, in Mₚₛₜ and M_fut, to the heading frame of the character, extracted from the current state mₜ. The origin of this frame is set to the character’s ground-projected root position, its x-axis points in the direction of the root’s yaw, and the z-axis is aligned with the global up vector.

Model and Training Parameters

Both the diffusion model M and style encoder 𝔼 are realized as transformer-encoders [45] with the same model parameters which can be seen in the inset table. These parameters are used across all experiments for both the humanoid and robotic characters. We train all models with 8 diffusion steps with a cosine noise schedule. Training is performed for 100 epochs and the model weights are optimized using Adam [17] with default parameters except for the learning rate, which is set to 10⁻⁴. During training we randomly mask past motion by setting it to 0 with probability 0.15. For the humanoid character we represent motion at 30 frames per second and set the future frames F=20 with past frames P=10. The robotic character uses 50 frames per second with F=30 and P=15. To ensure responsiveness to velocity commands, we trigger early autoregression after 10 and 15 frames, respectively, if the velocity commands change. For both characters, we sample style clips of lengths 1s to 5s. An important consideration is that the humanoid uses spherical joints while the robot uses revolute joints. For the diffusion model itself, we treat both joint types as if they were spherical joints, which allows the diffusion model to predict infeasible orientations for the revolute joints. We then post-process the diffusion model predictions by projecting the predicted orientations onto the set of feasible orientations using a swing-twist decomposition [5].

Motion Smoothing

To alleviate discontinuities between consecutive diffusion predictions, we apply a smoothing scheme to generate motion. Specifically, rather than generating a new motion every F frames, we trigger the diffusion model after only F-K frames, creating a K-frame overlap between consecutive predictions, as visualized in Fig. A.1. Then, the overlapping frames are blended together, using linear and spherical interpolation for positions and rotations, respectively. In practice, we set K=3.

Velocity Correction

For the feedback gains we set kₚ=k_ψ=1/FΔt where F is the number of future frames predicted by the diffusion model and Δt is the duration of each timestep, i.e., the inverse frame rate. This ensures that the error is corrected over the span of one diffusion prediction, without under-correcting or overshooting. Finally, we use the mean yaw error over the last P frames when computing the feedback update. This prevents the error correction itself from depending on when exactly in the gait cycle diffusion is triggered.

A.2 Reinforcement Learning

We use RL to train a policy π(aₜ | oₜ,gₜ) to track the generated motion. The policy predicts joint setpoints aₜ for proportional-derivative (PD) controllers based on observations oₜ and goal conditioning gₜ. The conditioning gₜ contains the character’s target state at timestep t as predicted by the diffusion model, converted into the character’s heading frame of step t-1. Additionally, we explicitly concatenate the joystick command to the target state. Proprioceptive observations consist of joint positions and velocities, root angular velocity, projected gravity and a history of previous actions.

Observations and Goals

In our tracking policy, we use the goal condition

gₜ\coloneq(xₜ,rₜ,qₜ,Xₜ,Rₜ,ẋₜ,ωₜ,ṽₜ),

(7)

containing the set of reference motion features mₜ (see Eq. (6)). However, note that here we represent the joint angles in minimal coordinates qₜ instead of using Jₜ, as is common for the simulation of articulated bodies. For the robot with revolute joints, J is projected to a feasible qₜ. In addition, gₜ includes the target root linear velocity ẋₜ and angular velocity ωₜ, computed from M_fut, as well as the velocity command after correction ṽₜ (Sec. 4.2). All rigid body positions and orientations are expressed in the root’s heading frame, making the policy independent of the global state. The proprioceptive observations oₜ are

oₜ\coloneq(q̂ₜ,q̇̂ₜ,ω̂ₜ,ĝᵖʳᵒʲₜ,aₜ₋₁,aₜ₋₂),

(8)

where the hat symbol (·̂) indicates measured values from the simulator or the real system. These observations include the projected gravity ĝᵖʳᵒʲₜ, angular velocity ω̂ₜ, joint angles q̂ₜ, joint velocities q̇̂ₜ, as well as the previous two actions aₜ₋₁ and aₜ₋₂.

Rewards

We use a combination of three groups of reward functions, consisting of tracking rewards r_track, regularization rewards r_reg, and task rewards rₜₐₛₖ. Tracking rewards ensure that the policy follows the prescribed motion, while the regularization rewards ensure that it does so in a smooth and natural manner that is deployable on real hardware. The task reward incentivizes following the joystick commands and helps with resolving unphysical target states, for example when the diffusion model generates motion with foot sliding. In such cases, the task reward encourages the policy to give less priority to exact tracking, resulting in more natural and stable motion. Tab. A.1 shows all the individual reward terms with their respective weights.

Training Environment
