We follow standard practices in the training of tracking controllers [36, 27]. During each episode we sample a random motion from the training set and iterate through it to get the individual goals of each timestep. Here, we also randomly sample the starting frame inside the goal motion and combine it with reference state initialization where the character is initialized in that exact state [27]. To allow the policy to reach any target state from any

starting state we choose the reference state during initialization from a different motion than the actual target motion with a probability of 0.2. Episodes terminate early if the pelvis or head contacts the ground. The policy itself is trained with PPO [34] with the hyperparameters given in the inset table.

Training Data

To generate the training data for the policy we generate a large-scale dataset using diffusion model rollouts with randomized commands. For each clip of motion in the training set of the diffusion model, we generate 10 minutes of motion. To do so, we randomly resample velocity commands every 1.5s to 4.5s and randomly resample the chosen style reference window from the clip every 5s. Additionally, we generate another set of 10 hours of motion where we sample velocity commands in the same manner while also randomly sampling the style reference over the whole training set, to ensure that the policy can transition between different styles.

Robustness and Sim-to-Real

In order to improve the robustness of the policies and ensure feasibility of transferring them to the real world we apply disturbances and domain randomization [28] with their respective values shown in Tab. A.2. A curriculum is applied to the magnitude of disturbances, which ramps linearly from 0 to the specified maximum values between PPO iterations 300 and 2000. Finally, the policies are trained on rough terrain where height field values in the range [-2,2]cm are uniformly sampled and placed on a grid with spacing of 10cm. The grid points are then linearly connected to generate the ground terrain. For the G1 robot, we use the same actuator parameters as in [46].

A.3 Evaluations

Evaluation Setup

We train the diffusion model for 100 epochs. When training on 100STYLE [23] this corresponds to roughly two days of training on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. With the inclusion of AMASS [22], training time increases to roughly five days. To ensure convergence, the RL policies are trained for five days on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. However, reasonable performance is already achieved after a few hours of training. For all experiments involving attention biasing we set w_syl=2.0,wₚₛₜ=-1.0 and for CFG we set γ_CFG=0.6. To assess the diffusion model quality, we generate 20 minutes of motion for each of the 100 styles in 100STYLE. For the transitions, we generate 5 transition motions from each style to every other style in 100STYLE. Here, we first generate 5s of motion in style i, then switch the style reference to style j and generate another 5s of motion. Velocity commands are randomly sampled for both the diffusion model and transition evaluations. For the evaluations of the RL policies we generate and track 20 hours of motions with randomized commands.

Evaluation Metrics

For the evaluation of the diffusion model we rely on a number of metrics to assess motion quality, adherence to commands as well as physicality of the motion. First of all, we use the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [10] as a measure of distributional similarity between original MoCap and generated motions. The FID value is computed as

FID=∥μᵣ-μ_g∥₂²+Tr(Σᵣ+Σ_g-2(ΣᵣΣ_g)^1/2)

(9)

where μᵣ,μ_g and Σᵣ,Σ_g are empirical means and covariances of latent features of the real and generated data respectively. We extract these latent features from the activations of a classification model. This classification model is trained to classify 0.25s motion windows of the original 100STYLE dataset into its corresponding style and we use the final activations, prior to the classification head of the model, as latent representations. Importantly, FID score is computed on a per-style basis so that it captures stylistic features of motion rather than just generic similarity to the MoCap clips. Style accuracy is computed as the percentage of generated motions for which the style classifier predicts the style label that corresponds to the motion that was used as style reference. Position and yaw errors are simply computed as the difference between predicted position/yaw and their imposed condition counterparts. We compute foot sliding by measuring foot movement under estimated contact where a foot is classified as in contact if its heel height is less than 1cm. For transitions we compute the success rate based on the style classifier: when the model should transition from style i to style j, we count it as a success if the style classifier predicts label j after the transition is initiated. We do not impose a maximum transition time, so a transition counts as successful even if style j is only reached by the end of the predicted motion.

CFG

In our experiments, we compare against CFG on past motion, where each diffusion step is computed as

\beginsplitM⁰_fut&=γ_CFGM(Mᵈ_fut,d;Mₚₛₜ,Dₚₛₜ,C_fut,c_syl)+(1-γ_CFG)M(Mᵈ_fut,d;∅,∅,C_fut,c_syl)\endsplit

(10)

where γ_CFG∈[0,1] defines the guidance strength, with lower values prioritizing style adherence over past-motion consistency.

A.3.1 Qualitative Results

In this section, we show more qualitative results of our method.

Diffusion Model and Tracking

Fig. A.2 shows an example of a longer sequence of motion generated interactively. A user gives joystick and style commands as conditions for the diffusion model’s generation which is then tracked by an RL policy.

Qualitative Comparison to CAMDM

Fig. A.3 shows a comparison of motions generated by [3] and our model for the same set of joystick commands and style conditions. For CAMDM we select the labels corresponding to the clips we choose as conditioning for our model. We can see that while the style is recognizable for both models, our method performs it more expressively, for example, by reaching the arms out widely in the aeroplane style (right).

Sampling Scheme

We generate 5 consecutive predictions with and without our sampling scheme, given a fixed style reference as input. Fig. A.4 shows how the model collapses without our sampling scheme, repeating the same motion at every prediction. With our sampling the model adapts and predicts a continuous motion that follows the general style characteristics.

Attention Bias

Fig. A.5 shows qualitative comparisons of generating motions without any inference adjustments, with CFG and with our proposed attention biasing technique. Stylization is noticeably increased when using our biasing method. Additionally, Fig. A.6 shows how varying bias parameters affects performance. Increasing either weight’s magnitude leads to worse command adherence, as the model is forced to attend less to the command conditions. Increasing w_syl improves FID and style accuracy at the cost of increased foot sliding. Positive values of wₚₛₜ reduce motion quality significantly, as they induce frozen poses, leading to foot sliding values of 0. Our defaults of w_syl=2.0 and wₚₛₜ=-1.0 present a good trade-off between improved stylization quality and increased generation artifacts. We found these default values to work well across styles, embodiments and different models.

Unseen Styles

To showcase generalization capabilities of our method, we select a random subset of the styles in 100STYLE as a test set (10 styles), which we do not include during training. Our model can still generate motion that matches these styles during inference, as shown in Fig. A.7.

Velocity Correction

Fig. A.8 shows qualitative results of our assessment of the velocity correction mechanism. All trajectories correspond to roughly 30s of motion. The periodic trajectories (circle, figure eights, square, rounded square) are repeated multiple times. In all cases, the character stays significantly closer to the commanded trajectory when the velocity correction scheme is applied.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：风格编码器 + 自回归扩散出运动学参考，RL 控制器跟踪，速度与风格解耦可实时调。

要点：

  • 现有数据驱动控制器需要显式风格标签，只能模仿训练分布内的动作；这里用定制采样策略把风格与功能性移动解耦，风格编码器从未标注的大规模动作数据里学出风格嵌入。
  • 风格嵌入条件化一个自回归扩散模型生成运动学参考，再由强化学习控制器跟踪；推理时用户只给一段风格参考片段和摇杆速度指令。
  • 加入 attention 偏置与速度指令校正提升可控性与风格强度；在物理仿真人形与真机上都能实时运行、连续调节风格。

为什么值得看：这是「引擎里 AI 当核心系统」的典型样本：动画不再靠美术逐段调曲线，而是用参考片段直接改风格，同时保持物理合理与实时——对云端/真机角色控制都直接可用。

中文摘要：物理人形控制的核心难题是超越功能性行走、做出有表现力的步态风格，但现有风格化控制器多为固定目标或只能模仿窄分布动作，训练后很难泛化到新风格；CAMDM 这类实时方案又依赖显式风格标签。Walk Like This 提出实时框架，让速度与风格独立可调：用定制采样策略把风格与功能性移动解耦，训练一个基于 transformer 的风格编码器，其输出条件化自回归扩散模型生成运动学参考，再由 RL 控制器跟踪。推理时用户给一段任意时长的风格参考片段加摇杆速度指令，配合 attention 偏置与速度指令校正提升可控性，在仿真人形与真机上均实现鲁棒的实时控制。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-23

Walk Like This: Stylized Locomotion for Physics- Based Characters through Example-Driven Diffusion

Abstract

We present a real-time framework for expressive legged locomotion that enables independent control over velocity and style. Unlike existing data-driven controllers, which typically require explicit style labels for training, our method efficiently leverages large-scale unstructured motion data and generalizes to unseen styles. We disentangle style from functional locomotion through a tailored sampling strategy used to train a style encoder whose output conditions an autoregressive diffusion model. During inference, the user provides a style reference clip and a joystick velocity command. The diffusion model then generates a kinematic reference tracked by a reinforcement learning controller. To improve user controllability and stylization strength, we propose an attention biasing mechanism and a velocity command correction strategy. We demonstrate our method on a physics-based humanoid character in simulation and on a physical robot, showcasing robust real-time control and continuous style modulation. The results can be best seen in our supplemental video111https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=roFnS6N7nJ4.

Keywords: Motion Generation, Physics-Based Control, Stylized Locomotion

1 Introduction

A central challenge in physics-based humanoid control is to move beyond functional locomotion and to perform tasks in an expressive gait style. Although some stylized locomotion controllers exist, they are typically designed around fixed objectives or limited to imitating a narrow distribution of motions [24, 30, 29, 7, 31], offering little flexibility for stylistic variation and generalization after training. Similarly, while CAMDM [3] achieves real-time stylized character control, its conditioning on explicit style labels prevents generalization to new styles. Style transfer offers an alternative by mapping style onto target motions [1, 14, 54], but these methods are not designed for real-time robotic tracking or interactive control. On the other hand, motion generators [35, 43, 50, 49] can be grounded in physics but lack expressive control over style. Hence, a real-time framework that adapts to unseen styles on humanoid robots is currently missing.

To fill this gap, we propose a framework for the interactive control of humanoid robots that enables real-time user control via joystick commands and an example motion clip that contains the desired style characteristics. This gives users intuitive control over both what the robot does and how it performs these movements. To enable this, we build a stylized generative motion model based on autoregressive diffusion [3]. Crucially, we condition the model on a style embedding that is extracted from a style example through a transformer-based encoder. We jointly train the diffusion model and style encoder on unlabeled data, and use a tailored sampling strategy to disentangle style from functional locomotion. Our method both generalizes to new styles and gives users the flexibility to provide style examples of any duration. We highlight both aspects in our experiments by extracting a style directly from a recorded human video demonstration.

To enhance style adherence and enable rapid style transitions, we introduce an inference-time technique that re-weights the attention scores within the diffusion model, outperforming standard classifier-free guidance (CFG) [11] both in efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, we add a velocity correction scheme that mitigates drift when following joystick commands. Finally, we bridge the gap between generated motion and hardware dynamics by pairing the diffusion model with a reinforcement learning (RL) tracking controller. This combines the expressive power of a motion generator with the robustness of an RL low-level controller, as we validate with closed-loop simulation and hardware deployment.

Our core contributions: (i) A generative motion-control framework enabling user control over locomotion and style, trained from large-scale unstructured datasets and demonstrated on hardware. (ii) An autoregressive diffusion model and style encoder that disentangle style from functional locomotion through an effective sampling strategy during training. (iii) An inference-time attention biasing technique to modulate stylization strength alongside a velocity correction scheme to mitigate drift. We validate each design choice through ablations.

2 Related Work

Our work builds upon advancements in kinematic motion synthesis and physics-based control. Tab. 1 contrasts our work with prior approaches.

Stylized Motion Generation

Stylized motion generation traditionally relies on style transfer from reference to content motion [48], with modern approaches utilizing network activation matching [1, 39, 16, 2] or diffusion models [54, 32, 55]. While they produce high-quality results, these methods are usually too slow for real-time use and depend heavily on the source content motion. Even when coupled with generative models to mitigate this dependency [54, 55], they still lack the performance and controllability required for interactive applications. In contrast, purely generative approaches are better suited for real-time interaction [3, 9, 40, 23, 51, 41, 38]. Closest to our work is CAMDM [3], a state-of-the-art interactive generator that uses an autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on discrete labels. While CAMDM achieves real-time, high-quality synthesis, it is restricted to seen training styles, provides purely kinematic motion, and lacks explicit control over style intensity or transitions. We overcome these limitations by introducing a more general style conditioning mechanism, explicit control over stylization strength, and an RL tracker to enforce physicality.

Physics-Based Character Control

Physics-based RL is well-established for robust humanoid locomotion [33, 8, 57, 18, 21]. Compared to command-based strategies [33, 8, 19], tracking-based approaches offer superior style control [21, 36, 27], scaling from single references [27] to large datasets via mixture-of-experts [47, 20] or implicit rewards [24, 30, 29]. However, frameworks like CALM [42] fail to explicitly disentangle style from skills, and character-specific gait-design tools [7, 31, 25, 12] lack generalization. To enforce physical feasibility, recent trends combine kinematic diffusion with RL through iterative training [49], joint state-action prediction [13], or closed-loop fine-tuning [43], though these are often limited to simulation. RobotMDM [35] tackles the sim-to-real gap by fine-tuning the diffusion model. We instead train a tracking policy from scratch on a large dataset of diffusion-generated motions.

3 Background

We build on the framework of Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) [44, 52]. Given a noisy motion Mᵈ, whose noise level depends on the diffusion step d, an MDM M predicts the clean motion M⁰. Particularly relevant to our work is CAMDM [3], an autoregressive MDM that predicts the next F frames of motion M⁰_fut, conditioned on the past P frames of motion Mₚₛₜ, as well as future root trajectory C_fut and a discrete style label ℓ_syl:

M⁰_fut=M(Mᵈ_fut,d;Mₚₛₜ,C_fut,ℓ_syl).

(1)

The future root trajectory contains x-y coordinates and the root orientation of the character in all F future frames, computed by integrating world-frame velocity commands. M itself is a transformer-encoder [45] where all the inputs are tokenized individually. During inference, a pure noise sample is gradually denoised over multiple steps to reach the final clean prediction. We refer to [3, 44] for details.

4 Method

We develop a real-time interactive controller for stylized locomotion of physics-based characters, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Our framework contains two models: a kinematic, autoregressive diffusion model (Sec. 4.1) and an RL-based tracking controller (Sec. 4.3).

The diffusion model generates kinematic motions based on user velocity commands and a stylized motion clip. A style encoder learns to extract the style from the motion in a compressed latent space. Both the generator and the style encoder are trained jointly from an unstructured motion dataset. During inference, we propose two simple yet effective techniques to improve stylization and adherence to user commands (Sec. 4.2). First, we modify bias terms in the generator transformer’s attention layers. Second, we enable intuitive user control through a velocity correction module that mitigates global drift. To transfer the generated kinematic motions onto a physics-based character, we use an RL-based tracking controller. We train this controller on a large dataset generated through autoregressive rollouts of our diffusion model.

4.1 Kinematic Diffusion Model

We use an autoregressive diffusion model for predicting the character’s next F states M_fut, inspired by CAMDM [3] (see Sec. 3). We condition the model on the past P states Mₚₛₜ and motion differences Dₚₛₜ, future root states C_fut and a style condition c_syl:

M⁰_fut=M(Mᵈ_fut,d;Mₚₛₜ,Dₚₛₜ,C_fut,c_syl),

(2)

where M is a transformer-encoder. Inputs are tokenized individually per timestep through linear maps before being fed to the transformer, except the diffusion step d, for which we use a learned lookup table. We use a motion representation similar to [3], where the state at each timestep consists of the root position, orientation, joint orientations as well as link positions and orientations (details can be found in Appendix A.1). Unlike CAMDM, the future root states C_fut contain desired root yaw angles and not full rotations so that the character’s roll and pitch are fully controlled through the imposed style. Furthermore, we add past motion differences Dₚₛₜ as an additional condition, computed as position and rotation differences of consecutive frames in Mₚₛₜ. While the information in Dₚₛₜ is redundant, we found it to improve coherence during autoregressive rollouts, e.g., consistent swing directions of arms.

Encoding Style

We compute style embeddings c_syl by compressing a stylized motion clip M_syl to a latent representation using our style transformer 𝔼, i.e., c_syl=𝔼(M_syl). Contrary to discrete style labels [3], such inputs contain explicit information about the style and allow generalization outside the set of training styles [1]. The style transformer 𝔼 is also a transformer-encoder, where all frames of the style motion are tokenized through a linear projection. The transformer architecture is well suited to represent the various timespans S of different styles. In addition, we enforce ∥c_syl∥=1 through normalization which facilitates generalization [29, 15] and allows mixing styles through spherical linear interpolation. Inspired by the use of register tokens in vision transformers [4], we use an input-independent register token r in the inputs of the style transformer. It serves as a working space to capture relevant style information and we use its value after the final transformer layer as the output c_syl. See Fig. 2 for a visualization of the style encoder in the full model architecture.

Training

Both M and 𝔼 are trained jointly. We first sample a motion sequence from the training data and then sample P+F consecutive frames to get Mₚₛₜ and M_fut. The future root states C_fut are directly read from the motion. The model is then trained to reconstruct M_fut from a noisy version of it. For the style encoder, a different window of length S∈[S_\min,S_\max] is sampled from the same motion sequence to yield M_syl. Crucially, this dual sampling allows the style transformer to disentangle the style of the sequence from its content. We define content as the ground-projected root trajectory, while style encompasses all residual motion dynamics. The loss function combines a reconstruction loss with velocity, joint consistency, and foot sliding losses, adopted from [3].

4.2 Diffusion Model Inference

We deploy the diffusion model autoregressively, conditioning the prediction of the next F frames on its own past predictions, the style c_syl, and the future root states C_fut. The autoregressive nature of the model, however, comes with a number of limitations, which we address through inference-time adjustments.

Attention Bias

Conditioning on past motion gives the model a strong signal for how future motion should be generated, often leading it to ignore style conditioning and get stuck in a single style. To address this, we propose biasing the attention mechanism during inference. Specifically, attention in the transformer layers is computed as

attention(Q,K,V;B)=softmax((QK^⊤)/(√D)+B)V,

(3)

where Q,K,V∈ℝ^N×D are the query, key and value matrices, and B∈ℝ^N×N is the bias matrix with N being the number of tokens and D the model dimension. Typically, the bias matrix is set to 0, leaving the model full control over how different tokens attend to each other. We propose adding a bias w_syl≥0 to the attention scores of all queries toward the style token and a bias wₚₛₜ≤0 to those toward the past-motion tokens. This forces the model to respect the style token, facilitating style transitions and improving stylization strength.

Velocity Correction

The user controls the character through joystick commands (v_x,y,v_ψ) comprising heading, lateral, and yaw velocities, which are integrated over timesteps t∈{1,…,F} to form the trajectory conditioning signal C_fut for the diffusion model. During inference, the character can drift from the intended trajectory due to accumulation of prediction errors. Furthermore, the character is controlled through velocity commands expressed in the root heading frame. As the root naturally oscillates during movement, the generated trajectory depends heavily on where exactly in that cycle the diffusion model is triggered.

To alleviate these problems, we keep track of the character’s current position and yaw direction, pᶜᵘʳ_x,y and ψᶜᵘʳ, as well as the desired position and direction, pᵈᵉˢ_x,y and ψᵈᵉˢ. The current state is updated according to the diffusion model predictions whereas the desired state is computed by integrating the given joystick velocity commands (v_x,y,v_ψ). Whenever a new diffusion call is triggered, we apply a feedback correction to the velocity command to compute corrected joystick commands:

ṽ_x,y=v_x,y+kₚR_ψ(ψᶜᵘʳ)^⊤(pᵈᵉˢ_x,y-pᶜᵘʳ_x,y)(4)
ṽ_ψ=v_ψ+k_ψ(ψᵈᵉˢ-ψᶜᵘʳ).(5)

Here kₚ and k_ψ are feedback gains and R_ψ is the 2D rotation matrix about the yaw axis. These corrected commands ṽ are then used to generate the future root trajectory which is used as conditioning input for the diffusion model. By treating the deviation from the intended trajectory as an error signal, this formulation introduces a closed-loop correction that continuously steers the character back toward the user’s original commands. We prevent excessive corrections by projecting the desired state into a neighborhood of the current state during each timestep. Specifically, the desired position is clipped to be at most 0.5m away from the current position and the desired yaw is clipped into a 0.5rad range around the current orientation. We refer to Appendix A.1 for further details.

4.3 RL-Based Tracking Controller

We use RL to train a policy that tracks the generated kinematic motions, largely following related work [36, 27]. The policy predicts actions given observations and goal states. We refer to Appendix A.2 for details on the design of the action space, rewards, observations, and goal states.

Training Data

We avoid the computational overhead of querying the diffusion model during RL by generating a large motion dataset offline via autoregressive rollouts. To do so, we run the diffusion model conditioned on style clips randomly sampled from the diffusion model’s training data paired with randomly sampled joystick commands. This ensures that we cover the whole space of motions that can be generated by the diffusion model.

Deployment

We deploy the policy and diffusion model in an open loop: the diffusion model is conditioned on its own past predictions, rather than the real state of the character, which we found to improve stylization quality. Furthermore, an open-loop scheme allows training on a precomputed dataset instead of running the diffusion model online. This is feasible because we do not deal with precise object or environment interactions that require the diffusion model to adjust to the real-world data, as in other works [43, 53]. To avoid computational overhead from the style encoder, we precompute a set of style encodings and cache them during deployment.

5 Experiments and Results

We first compare our method to CAMDM [3] and analyze our style encoder. We then evaluate the attention biasing and velocity correction. Finally, we ablate our RL tracking policy and transfer our method onto a real robot. We refer to the Appendix for implementation details.

5.1 Diffusion Model

Quantitative Evaluation

We compare our diffusion model against CAMDM [3], the current state of the art in generative modeling of stylized motion and the only model directly applicable to our setting when evaluating seen styles (Tab. 1). Both models are trained on the 100STYLE dataset [23]. We report FID score [10], style accuracy, foot sliding, and positional and yaw errors with respect to the condition trajectory (see Appendix A.3). We summarize results in Tab. 2 and provide a qualitative comparison in Appendix A.3.1. Compared to CAMDM, our model generates motion that is closer to the real motion capture data, as indicated by the lower FID and higher style accuracy, while achieving similar results in terms of physicality and alignment to the trajectory conditions. Furthermore, we find that adding attention biasing at inference improves overall motion quality for both CAMDM and our model, which we discuss in more detail in Sec. 5.2.

Style Encoder

We highlight the interpolation and generalization capabilities of our style encoder. First, we encode styles from the 100STYLE dataset and spherically interpolate between the corresponding style latents. Next, we evaluate the generalization of our method by capturing videos of a person performing a given style. We then extract 120 frames of motion features from that video using an open-source pose estimation model [37] and pass them as input to the style encoder. Notably, no further processing after pose estimation is needed before feeding the clips to the style encoder. As seen in Fig. 3 and our supplemental video, our model interpolates smoothly between styles and even generalizes to a highly dynamic style such as jumping. For this experiment, we train the model on both the 100STYLE [23] and AMASS [22] datasets to improve generalization capabilities. Furthermore, Tab. 2 shows quantitative evaluations on a set of 10 styles of 100STYLE not included during training. Importantly, CAMDM is not applicable here, as it is inherently limited to seen styles. On unseen styles, our model reproduces their distinctive features and reaches style accuracy comparable to that on seen styles, but it struggles with finer details, leading to a higher FID. Visualizations of the motions generated for the test split can be found in Appendix A.3.1. Finally, we apply three additional probes to the style latents for further evidence of disentanglement between style and content (the ground-projected root trajectory). First, linear discriminant analysis [6] recovers style identity from the style latents with 95% accuracy across all styles of 100STYLE. Second, within-style variation of the style latents, computed across different clips of the same style, accounts for only 19% of the total style latent variance. Third, regressing content from the style latents alone yields R²=0.07, barely better than predicting the mean content.

Style Clip Sampling Strategy

We verify the importance of our style encoder sampling strategy by training a model where we always sample the same motion window for both style reference and past and future motion. Using the same motion window results in a sample diversity of 0.8\deg for joint angles across different generated motion windows, while using different motion windows (our approach) results in 5.5\deg. We refer to Appendix A.3.1 for qualitative results, which show that without our sampling scheme, the model collapses, causing all generated motion windows to repeat the reference motion. In contrast, with our sampling scheme, we can disentangle the style from the locomotion and generate diverse motion.

5.2 Inference Techniques

Attention Bias

We compare our proposed attention bias method to CFG [11] on past motion where the predicted motion is a weighted average of a fully conditioned and a masked prediction (see Appendix A.3). Tab. 2 shows how attention biasing significantly improves quality and stylization of generated motions. As it is a pure inference adjustment, we can apply it to both models, Ours + Bias and CAMDM + Bias, though the relative improvement is smaller for CAMDM because its discrete style labels are less informative than our style encodings. Improved stylization comes at the cost of more foot sliding, as negative weighting of past motion makes it more challenging to create coherent foot swings. Compared to CFG, attention biasing performs better in all metrics. We conjecture that this performance gap arises because the bias modifies the pre-softmax weights, so attention stays a normalized distribution over the same tokens and thus closer to the training regime. In contrast, CFG interpolates two separate in-distribution predictions at every denoising step, and the result of this guidance step may no longer lie in the training distribution. Qualitative results and a sensitivity analysis with respect to the bias weights can be found in the Appendix (Fig. A.5 and Fig. A.6 respectively).

We also investigate style transition behavior between the different methods more closely. As shown in the inset table, both our attention biasing and CFG achieve similar improvements over regular diffusion rollouts in transition success rates [3]. However, our method incurs much less computational overhead than CFG, which requires two model evaluations in each diffusion step.

Velocity Correction

We evaluate how closely the generated motion adheres to the intended trajectories, with and without velocity correction. To that end, we deploy the diffusion model with velocity commands corresponding to a number of predefined trajectories, such as squares, circles, figure eights, and randomized velocity commands. The quantitative results, reported in the inset table, highlight that our correction scheme significantly improves adherence to the given commands, indicated by the reduced drift and mean velocity error. We refer to Appendix A.3.1 and Fig. A.8 for qualitative results and details on the test trajectories.

5.3 Physics-Based Tracking

RL Tracking Policy

We evaluate how the choice of training data affects the RL policy’s tracking of diffusion-generated motions. Tab. 3 shows that training a policy on the original, non-diffusion-generated data has a significantly higher failure rate (falls per minute) when tracking diffusion output than when training on generated data. This happens because the policy trained on the diffusion output learns to correct artifacts, such as foot sliding, yielding improved stability at the cost of higher tracking errors and worse motion quality. We further compare our open-loop approach, where the diffusion model is conditioned on its own past predictions, with a closed-loop approach, where the diffusion model is conditioned on states estimated from the robot. The open-loop approach leads to better stylization since, in closed loop, the past simulated states differ in distribution from the past motions the diffusion model was trained on. Closed-loop execution leads to lower tracking errors, because the tracking errors enter the diffusion conditioning, pulling the generated motion toward what the policy executes rather than toward the intended style. Finally, we apply perturbation forces of 600N to the character root, resulting in lower motion quality, higher tracking errors, and significantly more failures for both open and closed loop. Open loop nevertheless remains more stable than closed loop. Recovery states can enter the diffusion conditioning in closed-loop mode, pushing the diffusion model out of distribution. In contrast, with an open-loop deployment the diffusion model’s generation stream stays uncorrupted and provides clean recovery targets for the policy. We found no degradation of motion quality over the whole time horizon of 20 minutes per rollout. The tracking evaluations discussed so far were performed for styles contained in the training set of both the diffusion model and RL policy. For styles that are generated by interpolating between style latents of training styles, as seen in Fig. 3, tracking performance stays consistent at an MPJAE of 7.9\deg and 0 falls. FID and style accuracy cannot be computed for such interpolated styles, as no ground-truth data exists.

Transfer to Physical Robot

We apply our method to a Unitree G1 humanoid robot (1.32m, 35kg, 29 DoF). After retargeting the human data to the G1 with ReActor [26], we train our model and deploy it zero-shot on the robot. Qualitative results, provided in Fig. 4 and our supplemental video, show that a single controller can robustly track diverse motion styles using different joystick inputs. The robustness of the open-loop mode carries over to hardware, including under disturbances. Throughout ∼4h of deployments, the robot successfully executed various trajectories and velocity commands across different styles without any failures. The diffusion model runs in real time on an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Thor at ∼11ms per inference step and ∼17ms command-to-motion output latency, compared to 8ms/12ms for simulation on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.

6 Limitations

While our work presents a framework for general, stylized locomotion control, several limitations remain. The RL policy can correct artifacts of the diffusion model (foot sliding, hovering, ground penetration). However, there can be a mismatch between the kinematic motions and the commanded velocity, which manifests as the tracking policy taking extra in-between steps to maintain stability. Introducing implicit rewards to achieve natural gaits could present a solution to these issues [24, 30]. Our method works with styles that are agnostic to the direction of movement, such as flailing the arms or walking in a wide stance. For styles that are tightly coupled to the direction of movement, such as a moonwalk or cartwheels, our method requires matching velocity commands. Furthermore, styles that are largely described through a distinct root trajectory, such as rotating clockwise while walking, specify the same quantity as the joystick, creating an inherent conflict in the interface, which we resolve in favor of the user command. Finally, our current framework lets the model learn the style implicitly. A more explicit parameterization could allow users to partially stylize, for example, focusing only on the lower or upper body behavior of a style reference.

7 Conclusion

We presented a real-time system for expressive legged locomotion that enables simultaneous user control over velocity and style via an example-driven, autoregressive diffusion model. Through a style encoder that is trained with an effective sampling strategy on short, unstructured motion clips rather than fixed style labels, we enable physics-based characters to generalize to completely unseen styles, including those extracted from real-world videos. This flexible interface opens the door to various other style input modalities, such as artist-created animations.

Acknowledgments

We would like to thank Ioannis Dadiotis for his support with robot deployments.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Kinematic Diffusion Model

Motion Representation

We represent the motion state, similarly to CAMDM [3], as

m=(x,r,J,X,R),

(6)

with the position x∈ℝ³ and orientation r∈ℝ⁶ of the character’s root, the orientations of all its N_J joints J∈ℝ^N_J×6, and the positions X∈ℝ^N_B×3 and orientations R∈ℝ^N_B×6 of all its N_B links. We represent all rotations in 6D [56]. For joint orientations, we represent a child’s orientation in the kinematic chain by its orientation in the parent’s coordinate frame.

To train a model that is agnostic to the character’s global state, we transform all quantities, except the joint orientations, in Mₚₛₜ and M_fut, to the heading frame of the character, extracted from the current state mₜ. The origin of this frame is set to the character’s ground-projected root position, its x-axis points in the direction of the root’s yaw, and the z-axis is aligned with the global up vector.

Model and Training Parameters

Both the diffusion model M and style encoder 𝔼 are realized as transformer-encoders [45] with the same model parameters which can be seen in the inset table. These parameters are used across all experiments for both the humanoid and robotic characters. We train all models with 8 diffusion steps with a cosine noise schedule. Training is performed for 100 epochs and the model weights are optimized using Adam [17] with default parameters except for the learning rate, which is set to 10⁻⁴. During training we randomly mask past motion by setting it to 0 with probability 0.15. For the humanoid character we represent motion at 30 frames per second and set the future frames F=20 with past frames P=10. The robotic character uses 50 frames per second with F=30 and P=15. To ensure responsiveness to velocity commands, we trigger early autoregression after 10 and 15 frames, respectively, if the velocity commands change. For both characters, we sample style clips of lengths 1s to 5s. An important consideration is that the humanoid uses spherical joints while the robot uses revolute joints. For the diffusion model itself, we treat both joint types as if they were spherical joints, which allows the diffusion model to predict infeasible orientations for the revolute joints. We then post-process the diffusion model predictions by projecting the predicted orientations onto the set of feasible orientations using a swing-twist decomposition [5].

Motion Smoothing

To alleviate discontinuities between consecutive diffusion predictions, we apply a smoothing scheme to generate motion. Specifically, rather than generating a new motion every F frames, we trigger the diffusion model after only F-K frames, creating a K-frame overlap between consecutive predictions, as visualized in Fig. A.1. Then, the overlapping frames are blended together, using linear and spherical interpolation for positions and rotations, respectively. In practice, we set K=3.

Velocity Correction

For the feedback gains we set kₚ=k_ψ=1/FΔt where F is the number of future frames predicted by the diffusion model and Δt is the duration of each timestep, i.e., the inverse frame rate. This ensures that the error is corrected over the span of one diffusion prediction, without under-correcting or overshooting. Finally, we use the mean yaw error over the last P frames when computing the feedback update. This prevents the error correction itself from depending on when exactly in the gait cycle diffusion is triggered.

A.2 Reinforcement Learning

We use RL to train a policy π(aₜ | oₜ,gₜ) to track the generated motion. The policy predicts joint setpoints aₜ for proportional-derivative (PD) controllers based on observations oₜ and goal conditioning gₜ. The conditioning gₜ contains the character’s target state at timestep t as predicted by the diffusion model, converted into the character’s heading frame of step t-1. Additionally, we explicitly concatenate the joystick command to the target state. Proprioceptive observations consist of joint positions and velocities, root angular velocity, projected gravity and a history of previous actions.

Observations and Goals

In our tracking policy, we use the goal condition

gₜ\coloneq(xₜ,rₜ,qₜ,Xₜ,Rₜ,ẋₜ,ωₜ,ṽₜ),

(7)

containing the set of reference motion features mₜ (see Eq. (6)). However, note that here we represent the joint angles in minimal coordinates qₜ instead of using Jₜ, as is common for the simulation of articulated bodies. For the robot with revolute joints, J is projected to a feasible qₜ. In addition, gₜ includes the target root linear velocity ẋₜ and angular velocity ωₜ, computed from M_fut, as well as the velocity command after correction ṽₜ (Sec. 4.2). All rigid body positions and orientations are expressed in the root’s heading frame, making the policy independent of the global state. The proprioceptive observations oₜ are

oₜ\coloneq(q̂ₜ,q̇̂ₜ,ω̂ₜ,ĝᵖʳᵒʲₜ,aₜ₋₁,aₜ₋₂),

(8)

where the hat symbol (·̂) indicates measured values from the simulator or the real system. These observations include the projected gravity ĝᵖʳᵒʲₜ, angular velocity ω̂ₜ, joint angles q̂ₜ, joint velocities q̇̂ₜ, as well as the previous two actions aₜ₋₁ and aₜ₋₂.

Rewards

We use a combination of three groups of reward functions, consisting of tracking rewards r_track, regularization rewards r_reg, and task rewards rₜₐₛₖ. Tracking rewards ensure that the policy follows the prescribed motion, while the regularization rewards ensure that it does so in a smooth and natural manner that is deployable on real hardware. The task reward incentivizes following the joystick commands and helps with resolving unphysical target states, for example when the diffusion model generates motion with foot sliding. In such cases, the task reward encourages the policy to give less priority to exact tracking, resulting in more natural and stable motion. Tab. A.1 shows all the individual reward terms with their respective weights.

Training Environment

We follow standard practices in the training of tracking controllers [36, 27]. During each episode we sample a random motion from the training set and iterate through it to get the individual goals of each timestep. Here, we also randomly sample the starting frame inside the goal motion and combine it with reference state initialization where the character is initialized in that exact state [27]. To allow the policy to reach any target state from any

starting state we choose the reference state during initialization from a different motion than the actual target motion with a probability of 0.2. Episodes terminate early if the pelvis or head contacts the ground. The policy itself is trained with PPO [34] with the hyperparameters given in the inset table.

Training Data

To generate the training data for the policy we generate a large-scale dataset using diffusion model rollouts with randomized commands. For each clip of motion in the training set of the diffusion model, we generate 10 minutes of motion. To do so, we randomly resample velocity commands every 1.5s to 4.5s and randomly resample the chosen style reference window from the clip every 5s. Additionally, we generate another set of 10 hours of motion where we sample velocity commands in the same manner while also randomly sampling the style reference over the whole training set, to ensure that the policy can transition between different styles.

Robustness and Sim-to-Real

In order to improve the robustness of the policies and ensure feasibility of transferring them to the real world we apply disturbances and domain randomization [28] with their respective values shown in Tab. A.2. A curriculum is applied to the magnitude of disturbances, which ramps linearly from 0 to the specified maximum values between PPO iterations 300 and 2000. Finally, the policies are trained on rough terrain where height field values in the range [-2,2]cm are uniformly sampled and placed on a grid with spacing of 10cm. The grid points are then linearly connected to generate the ground terrain. For the G1 robot, we use the same actuator parameters as in [46].

A.3 Evaluations

Evaluation Setup

We train the diffusion model for 100 epochs. When training on 100STYLE [23] this corresponds to roughly two days of training on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. With the inclusion of AMASS [22], training time increases to roughly five days. To ensure convergence, the RL policies are trained for five days on an NVIDIA RTX 4090. However, reasonable performance is already achieved after a few hours of training. For all experiments involving attention biasing we set w_syl=2.0,wₚₛₜ=-1.0 and for CFG we set γ_CFG=0.6. To assess the diffusion model quality, we generate 20 minutes of motion for each of the 100 styles in 100STYLE. For the transitions, we generate 5 transition motions from each style to every other style in 100STYLE. Here, we first generate 5s of motion in style i, then switch the style reference to style j and generate another 5s of motion. Velocity commands are randomly sampled for both the diffusion model and transition evaluations. For the evaluations of the RL policies we generate and track 20 hours of motions with randomized commands.

Evaluation Metrics

For the evaluation of the diffusion model we rely on a number of metrics to assess motion quality, adherence to commands as well as physicality of the motion. First of all, we use the Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) [10] as a measure of distributional similarity between original MoCap and generated motions. The FID value is computed as

FID=∥μᵣ-μ_g∥₂²+Tr(Σᵣ+Σ_g-2(ΣᵣΣ_g)^1/2)

(9)

where μᵣ,μ_g and Σᵣ,Σ_g are empirical means and covariances of latent features of the real and generated data respectively. We extract these latent features from the activations of a classification model. This classification model is trained to classify 0.25s motion windows of the original 100STYLE dataset into its corresponding style and we use the final activations, prior to the classification head of the model, as latent representations. Importantly, FID score is computed on a per-style basis so that it captures stylistic features of motion rather than just generic similarity to the MoCap clips. Style accuracy is computed as the percentage of generated motions for which the style classifier predicts the style label that corresponds to the motion that was used as style reference. Position and yaw errors are simply computed as the difference between predicted position/yaw and their imposed condition counterparts. We compute foot sliding by measuring foot movement under estimated contact where a foot is classified as in contact if its heel height is less than 1cm. For transitions we compute the success rate based on the style classifier: when the model should transition from style i to style j, we count it as a success if the style classifier predicts label j after the transition is initiated. We do not impose a maximum transition time, so a transition counts as successful even if style j is only reached by the end of the predicted motion.

CFG

In our experiments, we compare against CFG on past motion, where each diffusion step is computed as

\beginsplitM⁰_fut&=γ_CFGM(Mᵈ_fut,d;Mₚₛₜ,Dₚₛₜ,C_fut,c_syl)+(1-γ_CFG)M(Mᵈ_fut,d;∅,∅,C_fut,c_syl)\endsplit

(10)

where γ_CFG∈[0,1] defines the guidance strength, with lower values prioritizing style adherence over past-motion consistency.

A.3.1 Qualitative Results

In this section, we show more qualitative results of our method.

Diffusion Model and Tracking

Fig. A.2 shows an example of a longer sequence of motion generated interactively. A user gives joystick and style commands as conditions for the diffusion model’s generation which is then tracked by an RL policy.

Qualitative Comparison to CAMDM

Fig. A.3 shows a comparison of motions generated by [3] and our model for the same set of joystick commands and style conditions. For CAMDM we select the labels corresponding to the clips we choose as conditioning for our model. We can see that while the style is recognizable for both models, our method performs it more expressively, for example, by reaching the arms out widely in the aeroplane style (right).

Sampling Scheme

We generate 5 consecutive predictions with and without our sampling scheme, given a fixed style reference as input. Fig. A.4 shows how the model collapses without our sampling scheme, repeating the same motion at every prediction. With our sampling the model adapts and predicts a continuous motion that follows the general style characteristics.

Attention Bias

Fig. A.5 shows qualitative comparisons of generating motions without any inference adjustments, with CFG and with our proposed attention biasing technique. Stylization is noticeably increased when using our biasing method. Additionally, Fig. A.6 shows how varying bias parameters affects performance. Increasing either weight’s magnitude leads to worse command adherence, as the model is forced to attend less to the command conditions. Increasing w_syl improves FID and style accuracy at the cost of increased foot sliding. Positive values of wₚₛₜ reduce motion quality significantly, as they induce frozen poses, leading to foot sliding values of 0. Our defaults of w_syl=2.0 and wₚₛₜ=-1.0 present a good trade-off between improved stylization quality and increased generation artifacts. We found these default values to work well across styles, embodiments and different models.

Unseen Styles

To showcase generalization capabilities of our method, we select a random subset of the styles in 100STYLE as a test set (10 styles), which we do not include during training. Our model can still generate motion that matches these styles during inference, as shown in Fig. A.7.

Velocity Correction

Fig. A.8 shows qualitative results of our assessment of the velocity correction mechanism. All trajectories correspond to roughly 30s of motion. The periodic trajectories (circle, figure eights, square, rounded square) are repeated multiple times. In all cases, the character stays significantly closer to the commanded trajectory when the velocity correction scheme is applied.

item.title: RLMuscle：让强化学习去找每块肌肉的激活量，动画师不用再手调 ｜ RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation via Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
一句话：RL 控制器跟参考动作反解肌肉激活，1D 代理留在环内、3D 体模拟出最终形变。

要点：

  • 现有 RL 肌肉控制器只到 1D 肌肉；这里把 1D 模型留在控制环内当快速代理，再用 3D 体模拟产出最终形变，两级共享同一本构模型，因此形变与驱动它的激活严格一致。
  • 加入实测肌电（EMG）先验，把欠定的激活解引导向真人募集模式；求解器是面向 XPBD 的几何多重网格，建在粗四面体笼上、用重心坐标延拓并在四面体网格上闭合 V-cycle，全 GPU 并行。
  • 在同一 GPU 求解器里以基于能量的纤维约束注入 Hill 型力—长度关系，把逐纤维激活变成可信的肌肉收缩与隆起。

为什么值得看：角色动画里肌肉/形变一直是「美术手 K + 布料式近似」，把激活反解交给 RL 且共享本构，是能落地到动画管线的具体做法。

中文摘要：肌肉收缩带来的体表形变对角色动画的真实感很关键，但现有 3D 动画管线多由美术手动指定肌肉激活，费时且不保证物理真实。RLMuscle 让强化学习控制器在无需手调的情况下发现逐肌肉激活以跟踪参考动作：把 1D 肌肉模型留在控制环内作为快速代理，再用 3D 体模拟产出最终形变，两级共享同一本构模型，从而保证形变由产生运动的同一组激活驱动。作者还引入实测肌电先验，把欠定的激活解导向真实募集模式，并提出基于粗四面体笼、重心坐标延拓与 V-cycle 的 XPBD 几何多重网格 GPU 求解器。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-21

本期推送：2026-10-23

RLMuscle: Muscle-Driven Character Animation
via Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

Body deformation caused by muscle contraction plays a vital role in the visual realism of character animation, yet in most 3D animation pipelines artists have to manually specify muscle activations, which is time-consuming and gives no guarantee of physical realism. To address this, we propose a new method in which a reinforcement learning (RL) controller discovers per-muscle activations that track reference motions without manual tuning. Existing RL muscle controllers stop at 1D muscles; we go one step further, keeping the 1D model inside the RL control loop as a fast surrogate, and using a 3D volumetric simulation to produce the final deformation. Because both stages share the very same constitutive law, the muscle deformation is produced by the same activations that generated the motion. We further add a measured electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward real human muscle recruitment. To achieve stable, efficient, and realistic simulation, we propose a novel geometric multigrid for Extended Position-Based Dynamics (XPBD) that is built on a coarse tetrahedral cage with barycentric-coordinate prolongation and closes a V-cycle on tetrahedral meshes. Within this GPU-parallelized solver, we inject the same Hill-type force–length law as an energy-based fiber constraint that turns per-fiber activation into realistic muscle contraction and bulging. We demonstrate volumetric muscle simulation on a 194-muscle human body with a diverse set of motions (walk, kick, swim, overhead-squat, etc.), simulating the full-body model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090. Our work takes a step toward character animation that is not only visually convincing but also biomechanically grounded. The website with code and videos is at https://chunleili.github.io/project-page-rlmuscle/.

Index Terms:

Muscle simulation, XPBD, reinforcement learning, physics-based animation, character animation.

I Introduction

In animation, film, games, and virtual reality (VR), realistic muscle behavior is essential for believable character animation. Yet production pipelines still rely on hand-authored muscle activations, produced by one of two major authoring methods. The first is a tension line: the artist binds a line onto the skeleton, and the muscle associated with that line is activated once the line contracts below a set length threshold, so activation is triggered geometrically by bone motion. The second is keyframing: the artist directly animates each muscle’s activation value over time as a keyframed curve. Both encode activations chosen for visual plausibility, not physical plausibility. Consequently, there is no guarantee that hand-crafted tension can produce physically valid motions, because artists effectively decouple muscle deformation from motion dynamics. This expertise-driven workflow is not only labor-intensive; it also cannot answer the question at the heart of physics-based animation: what muscle activations actually produce a given motion? This is the muscle inverse problem: recovering the hidden control signals from observed motion. A principled solution would replace hand-tuning with physically consistent activations derived from the target motion, so that the resulting muscle deformation reflects the underlying dynamics rather than a visually plausible guess.

On the other hand, recent works on muscle simulation driven by reinforcement learning (RL) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] are mainly limited to a simplified 1D Hill-type muscle model, which falls short of the 3D volumetric muscle deformation needed for visual realism. The muscle inverse problem is challenging because the map from activation to joint motion is highly nonlinear, and the control space is high-dimensional (hundreds of muscles), which leads to intractability of analytical inversion, and extremely low sample efficiency in RL training.

We solve the muscle inverse problem by forward dynamics, i.e. searching for the activations that, once simulated, reproduce a target motion. This poses two challenges:

  • 1.

    Control. The map from muscle activation to joint motion is highly underdetermined and nonlinear, so analytical inversion is intractable, and naive RL exploration in this space is sample-inefficient.

  • 2.

    Physics. The numerical solver must handle volumetric muscle that is nonlinear, anisotropic, and nearly incompressible while remaining both stable and efficient.

    • We present the first system that addresses both challenges. Given a reference motion (motion capture or keyframed animation) and rest-pose 3D muscle/skeleton assets as input, it outputs a skeletal–muscular animation driven by physically consistent activations. Our work makes three technical contributions.

    Technical contribution 1: a muscle-control pipeline that decouples 1D control from 3D simulation under a unified constitutive law for fibers, solving the muscle inverse problem and freeing artists from hand-tuning (addressing Control). Existing RL muscle controllers [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] actuate 1D Hill-type muscles only, so they recover joint motion but not the 3D volumetric deformation that visual realism demands; conversely, optimization-based methods [6] that place the volumetric solver inside the control loop are unstable and did not converge in our tests. We propose to use the 1D model as a surrogate in RL and to produce the deformation from the 3D model. To bridge the gap between the two, we introduce a new fiber constraint based on the Hill–Millard constitutive curve, which is used in both the 1D and the 3D model. Following MASS [1], a policy network and a muscle network are co-trained in a single PPO [7] loop against a motion-mimicking reward [8] on the 1D surrogate. The recovered activations then drive the 3D volumetric muscles through the same Hill-type constitutive law [9] used by the surrogate, in a single forward pass with the 3D solver kept out of the control loop, so the volumetric deformation is consistent with the dynamics that produced the motion, reproducing realistic muscle bulging, stiffening, and contraction rather than a visually plausible guess.

    Technical contribution 2: a physiological electromyography (EMG) prior that steers the redundant activation solution toward measured human muscle recruitment (addressing Control). The activation-to-torque map is redundant, and existing muscle networks [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] reduce that redundancy from torque and effort alone, with nothing tying the result to a real recruitment pattern, so their activations drift away from measured human EMG. We propose to inject a measured surface EMG envelope [10] into the muscle-network loss, matched per synergist group and folded onto a common gait cycle, which pulls the recovered activations back toward the measured envelope (§IV-B).

    Technical contribution 3: a Petrov–Galerkin geometric multigrid for volumetric XPBD, integrated into a GPU-parallel framework that runs the full-body volumetric muscle model at 18 ms per frame on a single RTX 4090 (addressing Physics). Previous position-based hierarchies, such as HPBD [11], are formulated for cloth rather than tetrahedral meshes and never close a complete V-cycle, so they act only as a low-resolution driver; algebraic constructions [12] instead assemble a global matrix and thereby give up XPBD’s local, per-constraint solve. We propose to coarsen a tetrahedral cage geometrically, prolongate by barycentric coordinates, and close a full V-cycle with a Petrov–Galerkin restriction, which keeps the high-stiffness solve stable and efficient. The framework further contributes muscle–bone collision handling based on a signed distance field (SDF).

    II Related Work

    Position-Based Dynamics. PBD [13] is a popular framework for real-time deformable object simulation. It is widely used in applications such as PhysX [14] and Houdini Vellum [15]. Extended PBD (XPBD) [16] reformulates PBD as a dual-space energy minimization framework and introduces a compliance term to transform the infinite-stiffness to a finite-stiffness problem, which improves the convergence. Bender et al. [17] cast Finite Element Method (FEM) strain energy as position-based constraints, which makes it possible to apply various FEM-based constitutive laws in PBD. We refer readers to the survey [18] for more details. We use XPBD as our simulation engine and propose a novel muscle fiber constraint tied to the physiological properties of muscle.

    Multigrid. Multigrid [19] is a classical numerical method for accelerating and stabilizing simulation, running an iterative solver on grids of different resolutions to eliminate low-frequency errors. Unlike grid-based fluid solvers, which have a natural hierarchical structure, soft bodies provide no such structure, so building a hierarchy on them is challenging. Hierarchical PBD (HPBD) [11] introduces a hierarchical solver for PBD simulated cloth, whose coarsening is based on edge collapsing. For volumetric solids, by contrast, the hierarchy is built by coarsening the simulation mesh itself, and how easily this can be done depends on the element type: coarsening is straightforward and efficient on hexahedral meshes [20], but the tetrahedral meshes prevalent in computer graphics are harder to coarsen. Several strategies address this: some build a multilevel XPBD through gradual rigidifying [21], while barycentric-coordinate prolongation [22] constructs a hierarchy directly on tetrahedral meshes and has proved successful in FEM. Our previous work, Multi-Grid Position-Based Dynamics (MGPBD) [12], utilized algebraic multigrid to build the hierarchy. However, algebraic multigrid requires assembling a global matrix, which sacrifices the flexibility and lightweight nature of XPBD’s local, per-constraint solve; moreover, building the hierarchy purely from the numerical matrix lacks geometric and physical intuition. In this work we propose a novel barycentric-coordinate-based geometric multigrid for XPBD, which accelerates the convergence of the stiff volume and incompressibility constraints and yields more stable and efficient volumetric simulation than single-level XPBD.

    Volumetric muscle simulation. Muscle is a special type of soft tissue, characterized by anisotropic fiber forces and strong incompressibility. Kim et al. [23, 24, 25] proposed energy potentials for FEM that yield an inversion-free muscle material matching the constitutive law of real muscle. Angles et al. [26] used position-based elastic rods with volumetric scale to model muscle bundles.

    Muscle-actuated Hill muscle control by RL. In recent years, many researchers have used 1D Hill-type muscles to physically drive the dynamics of human motion (activation → muscle force → bone motion, i.e. forward dynamics). The Hill-type model approximates each muscle as a polyline anchored to local positions on the bones, and reinforcement learning is commonly employed to train a neural network that finds the activations producing the desired motion. OpenSim [27] provides 1D musculotendon simulation, and Myosuite [2] wraps it in an RL framework for muscle-actuated control. The most prominent of these is MASS (Muscle-Actuated Skeletal System) by Lee et al. [1], a two-level imitation-learning architecture that actuates 346 muscles; we adopt its dual-network design (§III-B). A line of follow-ups inherits the same control formulation: MuscleVAE [3], MAGNET [4], and MuscleMimic [5], alongside torque-actuated trackers such as DeepMimic [28, 8] with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [7]. These methods all drive only 1D line-segment Hill muscles; building on this 1D Hill-type RL control, we add a 3D volumetric muscle simulation driven by the same Hill law, turning the biomechanics into visually compelling muscle deformation.

    Inverse muscle activation for volumetric muscle. Some works also address the inverse muscle activation problem with 3D volumetric deformation, similar to ours, but they recover the activations by static optimization rather than inside a forward-dynamic control loop. Han et al. [29] solve a per-pose torque balance as a quadratic program (QP) and train an ML-deformer [30] to reproduce muscle deformation from joint state and activation, but such a static solve cannot guarantee that the recovered activations actually drive the target motion (activation → muscle force → bone motion). Lee et al. [6] embed Hill-type muscles in Projective Dynamics and obtain activations from a per-frame QP, which runs the volumetric solver inside the trajectory-optimization control loop, but in our tests it was very unstable and never converged. We instead learn the activations inside the RL control loop on a 1D Hill-type surrogate, so they are exactly the forces that drive the motion (§III-B), making the deformation genuinely physically actuated rather than fitted or pre-scripted.

    III Method

    Our system couples a 1D Hill-type muscle model (Nₘ=284) with an RL controller, then uses a volumetric muscle model (194 muscles) with the same Hill-type constitutive law to simulate the deformation. We first outline the pipeline (§III-A) and the RL co-training that solves the inverse problem (§III-B), then detail the 1D Hill dynamics (§III-C), the 3D volumetric simulation (§III-D), and the motion retargeting and muscle mapping that bridge the 1D and 3D models (§III-E).

    III-AOverview

    Figure 2 summarizes the system. The input is a 1D musculoskeletal asset together with a reference motion clip in Biovision Hierarchy (BVH) format. A reinforcement-learning imitation-learning stage solves the muscle inverse problem on this 1D asset (284 muscles), jointly producing the muscle-driven bone motion and the corresponding 1D muscle activation trajectory. A motion-retargeting step transfers the bone motion onto a 3D skeleton, while a muscle-mapping step lifts the per-musculotendon 1D activations to 3D activations. Both streams and 3D assets (bone and muscle geometries) are then fed to the XPBD-based 3D simulation engine (§III-D), which produces the volumetric muscle deformation used for the final 3D rendering. The 1D track therefore acts as a fast surrogate that solves the hard inverse problem once; the 3D track is a single forward simulation at inference. The RL co-training that solves the inverse problem (Fig. 3, Alg. 1) is detailed in §III-B.

    III-BReinforcement Learning Control

    The RL stage solves control challenges: it discovers the muscle activations (Nₘ=284) that make the simulated character track a reference motion. We split control across a policy networkπ_φ and a muscle networkμ_θ[1] and co-train them inside a single PPO loop against the motion-tracking reward (Fig. 3, Alg. 1) rather than learning them sequentially, so each rollout supplies a gradient for both and they adapt to each other. A third, training-only value networkV_ψ serves as PPO’s critic but never participates in control.

    III-B1 Two-Network Co-Training

    We train the controller for muscle-driven motion tracking with PPO, summarized in Alg. 1. Letting the policy explore the Nₘ=284 muscle activations directly is sample-inefficient, so the policy instead acts in the compact space of per-joint PD-target offsets: Stable proportional–derivative (PD) control [31] turns its action into a desired joint torque τᵈᵉˢ ∈ ℝ^N_θ (N_θ=50 degrees of freedom, DOF), the muscle network maps that torque to the activations a^Mₜ ∈ [0,1]^Nₘ (M for muscles), and the Hill model realizes the muscle torque that drives MuJoCo [32]. Both networks learn from the same rollout, PPO updating π_φ,V_ψ and a mean squared error (MSE) loss updating μ_θ. The observation is sₜ=[ bₜ, vₜ, φₜ ], where bₜ ∈ ℝ⁶⁶ stacks the center-of-mass position of each of the 22 non-root bodies in the root frame, vₜ ∈ ℝ⁶⁹ the world-frame center-of-mass velocities of all 23 bodies, and φₜ ∈ [0,1) is the phase of the reference clip (\dim(sₜ)=136).

    III-B2 Policy Network

    Motion-mimicking reward. Following DeepMimic [8] we use an exponential-kernel reward composed of pose, velocity, and end-effector terms, augmented with whole-body center of mass (COM) and pelvis-orientation terms for balance-critical motions; the pose error is the SO(3) geodesic between current and target joint frames:

    pⱼ=\log (Rⱼ^⊤ R^*ⱼ)^∨∈ℝ³,(1)
    rₚₒₛₑ=\exp (-kₚ∑_j∈J ∥pⱼ∥²),(2)

    rₜ=rₑₑ·(wₚ rₚₒₛₑ+wᵥ rᵥₑₗ+w_c r_com+wᵤ rᵤₚ),

    		(3)

    where rₜ is the tracking reward; Rⱼ,R^*ⱼ∈SO(3) are the current/target rotation matrices of joint j; \log(·)^∨ is the matrix log map returning the axis–angle vector; J is the set of tracked joints; and asterisks mark reference-motion targets. The remaining terms share the same kernel \exp(-k \lVert·\rVert²) applied to their own error: joint velocity for rᵥₑₗ, the positions xₖ of the five end-effector links for rₑₑ, the whole-body center of mass c for r_com, and the pelvis up axis u=Rₚₑₗᵥᵢₛe_y for rᵤₚ, which gives a yaw-free torso-tilt error (full expressions in the supplementary). End-effector errors are taken in the COM-relative frame so root drift does not corrupt limb-placement credit, and rₑₑ enters multiplicatively so gross limb misplacement suppresses local joint credit. The exponential kernel confines each term to [0,1] and saturates smoothly as the tracking error grows. Balance-critical motions (squat, single-leg kick) shift the task weights (wₚ,wᵥ,w_c,wᵤ) toward the COM and pelvis-up terms and add the root pose to J; without these terms the policy matches the pose but loses balance and falls. Kernel widths, per-task weights and the Mixamo [33] clips are listed in the supplementary.

    III-B3 Muscle Network

    The muscle network μ_θ maps the desired joint torque τᵈᵉˢ to per-muscle activations a^M ∈ [0,1]^Nₘ, solving the muscle inverse problem. This map is redundant: the Nₘ muscles far outnumber the N_θ DOFs, so infinitely many activation patterns realize the same torque. Classical biomechanics resolves the redundancy per frame with a quadratic program (QP); we instead use a simple supervised network to solve it. Layer sizes and training hyperparameters are given in the supplementary material.

    Muscle-network loss. The muscle network μ_θ is trained online with three losses (Eq. 4): a torque-realization term L_torque that inverts the activation-to-torque map τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)=L a^M+b (§III-C), a minimum-effort regularizer L_reg that breaks the activation redundancy, and a physiological EMG prior L_emg. The first two are standard in muscle-actuated control; L_emg is our contribution: existing muscle networks [1, 3, 4, 5, 2] are trained on torque and effort alone, so their activations have no reason to match how a human recruits muscle (§IV-B), whereas L_emg steers the redundant solution toward a measured human EMG envelope. The three combine as

    L_μ=\underbracemean [(\tfrac1κ(τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)-τᵈᵉˢ))²]_L_torque+w_reg \underbracemean[(a^M)²]_L_reg(4)
    +λ \underbraceL_emg_EMG prior,

    with torque scale κ=100, w_reg=0.01, and EMG weight λ (L_emg is defined in Eq. 6; setting λ=0 recovers the tracking-only loss for motions without a measured envelope). L_reg is the ∑a² minimum-effort criterion of classical static optimization [34], which on its own drives the activations away from physiological EMG measurements.

    III-B4 EMG Prior

    So far, we have obtained activations that generate physically plausible motion through muscle forces, but these activations are still physiologically implausible. We therefore steer the redundant solution toward real surface electromyography (sEMG) from Moreira et al. [10]. Two mismatches stand between that recording and our model (Fig. 4). The first is a muscle mismatch: the recording is coarse-grained, using only four right-leg electrodes, whereas our model is fine-grained. The second is a temporal misalignment: the recording is not aligned with the reference motion, so the two cannot be compared sample by sample. We apply two treatments, detailed in turn below: 1) we match each electrode not to a single fiber but to a whole synergist group; 2) we fold both signals onto a common gait cycle and compare only their shape and timing, not their magnitude.

    Synergist-group mean. Let ℂ be the EMG channels (the four right-leg surface electrodes of Moreira et al. [10]). A surface electrode integrates over a muscle region and the redundant solver distributes load within a synergist group, so channel c is matched not to one fiber but to the cross-section-weighted mean activation of its synergist group G_c:

    ā_c=∑_m∈G_cω_c,m a^Mₘ, ω_c,m=(f_0,m)/(∑_m^′∈G_cf_0,m^′),

    		(5)

    where f_0,m=σ₀A^Mₘ is the maximal isometric force of muscle m (Eq. 8), obtained from its physiological cross-sectional area A^Mₘ and the maximal isometric stress σ₀, the peak stress a fully activated fiber can sustain. Since σ₀ is uniform across muscles (value in the supplementary), the weight reduces to a ratio of cross-sectional areas, so the stronger muscles of a group dominate its mean. Matching the group mean rather than a single fiber also guards against a dead-unit pathology (supplementary).

    Gait-cycle alignment. Each rollout sample carries a gait phase φ=fmod(t, T)/T∈[0,1) recovered from its simulation time t, with T the gait-cycle period, and is placed on the 0 - 100% cycle as ((φ-φₕₛ)\bmod1)·100 to align it to right heel strike [35], where φₕₛ=0.254 is the heel-strike offset calibrated by forward kinematics on the reference foot. The prior is a phase-indexed MSE that pulls each group activation toward the peak-normalized human envelope ê_c(φ):

    L_emg=(1)/(|ℂ|)∑_c∈ℂw_emg,c (ā_c-s ê_c(φ))²,

    		(6)

    where s scales the unit-peak envelope into the activation range and w_emg,c weights each channel (the weight λ against torque realization is set in Eq. 4). The prior enters only the muscle-network loss; the policy’s motion objective (Eq. 3) is untouched, so it re-selects which activation realizes a motion without changing the motion itself. We use λ=1, s=0.3, and w_emg,c=1 for all channels; ê_c is the 13-subject Moreira cohort mean on a 101-bin gait grid. It is enabled wherever a measured envelope exists (the walk) and switched off (λ=0) otherwise; its effect on physiological plausibility is evaluated in §IV-B.

    III-C1D Hill-type Muscle Surrogate

    For motion to be truly actuated by muscle forces, the musculoskeletal system should closely match human anatomy. However, we empirically find that 3D volumetric muscles are overly flexible during RL training due to their excessive number of degrees of freedom, leading to unstable learning. Lee et al. [6] run the volumetric solver directly inside their optimization loop, which was also our initial idea. However, in our experiments, this approach was unstable and failed to converge. Therefore, we instead train against a 1D Hill-type muscle model [1, 3, 4, 5] as a surrogate, and then lift it to a 3D volumetric muscle model in the next section. The Hill-type model plays a dual role in our system: (i) as the 1D musculotendon surrogate that drives RL training, its scalar tension routed through MuJoCo tendon paths to the skeleton (Alg. 1); and (ii) as the constitutive law for the 3D XPBD volumetric muscle of §III-D, injected there as an energy-based fiber constraint (Eq. 19). We give the shared 1D formulation here and the 3D lift in §III-D. The 1D musculoskeletal asset (Fig. 5) is a rigid-body skeleton with spherical and revolute joints, actuated by 1D Hill-type muscles routed as polyline tendon paths between bone attachment sites.

    The Hill-type model (Fig. 6) places a tendon spring in series with a muscle belly, itself an active contractile element parallel to a passive spring. Each fiber generates a normalized scalar force:

    fₕᵢₗₗ=\underbrace\color[rgb]0.1211,0.4648,0.707a f^L(ℓ̃^M) f^V(ℓ̇^M)_\color[rgb]0.1211,0.4648,0.707active+\underbrace\color[rgb]0.1719,0.6289,0.1719f^PE(ℓ̃^M)_\color[rgb]0.1719,0.6289,0.1719passive+\underbrace\color[rgb]0.7734,0.3516,0.0664fᵀ(ℓ̃ᵀ)_\color[rgb]0.7734,0.3516,0.0664tendon,

    		(7)

    where a∈[0,1] is the muscle activation and ℓ̃^M the fiber length normalized by the optimal fiber length, so fₕᵢₗₗ is a dimensionless multiplier equal to 1 at that length (the 3D counterpart of ℓ̃^M, the along-fiber stretch λ_f, is defined in §III-D). We take the force–length curves f^L and f^PE from Millard et al. [9] and evaluate them through a look-up table to accelerate RL training; their piecewise-Bézier form and parameters are given in the supplementary. For simplicity we further assume 1) an infinitely stiff tendon and 2) no velocity-dependent force f^V, since only conservative forces admit an energy potential (§III-D4). We obtain the 1D muscle force by multiplying fₕᵢₗₗ by the peak isometric force f₀, which depends on the muscle (e.g., leg muscles are stronger than arm muscles). f₀=σ₀A^M (physiological cross-sectional area A^M). The resulting 1D Hill-type muscle force is

    F(a)=f₀(a f^L(ℓ̃^M)+f^PE(ℓ̃^M)).

    		(8)

    Muscle force to joint torque. Summing the segments of the anchor polyline gives the path length, hence the normalized fiber length ℓ̃^M that Eq. 7 evaluates; mapping the anchor forces through their point Jacobians makes the total torque affine in activation, τᵐᵘˢᶜ(a^M)=L a^M+b, with L the per-unit-activation moment arms and b the passive torque (root DOFs excluded; both derived in the supplementary). This closed-form, differentiable map is the Hill forward through which μ_θ is trained (§III-B) and the torque that drives MuJoCo.

    III-D3D Volumetric Muscle Simulation

    To achieve a stable, controllable, and realistic volumetric muscle simulation, three key challenges must be addressed: 1) anisotropic fiber force, 2) volume conservation, and 3) muscle–bone coupling. The first two drive the realism: the fiber force contracts the muscle along the fibers, while volume conservation makes it bulge in the orthogonal directions. Enforcing volume conservation is in turn limited by solver convergence: under the high stiffness muscle requires, an under-converged solve leaves visible artifacts and inverted tetrahedra. Muscle–bone coupling is governed by attachments: attachments that are too stiff distort the muscle, while those that are too soft fail to transmit force. We address them in turn. We embed the Hill-type curve into the constitutive law, so that per-fiber activation directly shortens the muscle along its fibers. We propose a GMG (Geometric Multigrid) solver for fast and stable simulation (§III-D2). Finally, we partition each muscle by masks into tendon and belly regions, attaching the tendons hard and the belly soft. We simulate the volumetric muscle with XPBD [16], giving first the solver update and the geometric multigrid that accelerates it, then the individual constraints.

    III-D1 XPBD Update

    The volumetric muscle deformation is driven by a set of position-based constraints: volume and shape preservation (§III-D3), anisotropic fiber contraction (§III-D4), attachment (§III-D5), and collision (§III-D6). Each is solved with the standard XPBD update:

    Δλ=(-C-α̃ λ)/(∑ᵢwᵢ\lVert∇C\rVert²+α̃),(9)
    Δxᵢ=wᵢ ∇C Δλ.(10)

    Here C is one of the constraint functions and ∇C its gradient with respect to the participating vertex positions. λ is the constraint’s accumulated Lagrange multiplier (reset to zero at the start of each time step) and Δλ is its per-iteration increment. α̃=1/(k Δt²) is the compliance, i.e. the inverse of the constraint stiffness k scaled by the squared time step Δt; a stiffer constraint thus has a smaller α̃. wᵢ is the inverse mass of vertex i, and Δxᵢ is the position correction applied to that vertex. Once all constraints have been projected, velocities are recovered from the position change over the step, v^f←(x^f-x^fₚᵣₑᵥ)/Δt. The individual constraints are defined next; each constraint’s gradient is derived in the supplementary.

    III-D2 Geometric Multigrid
