We thank Jun Xing, Tianshu Zhang and Zhixin Piao for the very early discussions on motion compression. This work was partially funded by the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong (Ref: 17216826) and by the Innovation and Technology Commission of the HKSAR Government under the ITSP-Platform grant (Ref: ITS/335/23FP, ITS/469/24FP).

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：把冗余定位到「熵模型」而不是逐骨架先验，0.01cm 精度下用 0.37 倍 ACL 字节。

要点：

  • 前作 CurveCodec 用稀疏锚点 + 学习先验重建每条关节曲线，均误差追平引擎标配 ACL 但最坏情况不行，且把码率按浮点数而非比特统计。
  • 这一版先做 ACL 的「解剖」测量，再系统实验回答两件事：骨架运动的冗余在哪，以及编解码器的哪一部分该交给学习模型——答案是熵模型。
  • 在留出测试集、0.01cm 精度下只需 ACL 的 0.37 倍字节，码流比特精确、单核 CPU 即可解码，一个模型训练一次覆盖所有骨架、无需重训。

为什么值得看：动画内存与包体是移动端项目的硬指标，非逐骨架专用、可比特精确定点解码的编解码器，比通用压缩更适合接进运行时动画系统。

中文摘要：骨骼运动按每帧每个关节的变换存储，但其中大部分冗余由身体结构而非动作语义决定。CurveCodec 2 是一个骨架无关的骨骼动画编解码器：先对生产库 ACL 做实测解剖，再通过系列受控实验回答骨架运动的冗余在哪里、编解码器的哪一部分应当交给学习模型，结论是把学习模型放在熵模型上。在留出测试集、0.01cm 精度下，它只需 ACL 的 0.37 倍字节；码流比特精确、可单核 CPU 解码，且一个模型训练一次即可编码所有骨架而无需重训，并给出明确的误差界。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-10-03

本期推送：2026-10-23

CurveCodec 2: Skeleton-Agnostic Animation Compression with a Learned Entropy Model

© , 2026

Abstract.

Skeletal motion is stored as every joint’s transform at every frame, yet most of it is implied by the body rather than by what the motion is about. Compression is one way to ask what a motion must still say once the body is known, and a production codec is where that question has to be answered for any skeleton, with a stated bound on the error. Our earlier codec, CurveCodec, reconstructed each joint curve from sparse anchors with a learned prior. It matched the mean error of ACL, the production library of modern game engines, but not its worst case, and it counted its payload as floating-point values rather than as bits. Here we ask where the redundancy of skeletal motion lies, and which part of a codec a learned model should take over. A measured anatomy of ACL and a series of controlled experiments give three answers. At production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each quantized curve from its own past, and the second from choosing per joint, in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples not to code. On the gaps such an encoder leaves, interpolation has little left to find: a nearest-neighbour oracle with millions of training samples as memory is no better than linear interpolation there, and none of the learned in-betweeners we tried paid for itself. What a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals the codec must send. CurveCodec 2 puts these findings into one codec. Every sub-track becomes a curve, rotations in the log map and translations in centimetres, quantized in closed loop and thinned to rate–distortion-selected keys, and its prediction residuals are entropy-coded under a small learned model whose integer inference is bit-exact across platforms. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL’s own worst case per joint, within a stated tolerance, or ACL’s mean error per clip. On a held-out test side of 4,472 clips from 33 datasets, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37× ACL’s bytes at ACL’s default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract and 0.22× at 0.1 cm under the mean contract. It decodes whole clips on one CPU core, typically in a fraction of a second, and transfers without retraining to a species absent from training.

Keywords:

animation compression, skeletal animation, rate–distortion optimization, entropy coding, learned probability model

1. Introduction

A skeletal animation clip stores rotations and translations for tens to hundreds of joints at every sample, yet much of this is not what the motion is about. A performer decides what to do; the body, its morphology and its dynamics, determines most of how each joint gets from one place to the next. Compressing these data matters in production, where animation libraries face strict memory and streaming budgets, and in motion research, where corpora reach hundreds of hours and a model should spend its capacity on the decisions rather than on kinematics the body already implies. A codec is one way to probe this separation: what it must still send under a stated error bound is at least what the body did not predict. This is our motivation, not a claim the bit counts prove. If the body is only a prior, the representation should not be tied to one body: a production codec must serve arbitrary skeletons and motion without retraining, and it must bound its error, because a single visible pop on one joint is a defect regardless of how small the average error is.

ACL [(Frechette, 2023)] is the industry standard. It folds the sub-tracks that do not move, reduces the range of the rest per clip and per segment, and quantizes each joint with one of a fixed set of bit widths under a per-joint error threshold. It decodes a pose in microseconds, but it models neither time nor the statistics of its own symbols. Learned motion encoders [(Ling et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024)] take the opposite trade: their latent priors couple the representation to a training skeleton and domain, and they do not reach production precision.

Our previous work, CurveCodec [(Shi et al., 2026)], placed the learned prior on the smallest skeleton-independent unit of motion, the local joint curve, and reconstructed each curve from sparse anchors with a shared transformer. It reached three times ACL’s ratio at matched mean error, but its worst case exceeded ACL’s, its payload was counted in floating-point values rather than entropy-coded bits, and its decoder needed a GPU rather than a CPU core.

This paper asks a different question: where is the redundancy in skeletal motion, and which part of a codec should a learned model take over? We answer it by measurement, treating the codec as an instrument: under an explicit error contract and an exact bit count, every candidate structure of motion either pays or does not. We dissect ACL stage by stage and test every place where a learned component could enter. Three findings shape the result. First, ACL’s ratio comes almost entirely from folding and from range reduction with variable bit widths. Its widths are nearly tight for independent samples, so an entropy coder on top of ACL’s own symbols would gain little; a substantially smaller stream needs its own quantizer, one whose integers remain predictable in time. Second, at production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each curve from its own past, and the next from choosing, per joint and in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples to omit. Leaving a sample out is by far the cheapest way to spend error, and its share of the stream grows as the precision loosens, until the two are comparable at the loosest precision we use. Third, on the gaps such an encoder leaves, interpolation has little left to find. A nearest-neighbour oracle with millions of training samples as memory, which clearly beats cubic interpolation on random gaps, is no better than linear interpolation on the gaps the encoder actually leaves, and the learned in-betweeners we placed inside the codec did not pay. On our data, the in-betweener at the core of CurveCodec has little left to learn; what a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals that the codec still has to send.

These findings lead to CurveCodec 2. Every animated sub-track is coded as a curve: rotations in the log map, which removes the precision floor of ACL’s dropped quaternion component; a quantization step and a key set chosen in closed loop against the object-space error of the whole subtree; and prediction residuals coded with rANS under a small learned model of the curve’s own past, a causal transformer or, in the worst-case configuration, an MLP. The model sees no joint identity, so the codec is skeleton-agnostic, and its integer inference is bit-exact on ARM and x86. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL’s own worst case per joint, within a stated tolerance, or ACL’s mean error per clip. A clip that fails is re-encoded with a margin or stored as ACL’s stream, and every number we report includes this fallback.

On a corpus of 906 hours from 33 datasets with a held-out test side, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37× ACL’s bytes at ACL’s default precision of 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract, and 0.22× at 0.1 cm under either contract; against ACL with its default keyframe stripping the ratios are slightly larger and the picture is the same. It decodes on a CPU, typically a clip in a fraction of a second on one core, but only whole clips: it is a storage and distribution format decoded at load time, not a replacement for ACL’s constant-time sampling.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A quantitative anatomy of motion redundancy, measuring where a production codec’s bits go and which structure a codec exploited in our hands: temporal predictability and, increasingly as the precision loosens, per-joint sample sparsity did; interpolation from the decoded neighbourhood, cross-joint structure, and transforms under a worst-case criterion did not.

  • •

    CurveCodec 2, a closed-loop, skeleton-agnostic rate–distortion codec under two explicit error contracts, with a stated fallback for the clips that fail.

  • •

    A learned entropy model in the role where a network pays: small, causal, and bit-exact across platforms, it models the distribution of the residuals the codec must send, the one place where, in our measurements, a network consistently earns its cost.

  • •

    A corpus-scale benchmark against ACL, with audits of ACL’s configuration and of our own contracts, and same-core speed.

    • 2. Related Work

    Skeletal animation compression is a long-standing problem in computer graphics. Early work focused on making animation data smaller and faster to decode in production systems; learned representations later showed that motion can be organized into compact spaces that support reconstruction and synthesis. Our work sits between the two: an explicit, verifiable codec in the production tradition, with a learned component placed where our measurements show that learning pays.

    2.1. Hand-engineered Animation Compression

    Before deep learning, animation compression removed temporal redundancy, inter-joint redundancy, and perceptually insignificant detail while keeping the motion faithful. Mesh compression began with static connectivity and geometry [(Rossignac, 1999; Karni and Gotsman, 2000)]; animated meshes were then compressed through their vertex trajectories, by principal components [(Alexa and Müller, 2000)] or space-time prediction [(Ibarria and Rossignac, 2003)]. [Arikan (2006)] moved the problem to skeletal motion: joint angles were converted into virtual marker trajectories, fitted with cubic Bézier curves, and projected into clustered PCA subspaces. Later work exploited low-dimensional structure with segment-level PCA and spline interpolation [(Liu and McMillan, 2006)], quadratic Bézier break-and-fit curves [(Khan, 2016)], wavelet coefficient selection [(Beaudoin et al., 2007; Lee and Lasenby, 2008)], and wavelets guided by perception [(Firouzmanesh et al., 2011)]; others indexed repeated motion patterns across a database [(Gu et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2011)]. ACL [(Frechette, 2023)] is the production standard. It prioritizes per-track processing and constant-time random access over compression ratio, and Sec. 5.1 quantifies where its bits go. Our keys relate to keyframe extraction [(Lim and Thalmann, 2001; Halit and Capin, 2011)] and curve simplification [(Barkowsky et al., 2000)], which choose samples from a local error or saliency criterion. CurveCodec 2 instead chooses them by rate–distortion optimization against the object-space error of the whole subtree, and Sec. 5.2 shows that this closed loop, not the key representation itself, carries the gain. Unlike transform codecs, which we find lose to sparse keys under a worst-case criterion, CurveCodec 2 keeps the time domain and predicts each sample from its own past.

    2.2. Learned Motion Representations and Codecs

    Motion manifolds and deep motion representations show that valid character motion occupies a much smaller space than raw joint rotations [(Holden et al., 2015; Holden et al., 2016)]. VAE-style priors support character control, action-conditioned synthesis, and pose estimation [(Ling et al., 2020; Petrovich et al., 2021; Rempe et al., 2021)]; tokenizers with vector or residual quantization compress motion into discrete codes [(Yao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024)]; phase-based models organize motion by periodic timing [(Starke et al., 2022; Shi et al., 2023)]; and Learned Motion Matching [(Holden et al., 2020)] amortizes an animation database into networks. Cross-skeleton methods learn representations for retargeting [(Villegas et al., 2018; Aberman et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2023)]. These representations target synthesis, control, or transfer at pose level, not a decodable bitstream at a stated precision; SAME [(Lee et al., 2023)] in particular learns an embedding shared across skeletons, which is a different goal from ours rather than a competing codec. The learned encoders measured in CurveCodec [(Shi et al., 2026)] under the shell metric reconstruct with errors two orders of magnitude above the 0.01 cm of a production codec, and the residual-VQ tokenizer we built has a precision floor of about 1.3 % of a track’s RMS (Sec. 5.4); we do not extend these bounds to methods we did not measure. Implicit neural representations fit signals with coordinate networks [(Park et al., 2019; Tancik et al., 2020; Sitzmann et al., 2020; Dupont et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021)], and NeMF [(He et al., 2022)] applies the idea to kinematic motion. We find the same fidelity floor for per-window neural fields. CurveCodec [(Shi et al., 2026)] is our direct predecessor. It made the learned prior skeleton-agnostic by working on single sub-tracks, and reconstructed each from a first-frame state, a Fourier descriptor, and extrema anchors with a masked transformer, in the spirit of learned in-betweening [(Harvey et al., 2020)]. CurveCodec 2 keeps the per-sub-track, skeleton-agnostic unit but moves the learned prior from the interpolator to the probability model, for reasons that Sec. 5.3 measures on our data.

    2.3. Entropy Coding and Learned Probability Models

    Lossless coding separates modelling from coding: an arithmetic coder [(Witten et al., 1987)] or an asymmetric numeral system [(Duda, 2013)] spends -\log₂P bits per symbol, so the compression depends only on how well the model P predicts the data. Predictive lossless coders such as LOCO-I / JPEG-LS [(Weinberger et al., 2000)] and CALIC [(Wu and Memon, 1997)] combine a fixed predictor with a context model of the residual, the structure CurveCodec 2 adopts per curve. Learned image compression [(Ballé et al., 2017; Ballé et al., 2018; Minnen et al., 2018)] showed that much of the gain of a learned codec comes from the learned probability model, and that decoding with a network requires deterministic, integer inference to keep encoder and decoder in sync across platforms [(Ballé et al., 2019)]. General-purpose neural compressors use recurrent or transformer models as the probability model of a byte stream [(Goyal et al., 2019; Bellard, 2021; Delétang et al., 2024)]. Learned probability models have entered animation compression before: Chen et al. [(Chen et al., 2022)] compress motion-capture sequences with a learned continuous-time latent model, and Qin et al. [(Qin et al., 2025)] code mesh animations with a deep entropy model over vertex trajectories; neither holds an object-space worst-case bound through a skeleton. CurveCodec 2 combines per-curve learned residual probabilities with hierarchy-aware quantization and key selection under explicitly verified object-space error constraints, and our experiments indicate that for skeletal motion the probability model is the role where a network pays, while the learned interpolators, transforms, tokenizers, and neural fields we tried did not pay for themselves.

    3. Preliminaries

    3.1. Skeletal Animation and Error

    A skeleton has J joints connected as a rooted tree; joint j has parent π(j). A clip of N uniformly spaced samples stores, per joint and sample, a local rotation qⱼ(t) (a unit quaternion) and a local translation tⱼ(t)∈ℝ³; BVH data carry no scale. Following ACL, the time series of one transform component of one joint is a sub-track. Skeleton-agnostic means that the same codec and weights apply to any joint count and tree topology without retraining. For comparability with ACL we use its raw size of ten 32-bit floats per joint-sample, but report rate mainly in bits per joint-sample and as our bytes divided by ACL’s on the same clips. Sizes include every header; shared model weights are reported separately.

    Shell error.

    We use ACL’s shell-distance metric [(Frechette, 2023)]. Forward kinematics gives the object-space transform of every joint,

    (1)

    qᵒⱼ=qᵒ_π(j)⊗qⱼ, xᵒⱼ=qᵒ_π(j) tⱼ qᵒ_π(j)̄+xᵒ_π(j),

    and the error of joint j at sample t is the largest displacement of three virtual vertices at distance δ=3 cm along its axes,

    (2)

    e_j,t=\max_a∈{x,y,z}∥Tᵒⱼ(t) (δêₐ)-T̂ᵒⱼ(t) (δêₐ)∥,

    where Tᵒⱼ and T̂ᵒⱼ are the original and decoded object-space transforms, so the error of a joint contains the errors of all its ancestors. The vertices sample the sphere, so Eq. (2) can understate the largest displacement on it (by up to a factor √2/3 for a pure rotation error); the ACL commit we benchmark uses this approximation, which its development branch has since replaced with the exact maximum (supplementary Sec. A). Both codecs are measured with Eq. (2), at the sample times only as ACL does; our implementation matches the clip maximum our ACL build reports within 10⁻⁴ cm.

    3.2. Two-Stage Compression Pipeline

    As in CurveCodec, we view compression as two stages (Fig. 2). The first, deterministic preprocessing shared by ACL and CurveCodec 2, drops the scale sub-tracks that ACL’s raw convention reserves and folds every sub-track that does not move within p into a single default or constant value. Production skeletons contain many such joints: on our corpus, dropping scale reduces ACL’s raw 647 GB to 453 GB, and at p=0.01 cm folding leaves only 53 % of the rotation and 3.6 % of the translation sub-tracks animated. CurveCodec 2 applies ACL’s folding rule unchanged, so both codecs start the second stage from the same animated sub-tracks.

    ACL’s compression stage.

    ACL drops the w component of each quaternion and reconstructs it from the unit norm. It normalizes every animated sub-track to its clip range and to the range of each 16-sample segment, and gives each joint one of 25 bit widths, chosen per segment by a search that raises widths until the object-space error of the joint and its descendants meets p. We use ACL’s development branch after release 2.1.0 (commit 3ee5685), whose newer search does not read ACL’s compression level; supplementary Sec. A describes it and compares the release. ACL performs no prediction and no entropy coding: every sample of a segment costs the same number of bits, which gives constant-time random access. It can also strip whole frames that linear interpolation of their neighbours reproduces within p (on by default). Our corpus becomes an estimated 32.6 GB, extrapolated from the test side. CurveCodec 2 replaces this stage (Sec. 4) with log-map rotations, steps and keys chosen in closed loop through forward kinematics, prediction, and learned entropy coding; the corpus then becomes an estimated 11.9 GB, plus one 870 KB model shared by all clips.

    3.3. Error Contracts

    ACL compresses to a precision p (default 0.01 cm) but does not guarantee it: its widths come from a fixed set and its dropped w has a precision floor, so a clip’s maximum error stays within p on only 1.5 % of our test clips at 0.01 cm. Comparing codecs at the same p is fair only if both are held to the same measured error. We check every clip against ACL’s result on that clip, with ē^ACLⱼ and μ^ACLⱼ the maximum and mean error ACL reaches on joint j, μ^ACL its clip mean, and f^ACL the fraction of joint-samples it leaves above p.

    Max gate.

    Every joint stays within 5 % of the larger of p and ACL’s own maximum on that joint, and the fraction of samples above p within half a percentage point of ACL’s:

    (3)\maxₜe_j,t≤1.05\max (p,ē^ACLⱼ) ∀j,
    \tfrac1JN|{(j,t):e_j,t>p}|≤f^ACL+0.005.

    This bounds a joint by 1.05 p where ACL meets p and by ACL’s own maximum where it does not; a joint ACL codes far below p may be coded up to 1.05 p. It holds ACL’s worst case within tolerance, not identically; Sec. 6.3 measures what the tolerances are worth.

    Mean gate.

    The clip keeps ACL’s mean mₚ=\max(μ^ACL,φp), each joint stays near its share, and a guard bounds the worst case:

    (4)\tfrac1N∑ₜe_j,t≤ρ\max (mₚ,μ^ACLⱼ) ∀j,
    \tfrac1JN∑_j,te_j,t≤τ mₚ,
    \maxₜe_j,t≤\max (γ mₚ, 1.05 ē^ACLⱼ) ∀j,

    with ρ=1.05, τ=1.02, γ=10, and φ=0. The guard is ten times ACL’s clip mean, not a multiple of p: at p≤0.1 cm the resulting worst case is below ACL’s, but at loose precision it admits large isolated errors, so the mean gate suits storage at tight precision.

    Verification and fallback.

    The encoder decodes its own stream and checks Eq. (3) or (4) on every joint. A failing clip is re-encoded with its internal limits scaled by 0.98, then 0.95, then 0.90; if none passes, or if the final stream is larger than ACL’s, ACL’s own stream is stored, which satisfies either contract by definition. All test-side byte counts include this fallback.

    4. CurveCodec 2

    Fig. 3 gives an overview. As in CurveCodec, the unit of coding is one animated sub-track, a curve: one joint’s rotation (three log-map components) or translation (three components) over time; each coded component becomes one integer column of the entropy coder. The skeleton enters the codec in one place: the encoder evaluates the shell error through forward kinematics to decide how coarsely each curve may be coded. The learned model never sees joint identity; its only hierarchy-derived input is a four-class depth bucket that the decoder computes from the skeleton’s parent array. Sections 4.1 to 4.3 describe the lossy part, which determines the decoded clip, and Sec. 4.4 the lossless part, which determines only the number of bits, so the network cannot violate the error contract.

    4.1. Representation

    Folding.

    Folding follows ACL’s rule. On long chains (tails, finger rigs) small folding errors can accumulate below each joint’s threshold yet push a descendant over its limit; when the unquantized state already violates the contract, we un-fold sub-tracks on the offending root paths, largest error first. In the benchmarked max-gate codec this runs only in the first quantization stage, which causes most loose-precision failures (Sec. 6.3).

    Log-map rotations.

    ACL stores the (x,y,z) part of a quaternion and reconstructs w, which amplifies quantization error near |w|≈0 and leaves a precision floor: on our curated set ACL’s maximum error is 0.071 cm at every precision from 0.01 down to 0.001 cm. We instead code the rotation vector [(Grassia, 1998)]

    (5)

    v=\Log(q)=2 atan2(\lVertq_xyz\rVert,q_w) (q_xyz)/(\lVertq_xyz\rVert),

    after choosing quaternion signs so that consecutive samples lie in the same hemisphere (qₜ·qₜ₋₁≥0, with q_w≥0 at t=0), so that \lVertv\rVert∈[0,2π]. Where \lVertq_xyz\rVert vanishes (the identity, or q=-1 after a full turn) the direction is undefined and the limit depends on the direction of approach; by convention we take v=0, a branch choice that \Exp maps back to the same rotation in both cases. The map needs no side information, bounds the rotation error by \lVertΔv\rVert, and lowers the curated maximum at 0.01 cm from 0.071 to 0.024 cm. It is continuous only short of a full turn: when a joint’s rotation relative to its parent passes 2π, v jumps from about +2π u to -2π u. Since v and v+2π u are the same rotation in SO(3) (their quaternions differ only in sign) and the contract is checked on the decoded clip, this costs a few keys, not correctness; it occurs on 0.33 % of the test side’s rotation tracks and costs below 0.2 % of the bytes (supplementary Sec. C, which also evaluates an unwrapping rule). Translations are coded in centimetres without any transform.

    4.2. Closed-Loop Quantization

    Each curve is quantized uniformly, nₜ=\rint(vₜ/s), v̂ₜ=nₜs, with the step on a logarithmic grid s=2^i/G, i∈ℤ, G=16, so that the header stores a small integer. Because a joint’s error is amplified by the chain it moves, we start from

    (6)

    sᵣₒₜ=(2 p)/(√3 Rⱼ√cⱼ), sₜᵣₐₙₛ=(p)/(√3 √cⱼ),

    where Rⱼ is the shell distance plus joint j’s longest child chain and cⱼ the number of joints on the longest root-to-leaf chain through j. A closed loop then grows each track’s step while the contract holds: every candidate is decoded, forward kinematics is recomputed for the joint’s subtree, and Eq. (3) or (4) is tested on every joint of the subtree. The search passes leaves to root and back, offering 1,2,4,… grid units and bisecting on refusal; because the error is not monotone in the step, it looks up to half an octave past a refusal, which alone saves 1 to 7 % under the mean gate. Under the max gate the three rotation components may then grow separately. The root keeps the finest steps; leaves end 2 to 5× coarser than Eq. (6).

    4.3. Rate–Distortion Keys

    Each track keeps a key set K⊆{0,…,N-1} with the first and last sample, and the decoder fills the rest by Catmull–Rom interpolation [(Catmull and Rom, 1974)] of the log-map values,

    (7)v̂(t)=h₀₀(u) v̂ₖ+h₁₀(u) Δₖmₖ+h₀₁(u) v̂_k^′+h₁₁(u) Δₖm_k^′,
    mₖ=(v̂_k⁺-v̂_k⁻)/(t_k⁺-t_k⁻), u=t-tₖ/Δₖ,

    with consecutive keys k,k^′, Δₖ=t_k^′-tₖ, neighbouring keys k^±, and cubic Hermite basis functions h_··; rotations are recovered with \Exp. The cubic saves 0.5 to 2.6 % over linear interpolation in the same rotation-vector coordinates; this is not spherical linear interpolation [(Shoemake, 1985)], which it matches only for coaxial rotations, and every interpolation baseline in this paper is log-linear. Keys, like steps, are chosen in closed loop through the hierarchy.

    Max gate.

    From the all-samples state, the encoder removes keys in greedy rounds: it proposes every fourth interior key of every track, decodes the affected window, recomputes the subtree’s error, and accepts the removal if every joint stays within its limit and the clip within its over-p allowance. A narrow failure may be rescued by moving the two neighbouring key values up to two steps towards their least-squares fit of the window. Rounds alternate leaf-to-root and root-to-leaf passes until nothing is accepted.

    Mean gate.

    Under the iso-mean contract the budget is a sum, so moves can trade between curves. A Lagrangian ladder [(Sullivan and Wiegand, 1998)] lets two moves compete: removing a key, with distortion ΔD the increase of the summed error over the window and subtree and rate ΔR estimated from the residuals it removes, and growing a step by g grid units, with ΔR=β·3 |K| g/G and β=2.5 calibrated against measured bits. At level λ every move with ΔD/ΔR≤λ that keeps Eq. (4) is accepted; λ starts at 10⁻⁴mₚ per bit and grows by √2 until the budget is spent, about 60 % on steps and 40 % on keys.

    Track modes.

    Each track is finally coded in the cheapest of four modes: static, all samples, one key set shared by its components, or per-component sets that may only thin the shared set, with a context-coded presence flag per component and key.

    4.4. Prediction and Learned Entropy Coding

    After the lossy stage a clip is a set of integer columns, the quantized values of each coded component at its keys (at most six per joint, 468 for a 78-joint clip before folding).

    Prediction and alphabet.

    Each column is predicted from its own past, rₜ=nₜ-n̂ₜ, with a predictor chosen per column among first and second differences, a second difference scaled by the ratio of key gaps, and an order-4 integer NLMS filter [(Haykin, 2002)] on first differences. A residual is split into a symbol (zero or the sign, the bit length of |rₜ|, and the first bit below its leading one; 159 symbols) and raw low bits. Each symbol covers an interval of residual values, so a continuous distribution over rₜ induces symbol probabilities through its cumulative distribution.

    Learned probability model.

    A network ℙ_θ sees only the column’s own decoded past through 36 integer features fₜ: the last eight residuals as signed log magnitudes, five exponential averages of |r|, first and second differences of the decoded integers, the key gaps around the position, the depth class (root, one to two, three to five, six and deeper), the sub-track kind, predictor, log step, frame rate, precision, and position in the column; none identifies a joint, a skeleton, or a dataset. ℙ_θ is a causal transformer, two pre-norm blocks of width 64 with four heads over the last W=128 positions (108 K parameters), whose head outputs a mixture of K=3 logistics [(Salimans et al., 2017)]; the symbol covering [a,b] has probability

    (8)

    P(a≤rₜ≤b|f_≤t)=∑ₖ₌₁^Kwₖ[Sₖ(b+\tfrac12)-Sₖ(a-\tfrac12)],

    with Sₖ(x)=sig((x-μₖ)/σₖ), quantized to 15-bit frequencies and coded with rANS [(Duda, 2013)]. Residuals are ordered time-major over all columns, so the model runs once per index as a batch over the active columns, and the decoder reconstructs each integer before the next features are computed. For the max-gate codec we use a 22 K-parameter MLP (36→128→128→9) over the same features, 4× cheaper to decode.

    Bit-exact inference.

    Encoder and decoder must compute identical probabilities. We export the network to fixed point: 16-bit weights with power-of-two scales, 64-bit integer accumulators, integer layer normalization, and lookup tables for softmax, sigmoid, and exponential. The residual stream is clipped to ±2²⁸, which bounds every operand downstream: linear-layer products stay below 2⁴³ and their sums over at most 256 terms below 2⁵³, so even a float64 matrix library adds exact integers [(Ballé et al., 2019)]; the attention logits and the layer-norm variance are accumulated in 64-bit integers within the bounds given in Appendix H. The guarantee is that every probability and every decoded integer is identical on any platform. The float reconstruction (dequantization, interpolation, \Exp) runs on those integers and reproduced x86 results bit for bit on an ARM machine in our tests, but it is deterministic rather than exact by construction (Appendix H).

    Training.

    The model minimizes the code length of Eq. (8) on residual streams of our training split (886 h, 41.2 G symbols), on 40 M windows with 128 context positions and 384 scored ones, with AdamW [(Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019)] and a one-cycle schedule, in about 1.5 hours on one RTX 4090. Supplementary Appendix G summarizes the bitstream layout; the reference decoder defines the details it leaves out.

    5. Where Is the Redundancy in Motion?

    These measurements motivate the design. Unless stated otherwise, they use two development sets that predate the full corpus: curated, 70 clips from 14 mocap datasets (15.9 M joint-samples), and dev, 15 clips. Every variant was verified against its contract on every clip; Sec. 6 tests the final codec on held-out data.

    5.1. ACL’s Bit Budget

    Fig. 4a follows ACL’s stages on the curated set. Two stages do the work: folding sub-tracks that do not move (2.84×, from 191 to 68 bits per joint-sample) and range reduction with variable bit widths (3.74×, to 18.1 bits); the 4× spread of ACL’s ratio across datasets comes from folding. Of the remaining bytes, 81 % are animated rotations and 13.5 % per-segment range metadata, a share that grows to 24 % at 0.1 cm on the test side because it does not shrink with the precision. Fig. 4b asks what a lossless back end could add. The zeroth-order entropy of ACL’s quantized samples is 97.7 % of the bits it spends, so its widths are nearly tight for independent samples; first and second differences reach 83.8 and 81.1 %, and real context coders 0.80×. These bounds hold for the models we tried, up to second-order temporal context; little is left because range reduction stretches every 16 samples to fill their integer range.

    Consequence. A substantially smaller stream needs its own quantizer. Ours is close to ACL in zeroth-order entropy (0.92 to 1.07×), but its first differences cost 0.57 to 0.62× ACL’s bits against 0.84× for ACL’s own symbols: the gain appears once time is modelled.

    5.2. Samples Predicted and Samples Not Coded

    Temporal predictability.

    Predicting each integer from its own past reduces the log-map stream by 39 to 55 % against its zeroth-order cost. The best predictor depends on the joint and capture: second differences beat first differences by 18 % at the root but only 4 to 7 % at depth six and below, where noise at the scale of the step dominates, and an adaptive (NLMS) predictor wins on 37 to 44 % of the curves, which motivates a per-curve choice.

    Per-joint sparsity.

    Not every sample needs coding. Under the max gate the encoder keeps 87 % of the root’s samples but only 57 % at depth six and below at 0.01 cm, and 51 against 22 % at 0.1 cm (Fig. 5a; five development clips, an earlier version of the encoder); the root keeps the most because its error reaches every descendant. ACL can only strip whole frames whose every joint is linearly interpolable, 0.38 % of the curated frames at 0.01 cm. Where keys pay, the gain comes from the closed loop: removing keys by a local per-curve error bound saves only 0 to 0.6 %.

    The price of a bit.

    At the margin, keys are the cheapest way to spend error. Fig. 5c compares the distortion the iso-mean encoder adds per bit it saves at 0.1 cm: growing a step by one grid unit costs 0.17 step units, a dead zone 0.31, and removing an RD-selected key about 0.03. This says which move to prefer, not how much each move contributes in total, which depends on how many cheap moves the precision leaves: on held-out data, removing keys from the final codec costs 8 % at 0.01 cm and 69 % at 1 cm, where it matches prediction (Sec. 6.5). Codecs that code every sample lose accordingly: a dyadic hierarchical codec with a learned in-betweener matches ours where keys keep 83 % of the samples (1.01×) but needs 1.55 to 1.78× the bytes where they keep 7 to 15 %.

    Consequence. Prediction is the largest saving at p≤0.1 cm and the choice of which samples to omit the second, with a share that grows as p loosens. The encoder needs both, with steps and keys competing for one budget.

    5.3. Interpolation Gains Little on the Gaps the Encoder Leaves

    Where keys carry the bytes, a better interpolator should buy more: one that halved the cubic error everywhere (k=2) would save 3 to 27 %. This is the bet of CurveCodec and of learned in-betweening; we tested it, and the results below bound what the estimators we tried achieved on our data, not what any interpolator could. The gaps the encoder leaves are short: under the max gate at p≤0.1 cm, 77 to 92 % hide at most two samples (Fig. 5b), whereas published in-betweeners train on gaps of 5 to 45 frames at errors 60× above our default precision. In our gaps the cubic residual is linearly unpredictable from the curve’s own context (ridge R²≤0.02).

    A retrieval oracle.

    As a strong nonparametric reference, an oracle searches every window of 510 training clips (4.2 M samples, held-out skeletons) for the best match of a gap’s decoded context and copies the matched interior as a residual over cubic interpolation. It is a nearest neighbour in context space over those 4.2 M samples, a 510-clip subset of the 886-hour training split the entropy model sees. On random gaps it beats cubic interpolation by 1.37, 1.29, and 1.23× at p=0.1, 0.3, and 1 cm and keeps improving with the corpus size (Fig. 6). On the gaps the iso-mean RD encoder leaves, it reaches only 0.85 to 0.90, no better than linear interpolation on the same gaps, and is flat over the 32-fold range of library size we measured. The encoder removes exactly the samples a smooth prior already predicts and keeps contacts, impacts, and direction changes with no precursor in the curve’s past. A better interpolator might also let the encoder drop keys it now keeps; we placed four learned in-betweeners inside the encoder, including a 3.4 M-parameter transformer with keys re-chosen for it. None paid (supplementary Sec. F): they changed the size by -2.5 to +5.7 %, no more than the null option of choosing per gap between cubic and linear interpolation would give.

    Consequence. Under an explicit error contract and an explicit bit count, none of the interpolators we built found enough information in the transmitted context to pay for itself. These experiments ran under the iso-mean contract; for the max gate, whose gaps are shorter still, the conclusion is an inference we did not test. CurveCodec 2 therefore keeps a fixed interpolator and moves the learned prior to the probability model.

    5.4. Where a Network Pays

    Tab. 1 summarizes every role we gave a network. Dense learned representations have a precision floor: a residual-VQ tokenizer cannot represent a track below about 1.3 % of its RMS and a meta-learned neural field not below 1.6 to 4.8 % of the window’s amplitude, while the contract asks for 0.01 to 0.1 %, so both degenerate into scalar residual codecs. In a lifting-wavelet codec of ours, learning the transform changed the size by ±1 % while learning its entropy model saved 7 to 12 %; learned image codecs report a similar division of gains [(Ballé et al., 2018; Minnen et al., 2018)], an analogy rather than evidence for our numbers. Over a hand-designed context coder, the MLP entropy model saves 3 to 7 % on mocap and 13 % on game assets. It does not predict the next residual’s value (R²≤0.02) but its distribution, from a slowly varying per-curve regime: the residual’s scale relative to the step, periodicity, and whether a curve is held, linear, or noisy. Eight positions of context give 60 to 70 % of the gain. Supplementary Sec. F reports that cross-joint structure (mirroring, pose-space PCA, interpolation context) and transforms under a worst-case contract did not pay on our data.

    Consequence. The network belongs in the probability model, where it models a distribution the codec must send anyway, and it can be small, causal, and local.

    6. Experiments

    6.1. Setup

    Corpus and split.

    We assembled 192,392 clips (906 h, 16.17 G joint-samples) from 33 datasets, including HiPHI [(Ji et al., 2026)], BONES-SEED [(Bones Studio, 2026)], Motion-X [(Lin et al., 2023)], BEAT [(Liu et al., 2022)], AMASS [(Mahmood et al., 2019)], MotionPersona [(Shi et al., 2025)], 100STYLE [(Mason et al., 2022)], CMU [(CMU Graphics Lab, 2019)], LAFAN1 [(Harvey et al., 2020)], ZeroEGGS [(Ghorbani et al., 2023)], and PFNN [(Holden et al., 2017)], retargeted and converted versions of several of them, hand capture, and 549 game-asset clips of 196 skeletons, at 20 to 120 Hz. Because the corpus holds retargeted, cropped, and converted versions of the same performances, we split by take group, a key that follows the original performance across datasets and conversions, holding out 2 of every 100 clips per dataset: the test side has 4,472 clips, 20.1 h, and 342.7 M joint-samples, and no take group appears on both sides. A quadruped dataset [(Zhang et al., 2018)] (dog) is held out of training entirely. The test side also contains the 71 development clips of Sec. 5 (5.1 % of its joint-samples); without them the ratios change by less than one point.

    Baselines and metrics.

    ACL [(Frechette, 2023)] (commit 3ee5685) runs with its default settings at p=0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.3, and 1 cm, with keyframe stripping off because our contracts take their targets from the no-strip result; we report our ratio against ACL’s default stripping as well. CurveCodec 2 runs under the max gate with the MLP entropy model and under the mean gate with the transformer, our product configuration. Learned motion encoders are not included; their errors are two orders of magnitude above ACL’s at these precisions [(Shi et al., 2026)]. We report bits per joint-sample, the ratio of our bytes to ACL’s on the same clips, and the mean, 99th-percentile, and maximum shell error over all joint-samples. Timing uses one pinned core of an AMD Threadripper PRO 7975WX for both codecs.

    6.2. Compression against ACL

    At ACL’s default precision of 0.01 cm, CurveCodec 2 needs 6.1 bits per joint-sample where ACL needs 16.4, 0.37× ACL’s bytes under either contract (Tab. 2, Fig. 7). The ratio improves as p loosens because ACL’s segment metadata and widths have a floor while our keys thin out. Under the max gate our P99 is within 1.08× of ACL’s and our mean error 1.4× higher; under the mean gate our mean matches ACL’s on every clip and our maximum is lower at p≤0.1 cm (0.094 against 0.213 cm at 0.01 cm). At 0.3 and 1 cm ACL itself exceeds p on part of the data, which both contracts inherit. Against ACL with its default keyframe stripping, which removes 4.8 % of the frames at 0.01 cm and 29 % at 0.1 cm without changing its error, our ratios are 0.380× and 0.25 to 0.26×. ACL’s compression level changes no byte in our build. The released ACL 2.1.0 writes 2 to 7 % more bytes at a tighter worst case, a comparison of bytes only, since our contracts were not re-matched to its errors. xz or zstd over ACL’s stream saves 2 to 5 % (supplementary Sec. A). Extrapolated per dataset (Fig. 8), our 906-hour corpus would take an estimated 11.9 GB at 0.01 cm, against the 32.6 GB that ACL would need.

    Fig. 9 shows decoded motion for a humanoid, a game character, a creature, and the held-out dog. At 0.01 cm, decoded and original skeletons coincide for all three codecs while our streams are 2 to 3× smaller; at 1 cm the largest joint displacement in the frames shown is about half a centimetre for all three (the clip maxima are in the caption), at 4.4 to 4.7× fewer bytes than ACL. A static frame cannot show popping; the evidence about the worst frame is the contracts, checked on every sample.

    6.3. Contracts: Tolerances and Failures

    The tolerances of the max gate are a convenience for the search, not a source of the gain. Removing them costs 0.7 to 1.0 % of the bytes on a 311-clip test subset, and a standalone contract that holds every joint-sample within p, which ACL itself meets on only 2 % of the clips, still gives 0.438× and 0.265× ACL’s bytes at 0.01 and 0.1 cm: ACL’s own overshoot of p is worth 4 to 6 % of our bytes. The fallback is a safety net, not a source of compression: at p≤0.1 cm the first encode passes on at least 99.6 % of the 4,472 clips under either contract, and before any fallback no stream is larger than ACL’s. The final check fails on 16 and 3 clips at 0.01 and 0.1 cm under the max gate, nearly all hairline misses of the over-p fraction, and on 4 and 3 under the mean gate; a margin re-encode or ACL’s stream resolves every one and changes no ratio by more than 0.001; the re-encodes of all failing clips cost about 7 core-hours in total. At 0.3 and 1 cm, 34 and 95 max-gate clips fail because the encoder’s late step refinement cannot un-fold a folded track that already exceeds the contract, and 36 and 92 streams, nearly all of them these clips, are larger than ACL’s before the fallback; after it, ACL’s stream is stored for 13 and 29 clips, the counts and ratios of Tab. 2 (details and an un-folding fix in supplementary Sec. B). Under the mean gate no stream is larger than ACL’s at any precision.

    6.4. Generalization

    Every dataset is smaller than ACL at every precision (Fig. 10, Tab. 3). The gain is largest on long, high-rate captures (BONES-SEED 0.236× at 0.01 cm) because smoother curves let a fixed budget buy longer key gaps, while ACL’s rate per sample barely changes with the frame rate. A looser bound pays only where there are samples to omit: from 0.01 to 1 cm the ratio of 120 Hz BEAT falls 27-fold (0.399 to 0.015×) and that of 20 Hz HumanAct12 1.5-fold (0.676 to 0.444×); the frame-rate classes are partly confounded with datasets. Retargeted data gain less because ACL is already efficient on them. The dog, a species absent from training, reaches 0.532×, 0.350×, and 0.168×. The entropy model is the only trained part: on the dog it saves 5.7 to 6.9 % over the codec without a network, 91 to 95 % of what a model trained on dog data saves. A model trained on one 120 Hz dataset alone is 1.34 to 1.43×larger than no model on the dog, so the product model is trained on the whole corpus.

    6.5. Ablation

    Tab. 4 adds components one at a time and removes each from the final encoders. Prediction is the largest component at p≤0.1 cm: against the quantized integers coded with a general-purpose compressor (first row) it is worth 2.0 and 2.2×, and 2.3 to 3.0× against the same context coder without prediction. Keys are second and grow as p loosens: removing them costs 8 %, 39 %, and 69 % at 0.01, 0.1, and 1 cm under the max gate (2.2× at 1 cm without the five weakness clips) and 32 % to 2.2× under the mean gate, so at 1 cm keys and prediction are comparable (1.9×). Each configuration spends a different share of the error budget, so the table ranks contributions under the contract as used, not at strictly equal distortion. The final step search and container save 1 to 8 %; the entropy model saves 3 to 6 % under the max gate and 7 to 10 % under the mean gate, of which the transformer contributes 4 to 5 % over the MLP; thinning saves at most 1.6 %. Supplementary Sec. D gives the development ablation on the curated set and the capacity of the entropy model: deeper models save another 1 to 2.7 points at 1.8 to 27.5× the decode cost.

    6.6. Runtime and Deployment

    On one core, ACL encodes 1 M joint-samples in 5.0 s and decodes them in 12.5 ms. The max-gate codec encodes in 24 s (4.8×) and decodes in 0.48 s (38×); the product encodes in 57 s (12×) and decodes in 2.1 s (168×, about 8,700 frames per second of a 55-joint skeleton), 0.76 s on four threads and 0.57 s on one GPU (pooled over all precisions). Decode time scales with the number of coded residuals; at 0.01 cm the median clip of a 93-clip timing subset decodes in 0.10 s with the max-gate codec and 0.57 s with the product, the 95th percentile in 0.86 and 4.5 s. The model weights take 870 KB (transformer) and 182 KB (MLP). Re-encoding the decoded clip into ACL (supplementary Sec. E) costs one ACL compression, which dominates the load time, and a second lossy stage (1.4 to 1.8× ACL’s mean error), so a pipeline that must deliver ACL’s error should run that stage at a tighter precision or keep the dense output; ACL at p/2 costs 10 to 16 % more bytes, and we did not measure the composite error at that setting. Our equal-error comparisons are therefore claims about storage and transport, not about runtime.

    6.7. Failure Cases

    CurveCodec 2 gains least on short, low-rate clips of small skeletons (HumanAct12 0.676× at 0.01 cm, Edinburgh 0.628×, BFA 0.609×; Fig. 11), where the header and the model’s cold start are amortized over few samples and few samples can be omitted. At loose precision, ACL’s own misses on HiPHI widen both contracts, and the mean gate’s guard, ten times ACL’s clip mean, admits worst-case errors up to 24.7 cm at 1 cm on a handful of clips; we do not recommend the mean gate at p≥0.3 cm. We do not compare against CurveCodec: its published numbers come from a different split with floating-point accounting and are listed in the supplement for context only.

    7. Limitations

    No random access.

    CurveCodec 2 decodes whole clips: the coder, predictors, and model step are sequential in time, so a single pose cannot be read in constant time, which ACL does in about half a microsecond, and a full clip takes 38 to 168× ACL’s decompression time on one core, still far faster than real time (Sec. 6.6). This is inherent to the design, not a matter of optimization: ACL is stateless and keeps the clip compressed in memory, decompressing only the poses a runtime’s evaluation pass needs, whereas CurveCodec 2 is a storage and distribution format decoded at load time, and re-encoding into ACL adds a second lossy stage. Encoding is 4.8 to 12× slower than ACL and runs offline, in parallel over clips.

    Contracts relative to ACL

    Both contracts take their targets from ACL’s result on the same clip, so the encoder needs ACL’s statistics and inherits its misses at loose precision; the max gate holds ACL’s worst case only within a 5 % tolerance, and errors are bounded at the sample times, not between them. A standalone contract in terms of p costs 4 to 6 % of the bytes on a test subset but was not run at corpus scale. At loose precision the max-gate encoder does not un-fold tracks (Sec. 6.3); the fix is not part of the benchmarked codec.

    Not validated as a representation.

    We motivated the codec by the hope that what it must send is closer to the motion’s decisions than to the body, but we test it only as a codec. Neither the stream nor the entropy model is evaluated on a generative or recognition task, and the findings that interpolation, cross-joint structure, and transforms did not pay hold for the estimators, data, and precisions we tried, each with one architecture and training run; they do not prove that no such model can do better. Whether the codec can serve a learned motion model is future work.

    8. Conclusion

    We asked where the redundancy of skeletal motion lies and which part of a codec a learned model should take over, and answered by measurement. Predicting each quantized curve from its own past is the largest saving at tight precision; omitting samples, chosen per joint in closed loop through the hierarchy, is the second, and its share grows until the two are comparable at 1 cm. On the gaps such an encoder leaves there is little left to interpolate: none of the interpolators we tried, including a retrieval oracle over millions of training samples, beat linear interpolation, so the learned in-betweener at the core of CurveCodec had little left to learn. A network pays as the probability model of the residuals the codec must send. CurveCodec 2 puts these findings into one skeleton-agnostic, bit-exact codec that needs 0.37× ACL’s bytes at ACL’s default precision under ACL’s own worst-case contract within tolerance, and 0.22× at 0.1 cm at its mean error, with one model that serves every rig we tried, including a species absent from training. The two parts that carry the gain, each curve’s slowly varying residual regime and the hierarchy-aware choice of which samples to send, are what a learned motion model would have to capture to work across bodies; building such a model on them is the next step.

    Acknowledgements.

    We thank Nicholas Frechette, the author of ACL, for detailed discussions of ACL’s design goals and technical details. We thank Jun Xing, Tianshu Zhang and Zhixin Piao for the very early discussions on motion compression. This work was partially funded by the Research Grants Council of Hong Kong (Ref: 17216826) and by the Innovation and Technology Commission of the HKSAR Government under the ITSP-Platform grant (Ref: ITS/335/23FP, ITS/469/24FP).

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: PREFER：把 LLM 当虚拟试玩员，按玩家画像改规则、再试玩验收 ｜ PREFER: From Player Experience to Personalized Game Refinement
item.description:
一句话：用心理测量维度约束 LLM 的体验评价，再据此改规则并复测，五个画像平均偏好分高 9.2%。

要点：

  • 只给总分看不出模型到底在评什么；PREFER 借用 PXI、CORGIS 这类成熟问卷的体验维度，让模型对玩法逐维度打分，从而刻画它作为「虚拟试玩员」的视角。
  • 用 persona 模拟不同玩家画像，按体验—偏好关系为每个画像挑改进目标，实际改写游戏规则与实现，再对候选版本试玩评估体验变化与预测偏好增益。
  • 五个画像的实验里，PREFER 的试玩后平均偏好评分比最强基线高 9.2%。

为什么值得看：把「LLM 帮忙调玩法」从拍脑袋变成有闭环的实验流程：定维度 → 改规则 → 复测，这套脚手架适合接在内部原型或关卡调优流水线上。

中文摘要：要拿 LLM 的反馈指导游戏设计，先要弄清它在评什么。PREFER 借用成熟玩家体验量表（如 PXI、CORGIS）的维度，构建共享体验维度集，用来基准化各模型对实际玩法的评价、并刻画它们作为虚拟试玩员的视角；同时用 persona 模拟不同玩家画像，依据体验与偏好的关系为每个画像选择改进目标，改写游戏规则及其实现，再对候选游戏试玩以评估体验变化与预测偏好增益。五个 persona 的实验中，PREFER 的试玩后平均偏好评分比所评测的最强基线高 9.2%。

主题：延伸阅读

来源：arXiv·生成式玩法（English）

原文发布：2026-10-13

本期推送：2026-10-23

PREFER: From Player Experience
to Personalized Game Refinement

Abstract

Understanding how large language models (LLMs) evaluate gameplay experience is important for using their feedback to guide game design. However, overall ratings alone provide limited insight into which aspects of experience are associated with these judgments and how they can inform concrete game changes. We introduce Prefer, a framework that uses a shared set of experience dimensions adapted from established psychometric questionnaires to benchmark how models evaluate gameplay and to guide persona-specific game refinement. Through these dimensions, we characterize the perspectives models offer as virtual playtesters by examining how their overall assessments relate to specific aspects of experience and to the gameplay they produce. To examine how the same dimensions can guide refinement for players with different preferences, we use personas to simulate distinct player profiles. For each persona, Prefer uses experience-preference relationships to select refinement objectives, revises game rules and their implementations, and playtests candidate games to assess experience changes and predicted preference gains. Experiments with five personas show that Prefer achieves 9.2% higher mean post-play preference ratings than the strongest evaluated baseline.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in game development, supporting the generation of playable prototypes and the evaluation of player experience [(Sun et al., 2024; Lankes and Stöckl, 2023)]. Gameplay experience involves multiple aspects, such as challenge, mastery, and immersion [(Sweetser and Wyeth, 2005; Vanden Abeele et al., 2020)]. Understanding how these aspects relate to models’ overall judgments is therefore important for characterizing the perspectives they offer as virtual playtesters and for using their feedback to guide game refinement.

Established player-experience instruments, such as PXI and CORGIS, provide structured dimensions for describing functional, psychosocial, and challenge-related aspects of gameplay [(Vanden Abeele et al., 2020; Denisova et al., 2020)]. Building on such instruments, [Dutta et al. (2026)] map player reviews to experience constructs and examine their associations with review scores. In parallel, MeepleLM generates ratings and critiques from game rulebooks under different player personas, illustrating how LLMs can provide feedback from multiple player perspectives [(Li et al., 2026)].

Building on these advances, we ask how different LLMs evaluate the experience reflected in actual gameplay. An overall rating alone does not reveal whether models agree on specific aspects of an experience, or how those assessments relate to their overall judgments. Characterizing their perspectives therefore calls for comparing both levels of evaluation and examining how these judgments relate to the gameplay the models produce. Beyond this analysis, a further question is whether the same experience dimensions can guide game refinement for players with different preferences, by specifying which aspects to change and in which direction.

To address these questions, we introduce Prefer, a framework that uses shared experience dimensions to benchmark how models evaluate gameplay and to guide persona-specific game refinement. We adapt experience dimensions from established psychometric questionnaires to assess gameplay trajectories, collecting overall ratings separately from dimension-level assessments. Different models evaluate the same trajectories, allowing us to examine how their overall judgments relate to specific aspects of experience and how their assessments agree or differ. We further compare their evaluations of trajectories produced through their own play and that of other models, and examine agreement in game-level rankings.

However, players differ in what they value in a game [(Tondello et al., 2019)]. To better simulate diverse real-world players, we follow MeepleLM [(Li et al., 2026)] in using personas to represent distinct player profiles. For each persona, Prefer relates experience dimensions to overall preference to select which aspects to change and in which direction. These objectives guide rule revisions, which are translated into function-level contracts that specify required behavior and guide implementation checks and repair. Candidate games are then playtested under the target persona, and acceptance requires both the intended experience changes and a positive predicted preference gain. Feedback from unsuccessful candidates guides further rule revisions.

We evaluate Prefer on familiar card games and their rule variants. The model benchmark identifies shared patterns in game rankings alongside differences in how experience dimensions relate to overall ratings. Across five personas, Prefer achieves 9.2% higher mean post-play preference ratings than the strongest baseline evaluated. A separate implementation study also shows a higher success rate in producing runnable games and higher rule-consistency scores than baseline.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce Prefer, a framework that adapts experience dimensions from psychometric questionnaires to gameplay trajectories, providing a shared basis for model evaluation and persona-specific game refinement.

  • •

    We establish a model benchmark that characterizes the perspectives LLMs offer as virtual playtesters by comparing their experience judgments, overall ratings, and game rankings, and relating these evaluations to the gameplay they produce.

  • •

    We develop a persona-specific game refinement method that uses experience-preference relationships to select modification targets, guides rule revisions with playtesting feedback, and supports implementation through function-level contracts and execution checks.

    • 2 Related Work

    Game-Based Agent Evaluation.

    Games let researchers observe how agents follow rules, choose actions, and respond to other players over several turns. clembench tests instruction following and task success through dialogue games [(Kranti et al., 2023)]. GameBench studies strategic reasoning across nine games [(Costarelli et al., 2024)]. TextArena offers competitive text games that involve skills such as negotiation and deception [(Guertler et al., 2025)]. Our benchmark uses shared experience measures to compare models without persona prompts against reference players given fixed persona prompts. We compare their evaluation profiles on shared gameplay evidence and relate these judgments to the play the models produce.

    Personas and Player Experience.

    Persona prompts ask an agent to follow a given role or set of preferences. TRAIT measures model personality through multiple-choice questions about everyday situations [(Lee et al., 2025)]. PERIL studies how persona prompts affect game strategies. It maps a model’s answers to personality questions into strategy parameters [(Licato and Steinle, 2025)]. MeepleLM uses player personas to rate games and explain their judgments from rule descriptions [(Li et al., 2026)]. PXI and CORGIS offer scales for player experience and perceived challenge [(Vanden Abeele et al., 2020; Denisova et al., 2020)]. We use these scales to describe gameplay. Personas guide our game revisions and provide reference players for model comparison.

    Game Refinement and Verification.

    Game refinement requires both useful feedback and code that follows the revised rules. Self-Refine uses model feedback to improve generated outputs [(Madaan et al., 2023)] and systems [(Yuksekgonul et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026)]. Cardiverse creates card game variants and playable implementations [(Li et al., 2025)]. Fly, Fail, Fix uses play records from a reinforcement learning agent to guide changes to game settings [(Zook et al., 2025)]. For code repair, LDB checks execution step by step to locate errors [(Zhong et al., 2024)]. PolyVer uses function contracts to verify programs written in different languages [(Chen et al., 2025)]. In our method, a target player’s experience guides rule changes. Fixed function contracts guide code repair, and playtesting checks the resulting experience.

    3 Method

    Prefer uses shared experience dimensions to study how LLMs evaluate gameplay and to guide game refinement for a target persona. We first describe the experience assessment. We then explain how persona preferences guide rule changes, how function contracts guide their implementation, and how playtesting provides feedback for further revision.

    3.1 Experience Assessment

    We describe gameplay through selected dimensions from PXI [(Vanden Abeele et al., 2020)] and CORGIS [(Denisova et al., 2020)]. These dimensions cover how a game supports and engages the player, as well as the demands of play. For example, challenge fit measures whether difficulty suits the player. Cognitive challenge measures the reasoning and planning required during play. We keep the dimension definitions and scoring scales fixed across models and personas. Appendix B gives the full definitions and scoring details.

    Let R denote the rulebook and τ a completed gameplay trajectory. The trajectory records the focal player’s observations, available actions, chosen actions, and outcomes. An LLM evaluator uses this evidence to rate each experience dimension. A separate assessment gives an overall rating of the same playthrough. We write the two assessments as

    x=𝔼ₘ(R,τ,p), y=Sₘ(R,τ,p),

    		(1)

    where m is the evaluation model, x∈ℝᵈ contains the d experience scores, and y is the overall rating. The optional persona p specifies the player’s preferences. Each experience score includes a short explanation based on the trajectory. The two assessments do not receive each other’s outputs, so y is not calculated from x.

    For model comparison, we omit the persona prompt and compare judgments of the same gameplay evidence. The pairs (x,y) let us examine how each model’s dimension scores relate to its overall ratings. For persona-guided refinement, the player agent and both assessments use the same target persona p. In this setting, y measures the persona’s preference for the played game.

    3.2 Rule Refinement

    Rule refinement starts from a game with rulebook R, code C, and a target persona p. We collect paired experience and preference measurements across games under this persona. A regularized linear predictor fₚ relates the experience vector to the preference score. We fit the predictor on other games before using it to refine the current game. Appendix B.1 gives the predictor and fitting procedure.

    The predictor assigns a weight wₚⱼ to each experience dimension j. In the original scoring units, this weight estimates the preference change for a one-point increase in dimension j, with other dimensions fixed. We use the sign of wₚⱼ to choose the direction of change. A positive weight suggests increasing the dimension, and a negative weight suggests decreasing it. We denote this direction by dₚⱼ∈{-1,+1} and skip dimensions with zero weight.

    Given the current experience vector x, we remove targets without enough room for change on the scoring scale. We rank the remaining targets by |wₚⱼ|. This ranking compares the predicted gains from equal-sized changes in individual dimensions. It sets the search order, while playtesting checks the effects of an actual rule change.

    For each selected target, an LLM proposes a revised rulebook R^′ using R, p, and the target dimension and direction. The proposal changes a game mechanic while keeping the game objective and unaffected rules fixed. The next stage implements this rulebook and checks the resulting code.

    3.3 Rule Implementation

    Contract construction. We compare R^′ with R to identify changed requirements and relevant rules that must remain unchanged. Each requirement keeps a link to its source rule text. We also extract function definitions and direct calls from the code’s abstract syntax tree. This information helps assign each required outcome to an owner function and identify functions that may supply its prerequisites.

    Following [Chen et al. (2025)], we express function responsibilities through assumptions and guarantees. We add provider links and timing conditions to form each contract clause

    κ=(f,A,G,ℙ,α,δ),

    		(2)

    where f is the owner function, A is its required entry condition, and G is its required outcome. The set ℙ lists possible prerequisite providers. The trigger α activates the obligation, and δ sets its deadline. For arguments u, state s before the call, state s^′ after the call, and return value r, the clause requires

    A(u,s) \Longrightarrow G(s,s^′,r).

    		(3)

    Both A and G are executable checks. We check that the plan covers the rule requirements, has valid function links, and can execute its predicates. Semantic review provides advice on whether the clauses match the rules. Once the plan is accepted, its predicates and clause identities stay fixed during code generation and repair.

    Local and joint checks. An implementation model updates the affected function bodies using the revised rules and accepted contracts. Local checks test an owner function in isolation. Each test supplies arguments and state that satisfy A, independently of the candidate provider functions. It then calls the owner and tests G. A failed guarantee or an exception under valid entry conditions identifies an owner failure. If the test input fails A, the clause remains untested.

    Joint checks test whether gameplay supplies the required entry conditions. A runtime monitor follows each obligation from its trigger α. It checks A when the owner is called and reports a failure if A is false. A required call missing at deadline δ also causes a failure. The monitor uses provider calls observed during this period to identify possible causes. For both checks, a lack of evidence is recorded as unknown.

    Repair scope. We use execution feedback to select which functions to repair [(Zhong et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025)]. Each supported failure i gives a set Eᵢ of candidate functions. A local failure gives Eᵢ={f}. A joint failure gives the providers supported by the execution record. We select a set that covers every failure while limiting edit cost

    S^*=\arg\min_S⊆F∑_f∈Sc_f subject to S∩Eᵢ≠∅ for alli,

    		(4)

    where F is the set of editable functions and c_f>0 is the number of source lines in f. Failures without supported candidate functions remain unresolved.

    Let U contain the failure sets not yet covered. If U is nonempty, we choose a set with the fewest candidates, E^†∈\arg\min_E∈U|E|. The minimum remaining cost is

    V(U)=\begincases0,&U=∅, [5.69054pt] \min_f∈E^†[c_f+V ({E∈U|f∉E})],&otherwise.\endcases

    		(5)

    Selecting f covers every remaining set that contains it. We solve this recurrence by branch-and-bound search. A branch is dropped when its accumulated cost exceeds the best complete solution. A completed search returns S^*. Appendix D gives the search limits and tie-breaking rules.

    The repair model receives the rules, fixed contracts, code, failure records, and selected functions. It changes only the selected function bodies and preserves their signatures. We keep a patch only if rechecking improves the results without new failures or loss of earlier evidence. Repair stops when the required checks pass, no supported repair scope remains, or the budget is exhausted. Only candidates that pass the required checks proceed to playtesting.

    3.4 Playtesting and Feedback

    The player agent plays each candidate with the target persona p. We assess the resulting trajectory using the same dimensions and scoring procedure as for the original game. Let x be the original experience vector and x^′ₖ the vector for candidate k. A candidate needs valid gameplay and complete experience scores before it can be accepted.

    A rule change can improve the target dimension but harm other parts of the experience. We therefore check both the target change and the predicted preference gain. For candidate k targeting dimension jₖ, acceptance requires

    {\beginaligned d_pjₖ(x^′_k,jₖ-x_jₖ)&≥ε, fₚ(x^′ₖ)-fₚ(x)&>0,\endaligned.

    		(6)

    where ε>0 is the minimum required change in the target dimension. The first condition checks progress in the selected direction. The second uses all experience dimensions to estimate the total preference change.

    We try targets in their ranked order and generate each candidate from the same original game. A failed implementation, incomplete playtest, or rejected candidate leads to the next target. We accept the first candidate that passes all checks. If no candidate passes within the search budget, we keep the original game and enter the feedback stage.

    Following [Madaan et al. (2023)], we use feedback to revise a failed proposal. We select the highest-priority rejected candidate with valid gameplay and complete experience scores. The feedback includes its rules, score changes, acceptance decision, and an explanation based on the trajectory. The generator changes the mechanic while keeping the persona, target dimension, and direction fixed. The new proposal goes through the same implementation checks and playtesting. Equation 6 compares it with the original game. If no suitable candidate exists or the feedback revision also fails, we retain the original game.

    4 Experiments

    Our experiments connect three questions: what experience dimensions reveal about model evaluation, how persona-specific preference relationships define refinement targets, and whether the resulting game revisions receive higher post-play preference ratings. We examine each connection separately before following the complete process in a concrete case.

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Model evaluation.

    We benchmark GLM [(Zeng et al., 2026)], DeepSeek [(Xu et al., 2026)], Kimi [(Team et al., 2026)], MiniMax [(Chen et al., 2026)], and Qwen [(Qwen Team, 2026)] on 91 card games with fixed rules and implementations. The models play against random opponents without persona prompts. Five neutral judges and five persona references assess the recorded trajectories with actor identities hidden. Overall ratings and 12 experience ratings are collected in separate calls. Appendix A details model configurations and analysis sets.

    Persona prediction and refinement.

    We adopt five profiles from MeepleLM [(Li et al., 2026)]: Efficiency Essentialist, Narrative Architect, Social Lubricator, System Purist, and Thrill Seeker. They provide reference evaluations for model comparison and serve as target players in game refinement. We validate preference predictions on held-out games and assess game revisions through persona playtesting and code implementation checks. Appendix B describes the evaluation protocols.

    4.2 Model Evaluation through Experience Dimensions

    We use experience dimensions to characterize how models evaluate recorded gameplay. Figure 3 presents two complementary views: the associations between individual dimensions and overall ratings, and the similarity of these association profiles to persona references.

    We first examine whether models broadly agree on which games they rate highly. With complete rankings, four judges define high-, middle-, and low-rated groups for the fifth judge to compare. Each group spans ten rank positions. Each judge is held out in turn. All five favor the higher-rated group. Averaging the high–middle and middle–low comparisons gives mean gaps of 1.10-1.87 points and pairwise agreement of 78.4-96.0%, shown in Table 1. Figure 5 illustrates this pattern with the highest, middle, and lowest five games by pooled score. Each column orders the displayed games by one judge’s mean rating over actor sources, and lines connect the same game across judges. High-scoring games generally remain above low-scoring ones. At the level of overall ratings, the models show broad agreement.

    We then compare how their overall ratings relate to experience dimensions and use persona references to interpret the resulting association profiles. Figure 3(a) shows positive mastery associations across models, alongside differences in immersion and challenge fit. The displayed mastery correlations range from 0.41 to 0.57, placing mastery among the two largest correlations for every model. The other prominent associations differ: GLM has an immersion correlation of 0.56, DeepSeek a challenge-fit correlation of 0.42, and Qwen a meaning correlation of 0.54. These patterns identify a common association with mastery while showing that the remaining dimensions relate differently to each model’s overall ratings.

    The persona references provide a way to interpret these differences in evaluation emphasis. Figure 3(b) expresses these evaluation patterns relative to the five persona references. System has the largest estimated similarity share for GLM, DeepSeek, Kimi, and Qwen, while Thrill has the largest share for MiniMax. Similarity describes a combination of evaluation emphases for each model. For example, MiniMax’s shares are 25.9% for Thrill, 22.0% for Narrative, and 22.1% for System. These shares describe relative resemblance between evaluation profiles, without implying positive raw correlations. Social has the smallest normalized share for every neutral model. DeepSeek yields the largest share for Social, 13.2%, whereas the corresponding values for the other models range from 7.7% to 10.1%. This suggests that the pool of neutral judges may provide uneven coverage of different reference perspectives, highlighting the importance of persona-based perspectives.

    4.3 Validating Experience-Based Preference Models

    The persona profiles in Figure 4(a) characterize differences in evaluation emphasis on common benchmark inputs. For example, emotional challenge is positively associated with Thrill’s ratings and negatively associated with System’s. These patterns motivate preference predictors that combine experience dimensions for each persona. We next examine whether the same experience dimensions predict preference when games are played under the target persona. This analysis uses a separate dataset of 455 persona-played observations from the same 91 games and five personas, with experience scores and preference ratings collected separately.

    Preference prediction.

    We compare separate regularized linear predictors for each persona with a persona-mean baseline and a shared predictor that uses common dimension coefficients with persona-dependent score levels. Figure 4(b) reports persona-wise prediction errors. Averaged equally over the five personas, the separate predictors achieve a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.740, compared with 1.090 for the persona-mean baseline and 0.785 for the shared predictor. As shown in Figure 4(b), our persona-specific experience-based preference predictor has lower MAE than the shared predictor in four of the five personas, with nearly identical errors for Thrill. Appendix B.1 gives the procedures.

    Experience and persona ablations.

    Table 4 compares the experience sources and persona conditioning using identical observations and held-out-game folds. MAE and R² are averaged over personas; Order measures accuracy for within-persona pairs with different observed ratings, with both games held out. The nine PXI dimensions achieve MAE 0.761 and ordering accuracy 81.8%, close to the combined representation’s 0.740 and 82.0%. Using only the three CORGIS challenge dimensions yields MAE 0.905 and ordering accuracy 72.6%. Removing both sources gives the persona-mean baseline. The - persona ablation retains all 12 dimensions but shares both coefficients and intercept across personas, without persona indicators (MAE 0.880; Order 81.3%). PREFER uses the relationships fitted on the original 49 games to select which dimensions to change and in which direction for each persona, guiding the game revisions evaluated in Section 4.4.

    4.4 Post-play Preference and Implementation Quality

    We compare Prefer with Cardiverse’s game-generation workflow [(Li et al., 2025)], Reflexion’s self-feedback refinement [(Shinn et al., 2023)], ReCode’s bounded recursive planning [(Yu et al., 2025)], and PromptBreeder’s mutation [(Fernando et al., 2024)]. We report mean post-play preference and implementation metrics in Cardiverse [(Li et al., 2025)]: Success Rate, Execution Rate, code-rulebook embedding similarity (ECon), and play-rule consistency (PCon). Appendices B and D detail the adaptations, datasets, and protocols.

    As shown in Table 2, Prefer achieves a mean preference of 3.333, a paired increase of 0.407 over the original games and 9.2% above the best baseline’s mean of 3.053. It also achieves the highest implementation success rate (86.67%) and PCon (7.377), with execution rate tied at 99.96%. The different method rankings under ECon and PCon highlight the value of checking actual gameplay alongside code-rulebook similarity.

    Table 4 reports paired preference changes from the original games for both directed refinement and its feedback extension, averaged over 30 games per persona. Directed refinement achieves a mean gain of 0.380 points. Persona-level mean gains range from 0.067 for Narrative to 1.167 for Thrill. These differences may reflect how readily persona preferences can be addressed through local rule edits. Such edits can reshape the immediate risks and consequences relevant to Thrill, but may offer fewer opportunities to develop thematic progression for Narrative or improve strategic control and balance for System. The feedback extension yields a small additional improvement, increasing the mean paired preference gain from 0.380 to 0.407 points, an additional 0.027 points. Overall, Prefer improves mean post-play preference in the evaluated card games, with gains varying across personas.

    4.5 Case Study: From an Experience Target to a Rule Change

    Figure 6 follows a Crazy Eights revision for Thrill Seeker with a fixed challenge-fit target. Revealing a player’s hand after extended drawing leaves challenge fit unchanged. Feedback then guides a stop-or-continue drawing mechanic with a three-draw limit. In the resulting playtest, challenge fit rises from 2 to 3 and post-selection preference from 2 to 6. The case illustrates how feedback guides a concrete mechanic change toward the same experience target. Appendix C.1 gives the full rule changes and evaluation record.

    5 Conclusion

    Prefer uses shared experience dimensions to connect model evaluation with persona-guided game refinement. The dimensions reveal differences hidden by overall ratings, predict persona preference on held-out games, and define concrete modification targets. Delivered revisions receive higher mean post-play preference than the original games and evaluated baselines. The implementation evaluation also reports higher success and play-rule consistency. Together, these results demonstrate how experience measurements can inform concrete, executable game revisions.
